# Of Saint Calixtus, Pope.

...good merit with eternal commemoration. And hearing this prayer from heaven, the cruel Dion <note>likely referring to the prefect of the city or possibly a corruption of the name Decius</note> ordered that the tongue of Saint Victoria be cut out. And when they cut it out, those who were there said that never at any time had such a thing been done as God commanded to be done. And when her tongue was cut out, as Saint Victoria’s tongue was severed, she threw it in the face of Dion, and with it, she made his eye pop out of his face. And Saint Victoria gave a great cry, saying: “Into darkness you have come, Dion; you who unjustly desired to consume the organ of my body, and you have cut the tongue that blessed God; justly have you lost your eye, because you despised the word of the Lord.” Then Dion, being very angry, ordered Saint Victoria to be shot with arrows. And as they launched two arrows at her—one to her heart and the other to her side—confessing God, she gave up her spirit. And God <note>The text likely implies the judge or authority acting by divine permission</note> then ordered in the court where he sat in judgment that Saint Anatolius be beheaded. And when he was beheaded, a very faithful Christian woman came, who was named Iniciana <note>likely Saint Lucina, a Roman matron famous for burying martyrs</note>, who from her childhood loved God. And with much honor, she buried the bodies of the holy martyrs, Saint Anatolius and Saint Victoria. And she had Saint Anatolius buried in her house, and she placed Victoria near the Gate of the River; and there she placed and laid in peace and honor the bodies of the holy martyrs, in this place which is the house of Iniciana, where many miracles are performed, to the honor and praise of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

<column-break/>

Saint Calixtus, Pope, suffered martyrdom in the time of Emperor Alexander <note>Emperor Alexander Severus, reigned 222–235 AD</note>. And in his time, the highest part of Rome was burned; the golden hand of Jupiter was melted <note>original: "regalada," meaning dissolved or melted by fire</note>. Then the priests of the idols came to the emperor, saying to him: that the gods should be loved, for they were angry <note>original: "fañudos," meaning scornful or indignant</note> with the sacrifices. And while they were performing a sacrifice on a day of Saint John, the day being clear, a lightning bolt struck and killed four priests, and burned the altar of Jupiter, and darkened the sun in such a way that all the Romans fled out of the city. And Palmatius the governor, hearing that Pope Calixtus dwelt in Rome, and that through him this evil came upon them, went there with his horses, and immediately they were struck blind. And Palmatius, being afraid, told it to the emperor. And he ordered that on Wednesday everyone should fast to perform a sacrifice to the idol Mercury, so that he might answer them concerning this deed. And while they were doing this, a virgin who was in the temple, as if possessed by the devil, began to shout, saying: “The God of Calixtus is the true God, and He is already very angry against your filthiness.” And hearing this, Palmatius went across the river to Saint Calixtus, and had himself baptized with his wife and all his company. And when the emperor heard this, he ordered him to be brought before him. And he gave him to the senator Simplicio, that he might flatter him if he could lead him out of this madness, because he was much needed for the common good; but Palmatius persevered in fasting and in prayer. And one came to him saying: that if he would heal his wife who was paralyzed, he would immediately believe. And he prayed to God for her, and she was immediately healed. And she went to Palmatius, and another <note>likely the husband</note> said: “Baptize me in the name of Jesus Christ, who took me by the hand and healed me.” And then Calixtus came and baptized her and her husband, and many others. And hearing this, the emperor ordered them all to be beheaded, except for Lalitius <note>likely a follower or official</note>, whom he ordered should not be given food for the space of five days. And seeing that every day he grew stronger, the emperor ordered him to be whipped every day; and he ordered him to be thrown out of a window and cast into a well with a stone around his neck. And a priest took him out of the well and buried him in the cemetery of Calepodius.

# Of Saint Acisclus and Victoria. In November. Folio 157.
<note>original: "E noctubre" – This is likely an OCR error for "En noviembre" (In November), as the feast day for these saints is November 17th.</note>

"We bless You, our God, who are in the heavens. And many thanks we give You, to You our Lord Jesus Christ, for You do not abandon us in this anguish and tribulation; rather, Lord, stretch out Your hand and extinguish and turn away and remove this fire from above us, which burns us. Let this cruel Dion <note>Dion refers to the Roman governor or prefect, often identified as Dion or Dionisus in Spanish hagiographies</note> not rejoice over us." As they were saying this, suddenly that fire spread, and it scattered and moved away from the martyrs, and it burned and killed one thousand five hundred and forty wicked men among those who were there as servants of the idols. And the holy martyrs rested, relaxing upon the wheels <note>The "breaking wheel" was a common Roman instrument of torture</note> as if they were in their beds or chambers, and the holy angels of God were there with them, comforting them. And seeing so many wonders, that very cruel governor Dion ordered the holy martyrs to be removed from those wheels, and he had them brought before him, and he spoke to them, saying: "It is enough for you, wretches, for you have already shown your magical arts. Come now to sacrifice to our gods who were never defeated, who have compassion for you and will forgive you." To which Saint Acisclus responded and said to Dion: "Do you not see with your blind eyes the great miracles that God our Heavenly Father, with His co-eternal Son our Lord Jesus Christ, performs as He delivers His servants from the evils of your hands?" Then Dion, looking from every side very angrily at Saint Acisclus, ordered the breasts of Saint Victoria to be cut off; and when her breasts were cut off, Saint Victoria said to him: "Dion, heart of iron and stone, cast out from all virtue of Jesus Christ, you order my breasts to be cut off; look how milk flows from them instead of blood." <note>This "miracle of the milk" is a common theme in the stories of virgin martyrs, symbolizing their purity.</note> And looking toward heaven, she said: "Many thanks I give to my Lord Jesus Christ, King of the heavens, that You saw fit that for Your holy name the impediments of my body should be taken from me; now, Lord, I see that the hour approaches when You command me to depart from this world to go to Your glory." And as she said this, that cruel and very wicked Dion ordered Saint Victoria to be put in prison. And many no-

<column-break/>

ble matrons of the city, hearing of those pains and torments that they were giving her and that Saint Victoria had suffered, brought her many of their goods and came to comfort her. And they found her seated in the prison. And as she spoke words of God, they threw themselves down before her on their knees and kissed her feet. And Saint Victoria spoke to them of the holy mysteries and secrets of God. And they, hearing her with much devotion, marveled greatly at her holiness and sufficiency; and seven of them believed in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. And the next day in the morning, the aforementioned very cruel Dion ordered the holy martyrs to be brought before him. And when they were brought, Dion said to Saint Victoria: "Now the time of your death approaches; convert to our gods, and if you will not, I will have your soul torn out." The blessed Victoria said: "O cruel Dion, from here on believe that you shall have no rest in this world nor in the next." And then the wicked Dion <gloss>ordered another</gloss> who was insulting him by saying those things to Saint Victoria <note>The grammar here suggests Dion ordered another official to act because Victoria's words offended him</note>. And he ordered her tongue to be cut out. And then Saint Victoria lifted her hands to heaven and said: "Lord God, Creator of heaven and earth and of all goodness, who never abandoned this your servant: deliver me now from Your holy throne, and command me to be consumed and finished in this place, for the hour already approaches for me to go to rest with You." And when she had said this prayer, everyone heard a voice from heaven that said: "Immaculate, and without fault, and neither contaminated nor defiled by the evil dog and the heresy of Dion, you who have worked so much for my love: come, for certainly the heavens are open to you, and you shall have very great rest in my kingdom of heaven forever and ever; for everyone blesses and glorifies my Father because of you, who since your childhood have worked much for me; and all the righteous are very joyful, seeing your cruel battle that you have won." And again another voice was sent to them from heaven, saying to them: "Come to me, my blessed saints. And you shall have crowns forever, and the palm of your victory."

# Concerning Saint Luke the Evangelist.

Each one of these faces belonged to an evangelist according to the qualities found within him, just as Saint Jerome says. Saint Matthew was represented in the form of a man, because he primarily wrote of the humanity of Jesus Christ. Saint Luke was represented by the calf, because he speaks of the priesthood of Jesus Christ <note>In the sacrificial system of the Old Testament, calves or oxen were primary sacrificial animals; Luke's Gospel emphasizes Christ's role as the ultimate sacrifice and priest.</note>. Saint Mark was represented by the lion, because he speaks of the resurrection. For it is said that lions lie as if dead when they are born until the third day. But afterward, the lion comes and roars over them, and wakes them on the third day <note>This was a common medieval belief from bestiaries used to symbolize Christ’s three days in the tomb before the Resurrection.</note>.
¶ Furthermore, it was because his beginning was in the sound of preaching. Saint John was represented by the eagle, which flies higher than all other birds, because he speaks of the divinity of Jesus Christ. And Jesus Christ, of whom they speak, possessed these four things within Himself: He was a man insofar as He was born of Saint Mary. He was a calf in His passion. He was a lion in His resurrection. He was an eagle in His ascent to the heavens. And regarding these aspects in which Saint Luke was shown—just as with each of the other evangelists—it can be said that he was ordained in these four ways.
By the face of the man, it is understood that he was ordained regarding the poor, whom he must show reason to by bringing the commandments and guarding them in their weakness.
¶ Furthermore, he was well-ordered regarding himself. By the face of the eagle, it is shown that he was very well-ordered toward God. With the eye of understanding, he saw God through contemplation. He shaped the face of his will in Jesus Christ through his thoughts. He cast off old age for the new life and through his conversations.
And furthermore, the eagle is of such sharp sight that it looks at the sun in its wheel <note>The sun’s "wheel" refers to its circular orbit or the solar disc.</note> and never closes its eyes. And when it flies very high, it sees the small fish beneath the waters in the middle of the sea. And it strikes its face against a stone when its beak is very curved, so that it does not hinder its eating <note>Another bestiary legend: as an eagle ages, its beak grows too curved to eat, so it breaks the excess off against a rock to renew itself.</note>. And when it is well-warmed by the rays of the sun, it throws itself into a spring with great force, and casts off its old age. The heat of the sun consumes the darkness of its eyes while looking at its feathers.
¶ By the face of the lion, it is shown that he was well-ordered regarding himself. He was noble in many good ways, and clever against enemies, feeling sorrow for those who are 

<column-break/>

afflicted. The lion is noble and the lord of the wild beasts, and it is clever. It hides its footprints with its tail when it flees so that it is not found.
¶ Furthermore, it suffers great pain when the quartan fever <note>A fever that returns every four days, historically associated with malaria or similar ailments.</note> takes it. And by the face of the calf, it is shown that he was well-ordered regarding his office, which was to write the Gospel. He began it with the nativity and childhood of Jesus Christ, and so little by little he continued until he finished it. And he began it with great wisdom. He began it after the other two evangelists <note>Likely referring to Matthew and Mark.</note> so that if they had left anything unsaid, he might fulfill it. But we can better understand and show how he was well-ordered in these four things if you look closer at his life.
¶ First, he was ordered toward God in three things. Primarily regarding his disposition, for he was filled with the Holy Spirit; and afterward regarding his thoughts, for he was a virgin in body and in soul.
¶ Furthermore, regarding his understanding, for he did everything he did for the honor of God.
¶ Furthermore, he was well-ordered regarding the poor, for he gave them aid. Just like Saint Paul, whom he never left in all his tribulations.
¶ Furthermore, he preached the Gospel and showed them the doctrine of the apostles, and also his own will. He desired for them the life of paradise.
¶ Furthermore, he was well-ordered regarding himself, for he was very moderate in eating, and just in his deeds, and pious.
¶ Furthermore, he was well-ordered regarding his office. His Gospel is of very great virtue, of much profit, and of great beauty and authority.

# ¶ The life of Saint Lupus, archbishop.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a bishop, identified as Saint Lupus (Sant Lobo), standing in clerical vestments and wearing a mitre. He holds a pastoral staff (crozier) in his left hand and a book in his right hand.</image-desc>

Saint Lupus was a native of Orleans <note>original: "Virles", a common variant for Orleans</note>: and he was very full of virtues: they made him archbishop of Sens <note>original: "Senonas"</note> and he gave all he had to the poor. And one day he invited many to eat: and they told him that there was no wine for the company: and he said, "I believe that God, who governs the birds, will give us wine." And then a poor man came who said that there were at the door at least one hundred measures <term>moyos</term> <note>A traditional Spanish unit of liquid volume</note> of wine. And all those of his palace wished him ill because he so loved the daughter of his predecessor, who was a virgin of God. And he took the path of the hand <note>Likely an idiom for taking her by the hand or supporting her openly</note> before those who wished him ill, and did so solely so that the words of the others would not harm her, if her will was pure. For this reason he loved her much, because she loved God much. And once, while coming through the city of Paris, the doors of the prisons opened and all the prisoners were released, and they came out to receive him with great solemnity. And one day while he was singing Mass, a precious stone fell into his chalice, and the king placed it among his relics. And one night while in prayer he felt thirst, and asked that they give him cold water. And seeing the deception of the devil who had entered the vessel, he placed the small pillow <term>faceruelo</term> <note>A small cushion or cloth cover</note> over the vessel, and trapped the devil there; all that night he remained trapped there, howling. And in the morning he departed from there very confounded, and went confessing through the plaza whom he had come to tempt in his pride. And one night while Saint Lupus was walking around the churches as was his custom, he heard the clerics quarreling about sinning with women. And he entered the church and prayed to God from his heart for them, and then they lost the temptation. And they came before him and asked him for pardon. And he, having many virtues in himself, reached his end and went to the glory of paradise.

<column-break/>

# ¶ The life and end of the lord Saint Luke the Evangelist.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of Saint Luke the Evangelist. He is depicted sitting at a desk, engaged in writing a manuscript. Beside him is his traditional symbolic attribute, a winged ox.</image-desc>

Saint Luke was from Syria and was born in Antioch. And according to what the ancients say, meaning he was among the seventy-two disciples of Jesus Christ: he was of such great perfection and of such holy life that he was well-ordered in his service to God, as well as four ways toward men and four toward his office. And according to these four ordinations, he thus had four faces: of a man, of a lion, of a bull, and of an eagle, as was shown to Ezekiel the prophet. And each one of the animals by which we understand the Evangelists had four faces and four wings. And so that we may better see these, let us imagine them on a wooden post in which there is a square head. And on the front part it has the face of a man, and on the right part there is the face of a lion, and on the left part it has the face of a calf. And on the back part, it has the face of an eagle, which is higher than all the others because it has the longest neck. And each one of these animals had four wings. We can think that each animal was square. And in each one were four species, and each species had a wing. And by these animals, according to the saints, we understand the four Evangelists writing of four great things: of the humanity, of the passion, of the resurrection, and of the divinity of Jesus Christ. <meta>This page concludes the life of Saint Denis (Dionysius) of Paris and his companions, Rusticus and Eleutherius, following the previous section on Saint Lupus. It then begins the account of the martyrs Saint Acisclus and Saint Victoria of Córdoba (noted here as León).</meta>

...city. He put into the heart of Emperor Domitian <note>Titus Flavius Domitianus, Roman Emperor from 81 to 96 AD, known in hagiography for persecuting Christians.</note> great cruelty against the Christians, saying: whenever they found any Christian, they should make him sacrifice to idols or die with many torments. And for this reason, the Governor, coming from Rome to Paris, found Denis preaching to the people; and he immediately ordered that they strike him with slaps, and that they spit upon him, and that he be bound with very harsh ropes <note>original: "rüēdas", likely referring to the rack or wheel-like restraints</note> along with Rusticus and Eleutherius, so that they might be presented before him. And while they were before the magistrate with great faith, a noblewoman <term>dueña hÿa dalgo</term> came, saying that her husband had been deceived by these sorcerers. And she immediately looked for her husband; and when he came, he remained very firm in the faith and was soon killed. And then the governor called twelve knights, and afterwards they put them in chains. 

And the next day they stretched Saint Denis upon an iron grill, and they set great flames beneath it. And Saint Denis began to sing, saying: "Lord, your word is even as fire, and I love it much." <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 119:140: "Thy word is tried to the uttermost, and thy servant loveth it."</note> And they took him from there and threw him to the lions and to other wild beasts that were dying of hunger; and the very fierce beasts rushed at them, but he made the sign of the cross, and immediately they became very tame. And they threw him into the fire, but the fire lost its strength and was extinguished. And they tormented him for a long time, and afterwards they put him in prison with many others. And while he was saying Mass and they were receiving communion, Jesus Christ appeared with a great light; and taking the host <note>original: "pabra", likely a scribal variant for "oblea" or "pan"</note>, Jesus Christ said: "Take this, my friend, and go with your companion, Jesus Christ." <note>The text suggests a mystical communion where Christ himself administers the sacrament to the martyr.</note>

And they presented them before the judge, and after giving them many torments, they took them to the idol of Mercury. And while they were professing the Holy Trinity, they beheaded them all and cut off their heads with axes. And the body of Saint Denis rose up, carrying his head between his arms. And an angel went with a great light from heaven from the place that is called the Mount of the Martyrs <note>Montmartre in Paris</note> to the place where his body alone lies buried, which our Lord chose. And there was such a great court of angels there that those who heard it believed immediately. And even Lerejia <note>original: "erejia", possibly a corruption of the name Catulla or a reference to a converted noblewoman</note>, the wife of the governor, who became a Christian; and immediately the false ones beheaded her. And so she was baptized in her own blood. And because they did not want the bodies of Rusticus and Eleutherius to be buried, 

<column-break/>

they ordered them to be thrown into the River Seine <note>original: "seta senan"</note>; but a good noblewoman invited those who had killed the saints to dinner, and while they were eating, she stole the bodies of the saints. And she buried them secretly in her field. And after the persecution ceased, she took them out and accompanied them with the body of Saint Denis very honorably. 

In Arles, while Bishop Regulus was singing Mass, he was naming the names of the apostles and the saints: Denis and Rusticus and Eleutherius. And he said this thinking that they were still alive; and he began to marvel at why he named them without knowing why. And immediately three doves appeared over the cross of the altar, which had the names of these martyrs written on their breasts with letters of blood. And as he observed them with great diligence, he understood that these holy martyrs were in the glory of Paradise with our Lord Jesus Christ.

# Of Saint Acisclus and Saint Victoria, siblings.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration depicting the martyrdom of two saints. On the left, a saint lies on a rectangular gridiron or rack over burning wood. Two executioners apply fire with long poles. On the right, another saint stands in prayer. Buildings are visible in the background.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

### The life and martyrdom
### of Saint Acisclus and Victoria, his sister.

It happened in Spain, in the city of León <note>While historically associated with Córdoba, this Spanish edition places the narrative in León.</note>, that there was a noble man who was called Martial, who had a noble matron for a wife whose name was Mona. They had as children Acisclus and Victoria, and others whom they called Vital, Feniculo, Facundo, Primitivo, Dedio, Luperco, and Candido, and two others. And Martial was a good lieutenant, a faithful Christian, and a powerful knight. The King of León was an idolater, and he held ill will and hatred toward the said Christian knight because of his great lineage and the many relations that he had.

<meta>This page provides the backstory of Saint Denis (Dionysius), connecting his identity as a philosopher in Athens with his later mission in France. Although the previous page described his martyrdom in Paris, this text details his conversion by Saint Paul and his mystical knowledge.</meta>

### Of Saint Denis In October. Folio clv.

the city where he lived; and that neighborhood was named Areopagite <note>The Areopagus, or "Hill of Ares," was the location of the high court of Athens.</note>: because the temple of Mars was there: for the citizens of Athens named the neighborhoods where they lived after their gods. And the Areopagus was the most noble because the court of the nobles was there, as well as the school of the seven [liberal] arts. And there lived Denis, a very great philosopher: and because of the great science that he knew, they called him *Theophotos*: which means "wise in God." And there were other philosophers there whom they called Epicureans <note>A school of philosophy that sought happiness through refined pleasure and the absence of pain.</note> because they placed all the well-being of man in the delight of the body. And others who were called Stoics <note>A school of philosophy that emphasized virtue and endurance over emotion.</note>: who said that the virtue of the soul was nothing but folly. 

And when our Lord received His Passion, the sun darkened throughout the whole world. And all the philosophers who were in Athens could not find a way to explain why the sun should darken, for it was not according to nature. And the philosophers having gathered inside, especially Denis, he said: "Either the God of nature suffers pain, or the whole world is about to perish." And for this reason, those of Athens made an altar in honor of that God of nature who was to come: and they placed upon it letters that said: **To the Unknown God**: for on every altar they placed its title, so that they might know which god it belonged to. And wishing to perform a sacrifice to him as they did to the others, the philosophers said that he had no need of it, but rather that they should bend their knees and love him thus: for he is not paid with the sacrifice of cattle, but with the devotion of the heart. 

And Saint Paul came to the city of Athens: and some called him a babbler <note>original: "palabrero", a term used in the Book of Acts (17:18) to mock Paul's preaching.</note>, and others said he was a messenger of the devils. And as he walked through the temple encircling all the altars, he found that altar of the Unknown God: and he said to the philosophers: "Men, that which you do not know—of this God I am the messenger. And I tell you that this is the true God who made heaven and earth." And he spoke further to Denis, because he knew more than all the others: "Denis, who is this God whom you do not know?" And Denis said: "This is the God who is to come among men and is not yet known." And Saint Paul asked him if he was only man, or a spirit. And the other, Denis, said that he was God and man, and for that reason we say he is unknown: because his life and his name are in heaven. And Paul said to him: "This is the one whom I preach,

<column-break/>

who descended from heaven to earth and took flesh from Saint Mary, and [suffered] death and passion, and rose again on the third day." 

And while Denis and Saint Paul were disputing, a blind man passed through the street: and Denis said to Saint Paul: "If you tell that blind man to see in the name of your God, and he sees, I will immediately believe in him." And Paul told the blind man to see in the name of Jesus Christ, and he immediately recovered the light in his eyes. And then Denis converted and had himself baptized, along with his wife Damaris and all his company. And Saint Paul showed him the faith for three years, and afterwards he was the Bishop of Athens. 

And with the preaching that he did, he converted the whole city along with the greater part of the land to the faith of Jesus Christ. And they said that Paul had revealed to Denis the things that he saw in the third heaven <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2, where Paul describes being caught up to the "third heaven."</note> when he was caught up, just as this Denis makes it understood in many ways. Therein he spoke so clearly of all the orders of the angels <note>Dionysius was the traditional author of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, a foundational text on the ranks of angels.</note> that it clearly seems no other man showed it to him, but that he [Paul] revealed it to him, and through the spirit of prophecy, as it appears in the letter that he sent to Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist when he was exiled on the island of Patmos; and he sent it in this manner: **"May God give you joy, you who are loved and cherished and desired; in that joy you shall escape the exile in which you are, and you shall return to the land of Asia, and you shall find there many likenesses of the true God; and you shall tell those who come after you."** 

And he was present at the death of Saint Mary, according to what he says. And hearing, Denis, that the Emperor Nero held Saint Peter and Saint Paul prisoners, he put another bishop in his place and came to Rome to visit them. And after the Apostles were dead, Saint Clement was Pope, and they sent him to preach in France. and in his company went Rusticus and Eleutherius. And he came to the city of Paris and converted many there to the faith of Jesus Christ and built many churches. And our Lord put such grace in Saint Denis that, though the bishops of the idols often moved against him with arms to kill him, without any other bravery he would go and throw himself at their feet, and they would flee in fear. And Judas the devil, having great envy because his honor was diminishing and that of the Christians was increasing...

# The Four-Part Work of Ptolemy

## These are the contents contained in this volume:

->The Four-Part Book of Ptolemy. <note>original: "Liber quadripartiti Ptolomei"; commonly known by its Greek name, the Tetrabiblos, this is the foundational textbook of Western astrology.</note><-
->The One Hundred Aphorisms by the same author. <note>original: "Centiloquium"; a collection of 100 astrological rules often attributed to Ptolemy in the Middle Ages, though now considered pseudepigraphical.</note><-
->The One Hundred Aphorisms of Hermes. <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of the Hermetic tradition.</note><-
->By the same author, on the <term>beibene stars</term>. <note>original: "de stellis beibenijs"; from the Arabic "biyābānī," referring to specific fixed stars of primary importance in astrological practice.</note><-
->The One Hundred Aphorisms of Bethem, and on the planetary hours.<-
->By the same author, on the meaning of the <term>triplicities</term> at birth. <note>The triplicities are groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element: Fire, Earth, Air, or Water.</note><-
->The One Hundred and Fifty Propositions of Almansor.<-
->Zahel on <term>interrogations</term>. <note>original: "de interrogationibus"; also known as horary astrology, where a chart is cast to answer a specific question.</note><-
->By the same author, on <term>elections</term>. <note>Electional astrology involves choosing the most auspicious time to begin an undertaking.</note><-
->By the same author, on the significance of times in judgements.<-
->Messahalla on the <term>receptions</term> of the planets. <note>Reception is a technical relationship where one planet is located in a sign ruled by another.</note><-
->By the same author, on interrogations.<-
->A letter by the same author with twelve chapters.<-
->By the same author, on the <term>revolutions</term> of the years of the world. <note>Mundane astrology used to predict world events, such as wars or harvests, based on the sun's entry into Aries.</note><-

# Table of Contents

The following index will clearly show you, if you read it through, the division of this present volume into books, treatises, and chapters. First, you will encounter the Four-Part Book of Ptolemy, divided into four treatises. After that follows his *One Hundred Aphorisms*. Next is the *One Hundred Aphorisms* of Hermes, and a short treatise on the <term>beibene stars</term> <note>original: "beibenyus"; these are specific fixed stars considered to have primary influence in medieval astrology</note> follows immediately after. You will also see the *One Hundred Aphorisms* of Bethem, as well as his work on the benefits of the planets and the significance of all the <term>triplicities</term> <note>groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note>. After that, you will find Almansor with 150 propositions. Next, Zahel shows <term>interrogations</term> <note>horary astrology, or answering specific questions based on the time they are asked</note>, as well as <term>elections</term> <note>choosing the best time to start an undertaking</note> and the significance of times in judgments. In the final place, Messahalla declares the <term>receptions</term> of the planets <note>a relationship where planets occupy each other's dignities</note> and also interrogations. He presents an Epistle of twelve chapters and indicates the revolutions of the years of the world. Finally, you can read a more detailed distinction of these things we have mentioned, noted by page number, if you wish.

# Girolamo Salvi of Faenza, Doctor of Arts and Medicine: To Domenico Maria of Novara, the Ferrarese Doctor of Arts and Medicine and most excellent astrologer, regarding the nobility of astrology. Greetings.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "P" depicting a scholar in a gown seated at a desk, looking at an open book, with architectural elements in the background.</image-desc>

There are many insolent and slandering people, and many who are simply ignorant (my dearest Domenico), who judge this part of our astronomy—which we call "judicial" <note>original: "iudicialem"; this refers to predictive astrology, the practice of judging the influence of stars on human affairs</note>—as something to be despised, rejected, and completely disregarded. They cry out against it daily. Some do so because, due to the dullness and, if I may say so, the thickness of their intellects, they cannot grasp even the smallest part of it. Others, seeing many astrological judgments prove to be failed, vain, and without truth, boldly and recklessly presume to declare that this part of astronomy we have mentioned is not a science, but rather a collection of fables and deceptions. We, however, leaving the ignorant to their ignorance and the slanderers to their slander, prove that our branch of astronomy must be included among the "speculative sciences" <note>A category of knowledge sought for its own sake (like physics or math), rather than for a practical craft</note>. Indeed, that it ought to be called a science will be easily apparent if we make known what a science is and how it is acquired. For what else is a science but a "habit acquired through demonstration"? <note>This is a classic Aristotelian definition: a reliable mental disposition toward truth reached through logical proof</note> And what else does a demonstration do but create a notion of a property belonging to its subject? Every science presupposes a subject of which it treats, and demonstrates the properties of that subject using principles believed within that science.

It will be clear to everyone that our judicial astrology is such a science if they understand with an open mind what we say about astronomy. We say, therefore, that although astronomy seems to be divided into two parts—the "demonstrative" and the "judicial"—it is nevertheless truly one science due to the unity of its subject. It is divided only by the different properties demonstrated within that same science regarding that same subject, as will be easily clear to an intelligent person from what follows immediately. Let us say, then, that the subject of astronomy is the "celestial body" <note>the heavens/planets</note> in terms of how it moves with these specific motions; and within it are powers, which, along with the motions, are the cause of "generation and corruption" <note>original: "gñationis 7 corruptionis"; the Aristotelian term for the cycle of birth, change, and death in the physical world</note>. The astronomer takes this subject as a given, as it has been sufficiently proven by the "Natural Philosopher" <note>Aristotle</note>. For the Philosopher proves that celestial bodies are the cause of birth and decay. And because they must be the cause of birth and decay, it is necessary that there be these specific motions within them, for a thing that remains the same and in the same state is naturally inclined to always produce the same result. Therefore, it is not the primary movement <note>the daily rotation of the sky</note> that is the cause of birth and decay, but rather the movement along the "oblique circle" <note>the Ecliptic or Zodiac</note>. For in this movement, there is both continuity and the shifting of two motions. The Philosopher also proved that it is necessary for this lower world <note>Earth</note> to be governed by the upper world. 

The astronomer, proceeding to further demonstration, investigates what these motions are, how they occur, and in what span of time they happen. He does this by concluding through geometric principles, demonstrating these things as we have said. This is what is called "demonstrative astronomy," all of whose demonstrations are mathematical and thus most certain, as you yourself well know. Immediately following this is our science of which we speak, acting as the later part to the prior part of the whole of astronomy. This second part of the science sets out to demonstrate what the powers of the celestial bodies are, how they work, and how they are the causes of birth and decay. The astronomer arrives at the knowledge of these things "from the effect" <note>original: "a posteriori"; reasoning from observed results back to their causes</note>, just as happens in other sciences; for philosophers began to philosophize out of wonder. Thus, the astronomer, seeing that among men one dies by the sword while another ends his final day in luxury, and believing that all of this comes from the celestial bodies, began to examine the causes of these different deaths. He found that such a star, arranged in such a way, preceded a luxurious death for one, while another star delivered a cruel death to another. From many such memories, the astronomer arrived at "experience," and from many experiences, he constructed a science. This is according to the Philosopher's statement in the prologue of the *Metaphysics*: "Experience indeed made art, but inexperience made chance." An "art" or "science" is formed when, from many experimental perceptions, one single universal concept is formed about similar things. Thus, from knowing "that it is," the astronomer arrived at "why it is," and returning from the "why," he demonstrated "that it is." Therefore, it is manifest that the judicial astronomer uses both types of demonstration: he reasons from the cause to the effect when he judges

<column-break/>

concerning the future, but he uses demonstration from the effect to the cause when he offers a judgment concerning the past, for he then reasons back from the result to the cause.

Up to this point, my dear Domenico, I believe it has been sufficiently demonstrated that this part of our astronomy which we call "judicial" ought most worthily and deservedly to be called by the name of "science." That it should be called "speculative" will be easily apparent if we set out the division of the sciences and declare what "speculative" and "active" (or "practical") entail. Let us say, therefore, following Avicenna <note>the famous Persian polymath Ibn Sina</note> in the first chapter of his *Metaphysics*, that sciences are divided into the speculative and the active. Speculative sciences are those in which one seeks to perfect the speculative power of the soul by acquiring knowledge of the result—namely, by attaining knowledge and belief regarding things that are not our own works or our own choices. In these, the end goal is the certainty of a conclusion or opinion. For the conclusion and opinion do not depend on the quality of our actions, nor is the beginning of our work the source of them. Practical sciences, however, are those in which one first seeks to perfect the speculative power of the soul by attaining knowledge regarding things that *are* our own works, so that, secondarily, the perfection of "practical virtue" in our behavior may follow. 

Now, it is clear from this that "practical" and "speculative" are not distinguished by the intellect itself—since the speculative power of the soul is perfected by both—but rather the distinction between them comes from the "object" being considered and the "end goal." Thus, a science must be called "practical" if it concerns things that are our own works or our own choices, intended to reach perfection in our moral behavior. Such are the "moral" and "civil" sciences. For what is considered moral among one people is considered a vice and blameworthy among another, as is clear with the Epicureans. Similarly, we see the statutes of cities can override civil law; the Emperor alone can override the law; and the whole of Canon Law could be changed by a new decree of the Church, for the Pope alone can override it. None of these things can happen in the matters considered by the speculative sciences <note>i.e., human laws change, but the laws of nature and the stars do not</note>. Avicenna later added that speculative sciences are divided into "natural," "mathematical," and "divine." He intended for all other sciences to be included under these three; therefore, our astronomy will be among their number, as we shall show more broadly below.

But since we are also physicians and have broken into this discourse, we wish to insert what we feel about medicine itself. We say briefly, whatever others may think, that according to Avicenna's intention, medicine must be counted among the speculative sciences, as can be seen from what has just been said. For the "speculation" of medicine concerns things that are not our own works, nor our own choices, nor does the perfection of moral behavior come through it. This same point was understood by the Prince <note>likely referring to Avicenna again as the "Prince of Physicians"</note> at the beginning of the first book [of the *Canon of Medicine*] when he determined that the whole of medicine is a science, although many commentators there try to twist his opinion. And in the second part of the first book, he said: medicine in its primary division is divided into two parts: a "theoretical" part and a "practical" part, yet both of these are "sciences of speculation." If anyone asks under which branch of the division it falls, we reply that it belongs to the "natural sciences." This is clear from the number of sciences that Avicenna himself lists in that same first chapter of his *Metaphysics*, when he shows that God is not the subject of any [particular] science, just as He is not the subject of metaphysics. Listing all the sciences except metaphysics, he said: "The other sciences are either moral, civil, natural, mathematical, or logical; and no science of wisdom exists outside of this division." It is clear, therefore, to one following the division, that medicine will be among the number of natural sciences. And he says in the same chapter that the subject of natural sciences is "bodies in terms of how they move and rest," and what is investigated about them are the "accidents" <note>properties or traits</note> that belong to them specifically in this way. It cannot be denied that both the subject of medicine and the accidents considered by it proceed according to this reasoning. Add to this that a science is to be called "natural" if it speculates on the "natures" of things pertaining to it—which we all know medicine does. Therefore, medicine is both a natural and a speculative science. Having inserted these very few points concerning medicine, let us return to where we digressed.

<summary>In this dedicatory letter, Girolamo Salvi defends astrology and medicine against critics, arguing that both are "speculative sciences" based on the unchanging laws of nature and the celestial bodies, rather than mere human opinion or craft.</summary>
<keywords>Girolamo Salvi, Domenico Maria Novara, judicial astronomy, astrology, speculative science, Avicenna, Aristotle, medicine, natural philosophy, generation and corruption</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Girolamo Salvi is addressing Domenico Maria of Novara, providing a philosophical defense of "judicial" (predictive) astronomy. He has just defined science as a habit acquired through demonstration and is now categorizing where astronomy fits within the hierarchy of knowledge.</meta>

...know that this astronomy of which we speak is to be counted among the **speculative sciences**. For it concerns those things which are not our own works, nor within our own disposition. Nor does the perfection of practical virtue in morals come about through it. For what man, or what nation, can vary the celestial movements? Or who can change the natures of the heavens themselves and the stars, or prohibit their influences? I know everyone will admit that none of these things can be done by humans. Therefore, the things the astronomer considers are not our works nor our dispositions; thus, it must rightly be called a speculative science. 

But immediately, the mathematician, wishing to contend with the natural philosopher, will say that astronomy itself ought to be included under his own category; for the demonstrations by which the astronomer proves the movements of celestial bodies and measures their quantities are all geometric and mathematical. 

The natural philosopher, however, desiring to maintain what is his, will respond to the mathematician, saying: "On the contrary, astronomy itself must be placed under the order of our category." This will immediately become clear to you if you recall to memory what our subject is and bring your own subject into the open. You will know our subject if you read what was said a little before, and what we intend to demonstrate concerning it, and how. 

But you might say: "Did not **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian philosopher and physician.</note> say in a frequently cited passage that the subject of the 'doctrinal sciences' <note>The mathematical sciences</note> is pure quantity, or that which has quantity? And its dispositions, which are sought within them, are those which happen to quantity, in the definition of which neither the species of matter nor the power of motion enters?" Is it not therefore common knowledge among everyone that mathematics abstracts from matter? Certainly so. 

Therefore, if you remember what we said above is the subject of astronomy, you will immediately concede that it is **natural** <note>In the sense of "Natural Philosophy" or physics</note> and not mathematical. For the astronomer himself is a subtle investigator of the movements of the heavens, the planets, and all the stars. How then does he abstract from motion? For he scrutinizes the natures of the stars in detail, and their influences and impressions upon these lower things <note>The Earth and human bodies</note>, as if upon a receiving matter. Observing also the disposition of that same matter proportioned to those impressions, he said that **Venus** makes a person born in Italy white, but in Ethiopia, less black <note>This refers to the medieval belief that planetary influences interact with geography and "humors" to determine physical appearance.</note>. How then can he be called anything but a natural philosopher, and how could he be said to abstract from matter? 

As to why you said the astronomer uses geometric demonstrations, I confess this is true; but I do not doubt that it happens by your own kindness: for you have lent him your propositions, just as we see often happens to many other scientists; for one often uses the propositions of another. 

<margin>*</margin> But perhaps someone (my dear Domenico) will speak against what we said: that astronomy is not concerned with those things which are our own works. The astronomer judges that **Mars** joined to the **Head of Algol** <note>original: "capiti algol"; Algol is a star in the constellation Perseus, historically associated with violence and beheading.</note> at the birth of someone will cause that person to be hanged; yet the person lives uprightly and is not hanged. Likewise, the astronomer judges that one born with **Mercury** so disposed will be neither learned nor wise; yet the person labors in wisdom and doctrine and becomes both wise and learned. Why these two contradictions? They follow the judicial [astrologer] because either he has lied, or because the science itself concerns those things which are our own works, inasmuch as they can be changed and varied by our will. 

To this we respond by denying both. For the conclusion of the judicial astronomer is this: that Mars joined to the Head of Algol impresses such a disposition in the newborn that, either because of robbery, or because of treason, or because of any other cause, the anger of a judge is easily provoked against him to hang him. For not every thief, nor every traitor, is hanged; but those who are born to this, that they might be hanged. Likewise, Mercury so disposed effects such an impression in the newborn that he attains wisdom and doctrine with difficulty; for not everyone laboring in wisdom turns out wise, but he who has this from nature, that he might be able to become wise. 

Who will say that making these impressions is our work? But that these impressions, which are the effects of the stars and the causes within us, do not follow through to secondary effects happens because of an **impediment** arising from the **will** of the one who received the impression. Therefore, the astronomer judged correctly, and his consideration was of those things which are not our works, even if the effect of the impression about which he offered judgment did not occur. I say, however, that when the 

<column-break/>

said impressions are strong, it will be very difficult for a person to habituate themselves otherwise according to their will. And **Haly** the commentator <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), an Egyptian physician and astrologer who wrote a famous commentary on Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*.</note> believed that this was impossible; since celestial bodies impress a complexion <note>The balance of humors (blood, phlegm, etc.) in the body.</note> upon bodies and their parts, according to which the organs—which ought to serve the soul itself—remain disposed in such a way as the soul uses them in its operations. For the soul, being joined to the body, does not operate otherwise than according to the disposition of the organs serving it. Nevertheless, when the impressions are weakened, a person can—through practice and their own will—adhere to the other side which they have chosen and succeed in it. 

And from this, the diversity in the whole army [of mankind] is clear: and why one profits more in them than another; and why sometimes one, ceasing from an exercise they began, attacks another. We, however, so as not to speak against the **Faith** regarding **Free Will**, believe that the judgments of astronomy can fail in those things in which a person can oppose an impediment through their will; because it is either easier or more difficult for a man to apply an impediment according to whether the impression was strong or weak. Nor for this reason is the truth of the science taken away, nor the speculation. But in those things in which the voluntary power of man does not extend, judgments can by no means be removed from the truth. 

Wherefore our **Ptolemy**, at the beginning of the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy, though likely of Arabic origin.</note>, says that the judgments of astronomy are between the **necessary** and the **possible**; and that the astrologer will be able to prohibit many evils by disposing the one who is to receive them toward a contrary disposition—which position, unless it be taken, that evil will infallibly seize the man. And in the other works of nature too, we see many errors and "monsters" <note>Biological anomalies or birth defects.</note> occurring because of some encountered impediment; yet the truth of natural philosophy is not thereby taken away, nor the speculation. 

And in the works of **Medicine** also, it is clear that not a few errors occur; its judgments likewise are very often frustrated and uttered without truth, as women and children have seen many times; yet medicine is not for this reason disparaged. On the contrary, physicians themselves are held in the highest veneration, so much so that the ancients did not fear to call physicians "gods." Add to this, if you please, that in both medicine and astronomy, many frustrated judgments are uttered by those who are themselves to be laughed at, since they wish to insert themselves among astrologers and physicians while being entirely alien to these sciences, possessing habits of ignorance in them. 

Why then, O fools, do you rush so insolently and insanely into such a brilliant and divine science? For if you were wise, you would call the astronomers—whom you disparage—earthly gods, and believe them sent from heaven to us like prophets. For by what science, tell me I pray, can a man become more like God than by astronomy? Is it not prophetic and divine to predict the future? Does it not exceed human strength to turn away future evils from you and to increase future goods? Desist therefore from your insanity and exalt astronomy; and worship astronomers as gods. 

As for us, my dear Domenico—so that this so brilliant and noble science, hidden until now by the envious, may be made manifest to all who desire it—we have taken care to hand over to the press **Ptolemy**, the King of Alexandria and prince in astronomy, as much as we were able to emend him, at the expense of the most accurate man, **Octavianus Scotus of Monza** <note>original: "Octauiani Scoti Modoetiensis"; a prominent Venetian printer from Monza.</note>. We have also added at the back certain small works of other approved men. And with this intention also: that we may take care to hand over to the press very many other works of approved men, so that even this most noble science—although difficult in itself—may shine forth to those desiring it through an abundance of books. 

It is also our decree that we should not waste time in praising either Ptolemy or any of the others, lest by believing we are extolling them, we make them seem cheap; for they are worthy of many more and greater praises than we believe we can note with a pen or express with a word. But if anyone wishes to know how much praise Ptolemy deserves, let him understand the book of the *Almagest* and this *Quadripartitum* <note>The *Tetrabiblos*.</note> book, and his *Centiloquium* very well. Likewise, by understanding the works of the others, he will perfectly know how much he can praise them.

->Farewell.<-

<summary>In this dedicatory letter, Girolamo Salvi defends "judicial" astronomy as a legitimate speculative science, arguing that its failures are due to human free will or material impediments rather than flaws in the science itself. He announces the publication of Ptolemy's core works by the printer Octavianus Scotus to make this "divine" knowledge accessible to all.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on the categorization of astronomy as a speculative science, this page moves into the formal prologues of the *Quadripartitum* (Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*). It features the dedication by the Latin translator, Egidius de Tebaldis, to King Alfonso X of Castile, followed by the opening of the commentary by the Egyptian scholar Haly Heben Rodan.</meta>

**First Treatise**

# The letter of Egidius de Tebaldis, a Lombard from the city of Parma, regarding the *Quadripartitum* of Ptolemy. Egidius spoke:

To know and to understand is glorious, because all knowledge is from God. Therefore, the soul that understands and discerns is glorious, and God greatly loves and has chosen that person in whom He has placed the understanding of the science of the superior bodies. The science of the superior bodies is, without a doubt, the art of the stars; for all other sciences are subject to it, and it is founded upon certain natural principles encompassing the whole world. It is necessary that one's entry be made through other sciences before this one can be reached. From this it is clear that this science is of the highest and most excellent things. Furthermore, no doubt arises that, with divine providence disposing the superior bodies, all inferior things are moved, for the heavens are the cause of all earthly events. Therefore, he who exerts himself in the understanding of such a sublime science loves to know the God of all created things; for the work of the stars is God's work, and they act as God’s vicars <note>original: "vicarie dei"; meaning the stars act as deputies or representatives of God's will on Earth.</note> in whatever happens in earthly matters. Likewise, since God is himself the same as intellect, the more one understands, the closer one is to God—whose name be blessed for everlasting ages. Therefore, let everyone study for the sake of understanding, for as Solomon says: the one who understands shall possess the rudders of governance.

I, truly a lover of science and of those who know, observing how the entire art of the stars—through rules and foundations according to the four-fold science and nature—is contained in one book of four parts composed by the most wise Ptolemy; and considering also that his words were so closed and so weighty with meaning that they could scarcely be opened by any of the wise—nay, rather, almost all were in error regarding it and varied in their opinions—and because of this, the fruit and effect of such a noble science was being lost, for no one walked in it by the right path: I have provided for the translation of this book from Spanish into plain and open Latin, so that its pure meaning might be more clearly revealed to students, along with the glosses of the most prudent physician Haly Heben Rodan <note>Ali ibn Ridwan (c. 988–1061), a famous Egyptian physician and astrologer whose commentary was essential for medieval students of Ptolemy.</note>, which he received from God and through his own wonderful consideration, so that the words of Ptolemy and whatever he wished to reveal through them might be more fully understood. This was done by the command and pleasure of Lord Alfonso, the most illustrious King of the Romans and of Castile <note>Alfonso X (1221–1284), known as "The Wise." He established a famous translation school in Toledo to bring Arabic knowledge into Latin and Spanish.</note>, for I intend nothing else in this work.

I therefore pray to God the Father that He deign to open the way of righteousness to me. First, however, the most glorious and excellent Alfonso, King of the Romans and of Castile, who loves knowledge and honors the learned, ordered this book to be translated from Arabic into the Spanish language. He searches for and acquires knowledge from the ends of the earth through all the climates of the world, from every sort of people and language; like a lord and master of all sciences and virtues, he has renewed many useful things through his own consideration and ordered many books to be organized from the sayings and opinions of the ancient wise men, which lay scattered and lost here and there. Without a doubt, future posterity will be enlightened by him. Truly, that munificent king, whose generous bounty is inestimable, whose health prevails over all, and whose honor passes to everyone—remaining in itself, neither diminished but increased—his intellect encompasses all things. His providence seems divine rather than human, for all these things are rooted and naturalized in him, as he is the fountain of all virtues. Therefore, he is truly called by his name, "Alfonso" <note>A medieval pun on the name Alfonso and the Latin word "fons" (fountain/source).</note>. This is a high fountain, a living fountain, whose streams water and adorn the orb of the earth with the dew of salvation and all virtues. And to encompass many things in few words: I say that the heavens and the favorable aspects of the planets, with their receptions and dignities, agreed in the making of such a man; nor do I believe that nature could have made a man of greater perfection. Be content, therefore, O my lord, for when the fame of other kings and princes shall melt away, your fame shall flourish, immortal for all time.

<column-break/>

# ¶ Here begins the first treatise of the glosses of Haly Heben Rodan on the first part of the book of the *Quadripartitum* of Ptolemy of Pelusium. Haly spoke:

Regarding the words spoken by the most wise Ptolemy in the art of the judgments of astronomy <note>At this time, "astronomy" and "astrology" were not yet distinct; Ptolemy's "judgments" refer to what we now call astrology.</note>: wishing to provide a commentary on these things, we say that the judgment of the stars is an art proceeding from certain principles, by which those things that happen in the present can be known. Some of these certain principles are proven in the science of nature <note>Physics</note>, and others in the science of the quadrivium <note>The four mathematical arts: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note>. You will understand these words in this determination when you read this book, if you apply your mind to it diligently. However, if you do not look well and pass over it lightly, you will be like one passing by a good tree and looking at it, but not taking its fruit; and thus it would have been better for you not to have labored in reading this book. But if with great will and complete study you apply your mind, you will be able to reach a high degree of this science.

It is expedient, however, that you pray to God to aid you in understanding the words of the good and most perfect man Ptolemy. God granted me the grace to understand them, for until now, no one has been found who could completely understand them well, nor distinguish the wonderful reasons within them. We speak of these according to our ability, attending similarly to the things that agree with the reason of his words, and we distinguish each of them so that one may be separate from another. We pray to God, therefore, to help us and direct us into the path of truth.

¶ First, however, it is appropriate that we propose eight things, which the masters always propose in their books, stating one reason before it is appropriate to proceed. For we say that there are some sciences which are knowledge without works <note>Theoretical or speculative sciences</note>, and others which are works <note>Practical sciences</note>. Among those that are works, some complete what nature lacks, such as medicine and agriculture; and others follow the things of nature, such as weaving and carpentry. And others are those that teach things that are to come according to nature, such as the judgments of astronomy, prophecies, and divinations. But through this art of the judgments of astronomy, a man can know that which was in times long past, that which is, and that which is to come.

Furthermore, this is a science that pertains to many parts of philosophy, such as knowing how many spheres there are, and how many kinds and how many celestial motions there are; by these, philosophers know how many spiritual movers there are. Because of this, this science is divided into two great parts: one is theoretical, and this is "quadrivial" astrology <note>The mathematical study of the heavens, i.e., astronomy.</note>, by which a man knows how many spheres are in the heaven and how many kinds of motions, which demonstrates the true unity of God by certain demonstration—whose name be perpetually exalted. The other part is practical, and this concerns the judgments of the stars, by which their powers can be known, and how they act in all things that are below the sphere of the moon. These things are the four elements, the vapors of the earth, minerals, vegetables, animals, and other things that follow, such as health (which follows the temperament of the air) and sickness (which follows its corruption). In this second part, called practical, the ancient wise men compiled many books; but the most prior and more complete of them all, and the one which follows right philosophy most closely, is the book of Ptolemy. This is the one of which we speak; and because it is very "closed" <note>Densely written or obscure.</note> due to the brevity of the noble things within it, and the many reasons compressed into few words, Ptolemy wished to follow the custom of the good philosophers who are called the "founders." These are of the sect of Plato and Aristotle, who compressed great reasons into few words so that none but the wise—who have a great will and desire for knowledge, and are neither ignorant nor lazy—might understand them. And for this reason, it is appropriate that we comment on this book, so that it might be easier to learn for those desiring to know something. We shall propose eight principal things, as we said before, which are: the subject matter of which the book speaks; the name of the book; the benefit found in it; its order; the name of its author; to which art it belongs...

<meta>The text continues from the translator's preface by Egidius de Tebaldis into the formal introduction of the "Tractatus Primus" (First Treatise). It establishes the authorship of Ptolemy of Pelusium, distinguishes him from the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt, and outlines the four-part structure of the work known as the Quadripartitum or Tetrabiblos.</meta>

### First Treatise

**Concerning how many parts it contains. In what manner it demonstrates its subject. Concerning the principles from which it speaks.**
I say that Ptolemy set down in this book all the rules and roots <note>Foundational principles</note> from which this art of judgments <note>original: "iudicys"; judicial astrology, the practice of predicting events from the stars.</note> is composed. Thus, whoever knows and understands them well will be able to speak at any time about those things that happen to all bodies that are below the sphere of the moon, both those things that pertain to them by nature and those that follow them by accident. Because of this, he is seen to know as much as the human intellect can attain. 

**Concerning the name of the book,** I say that Ptolemy, in these rules and principles, found them to be of various types; for this reason, he placed each in its proper part. He saw that there were four types, and so he placed them in four treatises, each being an entity unto itself that could be called by its own proper name. Because of this, he gave this book the name *The Book of the Four Parts of the Judgments of Astronomy* <note>original: "libri quatuor partium iudiciorum astronomie"; commonly known as the *Tetrabiblos*.</note>, so we may know that this science is divided into the four parts he will describe. 

**Concerning the benefit of this book,** I say it is a matter that can be well understood by the reason of which he speaks and the name of the book; for from this book, a man can know the whole of this science in a few summaries. 

**Concerning the order of the book,** I say that the principles and roots are accepted from the mathematical sciences <note>original: "astrologia quadriuiali"; refers to the Quadrivium: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note> through which a man knows the motions and figures of the stars, and likewise from the art of nature <note>Physics or natural philosophy.</note> by which the king of nature is known. Because of this, it follows that after these two sciences, this book should be read; it follows that this book should succeed mathematical astrology so that the science may come in an orderly fashion. 

**Concerning the name of the author,** I say it was Ptolemy of Pelusium <note>original: "Ptol. pheludianus"</note>, the one who made the *Almagest*. We intend this to be so because his sense and intellect regarding the words of this book are similar to his sense in the other words he spoke in all his other books, which he clearly made. It is of the material about which he was accustomed to speak; for all the books he made are of one likeness in their depth and great truth of knowledge, regarding both natural and mathematical things, and in the ability to comprehend great reasons in few words. Furthermore, we find in other books he made that he names and acknowledges this science, just as he said in his book *On the State of the Lights of the Stars*: that through the figures of the stars reaching their proper motions, all various and rare changes occur in quantity and quality in this world regarding generation and corruption <note>The cycle of birth and decay.</note>. Because of these figures, changes occur in the subject matters of this world. 

He also said in that book that the celestial bodies give powers to the things below them, similar to the things themselves having a natural aptitude to receive them. He stated such a reason in many places: in his book the *Almagest*, as he related in the 13th book when he spoke of the triple, fourth, sextile, opposition, and conjunction <note>Astrological aspects or angles between planets.</note>. Thus, when we inspect these two books of his diligently, we will see them to be very similar in their reasoning. He also spoke other words in his book *On Aspects*, and the words he spoke in his book *On the Map of the World* <note>Ptolemy’s *Geography*.</note> are similar to those he said in the second treatise of this book when he spoke of the division of the earth's population. 

This same truth is affirmed by the testimony of the ancient Lapidiones of Alexandria and other wise and skilled men of that time: that Ptolemy made this book, the same who composed the *Almagest*. Other wise men who came after them, such as Thabit ibn Qurra, Ya'qub al-Kindi, Hunayn ibn Ishaq <note>original: "Joannitius filius Isaac"</note>, and Abraham ibn Ezra <note>original: "Dabraam de avenagald"</note>, all affirm and are certain that Ptolemy of Pelusium, who composed the *Almagest*, made this book. If he had not made it, there would have been no one among the wise who possessed such power in sense and wisdom to make such a book as this is, except only this Ptolemy. Certainly, I do not think anyone would be so ignorant or so bold as to want us to believe someone else made it, except this good man. 

However, Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "albumasar"; a famous Persian astrologer.</note> and others who made chronicles—those who understood nothing but the text and received things by hearsay, not seeking what is truth or not—believed that this Ptolemy was one of the kings of Alexandria. This is because after Alexander, all those kings were called by such a name. They believed there was one king among them who so loved wise men, wisdom, and science that he sought and held as many books as he could of every kind of science, and he drew wise men to his land with great rewards. Thus he was named Ptolemy, the lover of sciences.

<column-break/>

That Ptolemy lived a long time before this Ptolemy who composed this book. For in all chronicles, we find that those kings of Alexandria who were named Ptolemy lived before the Roman Emperors. We find that this Ptolemy who composed the book *Almagest* names the locations of the stars according to their rectification in the time of the Roman Emperors, long after the time of the kings of Alexandria. Therefore, we understand that this Ptolemy of Pelusium was not one of the kings of Alexandria. Furthermore, we never find that the aforementioned Ptolemy, the lover of science, composed any book; he merely loved wise men very much and loved to hear sciences, especially books of Hebrew <note>original: "abraica"; likely referring to the translation of the Septuagint.</note>. John the Grammarian <note>John Philoponus.</note>, who was one of the good wise men of Alexandria, affirms well what we say: that we find for certain that Ptolemy of Pelusium, who composed the *Almagest*, made this one. 

**Concerning what science this book belongs to,** I say it is of the science of prognostications <note>The art of predicting the future.</note>, through which a man can know things that are to come before they happen. Just as physicians know through signs if a sick man can be healed or not, or if a healthy man may fall into illness or not, or what infirmity he may encounter—as you will find in the *Book of Prognostics* by Hippocrates, and in his book *On Airs, Waters, and Places*, and in the book by Galen <note>original: "Sal."; likely a scribe's error for "Gal." (Galen).</note> *On Crises* and the one *On Critical Days*. Similarly, laborers and miners or sailors have their art, which they understand through the rising and ascending of the stars and their setting, and by the winds that move. They recognize those things that ought to happen to trees, harvests, and mines, and what will happen to ships at sea, and what kind of weather there will be. 

Even diviners <note>original: "idiuvini"</note> have their art, through which they know future things by looking into the hearts, shoulder blades, and livers of beasts. Similarly, there are augurs and those who look to proverbs; many use these for one purpose and one mystery—that is, each one intends to know things that are to come before they happen. Thus, the science of prognostication is of many types; one part of astronomy is one of them. And we understand it is more certain than all others, truer, more general, and complete in all things. 

**Concerning the major parts of the book,** I say they are four, as was said before; for when Ptolemy looked into the general types, he found there were four. In the **first part**, he compiled all the general rules pertaining to all other parts of this science. In the **second part**, he compiled the rules by which a man can know great and general things that happen to many peoples or to one nation, such as the change of kings, new kingdoms, great battles, good or bad times for food supplies across great lands, and similarly great debts occurring in great lands; and of these, he made the second part. In the **third part**, he compiled all the rules by which one can know those things that happen to any person at the time of their birth; and of this, he composed the third part. In the **fourth part**, he compiled all the rules by which a man can know those things that happen to any person concerning external things, such as marriages, occupations <note>original: "misterium"; here meaning a trade or craft.</note>, and such; and of these, he composed the fourth part. And once you know that it is divided into these four general parts, it follows that each of them should have its own specific chapters, as you will find here. And because choices <note>original: "electiones"; the branch of astrology used to choose the best time for an action.</note> and reasons are understood by men through what science they are, he did not wish to involve himself in speaking of them, rather seeing them as very weak things. 

**Concerning the manner of demonstration,** I say that Ptolemy spoke in six manners: in composition, in resolution, in division, in definition, in induction, and the like. That he spoke in composition and resolution is seen when he said that such a planet, when by itself, shows such a thing, and when it has another participation, it demonstrates otherwise; and thus he demonstrates each thing by argument or experience. In division, as when he said that the common degrees of the zodiac share in such and such a figure. In definition, as when he spoke on the division of the planets and signs. In induction, as when he spoke of the complexion <note>The physical and elemental makeup.</note> of each planet; and thus it was considered regarding proof. In likeness, as when he demonstrates his reasons according to the likeness of others. 

In all these manners, he always speaks as much as he can according to nature: such as heat, cold, dryness, and moisture, and such natural things. For his operation is that all stars cause these things in the bodies that are below the sphere of the moon, and all other things follow them. All things in this science are thus, as you will understand later. After we have completely described these eight principal things, we wish to begin to gloss the words of Ptolemy, placing his words on one side and our glosses <note>Explanatory notes or commentary.</note> on the other, so that the book may be well divided.

<summary>This page serves as an introductory prologue to Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos, establishing its authorship, distinguishing the scientist Ptolemy from the Egyptian kings, and outlining the book's four-part structure covering general principles, mundane events, nativities, and external life circumstances.</summary>
