<meta>The text transitions from the general introductory remarks by the translator into the primary body of Ptolemy’s work. This page establishes the distinction between the two branches of stellar science: the mathematical study of planetary movements (astronomy) and the study of their effects on the earthly realm (astrology). It introduces the commentary of Haly ibn Ridwan, which will accompany the text.</meta>

# Here begins the Four-Part Book of Ptolemy, that is, of the four treatises on the discernment of the future rooted in the stars: both in the manner of their construction and their destruction; with the commentary of Haly ibn Ridwan <note>original: "Haly Heben Rodan"; Ali ibn Ridwan was an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer whose commentary on Ptolemy became a standard text in Medieval Europe.</note>.

## In whose first treatise there are 23 chapters.

### Chapter one of the first treatise of the four-part book of Ptolemy on the collection of the understanding of the science of the judgments of the stars.

#### Preface.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting two scholars in academic robes. One stands pointing towards a celestial sphere on a table, holding a book; the other sits or stands opposite him, working with a pair of dividers over the table. Various scientific or astronomical instruments are visible on the workspace.</image-desc>

**O**f the measures of things in which the perfection of the predictable science of the stars consists, we have found that there are two great and principal ones.

**T**he things by which the predictions of outcomes are perfected: the two greater and nobler ones are these.

<margin>Commentary: When he said "of outcomes" <note>original: "missori"; likely a variant for "of things sent" or "results"</note>, he means to say: "of the world." And he says this to show honor to those reading his book; you will find such a word of courtesy in the prefaces of all his works, as in the *Almagest* and the *Arithmetic*.</margin>

<margin>Commentary: When he also said "greater," he means to say of greater perfection; for the perfection of any science ought to be such that it is true, encompassing all the reasons that follow from it.</margin>

<margin>Commentary: When he said "nobler," he said it because the matter of which the quadrivial <term>Quadrivial: Referring to the 'Quadrivium', the four higher liberal arts: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</term> science speaks are the celestial bodies. The matter of which the judgments of astronomers speak are the bodies existing below the sphere of the moon. Therefore, this art is nobler than all others because the matter of which it speaks is the whole world. These words which Ptolemy said are one argument whose substance is what he said: that the things by which the predictions of outcomes are perfected are the greater and nobler ones. And what he said is predicated on there being two.</margin>

**Ptolemy** looked into all manners of predictions and found those that are effective for physicians, and similarly for all others who have spoken of such things. He found that each one in his own science was aided by the stars: thus, the physician speaks of the rising, setting, and falling of stars. And thus Haly spoke of the changes of illnesses, which follow the course of the moon. Likewise, laborers know the time when they must plant trees and vines, and when to give the male seed to the beasts. Similarly, sailors who direct their ships by the stars, and even men of the law in ordering the hours and festive days for their people. Yet in all these things, whatever they have of the science of the stars is a very small thing, such that it is not perfect. And after it is so, it follows that only the astronomer's art of prediction is complete. For the astronomer knows that which all these others know, and beyond that, he possesses the completion of the whole. And because of this, Ptolemy said that the things by which the art of prediction is perfected and completed are two greater and nobler ones: which are the "quadrivial" astronomy <note>Mathematical astronomy</note> and the art of the judgments of astronomy <note>Judicial astrology</note>.

<margin>Commentary: "Quadrivial astronomy" is this: that through it, a man knows the configurations of the stars according to their motions and the relationship of one to another. These configurations are the conjunctions and other aspects; and by the relationship of these aspects to the earth, whether they are near the earth or far, or when they rise or set in the eclipses of the two lights <note>The Sun and Moon</note> and such things. Because of this, Ptolemy spoke of the "configurations of the stars" so that he might make us understand. For the science of knowing what their natures are—whether they are light or not, heavy or not—is not from the science of the astronomer, but from the science of nature <note>Physics</note>.</margin>

**C** One of these, which precedes and is stronger, is the science demonstrating the configurations of the sun and moon, as well as the five wandering stars <note>The planets</note>; which is manifest as happening by cause of their motions and the comparison of one to another and of them to the earth.

**C** One of these is that which ought to be placed first in order and power: and it is the art by which the configurations of the two lights and the five planets are known according to their motion in comparison of one to another and of them to the sphere of the earth.

And the five planets of which he spoke are: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury. And when he said that the art of astronomy ought to be placed first in order, it was because if we do not know the configurations of the stars, we will not know how to judge what they work in inferior bodies <note>Physical objects and beings on Earth</note>.

<margin>And what he said regarding "power" was because all these reasons are firmer and stronger than those in the art of judgments; and this is because they are accepted from geometry and arithmetic.</margin>

<margin>Commentary: Furthermore, the matter of which this speaks is nobler than that of which the other speaks; for that is celestial, while this is earthly. Below and elsewhere, he spoke only of the seven planets, nor did he name the fixed stars. But because the planets are of light motion and change quickly from one state to another, according to their changes these inferior bodies are changed; and especially because the powers of the fixed stars follow in comparison to the powers of the seven planets. And whenever Ptolemy names the "two lights," he means the sun and the moon. And when he names other planets, he says "this planet" and "that planet," so that he may make us know the powers and the great prerogative which the two great lights have over the other planets. And if you look at his words, you will find that he names them thus. The things which ought to be considered are the changes and works which happen and are perfected by the configuration of the courses of the stars, which are their natural ones, and specifically in the things which they encompass. This is the science of the judgments of astronomy; for through it a man can know the changes and works happening in the things that are near us. And the changes of which he spoke are the six manners of motion: which are generation, turning, corruption, increase, decrease, and change from one place to another. And the "works" he mentioned are the things coming from these changes in the manner of a consequence, just as the virtues of the soul follow the composition of the body.</margin>

<column-break/>

**C** And what he said "happen and are completed," he said so as to exclude things that are done but not completed; such as time, which is always being made and never completed. In knowing what time is and why it comes: this is not of this science, but of the science of nature.

<margin>Commentary: But if someone were to say that Ptolemy has already spoken in this science concerning a thing that is made and not completed—namely when he spoke of a miscarriage <note>original: "abortiuo"</note>—we answer to this that the miscarriage was already completed in all its members; only the time of its life was not completed.</margin>

**C** However, what he said concerning "the configuration of the courses of the stars," he said because each planet has its own proper course. Because of this, he sets each of them apart in a configuration separate from the configuration of another; for that which at one time is oriental <note>rising in the east</note> is at another time occidental <note>setting in the west</note>. And that which is occidental may become oriental, and so in other configurations. For because of such configurations, works and changes happen in the things that are toward us; and they have this from nature, just as the lodestone <note>original: "lapis adamas"</note> has the power to draw iron to itself, and as scammony <note>A medicinal plant used as a purgative</note> purges bile, and other such things.

**C** The other science is that which explains the changes and works that happen and are completed because of the configurations of their natural circuits in the things which they surround. But since the first of these two is a science unto itself and is not accompanied by the other, it is necessary that the researcher seek and learn it for its own sake and gather this fruit here, even if he does not learn the [second] science. Since, therefore, it is manifest that this is so, the volume of the first science has already been completed for you by us, in which we have proceeded reasonably according to our ability.

**C** The first of the two sciences which we mentioned is a science separate and complete in itself. And it is such that a man ought to learn it for the benefit which is in it for its own sake, without involving himself in this other; for he can excuse this other second science which we mentioned. And that which was first was our purpose; and because it is so, we composed this book separate from the first science. We have proceeded, indeed, in the first way of demonstration according to our ability.

**C** After Ptolemy said that the science of the judgments of astronomy ought to be read after quadrivial astronomy, he now notified us of the power which is in each of them, so that no one should think that the quadrivial science was proposed only so that one might arrive at the benefit of the judgments of astronomy. Because of this, he said: that quadrivial astronomy is a thing that can exist for its own end without this science of judgments. For the separate book which he said he composed in astronomy is the book of the *Almagest*.

**C** In this book, we shall explain the second of the sciences, which is by no means explainable by itself, according as physical reason requires.

->Ptolemy's Quadripartitum<-

<summary>This page introduces the "Tetrabiblos" (Quadripartitum), defining the two branches of celestial study: mathematical astronomy (the "Almagest") and the art of astrological prediction. Ptolemy and his commentator Haly ibn Ridwan argue that while astronomy can stand alone as a perfect mathematical science, astrology relies upon it and focuses on how planetary movements affect earthly changes like growth, decay, and health.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introductory discourse of Haly ibn Ridwan’s commentary on Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*. Following the previous page’s distinction between the two branches of stellar science, this text delves into why the second branch—the judgment of the stars (astrology)—is more difficult and prone to error than the mathematical study of the heavens (astronomy).</meta>

### Left Column:

The second matter that we mentioned is not complete by itself: however, we wish to speak about it in this book according to Ptolemy's method <note>original: "viam prohie"; likely a contraction for "viam Ptolomei," referring to the specific systematic approach Ptolemy takes.</note>. The science of the judgments of the stars <note>The branch of astrology concerned with predicting events on Earth.</note> is not complete by itself, because it cannot be fulfilled without the science of the quadrivial astrology <note>original: "sciaz q̃driuiatīs astrologie"; referring to the Quadrivium, the four mathematical arts. Here it specifically means the mathematical calculation of planetary positions (astronomy).</note>, in which the actual operation is performed. For if a man lacks either of these two things, he does not truly know the truth, and he will not be able to work well in this science. When he said "according to Ptolemy's method," it can be understood that he wishes to speak according to natural science. It can also be understood as the whole reason why this science speaks: which is the argument in the manner of speaking that is fitting for Ptolemy, for the purpose of making things certain.

It is necessary for the investigator of this science to follow this intention: so that he may proceed in it by a straight path and a truthful way. However, he should not wish to compare the method for reaching this science to the method by which the other (astronomy) is reached, which is always of one and the same mode. Indeed, he will set aside and deny this science if he tries to make them identical. It happens to one wishing to intend this, that he should follow the way of a man seeking the truth. Let his purpose be this: that he does not wish to equate the way of this second science (astrological judgment) with the way of his first science (mathematical astronomy), which is stable and firm and always of one mode. For if he did so, he would immediately have to reject it and declare this science a lie.

He means to say that whoever seeks to know the prognostications of this science with the same certainty as the mathematical science (the Quadrivium) is in error; for the prognostications of quadrivial astrology—such as knowing when eclipses and conjunctions will occur—follow the courses of the planets and never change. However, the prognostications of *this* science are of another mode: because the materials <note>original: "māe"; abbreviation for "materiae." This refers to the sublunary or earthly matter influenced by the stars.</note> in which they operate through their own bodies are easily changed, and because they are not firm, nor do they remain in a single state. Indeed, the brief duration of the accidents of the matter in which this science is engaged is the cause of the variation in this second science. For this matter never persists in the same state. Therefore, one reaches a perfect knowledge of this science only with great difficulty.

The reason why this science varies is this: because the element <note>The four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> in which the operation occurs in this science is not stable, nor does it stay in one mode. For this reason, it is difficult to understand the manifestations that are in it. After he assigned to us the reason why quadrivial astrology is always certain, he gives us the reason in this occasion why the science of the judgments of the stars is of a different kind than the first. He says that these two sciences have one distinction: yet the error that falls into this science of judgments is due to the element in which the work of this science is done. He means to say that the four elements and all things composed of them—such as vapors, minerals, plants, and animals—receive operations through many types of matter, and none of them is stable in one state; for this reason it is difficult to know the things pertaining to them. From this, therefore, it can be understood that the error falling into this science is not because of the science itself, but because of the accidents of the matter in which it operates.

For this reason, however, it should not be set aside by anyone out of laziness; rather, one should strive to know from it what is possible to be known. It is indeed plain that what surrounds us is the cause of the many accidents and changes occurring in this world. Yet it does not follow, because of everything that might happen, that we should stop looking into the things that can be known through this science; for it is manifest that for the greater part, the accidents and novelties that happen among us do not come about through any other thing except through that which holds us in its circle <note>Refers to the celestial spheres surrounding the Earth.</note>.

After Ptolemy made it understood that the error falling into this science is only because of the matter which is not stable, he tells us: though this is so, we ought not to turn away; for we should look through this science into those things that a man can know of it, because it is manifest that the changes and the contingent works happening among us occur through the figures and courses of the stars. And since it is so, a small error should not turn us away from the great profit we can have from it.

Now, it is common for many to despise difficult things in their investigation; some, out of blindness of mind and lack of skill, were accusing and setting aside the first part of the science, while others the second. And because many deceitful men do things that are difficult to understand, there are those among them who arrive at such great

<column-break/>

### Right Column:

blindness that they call the first of these sciences a lie, and others who, disparaging the second, do the same.

The Quadrivium <term>Quadrivium: the mathematical arts of arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</term> of astrology is difficult to understand because there are strong arguments from geometry and arithmetic within it; and because of the corrections of the ancients who held various opinions; and because of the error that happens in the division of the instruments with which they observed; and because of the length of time that passes between one correction and another. And the science of the judgments of the stars is most difficult to understand because of the element which is not stable, as we said before; and because of the difficulty of understanding the composition of the powers of the planets—for example, one with another. And because of this, there are some who arrive at such great blindness. He means to say, the blindness of intellect of those who call the first science a lie. For they disparage many very good and more perfect things in Ptolemy's work because they are difficult to understand. And there are others who call the science a lie and disparage it for this same reason. Ptolemy, however, joined these two sciences in his account so that you may understand that each of them is quite certain in itself, and that the difficulty and error occurring in them is because of the weakness of human intellect and because of the nature of the element, which is not stable. And since this is so, neither of these sciences can be disparaged by itself.

The occasion that distracts them toward these views is perhaps this: they are either like those who, because they cannot know a thing due to its excessive difficulty, think that no one else can know it; or perhaps like those who, even if they have the power to know, reject it because it easily slips from the memory. For these causes, despising this science, they considered it as nothing.

And the reason why we can say this happens to them is: because there are some who, for the reason that they cannot understand a matter, believe it cannot exist in any way and that there is no one who can reach it. And others are of the opinion that a man should not look into a matter that is difficult to know, and they disdain it; for these reasons they do not look into the purpose of this science, and they say it is a matter that a man cannot reach.

Ptolemy speaks in this place, assigning the reason why many disparage the science of the judgments of astronomers. And he says it is because of two things. One, for which they do this, is either because they believe there are no men who can in any way understand matters that are difficult to understand; or because they see some people err there, because they cannot know the whole due to something that is lacking. Therefore they disdain it themselves, and they reckon it is a thing that no one can know, like the others we mentioned. But the science that lies between one opinion and the other is because of the first people we mentioned: they reckon there is no man who can understand it in any way. And others reckon it is a thing that can be reached, but it is so difficult that it should not be looked into, and for this reason they disdain the same.

We, however, before we manifest the particulars of this science, will strive to prove briefly: what is in this science, what can be known from the science of prognostication, and what fruit <note>The practical benefit or result.</note> follows; and from these two we will begin to explain how much it is, to which we can reach from this science.

We will relate, in order to make it understood briefly, how much of prognostication a man can reach from this science and how much is the profit that lies in it before we speak of the particular matters of this science. Starting with the most immediate, so that we may make understood how much it is that a man can reach of this science.

After he related the reason why error can fall into this art—saying that it is because of the element which is not stable, and because it is difficult to know the compositions made through the mixing of the powers of the planets, and because of this many are indignant toward it—he now begins to prove that it is a true and certain science. And he wishes to show how much a man can reach from it, and how much is the profit that lies in it, so that men may have a greater will for it and consider it more.

How we can arrive at the prognosticable science of the judgments of the stars, and how much it is that can be known from it. Chapter 2.

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Haly ibn Ridwan on Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*. It transitions from the theoretical justification of astrology to the physical mechanics of how celestial bodies influence the Earth, specifically through the "ether" and the four elements.</meta>

As much as it can be reached, the demonstration through reason <note>original: "r cū β demōstrat̄"; likely "et cum hoc demonstratur"</note> shows that this art is philosophical. And since this is so, why should anyone think that this was not a matter of experience? For this art is philosophical: yet no one has spoken on it with reason; indeed, if you look at the words they have spoken, you will find them very far removed from the truth of the matter, and the words of Ptolemy are filled with truths that cannot be falsified.

In some matter of the ether <note>original: "alathīr"; from the Arabic *al-athir*, referring to the fifth element or the substance of the heavens.</note> existing, which reaches all the way to terrestrial things and compels them to change; indeed, it forces those things. Likewise, nature receives mutability from the two primary materials placed under the lunar circle, which are fire and air. The motion of the ether surrounds and changes these, and they in turn surround the others, namely water and earth. Each of the vegetables <note>In medieval terms, "vegetables" refers to all plant life and things that grow but do not move.</note> is surrounded by these, and they are changed by their mutations; we believe there to be no doubt of this.

¶ The word is given regarding the noble substance <note>The celestial bodies.</note> which possesses a known power: and that which it has descends to all things that are above the earth, moving and changing them. These things also receive motion and change from the two elements which are under the sphere of the moon, and these are fire and air, which are surrounded by and receive motion and change from the movements of the noble body. And they likewise grasp and change by their motion other things which are in them: thus is the earth, the water, and all things that are in them, both vegetables and animals. The word is certain and manifest to all.

All celestial bodies are of a noble substance: and generally, they are all one in genus. They are of a nature and substance different from other things that are under the sphere of the moon, because the celestial substance is firm and durable and always of one mode; but the substance of the things that are among us is convertible and subject to many changes. And it is manifest that the power coming to us from the superior bodies works and makes changes in the superior bodies <note>The author likely means the bodies just below the heavens, like the upper atmosphere.</note>: because all who wish to look in a certain way will see that sometimes the air is made cold, or hot, and dry, or humid; all things existing upon the earth are changed because of this: likewise the water, the plants, and the animals. And Ptolemy proves this with a certain and right proof of judgment, which is called experience in this manner: for the laborers <note>Farmers and agricultural workers.</note> know by the course of the planets the coming times for planting trees, for sowing, and for making the beasts breed. And they are wiser regarding the labors of the earth; likewise, those who have worked in agriculture know from the stars that which will happen to the field and the tree at the hour it is planted, and that which will happen to them when they bear fruit. Sailors truly know from the stars how they ought to direct their ships; and those who are wiser understand the things that happen in the sea. And those who dwell on the shores of the sea know from the stars how the sea increases and decreases, or how it changes; and similarly, the rivers and springs are changed.
¶ Physicians also know from the stars and planets that the air gives health and infirmity. And he who knows more and looks more deeply into things can know the particular things pertaining to his mystery <note>term: "misteriū"; here meaning a professional craft or specialized trade.</note>. Thus Hippocrates said: if arriving infirmities come through any of the celestial things, it belongs to the physician who predicts them. For the master's word shows that Hippocrates knew and understood the infirmities coming from the celestial bodies. And because of this, he said that this science is no small part of the physical art <note>term: "ars phica"; the art of medicine or natural science.</note>. ¶ And Galen also studied and looked into his mystery so much that he found that the changes of infirmities follow the course of the moon. And if on a critical day <note>term: "die cretica"; a traditional medical term for the day a disease reaches a turning point.</note> the moon looks upon some good fortune <note>A beneficial planet like Jupiter or Venus.</note> of the patient's nativity, a good end and exit without pain will come to him. And if on that day it looks upon some misfortune, it will be the opposite. Galen also said such things in his books on physics. And likewise Hippocrates, who spoke before Galen on this reasoning in his book which he made on the embryo, when he spoke regarding the creature that lives in seven months and not in eight. And I say further that there is no man so ignorant that he does not know that because of the course of the sun there is heat and cold, and other things which are seen by the eye. Ptolemy, however, was not content to prove this judgment except by a right demonstration.
->¶ Because the sun and the air work in all earthly things.<-
->¶ Since the sun with the air works in all things existing on earth.<-
¶ Ptolemy does not wish to show by this word that the spheres of fire and air, which are changed by the celestial bodies, change all things that are among us, when the air is changed into heat, or brought into us by its operation, and in the things that are among us.

<column-break/>

¶ And that not only do alterations come to the earth from the four seasons of the year—such as in the perceptions of animals, the fruits of trees, the overflows of waters, and the changes of bodies—but also from the diurnal <note>daily</note> volubility in which it is daily contained. For because of this volubility, the earth grows hot and cold, is dried and moistened in one and the same way, because of similar figures in appearance which are formed according to their places from our zenith <note>The point in the sky directly above the observer.</note>. From the moon likewise: because it is closer to the earth, a great force is attributed to us, which offers many changes to things animate and inanimate. For the overflows of rivers and increases occur according to the diminution and increase of the moon. The seas also are altered at its rising and setting. Plants likewise and animals, in whole or in part, enter into increase and decrease according to its growth or diminution.
¶ And this is not only because of the changes that occur through the seasons of the year—such as the generation of animals, the fruiting of trees, the rising of waters, and the changes of other bodies—but it is also because of the revolution which the firmament makes once in a day. For it heats, cools, moistens, and dries according to a rule and order that follows the figures <note>Astrological aspects or positions.</note> which are similar in those manners which occur according to their places and the zenith of our heads. From the moon likewise, which is closer to the earth, a great force is attributed to us, because it provides many changes to animate and inanimate things. The overflows of the sea and the decrements occur according to this diminution and increase. The seas also are altered at its rising and setting. Plants likewise and animals, in whole or in part, find increase or decrease in its growth or diminution.
¶ After he said that the sun changes the air, and the air also changes the things it encompasses, he said that the sun does not do this only because of the seasons of the year, but it does this every day, in the same way that it does through the seasons of the year. For thus the sun, when it is directly over our heads, makes the air very hot; and when it moves away, it is much diminished in its heat. Thus it does every day, according to whether it is near or far from the middle of the sky existing above the earth. For in the morning, it makes the air more temperate, just like the manner of the springtime, relative to the air of that day. And he wishes to say that in the morning the air is more temperate as a rule. Similarly, from the middle of the sky, the air grows hot according to what it is in the summer time; and from the sunset, it grows moist according to what it is in the autumn time. And at midnight, it grows cold according to what it is in the winter time. For this is a thing which a man can easily understand if he looks at how the air positions itself every day. And since it is manifest that the sun is the greater cause in these things that happen through the seasons of the year—such as the generation of animals and the fruiting of trees—and that in those times they follow the composition of the air, it is also certain that the sun is the greater cause in changing these things that are among us every day with particular mutations. And Ptolemy sought until he found a demonstration from the side of the senses that the sun works in things that are among us, and many things, living and non-living, receive changes from it over time. For the fresh waters increase and decrease just as the increase and decrease of the light of the moon; and the changes of the sea are also changed according to the rising and setting of the moon. Similarly, plants and animals increase and decrease in whole or in part according to the increase and decrease of the moon. And the power of one operation upon another is based on how far the bodies are from one another: for then they are weaker, and the closer they are, the stronger they are. And because of this, Ptolemy said that because the moon is near us, a great power comes to us from it. And it is manifest that living things, such as plants and animals, and non-living things, such as waters, vapors, and minerals, all receive the operations and changes from the power of the moon, and from the things we see with our eyes. For we see rivers increase and decrease according to how the light of the moon increases and decreases; and many trees change their movements every day because of the rising and setting of the moon, or because it stands in the middle of the sky. And all these things the physicians, shepherds, laborers, and sailors know for certain, all of which you can know well through the books they have compiled: that plants, animals, minerals, and waters are changed in whole or in part according to the change of the light of the moon or according to the figure in which it places itself.

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Haly ibn Ridwan on Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos. Having established the theoretical basis of astrology as a physical science in the previous pages, the text now explains the specific mechanics of how "wandering stars" (planets) and "fixed stars" influence the earthly environment through the medium of the air.</meta>

# Treatise

The revolution of the wandering stars <note>original: "Erraticarum... stellaruz"; refers to the planets, which appear to move against the backdrop of the "fixed" stars.</note> and the fixed stars also causes heat, winds, and snows in the air surrounding us in many ways. Therefore, according to their composition, alterations happen to the things placed upon the earth.

And the courses of the wandering planets and fixed stars perform many and diverse works of heat and cold, of frozen winds and snows in the air that encompasses us: and because of that change, all things that are above the earth are changed by a similar mutation.

Ptolemy taught us that all celestial things are generally of one substance, and that the sun and moon perform many universal and particular works in the things that are among us. For this reason, he found that each of the planets and fixed stars have universal and particular works, just as the sun and moon do. And since they are generally of one substance, it follows that every genus has species which act with their substance, some universal work being their power. And it follows that all other species of that genus have similar power, and that they perform such works as has been said in philosophy. And since this is so, it clearly follows that the other planets and stars have a power with which they act in the things that are among us. Similarly, just as the sun and moon act as they do because of their motion and because of the power of the figures <note>original: "figuras"; in astrology, these are the "aspects" or geometric relationships between celestial bodies.</note> in which they place themselves, so it follows in the other planets and stars: that because of their motions and the figures in which they place themselves, they also perform works in the things that are among us. Now, regarding what he called "wandering planets": he said this because they have retrogradation <note>The apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky.</note>, direction, height and depth, and fast and slow courses; and these are the five we have named: namely Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury. And the "fixed stars" are those which he well said are all the other stars that are in the sky; and they are called fixed because they are positioned in one way, namely one distant from another, and similarly by their distance from the zodiac, because they all always move as one. Similarly it follows that, just as the sun has its orbit through a spherical space of another manner than the moon, so each planet and star has its own and diverse works, one from another. And just as the sun and moon act in things because of the change they cause in the air, so all the other stars perform what they do because of the change they cause in the air; and because of them and the air, there occur among us heat and cold, winds, frost, snows, and many other principles for the nature of any body.

And according to their figures toward each other, which they receive from their conjunction and the mixing of their strengths, various mutations of things occur.

The participation also of the planets and stars in figures—namely, one toward another—causes many and diverse changes when the powers descending from them are joined and mixed, one with another.

Since each of the stars has its own power with which they perform their works, we have the change which they make in the air, especially when they are joined in every figure that their powers desire, and their <term>complexions</term> <note>original: "complexiones"; the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a thing's nature.</note> are mixed, one with another. And from this mixture, another complexion is made from those which each had for itself. And because of this, it follows that they perform other works, greater and more diverse than each could perform by itself; and thus there are many and diverse works according to how many and diverse these mixtures are. Now, regarding what Ptolemy said in this place: he said that what all the stars do, they do because of the change they make in the air: all heat, cold, humidity, and dryness. And this is the end of the proposition which he holds in the works of the stars. Ptolemy now wants to explain what follows for all things which he said in this proof, and afterward he will show this inductively.

Besides the fact that the efficacy of the sun always proceeds orderly in the variations of things, it has prevalence over the others. The others, however, sometimes help it and sometimes hinder it: which happens more evidently and frequently in the moon, as in conjunction and <term>dichotomy</term> <note>original: "dicothomitate"; the phase where the moon is half-illuminated (first or last quarter).</note> and the full moon. In the other stars, however, it happens in a circuit of more time, not without indication of their <term>occultation</term> <note>The period when a planet or star is hidden from view because it is too close to the sun.</note>, namely that which is in the hours of their hiding and appearance, and their declination toward any latitude.

And since the power of the sun is victorious and dominant in all things existing by order: yet other planets help somewhat <column-break/> and somewhat not: which can be understood. And this is manifest in the moon and appears more and more often: as in the conjunction of the sun and moon, and when she is diminished and when she is full. Regarding the other planets and stars, however, this happens more over a long time and is shown more hiddenly: as in the time when they appear and when they hide or when they decline toward some part.

What he said—that the sun is victorious and dominant in things existing by order—is in this: that it appears in the four parts of the year, and the four parts of the day, and in all things that appear from the works of the sun. And what he said—that the other planets and stars help the sun in that which they perform in things that are by order, either by helping or diminishing its every work—and everything else he said through this place, he said to show the works of the stars and the mixtures that occur through the conjunctions of their powers, one with another. Similarly, he teaches us through these words: that all movements and temporal states in the things that are among us happen because of all the powers of the stars and because of their mixtures; and this we see in the times: that each day has diverse manners. For sometimes the time which is proper to the sun increases, and sometimes it decreases.

And since it is to be understood thus, that the other planets and stars sometimes help the proper power of the sun, they are similar to it sometimes by essence and sometimes by accident. By essence: because some planet or star may be of such a nature that it performs a work like that which the sun does. By accident: because it may be in a place where its power has a greater strength. And some of them are helpers of the sun's work and some are diminishers of its power. Similarly by essence or by accident. By essence: since its nature may be contrary to the sun's own nature: so that it holds back the work of the sun; such is Saturn. By accident: because it may be in some place that can diminish all the power of the sun. For this appears in the moon more and more often than in any of the others: which is much around its transit, we see, since they join with the sun, and when it is halved and when it is full. Regarding the other planets and stars, however, this does not appear so, nor so often: because this does not happen except when they appear or when they hide, or when they decline to some part of the north or south, or west or east. And what Ptolemy showed through these words as a demonstration of the work of the planets: through these same he shows us the way by which we can know what complexion each planet has by itself and each star by experience and observation. And when we wish to experience what the stars of any of them do by themselves: we will experience this through the things of the sun and moon: since we already know for certain what complexion these two are: since it is a thing that appears visibly. And when we know one thing about them, we will be able to know about the others. This is done by inspecting when it looks upon itself or is joined, if its power increases or diminishes, studying in this not for a little but for a long time. And when we have inspected for this space of time, we will find it is true: we will be certain of that which we have found: and we will have the way to find that which follows afterward. Namely, if we have found the power of some planet that increases the heat which the sun makes, and that it diminishes the humidity which the moon makes: then we will see that the planet or star itself diminishes the cold and increases the dryness: and we will experience this many times in it: we will be certain that the planet or star itself performs heat and dryness. For through this way the philosophers found the truth of all mixture and medicine in comparison to the natural heat of man. Now, however, Ptolemy shows the explanation directly to those wishing to know this science: so that if they wish to take the rule in these words, as they were placed in them by the ancient wise men, they can take them. And if they wish to experience this for themselves, they can do so through this way. And since this is the demonstration, there could not be a firmer way by which this science is known.

Since, therefore, the work of the stars is thus: it is necessary that what they perform by their works should appear not only in manifest things, but also in the beginning of the birth of seeds and fruits, so that their forms and modes are designated according to the qualities of the air in that very hour.

And it is necessary, since this appears from the works of these things in this way, that they do not only perform these things through their movements in things that we see and feel: but they also perform these in all living things and those giving seed and fruit. In such a way that they are generated and formed according to the state of the air encompassing them, of whatever manner it may be at that time.

Already Ptolemy has shown us a general word: that what the stars perform, they perform in all things that are among us, because of the change which they first make in the air: because by the power coming from them into the air, they perform it thus on the earth, in the waters, the vapors, minerals, vegetables, and animals.

# Book One

A 3

->The Quadripartitum of Ptolemy<-

In animals: now, however, because of this, Haly <note>original: "B"; the commentator Haly ibn Ridwan is often abbreviated as 'B' or 'H' in these editions.</note> wants to make his truth known to us, or rather to have us understand the matter in another way, more specifically and more particularly. For he wishes to show us the power of any beginning <note>original: "principii"; refers to the 'beginning' or 'inception' of a life or an event, essentially the moment used for a horoscope.</note>. For the beginning receives a certain complexion <note>The 'complexion' is the unique physical and temperamental makeup of a person or thing, determined by the mixture of qualities like heat and moisture.</note> from the mixture that occurs in the air due to the change and power of the stars. It is according to this that things are generated and formed, and the whole substance that is made at that time receives such a power and proportion. And it is manifest that the powers of the soul and the operations of the body always follow the complexion of the body, as Aristotle showed first, and later Ptolemy. And this same thing happens in all other beginnings of all things that have a beginning. It is also manifest that the power which a thing receives at its beginning will remain with it as long as it lasts. Hence, since this is so, we understand the works of the stars to be in two ways: one is what the beginning of a thing performs, and the other is what they perform after the beginning. That which a thing receives at its beginning remains with it as long as it lasts. But that which happens to it after the beginning does not last except for a time, and is afterwards destroyed. Through these words, Ptolemy proves the certainty of nativities <note>A 'nativity' is a birth chart or the moment of birth used to predict a person's life.</note> and of every beginning.

¶ From this it is that farmers and keepers of livestock have become experienced in many things: in the hour of the mating of animals, and of the sowing of seeds, they perceive what the future will be through the blowing of the winds.

¶ And according to this, laborers and shepherds—who observe these things more than others—understand the hour in which the male is joined with the female, and the hour in which the seed is sown, and what will happen in that generation through the winds running at that very hour.

¶ Ptolemy did not remain content with merely demonstrating this to us through arguments. Instead, he wanted to affirm and certify it through examples that the common people know, so that we might more certainly know and understand the great power that the beginnings of things possess. For laborers and shepherds observe these things most, such as Antonius <note>Likely referring to a classical author on agriculture, though the name may be a corruption in the transcription.</note> who made a book on agriculture, and a very good, wonderful, and very complete treatise. And similarly, the ancient sages made other books on this reasoning such as this one is. They understand, by the winds running at the hour when the male joins with the female, and when they plant or sow, what will happen to this generation. He does not speak of the winds running by chance, but speaks of them because of the change that happens in the air due to the power of the stars; for winds exist only because of the vapors made in the air and because of the movements of the air, and these two things are not made except by the powers of the stars which are mixed in the air.

¶ Similarly we also know that universal things, which are declared through the configurations of the sun and moon and also the stars, are plain and open. For those experienced in this art frequently recognize their prognostications through experiments.

¶ And generally we see that those universal things which we understand from the participation of the sun, moon, and stars manifest themselves greatly in their configurations; they appear visibly so that those who know nothing of the science can know and understand them through the primary prognostications, simply by looking at things and through the experience that others have had.

¶ He says that the roots of this science are so manifest that the common people, knowing nothing of the science, know and understand them by looking at them and experiencing them. It is clear from this, therefore, how much more the wise ought to know, who study to know natural things, such as philosophers and physicians.

¶ And those effects of the stars which happen with the greatest forces, and which are accustomed to happen naturally from them; indeed, they are even predicted by certain animals. For we see that even the most simple animals signal the variations of the seasons of the year and the changes of the winds which are called 'animal' winds <note>original: "aulia" or "aiales"; likely a corruption of "Etesian" winds, the predictable Mediterranean summer winds.</note>.

¶ And the operations that come from a greater force and run in a perpetual order are known by common people before they happen. And I say more: that many animals understand these things; for many animals show the change of the seasons of the year and the diversity of the winds which are called 'animal' winds.

¶ Now he has told us that any of the common people, whoever they may be, can know the reasons of this art and science a little bit by looking into them. Much more, therefore, do the wise know, who know the natures of things. For the works of the stars are so much stronger when running in perpetual order, such as the wind and the sun. The common people can understand them well. How much more those who wish to experiment and look into things a little. And not only do these humans understand it, but also many animals and 

<column-break/>

those that move themselves from one place to another and move at any certain time and place, such as cranes. Similarly, animals that breed at a known time, such as turtledoves. And animals that prepare their food at one time for another, such as bees and ants. All this teaches us that many animals understand and know the changes of the seasons which the sun makes. We see also that the unlearned commoners and many animals understand the diversity of the course of the winds which are called 'animal' winds; for these winds always run in the summer from the north during the middle of the day, and it is sometimes running faster and sometimes less according to the participation the stars have with the sun. Many mute animals understand this. And in this way there are other winds that are proper for each time of year, because each of them runs because of the force of the sun’s course; and the increase and decrease of each of them does not happen except because of the participation of other stars with the sun. Hence, none understand this except those who know the powers of the stars having participation in the configuration with the sun.

¶ Since the occasion of these signs is most frequently the sun, we do not doubt it. But those things which happen with lesser forces are not predicted except by those who have frequently experimented, such as sailors who know the individual changes of the winter air and the wind of a longer time.

¶ The reason why the sun overcomes this earth is because of its power; for other operations coming through another lesser power, those can understand the prognostications who have applied their minds to them and have been experienced many times, such as sailors who know the particular movements happening in the winter air, and the winds running through a course from a long time ago.

¶ Ptolemy glosses for us by these words the statement he said before, saying that the reason why the unlearned people and mute animals understand the great changes happening in order is the great force of the sun prevailing in the mixture that is made through the conjunction of the powers of the stars. And because of this, the changes that happen through another power lesser than those of the sun cannot be understood except by those who have looked there many times and have been experienced for a long time, such as sailors who know through the course of the stars what will happen in the winter air regarding its increase or decrease. And similarly what will happen in the winds coming from a long time ago. This you can know from sailors traveling upon the sea, and especially from those who have their life in the Indian sea.

¶ Moreover, it is manifest that this happens through the moon and the configurations of the stars with the sun.

¶ And how this happens to them is because of the participation which the moon and stars have with the sun in configuration.

¶ That all the things which sailors know through long experience—namely, what particular changes will happen in the air—all happen because of the participation of the moon and the fixed stars with the sun in any configuration. And this word or sentence follows those words spoken before. We say that laborers and shepherds do similarly.

¶ But because they were ignorant of the places of the stars and the hours of the aforesaid things, and the motions of those wandering stars which very much help the knowledge of the aforementioned things, they have been deceived many times in this science.

¶ And because these people do not have a great power of intellect to know the places of the stars, and the times of things which we said should be certified, nor are they completely experienced—neither through the sense of the course, nor through those wandering stars <note>original: "erratecos"; the planets.</note> which is the thing that gives the greatest help in knowing future things—it happens to them that they are many times mistaken in knowing these things.

¶ He wants to say that laborers, shepherds, sailors, and all others for whom it is expedient to experience things, as he said: because they do not know the course of the sun and moon and other planets and fixed stars, neither concerning their configuration nor other ways, nor have they been experienced in this many times as they ought, nor do they know the powers and works of the wandering planets, nor their course (which in operating has a much greater effect than the fixed stars), it happens that they err many times in the prognostications which they ought to know through the stars. And if they had known this completely, they would be able to know the particular things that ought to happen in the matters they need to know.

¶ Since this is so, he who has had knowledge of the configurations of all the stars and the motions of the sun and moon, so that he easily recognizes the places and hours in which their configurations are formed, and has also learned their natures through the experiments of many times and does not forget them: indeed, their substance...

It argues that the moment of a thing's beginning (its birth or inception) imprints a lasting character upon it through the influence of the stars on the air.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Haly ibn Ridwan’s commentary on Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos. The previous discussion established that just as sailors and farmers use celestial signs to predict the weather, a learned scientist can use the stars to understand more complex natural phenomena. Here, the text argues that even if the internal essence of a star is unknown, its observable effects—like heat from the sun—provide a reliable basis for a predictive science.</meta>

# Treatise

...does not know their natures but has recognized the effects they work: such as the sun heating, the moon moistening; and it is similar in others. And if one is strong in this knowledge by natural means, and in the good mixture of signification, he will grasp the mode by a good estimation.

¶ And after this is so, what thing will prohibit him who knows the motion of all the stars, and the sun, and the moon, so that nothing prevents him from knowing the times and places in which their configurations <note>original: "figuras"; refers to the geometric relationships or aspects between planets.</note> happen? And he knows the nature of each of them from the mixture of the ancient sages, which has been tested many times over long periods. One after another, even if he does not know the underlying nature, he may nevertheless know the texture of the moon with what it works; thus a man knows that the sun's habit is heat, and the moon's habit has softness. In this way, he may know the virtues of the other stars and have the power of knowing these things according to nature; and he has knowledge through good sense, possessing the properties of things that are made through the mixture of all this: for he shows the things that are likely to happen at any time.

¶ Things that have been experienced and made by proof, and which others have experienced, proven, and rectified: it happens that we shall extract experience and rectification. And for those things others have not experienced for themselves, it happens that we say they knew them through the teaching of others. And because a man’s life is limited in a way that it is not sufficient to prove all things by himself, it was necessary for him to know those things which others before him proved by the demonstration of those who experienced them. This is so that the fruit and profit of it does not delay. And because a man’s science is to know things that are future through the works of the stars, it is sufficient for a man to know the virtue of each of their works, and the works that are made by the mixture of their configurations. To know the underlying cause <note>original: "causam subiectam"</note> is not the task of the astrologer, but of the physicist <note>term: physicist - in this context, a natural philosopher who studies the physical causes of natural phenomena.</note> wanting to know about nature. Ptolemy did not speak about that in terms of having the power of knowing these things according to nature. He wants to say that he who has knowledge, through himself or others, according to the natural virtues by which the stars perform their works—which virtues are the four qualities that occur in the air containing us (namely heat, cold, moisture, and dryness)—can know all other things that belong to this science. And yet you will understand later when we gloss the words he says: "After it is so." And when he said that he will be able to know through good sense the properties of things made through the mixture of all this, he wants to say that the man who can know through the complexions <note>term: complexion - the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in an individual.</note> the virtues of the stars, knows through the mixture of complexions the virtue that can come from others; because their virtues are mixed through their configurations; and he who knows this well, there is nothing that could disturb them from knowing those things which the stars are likely to work at any time.

¶ For what indeed can prohibit him, when he always recognizes the future changes of the air: as when he predicts it will now be hotter, now moister. He will also be able to grasp through the qualities of the air the qualities of the nature of all men, so that he knows their body and the qualities of the soul will happen thus and so, and he grasps their future accidents <note>term: accidents - non-essential events or changes that happen to a person throughout their life.</note> at certain hours. Who also, when the surrounding air of their bodies behaves thus and so, will have a prognosis for their health, being more suitable for their better action. And when there is a defect, he will judge the defect.

¶ For confirming the proper changes of the air: and for saying whether it will be hotter or colder. And he will be able to know the proper complexion of any person from the state of the air containing us. And through this he will know the state of the body and its spirits; and he will know the accidents that will happen to them at some times. And when the air that contains us is of one manner, and the complexion of the body is of another, it will be tempered and will help the health of the body to strengthen it. And if it is of another manner, it will not be suitable for the man, nor tempered.

¶ He wants to say that an astrologer is a man who sees the virtues of the configurations that are made by the motion of the stars, and all else that is said of it; and he has the power of knowing and admiring the particular changes that are likely to happen in the air. Further, he gives an example: because he says this truly, in the future the air will be moister or drier than it usually is. And he says the same for any day, that on such a day the air will be hotter or colder than what is common for that same time: and through this he will be able...

<column-break/>

...to know the state of any person, of what complexion they were, and what their character will be, and what knowledge they will produce. Because when he knows the virtue of the complexion that will be made in the air through the conjunction of the virtues of the stars at the hour the body is formed and fixed, the virtue of the air in that man can know those things which will happen to that body in health or infirmity; and that which will happen to the virtues of the spirits of that body and its motions through its sciences; because all these things follow the complexion of the body, as natural philosophers and physicians have experienced through right demonstration. Likewise, he can know what will happen to any man at any time: because when he knows the complexion of a particular man, and knows the things that are likely to happen in the air, and what humor will abound <note>original: "vñabit" (venerabit); likely referring to the movement or predominance of bodily humors.</note> in the brain of this man at such a time, he will know that the character of this man at that time is such as is the character of a melancholic man. It is appropriate for you to look well into the words of Ptolemy which he spoke in this place. He says these things well among the stars; by this voice you shall do so in all the words he says, in such a way that you understand something for yourself.

¶ From the aforesaid things, therefore, and those similar to them, it is manifest that we can arrive at this work.

¶ Through these things indeed that we have said, and other such things, we can know that this science is a matter attainable in the manner that we can reach it.

¶ He spoke a very good word when he says that we can reach it; because by the way we know other sciences which are extracted from nature, like medicine; through this same way we can reach this science: and this is the way he taught us. This word he said is a response to some saying that this science cannot be reached through nature nor through rectification, nor by experiencing things, but only through dreams, or through visions, or prophecies. And Ptolemy answers and says through these words: It may well be true what you say, that through prophecies or visions this science can be reached; nevertheless, we can reach it through the way of nature, and of rectification, and of experiencing things. And I say that if you wish to understand well this way which Ptolemy spoke of, look in the book of Haly <note>Referring to the commentator Haly ibn Ridwan’s own writings on scientific method.</note> which he made concerning opinions; and understand well what he said concerning the opinions of the sect and of experience. For he says, as far as Ptolemy spoke in this science, that it can be reached by proposing words that agree with this reason.

¶ Those who said this science is to be blamed and postponed, though they had some frivolous excuses...

¶ For those who cast out this science, saying that it cannot be reached, give reasons, but they are not correct.

¶ After Ptolemy showed that this science can be reached and taught us the way by which we can reach it, he wants to destroy the sayings of those who say there is no matter that can be reached in a way where no reason remains that could contradict this science.

¶ The first of these is the great deception of those who do not attend to this science as an authority; since to inspect it is a great industry in many ways. Therefore, many have opined that it happens by chance when this science is true.

¶ And we know this by these reasons which we shall say. The first reason why they erred in this is that they did not look into this science, nor did many study it as they ought; because it is very great and of many ways; and because of this, some believed that the things which astrologers certify in this art happen by chance and fortune.

¶ He says that the first reason why some believed this art could not be reached is: because some astrologers do not look into it or study it as they should; and they pass over things that are in this art which they should not do, because it is a great art of diverse and many ways. Wherefore it happens in knowing it that one must have great labor and study. And because it happens to some not studying in it as they should to err with many errors: those who see them err thus believe that the things which they certify sometimes happen by fortune, and not by the right science or the root of this art.

¶ This occasion of theirs is inconvenient: because this deception does not happen by the nobility of this art, but by the temerity of those inspecting it.

¶ For this which they estimate is not true. And the error by which some err in this science is not from the weakness of the art, but of him who introduces himself into it.

It defends the art against critics by claiming that errors in prediction arise from the practitioner’s lack of study rather than a flaw in the science itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of astrology against its critics. In the previous section, the author argued that celestial influences are observable and natural. Here, he addresses why the field is often ridiculed, blaming the "laziness and negligence" of fraudulent practitioners rather than the science itself.</meta>

# Treatise

### First Book

Ptolemy dismantles the reasoning of those [critics] with a sound argument, stating: that the error which happens to some astrologers does not stem from a deficiency in the art itself, but rather from the laziness and negligence of those who dabble in it. And since this is so, it is manifest that the things certified by this art do not happen by chance, but through deep roots and certain, firm rules, just as he showed before.

The second reason is this: there are very many who, in order to turn a large profit, take the predictions belonging to other disciplines and falsely attribute them to this science. Many are deceived by them and driven to this opinion [that the science is false]; for these people predict many things by the power of this science in a way that exceeds the limits of its nature in their conjectures.

Another reason is that many, seeking gain, offer prognostications from other sources while claiming to know them through this science. They lead the people into sophistry and error, making them believe they know many miraculous things about the future. They even go so far as to speak of matters that are not of a nature that can be known.

This is why many believe this science is unattainable. We find not just villages but entire cities full of men who feign knowledge of the art of astronomy, though they are far removed from it. They cast the people into sophistry and error, making them believe they know many miraculous things about the future. They are so bold as to speak of things that are beyond the nature of human intellect to grasp. I wish to give you an example of one such person whom I encountered. A man came to us who considered himself a great philosopher. He spoke great arguments to us: "I marvel at you who estimate that the 'Heart of the Lion' <note>The star Regulus in the constellation Leo.</note> arrives at the 15th degree of Leo, yet no fire exits from the lion to burn the whole world." When I heard him, I laughed at him. Others standing there said: "He arrived from where he held himself," and I do not give weight to such words. And what of it when he began to speak of the horoscopes <note>original: "nativitatibus"</note> of those who write chronicles? He claimed that Mercury was in degrees that are "pits" <term>Putei: specific degrees in the zodiac considered "dark" or debilitating to a planet's power.</term>. He argued this demonstrated that there would be some damage to the intellect. This is the greatest ignorance for several reasons. First, the degrees of the pits are the weakest things possible. Second, he brings his science and those who practice it into ill repute. Third, even if what he said were true, Mercury could lose that misfortune through the aspect of other planets. I would like to know where he learned this or how he could have experience of it without those who came before him. 

Indeed, this whole speech shows it is a mere fantasy, as we know from his other claims. Perhaps he found Mercury in the degree of the "pits" in his own horoscope or someone else's. We know that Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note>, before he studied astronomy, was one who wrote chronicles. We find such things in the writings; thus he believed all others who wrote chronicles had the same disposition as himself. How could it be true that chroniclers must have a defect of intellect? We have found many of them to be of good sense and intellect, and from them we have received certain doctrines of things past. I once met a man with some knowledge of astronomy who told me he heard someone claiming to know a thing no one in this world could know. This man asked: "How can anyone know that when Mars enters the second house of someone’s horoscope, their personal garments will be stolen, and no other clothes or money?" I told him this is something a man cannot know specifically through this art. He later told me his associates pretend to know such things with great lies. Because of such people, some have believed this science cannot be grasped and have therefore rejected it. 

You will understand that many have rejected the science for this reason when you read the fables in books written by such people—fables that are profane, meaning false—written to show themselves off as wise. They have hindered us with many words and disturbed us from knowing the truth. I say that when I find a path heavily obstructed by many, I excuse myself from it and do not wish to be drawn into it. I strongly advise you to maintain your resolve: do not labor over their books or involve yourself with them. Instead, apply your mind and study solely to the way of Ptolemy, for it is the straight and certain path, a matter certified by the proof of arguments and truthful experience, in which there is no doubt.

Therefore, their work became the occasion for many to despise not only what cannot be known through the science, but even that which is knowable.

Because of this, they devised a way to claim they understood the matters of this science—which are found in nature—without having to study them. They spoke of them so dismissively, considering the matters themselves vain and assuming all things are vain.

I say that the actions of those we mentioned were performed by students who might have known something outside of this science. This greatly affects those who have no desire for study, as they imagine that everything said in this art consists entirely of fantasies, just as those people claimed. I have seen some students who could have known something, yet were affected by this. I saw those who studied the books of "thousands," "hundreds," and "eights" <note>Likely referring to numerological systems or specific astronomical cycles.</note>. They believed whatever Albumasar and his like said there was certain and true. They wanted to test it against past events, but found no certainty. I said: "It is a great wonder that you neglect to inspect the motions of the stars and great arguments, yet you wish to know future things simply through the count of years. If this were the true art of astronomy, then the things we can know through the stars concerning the future would be nothing." I believe for certain that such things as these are rules of the art that some have devised to lead others into error and to gain praise for themselves for a thing that is not the truth. For these are all things that those who hear them desire—like fables of things that never were—and they believe them to be something great. Regarding the sophists who seek arguments that appear to be so: he who examines them with uprightness and truth finds them all to be lies. People believe everything said about this art is of the same nature. And if those who spoke of such new things did not devise them but believed them to be true, their ignorance is even greater; they compiled books of the same and filled parchments with lies, realizing how they wasted their time on lies and vanities.

This is the second cause, as inconvenient as the first. Philosophy should not be held in contempt because of the stupidity and laziness of fools.

Therefore, it is not right to cast out philosophy or abandon it because of the malice of certain individuals who pretend to know it.

He says that it is not right or fitting for a man to assume everything said in this science is of one kind [i.e., all fraudulent]. For in this science, he who examines it properly as he ought will find no defect; rather, the defect lies in those who feign knowledge of it. They include things that are not part of it, nor belong to it. Philosophy should not be depreciated nor cast aside because of the malice of those who pretend to it. Similarly, this science should not be depreciated or rejected for the same reason.

It is also clear that even good and diligent researchers of science are sometimes deceived—not because of the aforementioned reasons, but because of the nature of the subject and their own frailty, as they are unable to grasp the full essence of this science.

It is manifest that even a man who studies the divine sciences with great will, correctly and with all his might, will fall into error in many things. This is not due to the reasons we stated [fraud], but because of the nature of the subject he studies—which is vast in itself—and much because of the weakness of the human intellect, which cannot grasp all that is in that science because it is so incredibly grand.

After he stated the reasons why many believed this science could not be attained and dismantled those opinions, he showed that the defects found in this science do not belong to the science itself, but arise from the weakness of those who involve themselves in it. He had already told us before this that in this science, error can occur because of the material receiving the power of the stars, which is neither firm nor stable. And because it is very difficult to know the composition formed by the conjunction of the stars' powers, he now wishes to dismantle this final point: to show us that this error is not due to a defect in the nature of the science, but because the subject matter is exceptionally vast.

***
