<meta>This page continues the discussion on why astrology is difficult to master. The previous page explained that errors in the field often stem from the practitioner's negligence or fraudulent behavior rather than a flaw in the science itself. Here, the author shifts focus to the inherent complexity of the subject matter and the limitations of the human mind.</meta>

# Treatise

<column-break/>

...true in itself. Yet the human intellect does not possess such great power that it can always understand very complex things, even if the thing itself is profoundly true. This is the case with the **sciences of the <term>Quadrivium</term>** <note>The Quadrivium was the medieval "four-way" curriculum consisting of Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astrology/Astronomy.</note>. Although these are prior to all other arts and rely on the firmest demonstrations—because no falsehood can exist within them—nevertheless, many can err in them. This is not due to a defect in the science, but because of the great weight of the subject and the weakness of the human intellect. Since this occurs in arithmetic, geometry, music, and the astrology of the Quadrivium, it is no wonder if the same happens in the astrology of judgments <note>This refers to "judicial astrology," the practice of making specific predictions or "judgments" about human affairs.</note>. This is especially true because its matter is not firm or stable, and because of the difficulty of understanding the complex <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "complexio"; the specific mixture of influences.</note> that results from the mixing of the stars. Therefore, when errors occur in this science, they are not due to its own deficiency, but to the frailty of the human mind, which cannot reach a full comprehension of all these very weighty matters.

It also happens generally that we do not arrive at a truly certain knowledge regarding any quality of this material, but rather an "opinion-based" one. This is especially true for that which is gathered from many and dissimilar things.

And I say generally that the state of this world cannot be directed in a way that reaches a very certain path without any doubt, except through the sharpness of the intellect of those few who can consider things more acutely than others—especially in these things which are composed of many and diverse elements.

Ptolemy teaches us in his book on the manners of the art that all we can know about the states of superior matter <note>Celestial bodies.</note> is not directed by this art to be known except through a sharpness of intellect in one person more than another, and through a subtle consideration of high things. For this matter does not always persist in one state, nor is it firm. **Abraham [ibn Ezra]** <note>original: "Abra"; referring to the famous 12th-century scholar and astrologer.</note> taught us the same in his physics when he said that "time is sharp." He meant to say: this matter does not stay in one state for a long time, but changes quickly from one hour to another. Now, Ptolemy did not say this regarding things composed of many and diverse elements; he meant to say that knowledge is received through the conjunction of many and diverse powers. Thus, it is very difficult to understand the certain temperament created by such things, just as Abraham said that "judgment is heavy." He meant that every known thing is argued unless it is approved by experience; it is not so firm that one should rely on it entirely while working through it.

In Ptolemy’s words, however, there are two words we must <gloss>explain</gloss>: **to consider** and **to think**. Among certain logicians, there are three manners of this. One is certain in itself because the thing cannot be otherwise. Or concerning this: because it cannot be known for certain, but one **thinks** that it is so. Another is regarding a thing that is very far from truth and certainty. The third manner is between these two. Therefore, I say that "to think," as Ptolemy said here, refers to that which is close to the truth that cannot be otherwise, because its certainty is demonstrated by a prior true demonstration.

Of **considerations**, however, there is another type close to truth. This is every thing that has a rule to guard it from error, like a figure a man makes using a **compass and a ruler**. For the compass and ruler make a figure certain by consideration, even if it is not by mathematical demonstration. Another is that which is very far from the truth, which is a thing happening by chance or luck during what a man is considering. And another is between these two. When we return to what we said before: you will find that finding knowledge through "consideration" is that which is close to the truth, for it is a thing joined to science on the part of certain demonstration. Since this is so, that science is guarded from error. If you look closely at what we have said, you will find that through this manner of "thinking" and "considering," the operation of all sciences—and especially physics—is performed.

It also happens because the configurations of the **wandering stars** <note>The planets.</note> formed in ancient times are those by which we consider the configurations of our own times that resemble them, and we judge their effects. We judge that which the ancient authors—men who were observers of things—grasped through the configurations of their own times, because our configurations are perhaps very or somewhat similar to theirs through their long cycles. But that these configurations should perfectly resemble them—so that everything in the heavens and everything on earth returns exactly to what they were then—is in no way possible. No one can say this unless they are a fool, mockingly professing to know perfectly that which no one has ever been able to know perfectly, or who claims to have reached a point which no mortal life is long enough to reach.

<column-break/>

And it similarly happens in that which is possible: that the partitions which the planets have through configurations in works that were experimented upon in ancient times are very far off. We judge according to what the ancient sages said, who were experienced and found it to be so. These resemble the configurations of our time, some more and some less, through the long revolutions of the courses of the planets that have occurred from then until this time. However, to find a complete similarity between what the ancient sages experienced in the configurations and works of those times and the works of this time—in which there is no diversity or change, so that everything in heaven along with everything on earth is returned to its very first state—is a thing that cannot be. No one can boast of reaching it, nor know a thing from among those which cannot be completely reached, nor from those which his life cannot attain, for the life of man is limited.

After he made us understand that the things we have reached in this art were reached by a "consideration" that is close to demonstration—and that it does not fail to show what it is, except because matter is not stable—he now wishes to explain further to those wanting to learn this art. He wants to ensure no argument remains, saying: the things we judge in this time through the operation of the stars upon the matter found now, we have from the rectifications of the ancients and from no other source. And because it happens that there will be such a constellation and such matter that resembles those from the time of the ancient sages—some more and some less—this comes through the revolutions of the stars occurring over long periods of time. Yet, to find such matter and such a constellation that is exactly the same as that which the ancient sages certified—so that it is neither more nor less—is a thing that cannot be. A man cannot reach it in his whole life, for his life is mortal, nor because of any other teaching. And through the errors that fall into teachings and long periods of time, it does not happen that a man can praise himself for perpetual truth in such a matter, unless he is one who wants to show the people that he understands nothing of wisdom.

Since this is so, it is not very surprising if some error falls into the attempt to equate things in heaven and earth at this time with things from the time of the ancient sages, given the long spans of time from then until now. With these words, he destroyed the opinions of some who say that all things return to the "head of known times" <note>This refers to the concept of the "Great Year" or *Annus Magnus*, where all planets return to the same starting position.</note> with the same conditions they had another time, neither more nor less, but exactly the same. They fell into this error through the long courses and many revolutions of the stars, because they thought there was a common number of the years and days of the world with which the locations of the planets and stars could be certified. They believed that when that number is completed, all the stars will have returned to the very same point, and through this, all things will return to being exactly as they were. Indeed, many have fallen into this error at some point, including many astrologers like **Albumasar** <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer.</note> and many others. But you will understand, if you know anything of arithmetic, that there is a great error here. I myself have studied to seek out that common number—to calculate with a known number with which I could set tables to find known days—and I was not able to find it.

For these reasons, we are sometimes deceived in the hours of prognosticating judgments, because the examples through which we learn do not perfectly resemble those by which we judge.

And because of this reasoning, error sometimes happens in other things which ought to be in its favor: because those things for which the ancient sages gave us an example cannot return to those same exact states without some diversity, be it a little or a lot.

I say that these words are open and do not need a <gloss>commentary</gloss>.

For when we scrutinize the <term>accidents</term> of the air <note>Meteorological phenomena or weather patterns.</note> in the air, they are difficult for us to find for this reason: because the discovery of the causes that exist in the air is difficult; even if we grasp the causes through celestial things.

Therefore, the reason why it is difficult to understand and inquire into the accidents that happen in the air is this: because such an appearance does not happen to occur with the same constellation as it did another time.

<meta>This page continues the argument that astrology is a complex science subject to many variables. While the previous page focused on the limitations of the human mind, this page addresses physical variables—specifically the "matter" of the world, such as air, genetics (seeds), and environment—that can alter how the influence of the stars is received on Earth.</meta>

# First

¶ Here Ptolemy teaches us that matter is neither stable nor firm; rather, he teaches us how we ought to demonstrate how it always presents itself in diverse ways. I begin, therefore, by speaking of what happens in the air, because that is where the generation of things occurs. Many things happen in the air because the works of the **superior bodies** <note>The "superior bodies" refer to the planets and stars.</note> are not received in every place in the same way. In some places, there will be mountains where winds are strong due to their height, and therefore that air cannot hold much heat. In other places, there may be vapors rising from the moisture of a city, or even the stench of dead bodies. Indeed, these are the things that corrupt the balance of the air and affect what reaches us. It is fitting, therefore, for the **astrologer** <note>original: "astrologo"</note> to inspect the state of the air before he offers a judgment.

¶ When we speak regarding the births of men, we perceive many significant and non-frivolous factors based on the collection of forces, which by themselves compel things to vary.

¶ In the home and in births, which occur according to the <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexio"; refers to the specific balance of humors and qualities in a person.</note> of virtues in any given thing, we find in them many reasons—no less than others—by which their properties are changed.

¶ He says that in births, similarly, many things happen that disturb them, so that they do not easily receive the works of the stars as they were meant to receive them.

¶ For the qualities of changes greatly assist the **seed** <note>original: "semini"; refers to the biological material of generation.</note>. For though any region and the air of that same region may be of one and the same mode, each difference of seeds possesses the power to form an image suitable to its own species—such as the seed of a man, a horse, or other beasts.

¶ This means that the matter of the seed provides great help in the properties of generation, because the air surrounds the area that determines the **horizon** <note>The horizon at the moment of birth was considered crucial in determining the "Ascendant" or rising sign.</note>. If both are of one state, any kind of seed will form a general shape suitable to its species, such as the seed of a man, a horse, and all other animals.

¶ He means to say that all things that exist by their **essence** <note>original: "essentia"</note> prevail in all things, because that which exists by essence cannot be transformed or changed from its nature. For example: the purpose that is in the seed by essence is only to make a form belonging to the species from which it comes. From the seed of a man, no form can be made except that of a man; from that of a horse, no form can be made except that of a horse; and so on for other animals, and similarly for the seeds of vegetables. Each of these follows the nature of its whole species. However, the **accidents** <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential traits, like hair color or height, as opposed to "essence" (being human).</note> that happen to the seed of any body of that species do not belong to the seed by essence. Instead, they happen and are formed along with it by the power of the stars in that town and horizon where it was, and according to the state of the air and that place.

¶ Likewise, the places of birth overturn things with great change.

¶ And the places of generation change the things that are generated in them with no small mutation.

¶ He means to say that in the places where generation occurs—such as the lands of the **blacks** <note>original: "nigrorum"; a reference to sub-Saharan Africa or "Ethiopia" in medieval geography.</note>—all who are born in them will gradually return to that generation, namely to the color of the land of the blacks, even if they were born of white parents. And if a very black man is born in a very cold land where men are white, he will gradually return to that other generation; and the same happens in their children. Once this is manifest, it is clear that heat is gradually removed from the seed, and nothing remains in it except what it has by essence and nature, which is the power of generation alone. It is necessary for us to look at the generation from which one is born, and the seed from which one descends, and the place in which one was born; and afterward, we will be able to judge. This is explained more fully in what follows.

¶ For when the seeds are of one species, such as the seed of men, and the qualities of the air are the same, those being born will still obtain many and great different qualities in body and soul according to the differences of the regions in which they are born.

¶ And when the types of that seed are of one mode, such as the seed of a man, and the state of the air

<column-break/>

surrounding them is of the same kind, great diversities will happen to those born in their bodies and seeds according to the diversity of the regions in which they are born.

¶ For example: he who is born in the East will be different in body and spirit from him who is born in the West, even if the **constellation** <note>original: "constellatio"</note> of both births is the same. This is because of the "accidents" pertaining to each region that are formed along with the seed. You will find this same thing in all other natural things.

¶ Different customs and their individual alterations will also assist you in predicting the future.

¶ Furthermore, the food and customs which they use, since they are diverse, assist on their part.

¶ You will see this visibly in the customs of men and in the foods they use. Among those who use **choleric** foods, **choler** <note>Refers to the "yellow bile" humor, associated with fire, heat, and a quick temper.</note> is produced, and they take on those customs and complexions, like those of choleric men. In those who use foods that produce **melancholy** <note>original: "meliaz"; referring to the "black bile" humor, associated with earth, coldness, and sadness.</note>, their complexions and customs are drawn toward the melancholic. The same happens in other complexions. Therefore, customs are contingent; for those who dwell and have their life with good people, even if they are bad by nature, are drawn toward their goodness; and the contrary is also true. You will find the entire reason for this openly in the books of the ancient wise men.

¶ But since all things do not always harmonize with the conditions in the air—although the power of the air is great in the existence of these things—it is a great cause of failure if those who prophesy solely through the movements of the superior bodies do not take these other things into account. Those who investigate only through the stars seek that which they cannot perfectly know, and they are sometimes deceived.

¶ And if these things do not harmonize with the conditions coming through the surrounding air—because the power of the air is very great, and although the air gives great force and much help so that things are as they are—if these things are not considered, doubt and error will happen to whoever wishes to judge by the mode of the **superior bodies** alone. Such a man would be trying to know things that cannot be completely known by themselves.

¶ Ptolemy says here: if a man does not consider the works of the stars that occur in the air, working with the conditions of the lineage, region, species, food, and customs, error will happen to him when he wishes to judge. And because of this, he spoke of the "surrounding air," because he said before that the conjunction of the virtues of the stars and their works are in the air. Since this is so, it is manifest that when we wish to be certain through this science, we should join the works of the stars with the things capable of being generated. We should look closely at each of them so that we do not say of a black man who is the son of a black man that he is white, just because the constellation of his birth demonstrates that he "ought" to be white. Rather, we should say that he is *less black* than he otherwise would be. Nor should we say that he who lives with thieves is a man of peace because his birth demonstrates it; rather, we should say that he will be *less evil* than the other thieves, until he leaves their society, at which point he will return to his nature. We must do the same in all other general and particular things: in the laws and customs of nations.

¶ Therefore, since this is so, the fact that we are sometimes deceived in this science does not mean the whole science should be despised or destroyed. Just as the skill of **sailors**, who frequently err while navigating, is neither despised nor rejected by us, but rather we ought to remain more attentive and diligent in it.

¶ Since these things are of this nature, it is not fitting for us to destroy this whole art because of some error that occasionally falls there. Just as we ought not to destroy the mastery of mariners in ships...

Ptolemy argues that the stars provide a general influence, but environmental "accidents" determine the specific outcome, using the example that a constellation might make a person "whiter" or "better," but only relative to their birth environment and companions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of astrology, moving from the limitations of the practitioner to the nature of the science itself. It introduces the "benefits" of the art—prediction of famine, plague, and war—and compares the astrologer’s method to that of a physician.</meta>

**Treatise**

...to be directed because of the errors that happen there, and because they happen frequently.
¶ After Ptolemy demonstrated what this art is, destroyed the opinions of those speaking against him, and taught us the places we ought to look when we wish to guard ourselves well from error, he said in this place that we ought not to destroy this entire art on account of some small error that happens there occasionally. He placed a great distinction between this art and the **mastery of mariners** <note>original: "magisterio marinaroꝝ"; referring to navigation and seamanship.</note>; for when we look into this art, errors happen only a few times, whereas in the mastery of ships, they happen many times. And since this is so, it is fitting that we follow and love this art of judgments more than others because of the great profit that lies within it, and the modest error that occurs when we have looked well into it.
¶ For it promises us arduous and inestimable things, and we should not doubt that which is possible to attend to from it.
¶ But it is proper that we seek and hold these things as truly noble, for in them are many good and miraculous benefits.
¶ These benefits that Ptolemy mentions are: such as protection from the harms of enemies, from **corrupt air** <note>original: "aere cozrupto"; a reference to "miasma" or pestilence believed to be carried by the air.</note>, and from the **scarcity of provisions** <note>original: "caristia victualiū"; i.e., famine.</note>, since we know these things before they happen.
¶ It is not fitting to seek all things through this art, but only by investigating what can be investigated. We also say it is necessary that we grasp their manners, nor should we interpose anything that is not suitable.
¶ And let us pursue those things which are written through this art. It is not appropriate to wish to know all things through this art similarly, except those that can be reached by man; and it also befits us to wish for that which pertains to its scope, and that we do not apply to it that which is not of it.
¶ The **gloss** <note>original: "glosa"; a marginal or interlinear commentary.</note> on what is said here is not needed.
¶ For just as we do not find fault with **physicians** <note>original: "medicos"; the text draws a parallel between medical diagnosis and astrological prediction.</note> when they seek the occasions of illnesses and the qualities of the sick, so it should not be troublesome for us to investigate the matters and regions, the types of food, and all the accidents that have passed.
¶ And just as we do not disparage **physicians** <note>original: "phicos" (physicos); here meaning medical doctors or natural philosophers.</note> when they inquire by what reason an illness came to the sick person and the state pertaining to him, similarly it is not fitting for us to refuse this art when we ask about generation, region, food, and all other accidents that occur.
¶ Physicians help themselves much in that which it befits them to know by inquiring about the life the sick person has led, the place he is from, and all other things said in **medicine** <note>original: "physica"; in this context, it refers to the study of the physical body and medicine.</note>; and yet no one disparages them—rather, one praises him who inquires into this most effectively. And since it is so in medicine, which concerns present things, it is all the more so in this art, which is for foreknowing those things which are to come. It is therefore not to be wondered at if one inquires about generation and the other things Ptolemy mentioned.

### To demonstrate the utility of this work. Chapter 3.

<note>Decorative rectangular woodcut initial "Q" depicting a bird in a landscape.</note>
In what manner the prognostications of the stars are grasped: and how only those accidents which surround the globe of the earth and which occur to men by their occasion become known; and how these accidents of men pertain to the body and its strengths, as well as to works which are operated from the first years to the last; and what those things are which happen externally, which naturally and inevitably adhere to the aforementioned, by a certain connection of love which is between the body and the substance, as well as its partner; and the connection that exists between the soul and its progeny, and dominion, as much as will happen from them in other goods: this has been generally proven.
¶ We have generally demonstrated in what manner we are able

<column-break/>

to reach the prognostications of the stars. The sum of the whole that we can know of it are the accidents that occur in the body that surrounds us. And the accidents that occur to men happen for this reason alone. These accidents that occur to men are those that pertain to the spirit, the body, the habits, and works from the beginning, and that which follows after the works of that thing which was operating in him and in other times: and the things that happen outside them which have a natural and necessary participation with the aforementioned things, such as the participation between the body and that which it earns, and its partner. And the participation between the spirit, lineage, and dominion, and the things which the same man can have according to the times.

# Quicquid
Everything in this saying is from all those things he taught us before. But we wish to explain each one by itself so that you may better understand what he said: in what manner we might better reach prognostication through the stars. He means to say that he has already taught us how we might know future things through **astronomy** <note>original: "astronomiaz"; at this time, "astronomy" and "astrology" were often used interchangeably for the science of the stars.</note>. And that which he said: "The sum of the whole that we can know are the accidents that occur in the body that surrounds us," he means to say that the place from which they come are the accidents that happen in the air through the works of the stars. And the accidents he said happen to man for this reason alone, he means to say that the things that happen to men because of the power of the stars do not happen for any other reason except the works that the stars perform in the air surrounding us, and because of the mixing of the virtues of the stars that remain in the air. And this which he said—that these accidents which happen to men are those that pertain to the spirit and the body and the habits and works from the beginning—he means to say that the accidents that happen to men are only according to the **matter** <note>original: "māz" (materiam).</note> from which they are generated and the **complexion** <note>original: "cōplōnē"; the specific balance of the four humors in a person.</note> that is formed in them because of the mixture of the virtues of the stars that occurs in the air at the hour they are born. And that which he said regarding what follows the times of that thing which will operate in him and in the times, he means that which follows the body and spirit of a man because of the complexion he receives from the beginning; these complexions, after they happen, cannot operate in him otherwise except by adding to it or by moving things that happen outside them, which have a natural and necessary participation with the aforementioned things. He means things that follow the body and spirit from things that are outside them. And that which he said—the participation between the body and that which it earns and its partner—he means the food by which the body lives, and the wife and children, which are things by which the body helps itself. And the participation between the spirit, lineage, and dominion, he means that since the spirit is the generator of the body, the spirit desires that its form remain; and since this same form cannot remain, another similar one remains through generation. And the spirit loves dominion because it enters into man and he gains honor through all the things he needs. By this certainty you will understand the affection we have for children, because we all love them naturally, and because many have life and dominion by seeking it according to their power. And that which he said regarding what he can have according to the times, he means what a man can have from these things at one time and not another, such as a woman whom a man cannot have until he is of age. All these things Ptolemy has taught us generally, and from here on, all things particularly when he arrives at their specific places.
¶ Now, however, we will indicate the remainder of the promises, which is to briefly investigate the utility of this work.
¶ We wish to say briefly what remains of the reason we receive, to demonstrate the profit that lies in this art.
¶ He said briefly that if he wished to tell the whole profit that lies in this art, the account would be prolonged too much.
¶ But we have proposed first to explain the manner and intention of knowing the quantities of the fruits of this science.
¶ And we begin first to narrate the end of our purpose, from which we wish to know the virtue and profit of this art.

It explains that celestial influence works through the surrounding air to shape a person's physical and spiritual "complexion" at birth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the defense of the utility of astrology (referred to as "this art"). Having previously compared the astrologer to a physician or a pilot, the author now addresses how the science benefits the soul, the body, and even one's social standing, while refuting critics who claim that knowing the future is useless.</meta>

### Book One

He wishes to say that he will demonstrate the profitable purpose that a person can derive from this art.

We say, indeed, that if we wish to consider the extent of this utility as it pertains to the soul, we should conclude that there is nothing else from which the soul’s inclinations take such great improvement. In other words, we say there is nothing in which the soul gains as much as in this kind of **prognostication** <note>original: "prognosticatione"; the art of foretelling future events based on signs.</note>. For through it, we arrive at the knowledge of both divine and human matters.

We say, therefore, that if we look into the power of the profit that lies within it regarding the spirit, we find there is nothing that benefits the soul so much—nor does it so gladden <note>original: "erbillaret," likely a scribal error for "exhilararet."</note> or direct it—as knowing what is to come through this art. For through it, a person reaches toward human and even divine things.

When we have learned through this art the **character** <note>original: "mozes" for "mores"; referring to a person’s moral nature or habits.</note> that comes through the powers of the spirit—following the **complexion** <note>original: "complonē" for "complexionem"; in medieval science, the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person’s temperament.</note> of the body—we are able to direct or even amend them before any malice appears in them. This is done in the manner that the philosophers described in their works on Ethics. Likewise, if we understand through this art that good character traits are present, we will increase and strengthen them further. We can do this more easily in childhood than in later age, because when characters appear fully formed, it is then very difficult to change them. Furthermore, since we have learned through astronomy whether the spirit is more prepared or more distant from receiving certain things—such as the mastery of a science or laws—we will take care to apply the soul to that which it is most prepared to receive, and we will set aside that for which it is not prepared. In this way, we avoid the pain and labor of both body and spirit, for a person labors in vain on a thing for which the soul is not prepared. Such things we can achieve through this art alone, and not through any other. And since this is so, there is nothing by which we can better uplift and gladden our souls than through this art, nor is there any greater profit one can make for oneself. Since we learn better and more easily those things for which we are prepared if we apply ourselves to them: these are the "human things" he mentioned. The "divine things" he mentioned are the **living form** <note>original: "forma vā" for "forma viva."</note> which a person can possess who has been prepared for it; and this "living form" is to know God, as the ancient philosophers taught.

There is also a utility for the body, since we cannot arrive at those things which are suitable for each person's complexion except through the knowledge of this work.

And similarly, the perfection of the body, which we can know through this art: those things which are appropriate and beneficial to any given complexion.

The profit for the body is to preserve health and to alleviate infirmity from it. Since we will know through astronomy what complexion a body will have and what kinds of infirmities will happen to it in future times, we will know how to prepare that body to preserve its health and defend it from illness. Since this is so, there is nothing that benefits the body more than knowing through this art the things that are to come.

Regarding riches, dignities, and similar things, we can say the same as what we consider in all of philosophy. For it is not the nature of philosophy itself to lead anyone to the gain of the aforementioned things, yet it is not right for it to be blamed by men on that account. Similarly, this science should not be blamed for that reason, nor should its great utilities be set aside.

Regarding the honors and great riches given to an astrologer through this art, we should say what we say about philosophy: that through philosophy, philosophers do not intend to gain great riches and such things, yet it is not right for philosophy to be dishonored because of this. Similarly, we ought not to dishonor this art nor set aside the other great profits we can have from it.

He wishes to say that philosophy does not possess by its own nature the power to give riches, but through it, a person arrives at knowing the ways by which they can better earn. Similarly, this art does not by its own nature—through the knowledge of these things—always lead a person to great riches, but it teaches people to do things by which they greatly help themselves in earning honor and many profits. Therefore, it is not right to dishonor philosophy in this

<column-break/>

art because it does not provide great riches immediately, nor because a person might set aside the great honors and profits they can have for body and soul, as was said.

Similarly, the arguments of those who blame this science and say it is of no utility will be revealed as untruthful to those who pay attention. For their foolish deliberation led to this conclusion: that the prognostication of things that happen inevitably is superfluous and useless. These words of theirs are "dissolved" <note>meaning weak or logically unsound.</note>, lacking subtle insight and proper knowledge.

And generally, I say that you will easily understand that those who dishonor this art by saying there is no profit in knowing it do not hold to the truth. And others who said there is no profit in knowing things before they happen spoke empty words without discretion.

He wishes to say that those who said there is no profit in knowing the future have not looked well into their own words, but let loose words as they occurred to them, and they are not determined by proof.

For first, we should know that when things that happen by necessity occur to someone, they will perhaps not harm them at all unless they are feared; otherwise, they might take away one's sense and memory, or bring such great joy or sadness that the same result occurs.

For it is entirely fitting for us to know future things, because unless we knew them beforehand and prepared ourselves for them, we might find such a thing in that hour that it would cause us to lose our senses—whether a disaster comes upon us, or such great joy or sadness that it does the same.

This is seen visibly every day. We know people who found a treasure in a sudden hour without foreknowledge and lost their senses because of excessive joy, which they were never able to recover; they were ruined by this cause. And others, when a disaster came upon them suddenly, were so terrified that they lost their senses out of excessive fear. Yet he who can foreknow the future will not lose his senses but will remain firm in his memory. For a person has this profit regarding those things from which they cannot be liberated in any way—because of a **constellation** <note>original: "ostellatiōnē" for "constellatione"; the positioning of stars at a specific time.</note> demonstrating this very strongly. But if it should be otherwise—where some preparation might be of use—the profit is much greater.

Prognostication applies and draws the soul to frequent memories of things still far off, so that it holds them as if they were constant and present; it fits the soul plainly and sweetly for the reception of whatever future thing may come.

Prognostication changes the spirit by use, gradually bringing into the mind those things which are far off and preparing them for itself as if they were present, very gently and without sudden force.

When a person knows a future thing that cannot be avoided by any means, they bring it to mind often and temper themselves in it, so it does not come upon them impetuously, since they prepare themselves for it every day. Similarly, if someone foreknows that they will find or earn something at a certain time, they will think at leisure how to guard it or by what path they might have it sooner. Thus, if one looks well into such particulars, they will find it as Ptolemy said. And since such great profit lies in knowing things that are to come before they happen—by soothing the will and the senses in those things from which a person cannot be liberated, and even more so if they could be liberated by some preparation—then what they said about there being no profit in knowing prognostication is not true.

Furthermore, it should not be thought that the superior bodies [the stars] proceed toward their significations inevitably, like those things which happen by divine disposition, which are by no means to be avoided and which happen truly and by necessity.

And because of this, it is not fitting that we think that everything that happens to men through the celestial bodies is necessary—

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the utility of astrology, specifically focusing on the distinction between "divine" necessity and "natural" occurrences that can be mitigated through human preparation. # Treatise

...matters like divine things which man cannot remove <note>original: "vt diuina que homo remouere nō pōt"</note>.
¶ And he said that by "celestial bodies" he means the mixtures that occur in the air surrounding us because of the patterns and courses of the stars. The difference between a divine matter and any other is this: a worldly thing cannot disturb that which comes from God, and from that, no one can be set free. But other matters are not like this. Ptolemy <note>original: "Ptolō."; referring to Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and author of the *Tetrabiblos*.</note> said we should not believe that all operations of the stars are always necessary or divine; yet there are some that are indeed such, and others that can be changed, and thus a person can be set free from them. Since this is the case, it is clear that when we know which things can be changed, we can protect ourselves through some preparation; and then the profit of this art will be great and manifold.
¶ Indeed, we should know that the powers of the heavens are of divine disposition, which cannot be prevented from truly coming to pass. And likewise, the variation of terrestrial things proceeds by a natural path, which varies according to the first occasions of the beginnings of things, and they receive these variations accidentally. Some accidents occur to men through a general harm, not from the specific property of any one thing, such as in a great change of the air. We can hardly protect ourselves from this, and it results in the death of many people, whether it happens through an excess of the air, or a plague <note>original: "mortalitate"</note>, or drowning. These things happen because a great and strong occasion always overcomes a brief and weak occasion. Furthermore, some accidents are natural and occur according to the proper **complexion** <note>original: "cōplexiōis"; the specific balance of humors in an individual.</note> of each person, due to some change of contrary mutations.
¶ Indeed, it has come to our knowledge that the movement of the celestial bodies is a divine matter, which no worldly thing can disturb in any way, because it is necessary and cannot be otherwise. However, the changes of terrestrial things are natural and changeable, receiving their specific properties from the celestial bodies in the manner of an accident following them. One part of the accidents happening to men comes through general and universal plagues, and does not happen from the specific nature which each thing has in itself. This occurs when the air is corrupted by a corruption so great that men can hardly protect themselves from many of them dying, either because of great heat, or because of the air's putrefaction, or because of evil winds that cause many to perish at sea; for a greater and stronger thing always overcomes a weaker and smaller one. Other accidents are those occurring from the natural and proper complexion of anyone, due to some change among contrary influences.
¶ All of this is an **aphorism** <note>original: "afoᵐ"; a concise statement of a principle, likely from Ptolemy's *Centiloquium*.</note>... its **gloss** <note>original: "glosa"; a commentary or explanation of a text.</note> is in this manner: The movements of the stars and the virtues that result from their movements are necessary things. They are of God's making, which nothing can disturb, nor is there any thing that can be changed or overturned in any way. Nevertheless, the way terrestrial things receive the works of those virtues is a natural and changeable matter. For terrestrial things are subject to change and receive the operations of the celestial bodies in the manner of an accident and a following state; just as a divine thing receives the works of perfection more readily, or as a transparent object receives light through its potential to be transparent, which then becomes transparent in act. These words demonstrate a great power. Ptolemy, in knowing divine and natural things, shows that all his words clearly demonstrate great wisdom and his ability in speaking on all parts of philosophy. And regarding what he said—that some accidents happen to men through general and universal plagues and not from the specific nature each thing has—he means that every natural thing receives the proper virtue of the stars in all its changes. And when a more general and greater virtue happens through the stars than that which pertains to any particular thing, that greater general virtue destroys the particular accidents. And one has the power to change all these things; thus it happens in times when the air surrounding us changes with such a mutation that one can hardly protect oneself from it, because there will be excessive heat, or cold, or it is corrupted by putrefaction, which in many places

<column-break/>

causes mortality. Or it happens in great battles <note>original: "ꝑlys" likely for "proeliis"</note> where many people die, or when great floods of water occur in which many perish. And Ptolemy, in such matters, gives the reason for all this: it is because a greater thing conquers a smaller one, and a stronger thing conquers a weaker one. And he said that the accidents pertaining to each thing—according to how they receive the natural goods generated by the celestial bodies—are also changed by these general events. Since this is so, it is manifest that all terrestrial things do not receive the operations of the stars of necessity, in a way that they cannot be changed. Among them, however, are those that can be changed, and in such cases, knowing the **prognostications** <note>original: "ꝓnosticatiōes"; forecasts of future events.</note> is a very great benefit.
¶ Since these things are so, it is proven in both general and individual matters that those accidents whose first cause is stronger and greater than all their own specific causes will happen of necessity. It should also be known that those which are not so—when they receive a cause of equal strength—will be easily changed. Those which do not encounter such a cause will follow their first natures.
¶ And since these things are as we have said before, we understand well that in all things, both universal and particular, to which accidents happen: if the specific thing is stronger and greater than the external properties, then without doubt it is necessary that the greater entirely overcomes the smaller. But those which are not so, but are equal in their weakness, can easily be changed with some preparation. And if a contrary accident does not come, the specific nature will follow.
¶ He wishes to say that the works which the stars perform in terrestrial things—both universal and particular—are of one kind in this: that those which had a stronger beginning will entirely come to pass. The profit that a person has in knowing this prognostication is that it soothes the will, lest the thing itself happen to him violently. Those which have properties of equal virtue can be changed easily, and one of them can be diverted by some preparation. And if preparation is not made in this, the accident will happen just as the first principle demonstrated.
¶ That laziness and foolishness do not happen by necessary forces.
¶ This, however, will be through great ignorance and lack of necessity.
¶ He wishes to say that the works of the stars which have a great lead in virtue do not pass to us except by our own necessity, because we do not make the preparation for deviating those things which are not necessary to happen. In these matters, knowing the prognostications is a great benefit, because we will be able to deviate an evil in a way that it will not come. For example: when we know that the power of Mars will cause someone an illness of **yellow bile** <note>original: "chola"; one of the four humors, associated with heat and fire.</note> in the head in one month's time, we can oppose this by purging the bile and tempering his complexion with cold and moist things. When we have done this, we can free him from this sickness. Likewise, if it does happen, it will be very little in respect to what it would have been if we had not done so.
¶ The same is seen to happen in all things whose beginnings are natural, as in the natures of certain stones and plants, as well as in wounds and **abscesses** <note>original: "apostematū"</note> and illnesses, which necessarily perform some operation; some of them are such that they perform it unless they are contradicted by some contrary thing.
¶ we see this same thing happen in all other things having natural principles; for it is from the nature of certain stones and plants, animals, wounds, and illnesses to perform a certain thing of necessity so that it cannot be otherwise. And some of them perform this unless the things have their own specific counter-operations.
¶ He says that what he has stated is not only in the works of the stars, but also in the works of other natural things, because none of them has in its work a specific thing that can disturb it. Just as with a great fire when it falls on dry grass, or a very strong poison, or great and deep wounds from which a man cannot be freed, or from the strong onset of a great illness, or from very dangerous and strong illnesses. For among these are some from which a man cannot be freed by any preparation he makes. And there are some that have a specific means by which a man can be set free and that accident can be disturbed. Ptolemy, however, added...

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 6 regarding the practical application of astrology. # First Book

...the works of the stars and the works of terrestrial things, so that he may make us understand better that both are natural things <term>res naturales: the physical realities of the world governed by natural laws</term> that can be changed; though some of them can in no way be disturbed, it is advantageous that they exist entirely as they are. And there are those things that have a contrary, which can oppose them.

¶ Similarly, it is appropriate for everyone constant in this science to consider the accidents <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to events or conditions that happen to a person that are not part of their essential nature.</note> that happen to men, and to prognosticate naturally within them; so that they do not cling to false opinions. For some things cannot be avoided because the occasions from which they proceed are many and great; yet there are other alterations contrary to these that they may receive. This is just like physicians to whom the infirmities of men become known; they predict which of them are curable and which are not at all.

¶ It is also fitting that those who wish to know about this science understand the accidents that happen to men in this way, and that they judge with foresight according to nature, not looking toward empty opinions in their judgments. For there are some things from which a man cannot guard himself in any way, because the causes from which they come are very strong and great; but there are others of a kind that can receive change, according to what physicians <term>physici: used here to mean doctors of medicine or natural philosophers</term> ought to understand about infirmities: which of them are mortal and unable to have a remedy, and which can have a remedy because of medicine.

¶ Regarding what was said about judging according to nature: he means that when a man has judged and judges thus in those things which can be changed through the way natural things change; he does not speak of a thing that must entirely be and cannot remain otherwise, unless it is among those things that come through great, many, and strong causes. For of such things it is judged that they will happen in every way. And as for what he said about them being of a kind that can receive change: he means they are those from which we can be liberated by some "custody" <note>original: "custodia"; meaning protection, care, or preventative measures</note> because they come from a weak cause. In such cases we ought to say: "This will happen unless protection is applied there." As for what he said about how physicians proceed to know about infirmities—which are mortal and which can be delivered through medicine—he means that it is fitting for an astrologer to know which works of the stars are necessary from which no one can be liberated, and to judge that on one hand; and on the other hand, to know those from which one can be liberated. Just as good physicians do, who, when they see an infirmity that cannot be cured, do not involve themselves with it because they do not wish to labor over a useless matter; but when they understand it can be delivered, they apply their mind there and cure it.

¶ In those matters also where alteration can exist, we ought to pay attention to the methods of judgment, which I shall subjoin. When in anyone’s nativity <note>A birth chart used to predict a person's life and health.</note> the astrologer says that since such will be his temperament <term>complexio: the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, bile, black bile) in an individual</term> and such will be the change of the air—and because the tempered constitution will have been altered according to increase or decrease—such an infirmity will follow. Just as a physician will say that this infirmity or these ulcers will increase and become putrid. And similarly, if someone knowing the natural power of "magdania" <note>likely a corruption of "magnesia" or "magnetis"</note> says that a magnet attracts iron: each of these will necessarily happen and proceed by the power of its own nature if the "servant" <note>likely referring to the practitioner or patient</note> is not prepared due to the artist's laziness. And the ulcers will not increase or rot when medicine encounters them. Likewise, the magnet stone will [not] attract iron if it is smeared with other things <note>A common medieval belief was that garlic or goat's blood could negate a magnet's power.</note>.

¶ Furthermore, in those things which can be changed, it is fitting that he judge in this manner which is said: for example, when someone has judged another's nativity, he should say if the temperament is of this kind and the specific air will be changed in this manner, provided that the tempered constitution is changed toward bad or less, such an infirmity will happen as the beneficial person says. This infirmity will grow more or this wound will have to putrefy; or as he who knows about minerals says that a loadstone <note>original: "adamas"; while often meaning diamond, in medieval scientific texts it frequently referred to the loadstone or magnet.</note>

<column-break/>

will draw iron if it is placed near it. And whichever of these things is omitted through ignorance, because no contrary thing is worked within it to defend it, that thing will happen in every way and follow its primary nature. But if "custody" is applied there with a contrary, the wound will not increase nor putrefy, nor will the loadstone attract iron if it is smeared with garlic <note>original: "allio"</note>.

¶ He means that it is fitting for the astrologer to foreknow things through the works of the stars that can receive change: which are clearly causes that can have a contrary by which they are disturbed. And let him who has to judge apply "custody" there and temper them with his counsel, just as physicians do; for if they did not apply medicine, the wound could putrefy and the man die from it. The other thing he said in the commentary <note>original: "glosa"</note> needs no explanation.

¶ These things which are predicted are not prevented except by those things which are naturally contrary to them, and according to what has already been indicated. And in those things it will happen that when accidents occur to men, they will be ignored; or when they are known, if no wisdom opposes them, the first order of nature necessarily follows. But if they are foreknown and someone is found who knows how to heal them, either the things previously indicated will not happen at all by the natural way, or if they do happen, they will happen only in a small way.

¶ These same things we have mentioned we can avoid: so that they do not come to such states by opposing them through nature and through interrupted judgment. Thus will those things be if a man remains ignorant of the accidents that happen to people; as if they are known and he does not prepare any of the things which happen in those ways, the ordination of the primary nature follows in all ways. But when some things are known to happen and someone appears who knows how to give a remedy, they will not happen; or if they happen, it will be a small thing.

¶ Regarding what he said, "these same things which we have mentioned which are defended by these things": he means the kinds of medicine by which the works of natural things are changed through the contrary that is in them. In the same way, they are from the works of the celestial bodies, which can have a remedy; because just as terrestrial works always follow their course unless they are resisted in some work, so the works of the celestial bodies follow their own nature unless they are known through some work or medicine. Thus they will be healed or destroyed in total and will not be, or if they are, it will be a very small thing.

¶ For in general things and in individual things the power is the same. It is a wonder why it is conceded by men that a prognostication of general things can be had and that they can be guarded against. For there are many who [predict] the prognostications of the seasons of the year and of the fixed stars, the clouds, and the patterns that precede them; many people are occupied with these, and also guard themselves from the things that are to come through them. They reserve things that are cold in the summer, and in the winter things that are warm. Similarly, regarding their temperaments: they strive to draw in tempered constitutions. Also, when they wish to guard themselves from misfortunes and accidents that happen at sea, they pay attention to the clouds of the fixed stars. In the conception of beasts and the planting of plants, they observe the phases of the moon which are formed according to the portion of its light. And what shall we do? We have seen no one who ever denied this or said it could neither be useful nor exist. But some there are who judge that in the prognostications of individuals in their own temperament, no one can arrive at a conclusion—as in the increase or decrease of heat or cold, and similarly in the specific temperament of any thing. They even think there are many things from which no one can guard himself. But if it is clear that when we naturally chill our bodies before the arrival of general heat, less heat burdens us, we can do the same in individual things that increase heat, so that the causes are converted away from intemperance.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page, further developing the analogy between the physician and the astrologer. # Treatise

**Column 1**

AND since this power <term>virtus: the natural influence or "virtue" exerted by celestial bodies</term> is one and the same in both universal and particular things, it is a wonder by what reasoning it happens that men do not know those things which are to come in particular matters; nor do they provide the preparation and protection which is expedient against them. For almost all common people, as is generally known, recognize the truth that they can foreknow the seasons, the clusters of the fixed stars, and the phases of the moon; they look much into these things to protect themselves from what might happen. They prepare cold things in the summer and hot things in the winter, and they study to bring about a temperate balance <term>complexio: the combination of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a person’s health or the "temperament" of a season</term> for the time. Furthermore, they look to the clusters of the fixed stars when they wish to protect themselves from things that happen at sea. Similarly regarding beasts: they are careful when they give the male to the female; and in planting trees, they look to these phases of the moon, whether it is full, or waning, or waxing. Nor have we ever seen anyone who would choose otherwise, or say that this is a lie, or that it cannot be, or that it does not bring great profit. There are, however, some who say regarding particular things that a man cannot know what will happen there, even though they follow their own senses regarding the temperament of things—such as when there will be more or less cold, and similarly heat—and say that a man will not be able to guard himself from particular events. But since it is manifest that what is to come must happen, we shall cool our bodies so that we will not have such great heat when it comes; <term>B</term> <note>original: "B" — likely a reference mark or abbreviation for a specific proposition</note> the same we can well do for particulars: and we can well increase the heat so that it will be greater by this same reasoning.

¶ All these are the words of <unclear>Solomon</unclear>: <note>original: "So. m⁹" — possibly referring to Solomon or a specific commentator; "m⁹" is a common abbreviation for "mus" or "mon."</note> he means to say that since the power is one and the same in universals <term>universales: general categories or global events like the seasons</term> and particulars <term>particularia: specific, individual events or circumstances</term>, just as he taught us before in the works of the stars which receive change. One should not wonder by what reason all men happen to be so ignorant that a man cannot know those things which are to come before they exist in universal things, such as the seasons; and those things which shepherds, laborers, and sailors know, and the other things he mentioned; and he will see that in knowing these things before they happen lies great profit, because of the protection that is applied there. And similarly it happens in particulars: if protection is applied there, which indeed is easier to do in particulars, a man can do more. This, indeed, is the reason for this whole saying. For the truth, though it is somewhat obscure, I wish to explain it better to you. And when he said they study to provide a temperament for the seasons, he means to say that he makes things by which all times of the year are tempered for the preservation of health; and you shall find the power of this through the books of physics <note>original: "physice" — in the medieval sense, this refers to natural philosophy or medicine.</note> which speak of the governance of the healthy. And that which he said regarding the breeding of beasts—namely, giving the male to the female—and in planting trees while looking at the phases of the moon: he means to say that which the wise laborers and shepherds do, the certainty of which you shall know from books of agriculture. And concerning the clouds, and that which he said regarding the temperament of things by adding heat or cold: he means to say concerning the mixtures that are made because of the conjunction and position of the stars, which increase in the power of the sun or diminish it. And that which he said, that similarly we could add to the heat by this same reasoning, he means to say that just as we can diminish the heat by the things we do, so we can increase it by the things we have done, and the same in the cold.

¶ Since, however, the occasion of this deception is the difficult prognosis of individual things, and because very few have it in use.
¶ Since, however, the gravity of this error lies in the difficulty of knowing particulars before they happen, because men use this very little.
¶ He says that the reason why they are otherwise unknown, so that a man cannot know particulars before they exist, is because of the difficulty of knowing the prognostications of particulars, and because men do not use these as much as they use universals.
¶ So much so that it is almost the occasion that other things are in no way believed. For things having the powers of contrariety are not easily found without the things through which the powers are prognosticated; and therefore

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

in the greater part they are not found perfectly.
¶ So that because of this error men believe nothing concerning particulars: because that which has in itself the force of contrariety cannot generally be found as the signs of any prognosis are known. Whence this would be a thing that cannot be found completely.
¶ He teaches us by this saying what the reason for the difficulty of particular prognostications is: because the mixture which is made of contrary things cannot be understood easily because of the weightiness that is in it; and because of this, it is a burden for a man to know them completely.

¶ Wherefore, since the primary natures are by themselves without hindrance and are victorious, they thought that they would do whatever is inevitable, and in such a way that it cannot be prohibited.
¶ And because those higher natures are superior and do not receive disturbance in their motion, they believed that all things happen in the world of things which cannot be changed, nor can a man protect himself from them.
¶ And because the stars are much higher than the whole world, and their powers are so strong that they overcome all other powers and have no disturbance of their motion: many believed that their works similarly were turned and could not be changed, nor can a man protect himself from them in the manner they occur, nor by their motions. Nor would this belief be empty if the matter receiving the work did not receive works from many other things. But since it must receive from many things, by right it will not receive the works of the stars if there should be anything in them contrary which is equal to the works of the stars.
¶ And as it seems to me, they thought the same in the prognosis itself. But although it might happen that in the greater part the prognosis might fail, it would still be appropriate that we investigate it subtly, because some utility lies within it; just as in the science which stands for the preservation of health, although it is not the occasion of health for all men, since it is nevertheless for some, although it may be small, it is still to be desired and loved: and in this we ought to think there will be great profit.
¶ Even so that which they believed concerning prognostications: for although the majority err in them, that little bit which is found true in them ought by right to be loved and sought out; because it is a discovery of things for the protection of health. And if this which we do cannot protect all men, nor is it a protection for the whole people, it is nevertheless for the health of some of them; and though this be small, it is nevertheless fitting that we more truly seek it out and procure to know it, and hold it as a very good and noble thing.

¶ He says similarly, I hold it fitting that since those considering these matters in the prognostications of astronomy err much: yet that little bit of certainty which is in them, it greatly behooves us to love and to procure in the manner in which we do in protecting health. And although in that which we do the protection for the whole people is not hidden: because nevertheless from that small amount some are to be protected, it is fitting that we hold it as a very noble and good thing. If it is done well, even if it be little: for because of this saying, <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>original: "Ptolo." — Claudius Ptolemy, the most influential astronomer/astrologer of antiquity.</note> teaches us that it is fitting for us to follow this art greatly, although its certainty be small. Not because he has already proved and demonstrated to us that if we apply our minds well to it, whatever we find in it will be truthful and certain—unless perhaps sometimes, from one slow time to another, because of some error.
¶ It is also clear that the Egyptians demonstrated the powers of this work all the more because in all their books of healing, they joined the science of the stars with prognostications; because they knew this would be the case, nor would they at the same hour join those things together to make incantations and medicines to delete present or future impediments, whether general or particular, happening through the surrounding body <note>original: "per corpus circundans" — likely referring to the air or environment affecting the physical body.</note>, unless they had the opinion that they could be prevented, changed, or turned.

# First

They assimilate <note>original: "Assimilant"</note>. For the sages of Egypt, who truly taught this art, placed natural science <term>physica: in this context, the study of the physical body and medicine</term> alongside astrological predictions in all their books, because they knew these matters were of this nature. And they would not have joined the arts of power <note>the "virtues" or influences of the stars</note> with this medical practice, providing a defense against pestilences coming openly from the celestial body—whether present or future, whether general or specific—unless they saw that through that act, things would not be destroyed nor would they succumb to the pestilences themselves.

¶ Thus it taught us that the universal or particular works of the stars can be changed through preparation; and in affirming this, it takes testimony from those ancients who taught this art, and these are the ancient sages of Egypt. For they, as we hear, taught men all sciences and harvests; and Ptolemy affirms this, and the same Ptolemy teaches us by those things he did when he placed natural science alongside astrological predictions. Because they knew these things were of this manner, he means to say that they knew the works of the stars could be changed: they placed the work of natural science with the works of astronomy, so that natural science might remove the harm that came through the stars. When, however, he said "unless they held that through that knowledge things would not be destroyed," he means to say that the sages of Egypt set out to free earthly works from celestial works through mixtures and incantations, and things possessing powers <note>talismanic properties</note>, which they placed around the neck and upon objects.

¶ Wherefore, that which belongs to this nature and those things that follow it—namely, having the power to contradict in the second order—they placed in power and possibility.

¶ And because of this, they placed things having a nature contrary to this in the second grade of the power of incisive judgment.

¶ He means to say that the sages of Egypt placed the works of the stars in the first grade of power, and those things by which we counteract them they placed in the second grade.

¶ And they joined the strengths of the utility of that work with the strengths of prediction in the books which are called the *Showers of Medicine* <note>original: "ostensores medicine"</note>; specifically, so that they might understand the qualities of existing complexions <term>complexio: the specific balance of humors—blood, phlegm, bile—in an individual</term> through the stars, as well as the accidents <note>unforeseen events or symptoms</note> that are to occur through the surrounding body <note>the "circumambient" atmosphere or heavens</note>. This was so they might also be strong in the knowledge of these things, and in the doctrine of curing curable things for the most part; for it is impossible that all bodies should be of the same quality of imbalance <note>intemperie</note> in their infirmity. Thus, through medicine and through things suitable or unsuitable to each individual body, they might exist more strongly in the guarding against future infirmities; and also so that they might heal those things which have already occurred with a remedy in which there is neither imperfection nor any deception; and so that from this, they might reach the highest perfection to which anyone might attain.

¶ And the ancients placed the profitable power of this art in one grade with the power of predictions, which they named in their books on natural science: so that they might know through the stars the states of the complexions of the seasons and the infirmities destined to happen in the works of the celestial body, and what will happen to those same infirmities. Because from these things they would know the mixtures which they had to make—for the most part—since all bodies could not be in all infirmities of that state or of one temperament. And so that they might know natural science well, they commanded that each person be guarded with the guard suitable to each body and infirmity; so that they would not incur those infirmities destined to come by such medicine in which there would be no error or defect, and from that cure—

<column-break/>

—they might reach a fitting end.

¶ He means to say regarding all this that the sages of Egypt recognized that this art held very close to natural science; they included one part of it in their books of natural science, so that they might know through astronomy the complexions that are specific to each person, and those things that happen in the air by which bodies are changed, and what kind of accidents come from those same mutations. And when he said, "because they know these things and the mixtures that happen for the most part," and the other thing he said, he means to say that when they saw that bodies and infirmities are of many and diverse kinds, and they looked into this art for knowing the accidents that happen in the air, they gained this art for knowing the accidents that happen in the air <note>The OCR repeats this phrase; it refers to environmental influences on health</note> for each accident. Through these two arts, they had a great power of governing and guarding the health of bodies and for medicating whatever infirmities might happen, in a way that error would not occur there, nor defect in their work. This saying indeed teaches us the perfection and great goodness of the ancient sages of Egypt, who were of great sense; and I well believe that Hippocrates and Galen and all the Greek physicians held this way, for we find in their books that they command us to apply our minds to such things.

¶ This, therefore, in speaking generally, was to be set forth first.

¶ These things are what were fitting for us to put forward generally.

¶ He means to say that whatever he has said from the beginning until here is a matter which it behooves a man to understand and look into, so that he may know they are general sayings; and because of this, they will better understand the particulars of this art.

¶ Consequently, having given these things, we will now proceed in an introductory manner.

¶ And then we wish to set down the things we shall say in an introductory way.

¶ He means to say that those things which he will teach us in this book from here onward are rules and roots of this art, such that when we understand them well, we will be able to proceed through whatever part of this art we wish. And this whole book will be introductory, by which we understand all the reasons of this art.

¶ And we will first manifest their works, by which the alterations of celestial things properly happen.

### Beginning to speak of the works that cause changes specifically to celestial things.

¶ He means to say that he will begin to state the rules and roots pertaining to each of the celestial bodies—that is, to each one separately by itself—and that all parts of this art are composed of these simple things.

¶ And we shall execute this by the experiments of the ancients arranged in natural order; and from these, we shall first treat the works of the wandering stars <term>erraticarū stellarum: the planets</term> and the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note>, God willing.

¶ And we shall follow those same ancient sages who are arranged in a natural order, speaking first of the works of the two luminaries and the wandering stars.

¶ He says that whatever he wishes to say in this book is according to the proof and rectification of the ancient sages; and thus they were experienced in how it is fitting to set aside by nature only those things which do not suit nature.

¶ For he first begins with the two luminaries and the five wandering planets, because he finds them to be of greater work in earthly things than all other celestial bodies; because their own motions are so diverse by nature and of many changes—just as earthly things are—and of great question; and because through these we can reach the knowledge of the powers of other celestial bodies. For here ends the reasoning which he stated in the 15th chapter.

¶ And it is fitting that you hold all past reasons present in your memory, when you read each of the things he said before; and thus you will be able to understand whatever he wishes to say, in what manner he says it, and you will understand this if you do so. Here, however, we wish to complete this treatise of the gloss, and we shall begin the second treatise of the gloss of the fourth chapter of the first part by Ptolemy, because up to here it was all of one reasoning, but from here on it speaks of another reasoning.
