# The second treatise of Haly's gloss on the first treatise of Ptolemy's book.

->Haly said:<-

In the first treatise, we provided a gloss <note>a "gloss" is a scholarly commentary or explanation of a text</note> on those things which are suitable to be proposed regarding the specifics of this art. In this next part, we shall provide a gloss on the sayings of Ptolemy regarding each planet individually. We shall prove that his opinion in this matter is greater than all others. You should know that we have never found another gloss on this book. I believe, however, that the ancient sages would not have left it without a gloss, but it has never reached us nor our land. It is fitting, therefore, that you give thanks to God that he has deigned to open to us the words of this good man, which were so enclosed. Nevertheless, if you find any error in these words of ours, you ought to correct it yourself; do not impose the blame upon us, for there is no man who can avoid all errors.

---

## On the strengths of the luminaries and the wandering stars. Chapter 4.

This is the fourth chapter, in which he speaks of the power of the two luminaries <term>luminaria: the Sun and the Moon, the "lights" of the sky</term> and the wandering planets. In everything he speaks of in his books, Ptolemy holds to the path held by Aristotle in those works he produced. It is clearly apparent that Ptolemy was one of the "walkers" <note>original: "andatores"</note>, that is, those who go around, which is to say the Peripatetics <note>original: "peripatetici"; a school of philosophy founded by Aristotle, so named because he taught while walking about</note>. For they used to circle the schools, teaching their disciples as they went through the schools. These men taught the most manifest things first before those which were more hidden; and so they went on until they reached the most enclosed parts of that reasoning. Since Ptolemy was of that sect, he begins first with the two luminaries, because their works are more visible and manifest than the works of the others. Afterward, he spoke of the five wandering planets <note>the "wandering stars" or planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, because their works are more manifest than those of the other stars.

It is manifest that from the substance of the sun, its work is to heat slightly and to dry. This work is sensed more appropriately than other works; its knowledge is easier because of the great size of the sun and the manifest change of the seasons. For the more the sun approaches the point of our zenith <note>original: "zenith nostroum capitulū"; the point directly overhead</note>, the more it heats.

It is a known thing that the work of the substance of the sun is to heat and to provide a certain amount of dryness. And these works are felt more and are more easily known than all others because of the magnitude of the sun and because of the manifest change it makes through the seasons of the year. And the more it approaches above our heads, the more it heats.

Regarding what he said—"it is a known thing concerning the work of the sun's substance"—he means to say that it is manifest to all men in the world who have any sense that the sun's work is to heat greatly and to dry somewhat. For this is the substance of natural heat which is in the world, and this is the element of fire. You can know that the more it comes over our heads, the more it heats; and in heating, it dries somewhat, because it draws out moisture <note>original: "exuggat hūiditates"</note>, pulling it from the bodies of animals, as the physicians have said. It also draws sweet waters from the sea, as the natural philosophers <note>original: "phici nales"</note> have said. And Haly proved that all natural virtues, through such heat that is like this composition of the sun, perform all their works. When he said, however, "these works are more felt and more easily known," he means that the senses perceive the works of the sun more than those of other stars. A person understands that if the senses perceive them easily, they should also understand what is observed of the other planets; for it is not necessary to look too deeply there, because the matter is visible and manifest. Ptolemy gives the reason why this appears more in the sun than in other stars, saying it is because of the magnitude of the sun and because of the changes that appear through it in the four seasons of the year. When he mentioned "magnitude," he said it because it is the largest body in the whole world that can be perceived, as was proven in the fifth treatise of the *Almagest* <note>original: "almagesti"; Ptolemy’s influential 2nd-century work on astronomy</note>.

<column-break/>

And because of this, it follows that its power is greater than all other powers of all other bodies in the world. For the power of any body is proportional to its size, as has been proven in the study of nature. We understand this from what appears of the sun's works in the works of the year. Ptolemy, however, returns briefly to speaking of the sun's works, though he does not speak of its substance, to make us understand that the works of the stars that reach us are by power of their influence <note>original: "vtute ogis"</note> only, and not because of the quality of their substances which are of the nature of the works; for to speak of this belongs to the study of nature, not this science. In this science, we do not have to look as if at the qualities of nature, but rather at the work. Nevertheless, it clearly appears from the reason of Ptolemy’s words that his opinion was one with that of Aristotle: that the substance of all celestial bodies is an essence that is not hot, not moist, not cold, and not dry. From the words he said about the sun, Ptolemy teaches us four rules. One is general to the sun and all other stars, which is that the power of the stars follows the magnitude of their bodies. To give a demonstration of this is easy: since the stars are of one general substance, it is fitting that all things of this substance are overcome by the species and persons of each. And it had already been proven that this substance performs works in earthly things that are of one general nature; the sun is one species of this genus, and its power follows its size. Afterward, it follows that the power of other species of this genus follows the size of their bodies; these species are all the other stars. The second rule is that since the power of the sun is greater than the power of other stars, it follows that among the things that are between us, it possesses those which pertain to such power—such as sovereignty, kings, nobility, the ability to appear good, greatness of heart and intellect. According to this rule, it follows that each of the other stars possesses such things as pertain to its own power. The third is that because the sun heats much and dries out a little, it follows (as we said in the first treatise) that the effects they produce in the bodies and characters of animals are suited to this composition. Because of this, it follows that it governs the heart and its veins of natural heat, life, the age of youth, and all works of the spirit, so that one might be free and ready; and it is understood to love clarity, light, and every bright thing. The fourth rule is: those things that are composed of what was said in the other three rules, such as having a good will, loving to play, and to praise—which is something that follows clarity and intellect. When you look into these four rules concerning all other things, you will be able to know all things that are in the sun. For according to this, it follows that among minerals it possesses the precious hyacinth <note>a blue or reddish gemstone, often identified as zircon or sapphire</note> and gold, and among animals and plants, the noblest among them. And because its power is greater and stronger, it follows that it operates thus more greatly in all things, and that all other stars have a participation with it in its work.

---

->On the power of the moon.<-

The greater power of the moon is to moisten. For it is nearer to the earth, from which moist vapor ascends from the bottom all the way to it. Therefore, in this manner, it changes bodies with a manifest change. For it changes and putrefies most parts of those things existing within the body. It also shares a slight partnership in heat with the sun, because it receives light from it.

For the greater power of the moon is to moisten, because it is very much around the earth, and because of the moist smokiness <note>original: "fumositatē"</note> which is raised from the earth through it. And because of this, it changes bodies to such a state with a manifest change, which causes bodies to change and putrefy for the most part. And it also has a small participation in heat with the sun because it receives light from it.

After he taught us that the powers of the stars follow the magnitude of their bodies—and the body of the moon is small, as he showed in the *Almagest*—and its work is like that of the sun in one part, he says here that this is because it is very much around the earth. Its power reaches us before it is changed, and because of this, its work appears more than that of the other stars; and we see visibly that it draws humors...

<summary>This page introduces Haly's commentary on the individual planets, focusing on the Sun as the primary source of heat and the Moon as the primary source of moisture. It establishes the rule that a celestial body's influence is proportional to its physical size and proximity to Earth.</summary>
<keywords>Haly Abenragel, Ptolemy, Sun, Moon, planetary influence, Peripatetics, heat, moisture, Almagest, natural philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 37 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Moon's influence on the Earth's moisture, specifically addressing criticisms from Albumasar before moving on to describe the essential qualities and astrological powers of Saturn and Jupiter.</meta>

[it draws] the humors of the earth and of the bodies that follow it. Because it receives its light from the Sun, it produces a slight, accidental heat in earthly things. With this heat, it causes the humors existing in bodies to putrefy <note>In medieval science, "putrefaction" often refers to the breakdown or transformation of substances through heat and moisture, not just rotting.</note> and change, just as has been shown in the study of physics and nature. It is evident that light produces heat; this can be proven by mirrors that burn things and similar instruments. Since the Moon has its light from the Sun, it is fitting that it has a small amount of heat, as it acts as if by accident. This is what Ptolemy means to say. 

Because Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a famous Persian astrologer.</note> did not understand this, he believed Ptolemy had erred in his saying, asking: "How can moist vapors ascend to the Moon, when vapors cannot rise higher than 16 stadia <note>A "stadium" was an ancient unit of distance; 16 stadia is roughly 1.8 miles or 3 kilometers.</note>, and the Moon is much further away?" 

I, however, laughed at such sayings and said: "How did he understand this?" Ptolemy did not wish to say that moist vapors physically ascend from here to the Moon; rather, he said that the ascent of moist vapors is *toward* the Moon. This teaches us that the Moon draws the humors of the earth and of other bodies following it, just as a magnet <note>original: "adamas"</note> draws iron. Since he said that men understand these things from the movements of the tides of the sea and of moist bodies, it is sufficient for this reasoning to say that the vapor rises toward the region where the Moon is. 

Ptolemy also gave us three rules concerning the Moon. The first is that the power which is near the Earth has the greatest effect, because it reaches the Earth before it can be altered. When we join this rule to what was said about the size of a body, we will find a way of knowing the virtues of the stars—namely, which is stronger or weaker—and because of this, we shall know those things which pertain to them according to their power. When we join these two things, it is fitting that the Moon has things that follow the Sun and are in its second degree. For example: if the Sun’s influence lasts for years, the Moon’s work will last for months; if the Sun possesses gold, the Moon will possess silver; if the Sun possesses drink <note>original: "bauere," likely a corruption of "bibere" (to drink) or "vivere" (to live)</note>, the Moon will possess bread; if the Sun possesses kings, the Moon will possess those who will inherit their kingdoms; and other things that follow secondarily to the power of the Sun.

The second rule is: since the Moon creates moisture by accident, it is fitting that the Moon governs waters and all other moistures, and those things that come through them, such as the slight cold that follows because of moisture. The third gloss is: since the Moon heats a little by accident, it is fitting that it causes things to change and putrefy, and that it has works and substances suitable to such a thing. 

Ptolemy does not name the rule taken from the movements of the stars because it is a manifest thing. For there is a rule in the Sun: because the movements of all stars follow its motion, it is fitting that it be the prince over all stars. And in the Moon it is because in any quarter <note>referring to the lunar phases</note> it applies to all stars; it is fitting that it has the power of connecting the virtues of other stars with its own. Because of this, it is fitting that the power of the Sun and Moon dominates over the powers of the other stars. And because the Moon is swift in its motion, it is fitting that it governs those earthly things that pertain to such a quality, such as messengers and couriers. For it is fitting that we look thus at everything pertaining to each of the planets.

### On the power of Saturn.

The star of Saturn, according to the greater part of its work, cools; and by its very great coldness, it dries slightly. This seems to happen because of its great distance from the heat of the Sun and from the moist vapors that are near the Earth.

The greatest and strongest work of Saturn is to cool and to dry slightly due to the strength of the cold. It seems to be because it is moved very far from the heat of the Sun and the moist vapors of the earth. He means to say that it does this because its work is very far-

<column-break/>

-removed from the work of the Sun, which is the work of heat, and from the Moon, whose work is to draw humors. As we said in another treatise: when one looks at the comparison of Saturn with the Sun and Moon, one sees that it is the opposite of both; because of this, he said that it is fitting for it to be cold and dry. Ptolemy himself explained this comparison in what follows.

*Indeed, the knowledge of the power of this star and the other stars proceeds from the experiments of their configurations <note>original: "figurarum," referring to aspects or planetary alignments</note> which are found in their relationship with the Sun and Moon. For in the orders of changes, which differ according to increase and decrease, we see certain qualities of the air vary in one way, and others in another.*

To know the power of this planet and the others will be through the verification of the configurations that are in respect to the Sun and Moon; for from some we see them changing the air in one manner of change, and some in another manner in various orders of increasing and decreasing change.

If you remember what we told you about how we can prove the powers of the stars, this saying needs no explanation. But if you have forgotten this, listen: I say that because the works of the Sun and Moon appear more than those of all other stars, and are more manifest to us, they always follow one path. And the works of the remaining stars seem hidden because of these manifest ones. It is fitting to look to the stars having community with the two luminaries through configurations, whether they increase in their works or decrease from them. And so you shall go on inspecting all of them until you know the certainty of all—not once, but many times. And if you find that it always follows one manner of operating, you will know for certain what kind of power they have.

### On the power of Jupiter.

*The body of the star of Jupiter is of a temperate complexion; for the place of its motion is midway between the coldness of Saturn and the fervor of Mars. Therefore, it both heats and moistens at the same time; and because its nature is more to heat, and it is carried above the other heavens, it is the author of winds that make things grow.*

The work of Jupiter's power is of a temperate complexion <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body</term>. The place of its motion is midway between the coldness of Saturn and the heat of Mars; because of this, it is fitting that it heats and moistens. Because its heating is greater, it is fitting—on account of the spheres that are below it—that they generate winds.

Many believed, when they heard this word of Ptolemy, that the works of the stars, according to his opinion, follow the locations of the spheres according to how one exists above another, as Pica Avenquinton <note>Likely referring to the Andalusian philosopher Ibn Bajjah (Avempace).</note> and Al-Kindi <note>Al-Kindi (c. 801–873), a pioneering Arab philosopher known as "the Philosopher of the Arabs."</note> and others believed, who hindered us with such reasons. I, however, say that if the works of the stars are according to nature, how can they be known through quadrivial <note>The "Quadrivium" consisted of the four mathematical sciences: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note> propositions? For the roots of these two sciences are different from one another. Furthermore, if all celestial bodies do not possess any complexion of hot, cold, moist, or dry—as Aristotle proved—how can the complexion of Jupiter be tempered just because its sphere exists between those of Mars and Saturn? For if you look well at Ptolemy's saying, you will find it is not as they believed. After he taught us the way by which we shall know the powers of the stars, he puts this another way in this place...
Quadri. Ptol.

...tension. For when we examine the movement of [Jupiter's] influence, and how it works in the air surrounding us, we find that it is a middle ground between the great cold produced by Saturn and the great heat produced by Mars. This confirms the statement that it heats and moistens. If he had said Jupiter does this simply because its sphere exists between one sphere and others, it would follow that it is merely temperate, and neither hot nor moist. I say that when Ptolemy proved the work of Jupiter in comparison to the work of the Sun and Moon, he stated that it produces a heat that is not excessive; for this reason, he said the movement of its influence is between the work of Mars and that of Saturn.

<unclear>Ptolemy</unclear> however said that because of its heat, it primarily produces "generating winds" because of the spheres located beneath it. He means to say that because Jupiter leans toward a temperate state of heat and moisture, when its influence mixes with the works of other planets existing below it, it produces life-giving winds. These "winds" are those found in seeds and sperm <note>In medieval science, "wind" or "pneuma" was often thought to be the vital spirit or gas that carried the power of life in biological seeds.</note> and other such breaths that are suited for life. And if you look at the mixture that results from the powers of the planets existing below it combined with its own power, you will find it must be so.

### On the power of Mars.

The star of Mars essentially dries. The force of its nature is to burn; its heat is likened to fire, and it holds a place next to the Sun, whose carrying sphere lies beneath it.

Mars essentially dries and burns by the force of its nature, because it has a fiery heat and because it is near the Sun, and because the sphere in which the Sun exists is placed beneath it.

He means to say that when we test the effect of the power of Mars, we find it to be of great dryness. Regarding what he said—that the power of Mars burns because it has a fiery heat—I say that the stars are of a simple substance <note>A "simple substance" refers to the celestial fifth element (aether), which is not made of the four heavy earthly elements.</note> and not composed of different elements. The appearance of its heat is direct, because there is nothing there to change the heat coming from that same substance. Ptolemy teaches us through this statement a rule by which we may know the power of a star; since we cannot understand it directly through our senses, we can understand it through its heat. In this statement, there is a doubt that we ought to resolve. For many believe that heat does not reveal the true power of a thing; this is true in earthly matters because of the mixture of elements within them, yet in celestial things it is not so, as they are not composed of any element. Because of this, the author returned to prove this power in another way, saying that it exists near the Sun, and that the sphere in which the Sun resides is placed beneath it. He means to say that this fact happens to be true: the power of Mars burns because it exists near the Sun, and because the Sun is beneath it, its power mixes with that of the Sun, becoming very hot and dry in such a way that it burns without any tempering.

### On the power of Venus.

The star of Venus also, because of the temperament of its constitution, completely imitates Jupiter in its effects, except that in Venus the order of Jupiter is reversed: for it heats moderately because it is near the Sun, and it moistens as much as the Moon does because of the great quantity of its light; therefore, it draws to itself the vapors that rise from the humors <note>In this context, "humors" refers to the elemental liquids of the earth, like water and mist.</note> surrounding the earth.

And Venus itself performs the works of Jupiter because of the temperament of its constitution, except that it is of one nature contrary to Jupiter: it heats a fair amount because it exists near the Sun, and it moistens like the Moon because of the great light this 

<column-break/>

planet possesses: because it draws to itself the smokiness <note>original: "fumositates"</note> that rises from the humors of the earth.

He means to say that its heat is much less than that of Jupiter; because of this and because of the moisture it produces, we say it is in some way cold and more moist. But he said "because it exists near the Sun" because its power moves with that of the Sun. And where he said "it moistens like the Moon," he means that Venus produces a moistening effect similar to what the Moon does. And where he said "because of its great light," he means that its moderate heat causes the humors to flow.

### On the power of Mercury.

The effect of the star of Mercury is for the most part to dry and equally to moisten. Indeed, at certain hours it dries humors, because it is never too far removed from the heat of the Sun. At other times, however, it moistens, because its place is above the lunar sphere which is closer to the earth; and in both of these, its change is rapid. It is also a source of winds, because its motion around the Sun is very fast.

The dryness and moisture of Mercury are equal to one another: since sometimes it dries and sucks up humors, because it is never far from the heat of the Sun at any time; and sometimes it moistens, because it is placed above the sphere of the Moon, which is closer to the earth than all other spheres; and it changes between these two states, and produces winds because of its sensitive changes all around the Sun.

He means to say that the work of Mercury is not one single thing: since sometimes it dries and sometimes it moistens. When it dries, it is when it applies itself to the Sun; then its work in heating and drying is similar to that of the Sun. Its moistening, however, is because of its force which is mixed with that of the Moon, which is placed beneath it; and its work is like the work of the Moon. When Ptolemy made a comparison of Mercury’s work with that of the Sun, he found that sometimes it performed a work such as the Sun's; and then when he compared it with the Moon, he found that sometimes it performed a work such as the Moon's. He tested this many times and found that it always performed one of these two works easily; he knew for certain that its work follows the work of the other stars with which it is involved, and it has no work of its own within itself. Because the course of Mercury is always around the Sun, it happens that the power of Mercury changes the work of the Sun with various mutations according to the stars with which it is involved. And because its power is much involved with that of the Moon, and because it works in changing the power of the Sun, it results in it producing winds of various kinds. 

Here is completed what Ptolemy spoke concerning the powers of the seven planets; and it is manifest, as we understand and have glossed, that he showed all of this according to nature <note>i.e., physical observation and the properties of matter.</note> and not according to the quadrivium <note>The "Quadrivium" refers to the four mathematical arts: Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy. The author argues Ptolemy is using physical logic rather than just mathematical theory here.</note>. If people were to say that the spheres were placed in this manner by nature because of the powers of their works, we would say that this power is possible in itself; however, they cannot know the powers of the stars any better through that. Furthermore, if we understood by Ptolemy's statement about Saturn—that it is cold because it is far from the heat of the Sun—that he said this because its sphere is far from the sphere of the Sun, it would follow from this opinion that all the fixed stars would be colder than Saturn, because their sphere is much further from the sphere of the Sun than Saturn's is; but this is not so. Therefore, what we have said is true. You will find us to be with the truth if you look well into Ptolemy's words. And we have already taught you the rules which Ptolemy gave us regarding the Sun and Moon; and it is fitting that you seek such rules for the five wandering planets and other stars. And regarding what he said...

And accordingly, it follows that he governs men-at-arms and soldiers, and all war and strife, and every kind of weapon. ¶ And by what he said—that the power of Venus is like the power of Jupiter, except that it is somewhat smaller—it follows that she governs all such styles and ornaments of women, joys, games, and every delight and good manners. ¶ And by what he said—she moistens like the Moon—he gave us a rule that she possesses all the moistures appropriate to her, such as wine and every flavorful drink and the like. ¶ And by what he said—that Mercury is mixed with other stars—he gave us a rule that he possesses things belonging to other planets in comparison to the Sun; and it follows that he governs secretaries, kings, scribes, <term>accountants<note>original: "numeratores"; those who calculate or keep accounts.</note></term>, <term>administrators<note>original: "adredatores"; likely meaning those who prepare or arrange affairs.</note></term>, and other things named as pertaining to Mercury. And if you hope in our words, you will be well able to understand in what manner the powers of the stars are applied to those things that are near us; for they are applied through rays in straight lines. And you should not wonder that we find all things perceived among us in this way, because the powers of sight, hearing, and smell all come to us by means of the air. Furthermore, when we wish to place the <term>big toe<note>original: "poleguz"; a corruption of the Latin 'pollicem', usually the thumb or big toe.</note></term> of the foot, we move it with our will whenever we wish, and without doubt, because the power of motion comes from the brain in a single moment to the toe. And since it is so, it is manifest that whenever two stars are joined by longitude and latitude, their two powers are mixed and a third, celestial power is made, reaching down to us; and without doubt, the powers of the stars are changed because of their conjunctions.

## ¶ On Fortunes and Infortunes. Chapter 5.

<image-desc>A large woodcut decorative initial 'C' containing a scene of a scholar or physician seated at a desk with books, set within an ornate square border.</image-desc>
Since, therefore, the aforementioned figures are as we have said, and they are of four natures: two, namely heat and moisture, are procreating and effective, for nothing receives growth except through them; and two, namely coldness and dryness, are destructive, for through them things are diminished and cease to be.

¶ Since these things are so, and two of the four natures—heat and moisture—are generative and active, because all things are mixed and grow through these; and the other two—coldness and dryness—are damaging and destructive, because all other things are harmed and destroyed through these two.

<column-break/>

¶ He means to say that after these rules have been given in this way, we find that through heat and moisture all generation and all growth occur; and that through coldness and dryness all corruption and all change occur. We say that this is proven in the science of nature and in physics; and therefore he accepted this as a matter of experience. And he means to say in this place regarding heat and moisture that they incline more toward a temperament <note>A "temperament" or "complexion" refers to the balanced state of the four qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry).</note>, and regarding coldness and dryness that they depart more from a temperament. And you will understand from his own words that this is true. You will find that <term>Aristotle<note>The Greek philosopher whose works on natural science were fundamental to medieval university education.</note></term> proved in that book *On Generation and Corruption* that coldness and heat are the active operations, and moisture and dryness are the recipients of their work. And this is the opposite of what Ptolemy said, and for this reason, I wish to resolve this doubt, saying that Ptolemy did not contradict Aristotle except in this place, according to the reason of which he speaks: for he applied the name of "operators" and "generators" to those through which things are born and grow, and he used the name "damners" for those through which things are corrupted; and he placed moisture with heat because through these two all things are created. And he placed dryness with coldness because through these two all things are harmed and destroyed. And it is manifest that when two different things are joined, whichever of the two prevails takes the name. And so Ptolemy did in this book.

¶ Two of the wandering stars—namely Jupiter and Venus—and also the Moon, according to men of ancient authority, were said to be "fortunes" because their complexion is temperate and because much heat and moisture are in them.

¶ The ancients said that three of the wandering planets—which are Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon—likewise grant good fortune, because they are of a temperate complexion and are drawn more toward heat and moisture.

¶ Here Ptolemy explicitly said that the heat and moisture of which he spoke are those that incline most toward a temperament. For when we take the rule of Jupiter, it heats and moistens temperately; it is appropriate according to this work in generation and growth, and to the one doing such a thing, it is fitting to give good fortune. And when we take the rule of Venus, the work falls near that of Jupiter, because it moistens more; and its power is always mixed with that of the Sun, because it moves around it, and its motion is everywhere around the Sun. It is composed of the moderate heat which Venus has with the heat of the Sun, and the moisture of Venus combined, performing all generation and growth; and to the one doing such a thing, it is fitting to give good fortune. Similarly regarding the Moon: because its motion is swift and its light is from the Sun, and its power follows the power of the Sun in operation and is always mixed with the power of the Sun (which rules over all generation), it follows that the work of the Moon is all generation and growth. For nature placed in her a great moisture, so that she might enlarge the bodies of all earthly things to temper the power of the Sun's dryness.

¶ They testified that the works of Saturn and Mars are naturally contrary to the works of the aforementioned stars, because one of them works through intense cold and the other through intense dryness.

¶ And they said that the natural work of Saturn and Mars is contrary to those planets, because one is cold and the other dry beyond the middle point.

¶ Here he also explicitly said that the coldness and dryness of which he spoke are those that have excessively departed from all temperament. And it is manifest that since Saturn cools so much, he takes away moisture from all things. And it follows that the work of that nature, being such, is [the opposite of] the work of Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon. And I wish to say that its natural work is of corruption, diminution, and the destruction of things. And he has already told us plainly that Mars works more by dryness than by heat; and a little heat when mixed with great dryness burns. And if anyone believes that the natural work of Mars is great dryness, and when it is joined with the work of the Sun it becomes the same compound that burns, I say that here Ptolemy wished to say...

Because there are indeed two primary kinds of the parts of nature: namely, masculine and feminine.

¶ Furthermore, because the principles of nature are two: and these are masculine and feminine.

When nature begins to make a human, it starts by making the body so that it can receive the spirit; and afterward, it changes that body to the state of a living being until the spirit is in it; and it changes it afterward until it becomes a soul; and afterward, it changes it from the state of a living being to the state of a human: and in this way nature works all things, as is proven in natural science. And since it is so: those things that nature makes receive every work from the celestial bodies; it is manifest that the virtue of masculine and feminine follows the first four qualities. Concerning this, he said that there are two kinds: masculine and feminine. He means to say that these two are derivatives <note>original: "filia", literally 'daughters'; here used to mean the primary products or branches of natural processes.</note> in all of nature. And in those things that are of moderate perfection, it made the masculine and feminine mixed: for in the seeds of vegetables and the fruits of trees, the masculine and feminine virtues are mixed; and you should understand in this place the name of nature, which is the force and virtue that God placed in all things for governing, completing, and preserving them.

# Book One

After Ptolemy showed what the planets perform naturally by having masculine and feminine power, he now shows us how they perform the same by "accident" <note>original: "p accñs" — by circumstance or position rather than inherent nature</note>, telling us first what they perform in respect to the Sun, and primarily showing what they perform in respect to the East, as he gives us through these rules. From this, it follows that the first quarter, which is eastern, is of a masculine nature; and the western quarter is of a feminine nature. And because things which are opposite have equal power, it follows that the quarter which is from the west to the Midheaven beneath the earth has a power as great as the eastern one, because it is opposite to it. And the quarter which is from the Midheaven beneath the earth to the east has a power as great as the western quarter opposite to it. For by these words, Ptolemy gave us a rule by which you can understand many other things. And he gave you a way to understand the nature of the twelve houses <note>The twelve divisions of the zodiac used in a horoscope</note> which are made in the firmament by accident; and he will express this to you later.

->On Diurnal and Nocturnal [Planets]. Chapter 7.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q depicting a scholar or astronomer pointing toward an armillary sphere or celestial globe mounted on a stand.</image-desc>
Since there are likewise two spaces from which time is made: of which one is the day, which is properly masculinized because of its heat and its effective and moving power. The other indeed is the night, which is feminized because of its moisture and rest.

Because the stars perform primary qualities <note>Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note> on the earth, it follows that they should divide into other opposites; and according to this, some of them belong to the day, others indeed to the night. And similarly, because these two are the parts by which time is made, the day is properly masculinized because of the power and the active heat which exists in motion during the day; and the night is feminized because of the coldness and the active power which is rest and tranquility.

**Time** is made of continuous things, and every continuous thing always receives division: and because of this, time is divided into years, months, days, and hours, and parts of these, and other fractions. And in the day is the time in which the sun completes one revolution from the part where it rises until it rises another time; and this is divided into day and into night. And the day is not divided into another nature: because it is one part of it, and similarly the night. Whence it follows that the parts of the day by which time is clearly composed are night and day. Yet the day is of greater power: because the power of the sun extends itself through the earth, with which animals move and vegetables grow. And generally in animals and all things moving themselves, the sun has a greater power by day than by night; so that the power of the sun is that which moves all things without any other medium. Night, however, is of a more hidden power: because the power of the sun is hidden beneath the earth; and because of this, it follows that animals rest. Furthermore, heat is more manifest by day than by night; for by night moistures grow, because we have moist vapors which

<column-break/>

are joined more in the air at night, and are expelled by day. Whence from all this, it follows that the diurnal nature is masculine, and the nocturnal is feminine.

They said that the Moon and Venus are nocturnal, while the Sun and Jupiter are diurnal. Mercury indeed, as we said before, they made a companion to both.

They said that Venus and the Moon are nocturnal by following their first reasoning: and that the Sun and Jupiter are diurnal; and Mercury has a participation with these, as we said.

When he said "following his reasoning," he means to say that they knew which were diurnal and nocturnal stars by the logic of masculine and feminine. And what they knew by reasoning, they afterwards verified by experience.

And they reported that it [Mercury] is diurnal when in the east, and nocturnal when in the west.

Because Mercury, when it is in the eastern part, is diurnal; and when it is in the western part, it is nocturnal.

Ptolemy indicates to us in what he said about Mercury: that the stars perform by accident; since in the east, when the stars appear in it as they rise, and then the *Solanus* <note>East wind</note> wind moves, it follows that it has a greater and more manifest power than the west; because in the west the stars set, and the western wind moves from there. And because Mercury makes a middle temperament <note>original: "medianā cōplōnē" — a balanced mix of qualities</note> between heat and coldness, it follows that when it is in the east, it pertains to the masculine and diurnal, and when in the west, to the feminine and nocturnal.

They divided the two "unfortunes" <note>original: "ātrāq;" (utramque) — both malefics (Saturn and Mars)</note> according to these two modes; except that they did this not naturally, but through contrariety.

And they also partitioned into these two manners the two planets that possess the substance of corruption and destruction. Whence they do not follow the first natural reasoning in this, but another different one.

Ptolemy told us this openly: that whatever he said up to this point is according to the reasons of nature. And this which he now said is of another manner. He means to say that this of which he now speaks is with a reason of natures different from what he said before.

For when similar things are mixed with things whose temperament is suitable, their health is improved.

And indeed, when similar things are mixed with things of a good temperament <note>original: "bone complexionis"</note>, their benefit increases more.

And this is manifest: because good things, when they are mixed with other similar things, are of greater benefit. And concerning this, the same is true: for bad things, when mixed with similar things, are of greater harm.

But when dissimilar things are mixed with destructive things, their harm will be diminished.

And when things that are not similar are involved with evil things, they diminish much of their harm.

This is another statement manifest in itself: because if things causing harm are mixed with beneficial things, they diminish much of their harm. Ptolemy, however, proposed these reasons by confirming what the ancient wise men proved by experience and found to be certain, and by proving this reasoning.

Because of this, they likened Saturn—which cools—to the heat of the day; and Mars—because it dries—to the moisture of the night. Therefore, namely, because each of these, through its tempering, the temperament will be likened to the quality of a temperate temperament <note>The idea is that mixing extreme qualities (like Saturn's extreme cold with the Day's extreme heat) results in a "temperate" or balanced state.</note>.

And because Saturn is very cold, they placed it with the heat of the day; and because Mars is very dry, they placed it with the moisture of the night. And each of them, when its temperament becomes moderated, becomes suitable to the state of a temperate temperament.

For it is nature that tempers every thing. And since Saturn is excessively cold, he placed it as diurnal: so that the nature of the day might temper it with its heat; because

if he had made it [Saturn] nocturnal, he would have increased its harm too much, beyond measure. Similarly with Mars, because it is excessively dry, he placed it as nocturnal so that the moisture of the night might diminish some of its great dryness; for if he had made it diurnal, its dryness would have increased beyond measure, much to its own detriment. And when the ancient sages tested the nature of these two planets, they found Saturn to be diurnal and Mars indeed nocturnal for other reasons diverse from that which I have said: they followed the first reason. For they found this reasoning regarding the tempering of nature to be fitting, as you may understand from the words of Ptolemy, because in the combination of fortune they sometimes do good, since they diminish the works of others that are harmful to them by their own efforts. It is also beneficial that you look into this in whatever place happens to you in this regard.

->**On the strengths of the figures that are formed according to the sun's position.**<-

<margin>Chapter 8.</margin>

<margin>Haly said:</margin>

## Ptolemy

<margin>He wishes in this chapter to show how you may know the virtues which the stars have by accident <note>original: "p accidēs" — astrological strength gained through position or circumstance rather than inherent nature</note>; thus he has recounted up to here how you can know the virtues they have by essence <note>original: "p cēntiā" — essential dignity or inherent nature</note>.</margin>

Up to here, you could know the virtues they have by essence. Likewise, the one [Moon] and the three wandering stars placed above the Sun <note>The "superior" planets: Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note> assume an increase and decrease in their own proper strengths according to the figures they form in relation to the Sun.

**The Moon and the three wandering planets that are received above the Sun [increase] and decrease in their own virtues according to the figures they have in comparison to the Sun.**

He [Ptolemy] wishes to say that their own proper and natural work increases and decreases in the figures of those planets in comparison to the Sun. For he taught us before that the planets which are above the Sun are Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. And therefore he called them "wandering" <note>original: "erraticos" — from the Greek 'planētes,' meaning wanderers</note> so that you may distinguish those stars that are also above the Sun.

For the Moon, from its first "horning" <note>The crescent phase</note> until its first dichotomy <note>The first quarter moon, when it appears half-full</note>, provides moisture; and from then until the full moon, it heats; and from then until the second dichotomy, it dries; and then until it is hidden and exists directly with the Sun, it cools.

Because the Moon, from the hour it is born until it is in the middle of its first light, works specifically with moisture; and from the hour of the middle of the first light until it is full, it works with heat; and from the hour it is full until the hour of the second middle, it works with dryness; and from the hour of the second middle until the hour in which it is hidden and separated from the Sun, it works with coldness.

The proper work of the Moon is of moisture. And because after it begins to grow in light, heat happens to it, increasing every day—and heat always opens the pores, stirs thick and frozen moisture, and makes it flow—it follows that the Moon, from the hour it separates from the Sun until it is halved in light, mostly works only on moisture. And after it separates from the left quarter [square] of the Sun and goes toward its opposition, its heat increases more because of the great light it has. And after it separates from the opposition of the Sun and goes toward its right quarter, its heat increases even more because its light is much above the earth, and because of this it dries up moistures; and so it happens that it works with dryness. And after it separates from the right quarter of the Sun and goes to be joined with it, its light is much diminished every day; and it follows that coldness succeeds that moisture until it is separated [from the Sun], because the heat is diminished every day due to the diminution of its light. And according to this, there are four states in the Moon: the first is similar to the age of childhood and the season of spring; the second is similar to the age of youth and the summer time; the third is similar to the age of old age and the autumnal time; and the fourth is similar to the decrepit age and the winter time. Now, however, other rules have been gained through these occasions, which, when mixed with other essential rules of opposition regarding the Moon, will allow you to understand many things pertaining to the Moon: for example, that when it is moist, it signifies females, and males when it is dry. Similarly, when it is hot, it will signify males, and females when it is cold.

As for the stars that are "matutinal" <note>Rising in the morning before the Sun</note> from the time they appear from under the rays

<column-break/>

of the Sun until their first station <note>The point where a planet appears to stop before turning retrograde</note>, they moisten more; and from their first station until their evening rising, they heat more; and from then until the second station, they dry more; and from that until their occultation [hiding], they cool more.

The wandering planets are called matutinal only from the hour they come out from under the rays of the Sun until their first station, and they moisten more. And from the first station, when they rise on the first night, they heat more; and thereafter, as they rise on the first night until the second station, they dry more; and from the second station until they are occidental [setting in the west], they cool more.

The wandering planets that are called matutinal are the three existing above the Sun: namely, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars; for these alone appear coming out from under the rays of the Sun in the morning. And Venus and Mercury, in coming out from under the rays of the Sun, appear sometimes in the morning and sometimes in the evening. And the light of these three, when they are oriental [in the east], begins to increase every day until they place themselves in opposition to the Sun, rising on the first night; and after that, the light begins to decrease every day until they are joined with the Sun. Whence it happens that they have such a state for the increase and decrease of their light as the Moon does: so that when they are oriental until they are in the first station, they work with moisture by accident; and from the first [point] of their retrogradation, when they rise on the first night, they work with heat by accident; and while they rise on the first night until the station where they begin to move direct, they work with dryness. And while they are direct until they are joined with the Sun, they work with coldness in the manner that happens to the Moon. And you will find that the reason for this is what I wish to say. For I say that while they come out from under the rays, they are similar to the age of childhood. And after they begin to be retrograde until they are opposite the Sun, they are similar to the age of youth. And after they separate from the opposition until they begin to move direct, they are similar to the age of old age. And after they are directed until they are joined with the Sun, they are similar to the age of decrepitude. The reason for this similarity is this: because the virtue of the stars is mixed with the virtue of the Sun, and their movements are naturally bound with its movement; and all their virtues follow the virtues of the Sun and Moon. And because [Ptolemy] knew it was sufficient to make these states of the Moon known, it was not necessary to make the same known for Venus and Mercury. For it is not expressed in this place, but you must understand it: for there is an opinion of some that these planets perform this according to whether they are near the earth or far away. And this is a false reasoning; for because they are near the earth they do not perform anything else except that they are simply of greater power, and when they are far, of lesser power, because they are more elongated. And some go against Ptolemy in what he said before: that the more the planets are near the earth, the more their virtue appears. For as they said, "we find retrograde planets to be of weak work," and it is manifest that they are nearer the earth; but we do not say that it is so. And if God grants us life and favor in glossing the *Almagest* <note>Ptolemy's great astronomical work</note>, we shall distinguish this better. To these, however, we wish to respond according to how Ptolemy is understood by you: I say that retrograde planets are like traveling men who, even if they have great strength, cannot perform their works as well. The natural reason for this is: because the work of the three superior planets when they are retrograde is contrary to the work of the Sun, and the work of the Sun conquers and overcomes them, because it is mixed with their work due to the opposition; and their work is weakened because of the Sun, which strengthens itself over them. And when Venus and Mercury are retrograde, because their virtue is involved with that of the Sun, their work does not appear completely as it pertains to them. And if you say against this, "when they are more mixed with the Sun, we can better understand what changes they make in the Sun's work," I answer you with this same thing: and I say that they do not have complete virtue in themselves, except because they change the virtue of the Sun. And this virtue of the Sun is that which conquers and which works. For I want to tell you things about Venus and Mercury according to the figures they have in respect to the Sun. I say that Venus and Mercury, after they are separated from the Sun and are direct and appear on the first night until their direction is completed and they return to the Sun and are joined with it, they have four states...

...four phases according to whether they are far from the Sun or near it. For the first phase is that which moistens, until they are in the middle of their forward motion. The second phase is that which heats, until they reach their first station <note>The point where a planet appears to stop before turning retrograde</note>. The third phase is that which dries, until they are in the middle of their retrograde <note>backward</note> motion. The fourth phase is that which cools, until they are combust <note>original: "combusti" — so close to the Sun that they are hidden by its light</note>. 

<margin>This is situated for them according to what was said concerning the superior planets <note>The planets further from the Sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, and you yourself will be able to understand it from what we have said.</margin> 

And after they separate from the Sun while being retrograde, and they appear in the morning until their retrogradation is complete and they become direct, they also have four states similar to those four phases when they are moving forward in their exit from under the rays when they are occidental <note>setting in the west</note>; and those that are retrograde in their exit from under the rays when they are oriental <note>rising in the east</note>; and it happens that they have a greater power when they are occidental than when they are oriental. And others have said that they moisten when they are oriental, because their power is extended over the earth before the power of the Sun; and that they dry when they are occidental.

It is also plain that when these different qualities are mixed with one another, they work upon the air in many ways according to the victory of the proper strength of each one.

And it is manifest that when one is mixed, for instance, with another, they produce many kinds of diverse states in the air according to what is the proper power of each for the most part, and its motion according to the diversity of the configurations <note>original: "figuraꝝ" — the geometric relationships or aspects between stars</note> whenever it may be.

**He means to say:** that when the stars are mixed—one, for example, with another—they produce many types of mutations and very diverse natures in the air because of their essential and accidental powers, according to the number of diverse temperaments <note>original: "complexionē" — the specific balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> from which their powers are composed every day. And it is manifest that the winner in any of these compositions will be the one that has the greater power according to the locations of the planets and according to the power of each within itself, as you understood before. And that the essential powers of the stars are changed somewhat according to the diversity of their configurations and locations in respect to the Sun and the horizon. And since it is thus in the air surrounding us, it follows that the same happens in men and in all things regarding the work of the stars.

### On the strengths of the fixed stars. Chapter 9.

So that a treatise on the natures of the fixed stars <note>original: "stellaꝝ fixar'" — stars that do not move relative to each other, unlike planets</note> (which take their properties from the nature of their effects) may follow what was said before, let us hereafter begin to record their variations as discovered through experience.

And since this follows what we have said—to speak of the nature of the stars that are not wandering <note>original: "erratice" — planets</note> in those things which they have according to their own proper work—we wish to begin in this work by telling of the changes found in them when they have been verified.

**He means to say:** that speaking of the fixed stars follows that which he spoke regarding the wandering stars, because their own motion does not change. But what he said—that they have according to their "proper work"—he means to say that their effects of which he will speak are effects they have solely by their essence, and not from those they have by accident; for the accidental effects they have are of the same kind as he described regarding the three superior planets. And what he said—that they were discovered for them when they were verified—he means to say that their effects of which he will speak are those which were discovered for them through experience, according to the work of each of them on earthly things.

From which we may indicate their similarities with the wandering stars.

And we will show in this their similarity which they have with the nature of the wandering stars.

After Ptolemy spoke completely about the seven wandering planets—and the Sun and Moon are the lords and princes over all the stars, because their effects are more manifest and visible than those of all the others, and the rest of the wandering stars have temperaments similar to those of the Sun and Moon—and the appearance of their effects is midway between the great appearance of the two luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note> and the small appearance of the effects of the fixed stars; Ptolemy had to set the wandering planets as a rule for knowing the power 

<column-break/>

of the fixed stars in comparison to the wandering ones; thus he placed the two luminaries for knowing the powers of the wandering stars or planets. However, in some places, he placed the two luminaries for knowing the powers of certain fixed stars.

And first, indeed, let us record those which are in the figures of the circle of the signs <note>The Zodiac</note>.

And we will first name those which are in the figure of the signs of the zodiac.

The signs are the places from which the stars go and move from one sign to others; and they are twelve signs in number. In this way which I shall tell you: imagine now that there were parts of the circle in which the Sun goes through the surface, twelve equal parts; and that great circles in the sphere divide them. And it is manifest that these circles will join each other at two opposite points. That is, for others, the greatest space that is between one and another is in the circle of the Sun only. And the more the two circles are elongated from the circle of the Sun, the more they increase. But when you have imagined this, it results that you know the space which is made in the sphere intersected by the two [circles] is every sign; the zodiac, however, is a circle from the middle of these. And this circle from the middle of these is the place where the path of the Sun and Moon and the other wandering planets always is. And because Ptolemy found the fixed stars which are in the zodiac to be of more manifest effect—because their motion is always in the path of the moving stars, and their powers are mixed more with the powers of the moving ones—he spoke first of their effects rather than the powers of the others, and he named them one by one according to the order of the signs.

The nature, therefore, of the stars existing in the vertex of Aries, when their powers are combined, are likened to Saturn and Mars.

The power of the tiny stars which are in the head of Aries is similar to the mixture that is made from the power of Saturn and Mars.

The twelve signs were named from the names of the figures which are in the zodiac; so that the name of any of them takes the name of the figure that is in it around the zodiac; because a figure existing outside the zodiac can be such that it takes up two signs. And it is manifest that since the fixed stars move over a long time, it happens that the names of the signs change when the figure will change from one sign into another. And when Ptolemy found many fixed stars to be those which are in one place, he grouped them; because their powers are mixed and become as one power. And he spoke of them as if they were one star, as he reported in that place: because the stars which are in the head of Aries have a power similar to a power mixed from Saturn and Mars. And it has already been made clear to us that the power of Saturn is to produce great cold and a little bit of dryness; and that of Mars is of the greatest dryness, so much so that it burns. Whence, according to this, it happens that the fixed stars which are in the head of Aries are of the greatest and complete dryness. They are tempered between heat and cold, but they tend more toward cold; afterwards it happens that they are cooled a little and dried much. And because they are of such a kind, it is appropriate that they produce in earthly things such effects as pertain to such a temperament; and others, according to the rules which we said before, ought to follow. For it is fitting that you store this in your memory regarding everything Ptolemy said in this reasoning. And thus you will not need a large commentary; now, however, listen to what Ptolemy teaches.

Moreover, the powers of those which are in its mouth are said to be similar to the powers of Mercury, and also somewhat like the powers of Saturn.

And the power of those which are in the mouth of Aries is similar to that of Mercury and a little to the power of Saturn.

**He means to say** that they cool and moisten a little.

Furthermore, the work of those which are in its hind foot does not differ from the works of Mars; and those located in its tail follow the powers of Venus.

And those which are in the hind foot have power like that of Mars; and those which are in the rump are similar to the power of Venus.

He taught us that in all the stars which are in the figure of Aries, dryness wins out; and they tend more toward the temperament of Mars.

# TREATISE

¶ Of the stars that are in **Taurus** <note>The Bull</note>, the nature of the one that sits upon his shoulder is not far from the nature of **Venus**, and it is also somewhat similar to the nature of **Saturn**.
¶ And those that are in the tail of the Bull have a nature similar to the nature of **Venus**, and are somewhat likened to the nature of **Saturn**.
¶ This is the second figure of the signs, and it means to say that the power of these stars is cold and moist.
¶ From the chest, however, the nature is proven to be similar to a mixture of the natures of **Mars** and the **Moon**.
¶ And those that are called the **Pleiades** <note>The "Seven Sisters" star cluster</note> have a nature similar to the nature of the **Moon** and **Mars**.
¶ **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer</note> gave a comparison to the **Moon** for these; and according to him, it is agreed that the Pleiades have a nature tempered between moisture and dryness, and that they tend toward heat; and it agrees with him that you should understand from Ptolemy: that if the stars which belong to two planets were equal in their likeness to both, they themselves would be of a tempered nature, and both would perform works pertaining to both planets; and if not for an equal nature, both would tend toward the nature of one.
¶ But of the stars in the vertex <note>top</note> of Taurus, the brightest and of a clear redness bears a likeness—it is called **Aldebaran** <note>original: "aldebaran"</note>—to that nature from which the nature of **Mars** is not distant. Of the others that are in the same place, their nature is equal to the nature of **Saturn** and bears a likeness to the nature of **Mars** for a little while.
¶ And concerning those that are in the head of Taurus, the nature of the shining one which is among them—whose color tends toward a deep vermillion, which is Aldebaran—is likened to the nature of **Mars**. The others that are there have a nature similar to the nature of **Saturn** and a little of that of **Mercury**.
¶ He said **Aldebaran** is plain; yet it is consistent according to him that the other stars which are in the head have a very cold nature, and that they produce dryness more than moisture, though sometimes they moisten.
¶ Those positioned in the tips of his horns perform the same as **Mars**.
¶ And those that are in the tips of their horns have such a nature as that of **Mars**.
¶ Likewise, of the stars situated in the sign of **Gemini** <note>The Twins</note>: those that are placed in their feet do not recede from a **Mercurial** quality, and they associate a little with the quality of **Venus**.
¶ Concerning the rest of the figure, those that are in the feet of Gemini have a nature such as that of **Mercury**, and it is likened a little to the nature of **Venus**.
¶ According to this, it is fitting that they produce moisture more than dryness.
¶ The brighter stars positioned in their body are equal to the **Saturnine** nature. Also, two large stars are impressed in their two heads: the first of which is likened to **Mercury** in its effects and is called **Auellar** <note>Likely Castor</note>; the other imitates the nature of **Mars** and is called **Abzacaleus** <note>Likely Pollux</note>.
¶ And of the shining stars that are in their body, the nature is such as that of **Saturn**. And of the two great stars that are in the two heads: the power of the former—that is, of those—is such as that of **Mercury**; and these stars are called in Greek **Askaion** <note>original: "askaion"</note>; this is the foot of Gemini. And the other star of those two has a nature similar to that of **Mars**, and it is called in Greek **Hercules**; this is the hand of Gemini.
¶ Likewise, in **Cancer** <note>The Crab</note>, the work of the two stars that hold their place in his foot is one and the same: it is likened to **Mercurial** works and mo-

<column-break/>

-derately to **Martial** ones. The nature of those in his claws <note>original: "azubene"</note> is not repugnant to the nature of **Saturn** and **Mercury**; but the work of that which is located in his breast and bears the likeness of a cloud, and is called **Meelef** <note>original: "meelef"; the Beehive Cluster</note>, is equal to the works of the **Moon** and **Mars**.
¶ And of these that are in Cancer, the work of the two which are in his feet is one and the same: they have such power as the star of **Mercury**, and it is likened a little to that of **Mars**. And those that are in the forward claws have power such as that of **Saturn** and **Mercury**. And those that are in his breast, which are likened to a cloud—and it is called **Presepe** <note>The Manger or Beehive Cluster</note>—have power such as that of **Mars** and the **Moon**.
¶ All **Astrologers** are in agreement that the stars which have the nature of **Mars** and the **Moon** are properly hidden from sight; and I say this is because of the great contrariety <note>opposition</note> that is in this power.
¶ The powers of the two stars which are on either side of **Meelef**—and which are called the **Two Asses** <note>original: "duo asini"; the stars Asellus Borealis and Asellus Australis</note>—do not recede from the powers of **Mars** and the **Sun**; and it is manifest that this nature hides and destroys.
¶ And the two that are around the Manger, which were called the two Asses, have a power similar to that of **Mars** and the **Sun**. And it is manifest that such a nature is hiding and condemning.
¶ Here **Ptolemy** gave a comparison to the **Sun**; and he means to say that these two stars produce great heat and dryness, and he showed superstition and the power of wisdom and other such things.
¶ But of the stars in **Leo** <note>The Lion</note>, the two which are situated in his head: their work is likened to **Saturnine** works and also a little to **Martial** ones. Of the three that are in his neck, their works are made equal to **Saturnine** works, and they are likened a little to **Martial** works. The bright star positioned in the heart of the Lion, which they call **Regia** <note>The Royal Star, Regulus</note>, works in the manner of **Jupiter** and **Mars**.
¶ And the two stars that are in the head of Leo have power such as that of **Saturn**, and it is likened a little to that of **Mars**. And the three that are in his neck have power such as that of **Saturn**, and they are likened a little to that of **Mercury**. And the shining one in the heart of the Lion, which is called **Regal**, has power such as that of **Mars** and **Jupiter**.
¶ This is the **Heart of the Lion** <note>original: "cor leonis"</note>, to which the ancient wise men gave the name "Royal," because it is more upon the zodiac than the other large fixed stars; and for this reason, they ranked it in the first magnitude, although it is for certain in the second magnitude.
¶ Indeed, the star positioned in his back and the clear star located in his tail are made equal to the powers of **Venus** and **Saturn**, and they imitate **Mercury** a little in their works. The two situated in this [region] do not depart from the powers of **Venus** and **Mercury**.
¶ And that which is in his spine, and the other shining one which is in his tail, have power such as that of **Saturn** and **Venus**, and it is likened a little to that of **Mercury**.
¶ Likewise, in **Virgo** <note>The Virgin</note>, of those in her **Spica** <note>The "Ear of Grain," the brightest star in Virgo</note>, and of those in her eye, as well as those figured at the tip of her southern wing: their works are not removed from **Mercurial** effects, and they are likened a little to the works of **Mars**. Other bright stars also, which are formed in her northern wing as well as on her back, do not differ from the works of **Mercury**, although they bear a little likeness to **Mars**. But the bright star borne in her northern wing, which they call **Almucedeme alacaf** <note>Vindemiatrix</note>, works like **Saturn** and **Mercury**.
¶ And of those that are in Virgo: this is the sixth figure, composed of the figure of a woman and the Ear of Grain. Those that are in her head and the southern wing which is in the head...

# BOOK ONE

### The Stars of Virgo and Scorpio

Her wings have a power like that of **Mercury** and are slightly likened to that of **Mars**. Other bright stars in her northern wing and those on her spine have a power like that of **Mercury** and are a little like **Mars**. The bright star in the northern wing, which is called the "foremost" in its rotation, possesses a nature like that of **Saturn** and **Mars**. We understand from this statement that the influence of **Mercury** prevails in the stars of the entire sign of **Virgo**.

But the work of the star called **Azimech Alaazel** <note>original: "azimech alaazel"; the star Spica, the brightest in Virgo</note> does not depart from the powers of **Venus** and is somewhat like **Mercurial** influences. Those placed at the very tips of her feet, and in that part from which the hems of her garment are drawn out, are equal to the powers of **Mercury** and **Mars**.

And the star which is called **Alziniee Alagzel** <note>original: "alziniee alagzel"</note>, meaning "the highest," has a power like that of **Venus** and is slightly likened to that of **Mercury**. And those that are at the head of the feet of the **Virgin**, in the place where her robes are greatly drawn out, have a power like that of **Mercury** and **Mars** in **Libra**.

These stars are in the figure of the **Virgin**, and yet they are in the sign of **Libra**; for **Libra** <note>The Scales</note> is composed in one part from the figure of the **Virgin** and in one part from the figure of the **Scorpio**.

And those stars that appear at the extremity of the two **Azubene** <note>original: "azubene"; the "claws" of the Scorpion, which now form the Scales of Libra</note> of the **Scorpion**, by their inherent works, imitate **Saturn** and **Mercury**; and those that occupy the middle of them are likened to the powers of **Saturn** and follow a small part of the temperament of **Mars**.

And the stars that are in the two anterior claws of the **Scorpion**: those at their tips have a power like that of **Saturn** and **Mercury**, and those in their middle have a power like that of **Saturn** and are slightly likened to **Mars**.

And from those stars which are in this body of the **Scorpion**, the eighth figure begins here.

Indeed, of those stars noted in the **Scorpion**, the powers of that bright one which claims a place for itself in his forehead do not depart from the powers of **Mars**. Also, of the three that are in his mouth, the middle one—which is the brightest and has a little redness, and is called the **Heart of the Scorpion** <note>original: "cor scorpionis"; the star Antares</note>—is not separated from the works of **Mars** and assumes a small part of the powers of **Jupiter**. Those, however, which are placed in the joints of his tail are likened to the powers of **Venus** and **Saturn**. But those placed in his sting imitate the powers of **Mars** and **Mercury**. Moreover, those located in the **Alatha** <note>original: "alatha"; likely referring to the "cloudy" star cluster M7 near the sting</note>, which bears a resemblance to clouds and follows after it, do not depart from the powers of **Mars** and the **Moon**.

The power of the bright stars in his forehead is like that of **Mars** and a little like **Saturn**. Of the three in his mouth, the middle one is bright, having a color tending toward a fine vermillion, and is called the **Heart of the Scorpion**, having a power like **Mars** and being slightly likened to **Jupiter**. Those in the nodes of his tail have the power of **Saturn** and **Venus**. Those in the jaw—and there is one held at the head of the tail—have a power like **Mercury** and **Mars**. And the stars likened to clouds that follow these—called **Iacba** <note>original: "Iacba"; from the Arabic *Al-Jabhah*, the forehead, though here applied to the tail region</note> in Arabic—have a power like **Mars** and the **Moon**.

Likewise, among the stars in **Sagittarius** <note>The Archer</note>: that which indicates the tip of the arrow is equal to the powers of **Mars** and the **Moon**. Those that express the form of his bow, and those figured in the place where the hand touches it, work like **Jupiter** and **Mars**. Those

Those set in his legs do not rank behind the powers of **Jupiter** and **Saturn**. The four that are in his tail are likened to the powers of **Venus** and **Saturn**.

The figure of **Sagittarius** is composed of a horse and a man drawing one arrow with a bow.
