### The Stars of Pisces

The stars in the **spine** do not reject the works of **Jupiter**, and for a short time, they imitate **Venus**. In the northern **thread** <note>original: "filo"; the cord connecting the two fish in the constellation Pisces</note>, however, they act as if **Saturn** and **Jupiter** were at work. Indeed, the bright star positioned above its **knot** <note>original: "ligaturam"; the point where the two cords of the fish are joined</note> bears a resemblance to **Mars** and a small amount of **Mercury**.

And from those stars which are in the **Two Fish**: this is their twelfth figure. Specifically, those in the head of the southern fish's chest possess the work of **Mercury** and a little of **Saturn**; those in its mouth have the work of **Jupiter** and **Mercury**; and those in its tail and the southern thread have the work of **Saturn** and a little of **Mercury**. Those in the body of the chest itself and in the spine have the work of **Jupiter** and a little of **Venus**, while those in the northern thread have the work of **Saturn** and **Jupiter**. The bright star which stays in the **ligament** is the "bone of the fish" <note>original: "os piscis"</note> and possesses the work of **Mars** and a little of **Mercury**.

Here is completed everything that has been spoken concerning the figures existing in the **Zodiac**, and concerning the stars that are within them.

### The Northern Constellations

Likewise, let us speak of the stars that are in the figures to the north of the circle of signs <note>the Zodiac</note>.

->**Concerning the stars existing in the figures which are on the northern side with respect to the Zodiac.**<-

We have shown before that the fixed stars existing in the **Zodiac** are of greater power and more manifest work than others; now we wish to show that the fixed stars in the northern figures are of greater power and more manifest work than those in the southern figures. For we say that the powers of the stars and the rays of their light fall upon us either at right angles or through angles greater than the angles of the rays of the southern fixed stars. For this reason, more of the powers of the northern stars reaches us than those of the southern ones. Because of this, **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose "Almagest" is the source of this star catalog</note> arranged the northern figures before the southern ones.

The bright stars formed in the **Little Bear** <note>original: "vrsa minori"; Ursa Minor</note> do not withdraw from the powers of **Saturn**, and they embrace **Venereal** qualities, though but a little. Those located in the **Great Bear** <note>original: "vrsa maiori"; Ursa Major</note> agree with the temperaments <note>original: "complexionibus"</note> of **Mars**. The stars likened to the "lesser Alatha" <note>original: "alatha"; likely referring to a specific star cluster or nebula</note> formed under its tail do not differ from the temperaments of **Venus** and the **Moon**.

The bright stars in the **Little Bear** have the power of **Saturn** and a little of **Venus**; those in the **Great Bear** have the power of **Mars**. And the star which is likened to a cloud above its tail has the power of the **Moon** and **Venus**.

Some astrologers have proven that when a star is of such a temperament, it destroys because of the great humidity that is within them.

The bright stars that signify the place of the **Dragon** <note>original: "draconis"; Draco</note> are equal to the powers of **Saturn** and **Mars**. The qualities of those in the "Ficarius" <note>original: "ficario"; likely a specific grouping within Draco</note> do not disagree with the qualities of **Jupiter** and **Saturn**. Those placed in the nape of its back do not set aside the powers of **Mercury** and **Saturn**; indeed, they even follow the powers of **Jupiter** and **Mars** at times.

The bright stars in the **Dragon** have a power like **Saturn** and **Mars**; those in the "fifth figure" must have a power like **Saturn** and **Jupiter**; and those in the modes of the spine have a power like **Saturn** and **Mercury**, and sometimes like **Jupiter** and **Mars**.

This is a great mixing of powers, and because of this, they perform

diverse works.

The bright star of a reddish color called **Azimech** or **Ariamech** <note>original: "azimech ariamech"; here referring to Arcturus</note> bears a resemblance to **Jupiter** and **Mars**. But those in the **Alfelta** <note>original: "alfelta"; Alphecca, the brightest star in Corona Borealis</note> exist as similar to **Venus** and **Mercury**. Those positioned in the **Man Sitting on His Knees** <note>original: "viro sup sua genua sedente"; the constellation Hercules</note> do not turn their face away from **Mercurial** temperaments. Some of those in the **Assange** <note>original: "assange"; from the Arabic "al-sanj," meaning the Lyre</note>, which is called the **Falling Vulture** <note>original: "vultur cadens"; the star Vega</note>, do not cast off the powers of **Venus** and **Mercury**. The stars of **Andromeda** are proven to have **Venereal** powers. The stars of the **Triangle** <note>original: "trianguli"</note> do not despise having the temperaments of **Mercury**.

And the bright star whose color tends toward vermilion, called **Azimeth Colanza**, has the power of **Mars** and **Jupiter**. Those in the "Foca" <note>original: "foca"; likely a corruption of Alphecca</note> have the power of **Venus** and **Mercury**. Those in the **Knees** have the power of **Mercury**. Those in the **Arnig**, which is a musical instrument called in Greek **Lora** <note>original: "lora"; Lyra</note>, one of which is the **Falling Vulture**, have the power of **Venus** and **Mercury**; those in the **Hen** have the same power. Those in the figure of **She who stands in the Cell** <note>Cassiopeia</note> have the power of **Saturn** and **Venus**. Those likened to "snow" in the **handle of the knife** have the power of **Mars** and **Mercury**.

Those in the **Arrow** have the power of **Mars** and a little of **Venus**. Those in the **Flying Vulture** have the power of **Mars** and **Jupiter**. Those in the **Dolphin** have the power of **Saturn** and **Mars**. The bright stars in the **Horse** have the power of **Mars** and **Mercury**. Those in the **Asnade**, who is a woman who has no living husband <note>referring to Andromeda as the "chained woman"</note>, have the power of **Venus**; and those of the **Triangle** have the power of **Mercury**.

# First Book

...have a greater power in us and in the lands: in the southern regions, they possess a greater power than the northern stars.
¶ It is manifest that the bright star formed in the mouth of the **Southern Fish** <note>original: "meridiani piscis"; likely the star Fomalhaut</note> is similar to the powers of **Venus** and **Mercury**. Those located in the body of the same fish are equal to **Saturn** in their effects. The powers of the stars in the figure of the **Strongest One** <note>original: "fortissimi"; likely Orion the Giant</note>—specifically those in both of its shoulders—do not differ from the powers of **Mars** and **Mercury**. Meanwhile, the effects of the other bright stars in that figure do not deviate from the works of **Jupiter** and **Saturn**. The last and brightest star of the **River** <note>original: "riui"; the constellation Eridanus</note> imitates **Jupiter**, while the others imitate **Saturn**. Those that designate the image of the **Hare** <note>Lepus</note> are not inconsistent with the powers of **Mercury** and **Saturn**. All the stars situated in the **Dog** <note>Canis Major</note>, except for the one placed in its mouth, operate the same way and are likened to **Venus**. The bright star formed in its mouth—called **Albabor** <note>original: "albabor"; the star Sirius</note>—does not rank below the works of **Jupiter** and is associated slightly with the works of **Mars**. The complexion of the bright star situated in the **Little Dog** <note>original: "percane"; Canis Minor, specifically the star Procyon</note> equals the complexions of **Mercury** and a little of **Mars**. The works of the bright stars representing the form of the **Great-Hearted One** <note>likely Leo</note> are likened to the works of **Saturn** and **Venus**. Those placed in the **Cup** <note>Crater</note> do not despise **Venusian** compositions and imitate **Mercury** slightly. Those placed in the constitution of the **Raven** <note>original: "corni/coruo"; Corvus</note> are similar to **Saturn** and **Mars**. The bright stars expressing the image of the **Ship** <note>Argo Navis</note> are equal to **Saturn** and **Jupiter**. In the **Centaur**, those which maintain its human form bear a resemblance to **Venus** and **Mars**. However, the clear stars situated in its equine form operate like **Jupiter** and **Venus**. The bright stars placed in the form of the **Wolf** <note>Lupus</note> do not deny **Saturnine** powers, nor **Martial** ones, though only slightly. Those placed in the **Altar** <note>original: "turribulo"; Ara</note> are similar to **Venus** and somewhat to **Mercury**. And the complexions of the bright stars in the **Southern Crown** <note>Corona Australis</note> do not forget the **Saturnine** and **Martial** complexion.
¶ And Haly says: the bright star in the mouth of the **Southern Fish** has the power of **Venus** and **Mercury**, and those in the chest have the power of **Saturn**. Among those in the **Giant** <note>Orion</note>, those in the shoulders have the power of **Mars** and **Mercury**, yet other bright ones in it have the power of **Jupiter** and **Saturn**. Among the stars of the **Hare**, they have the power of **Mercury** and **Saturn**. All in the **Dog**, except the one in the mouth, have the power of **Venus**. The bright one in its mouth—which is **Albabor** <note>Sirius</note>—has the power of **Jupiter** and a bit of **Mars**. The bright ones in the **Raven** have the power of **Mars** and **Saturn**, and the bright ones in the **Ship** have the power of **Saturn** and **Jupiter**; the larger of these is called **Rubayl** <note>an Arabic name for a star in Argo Navis, possibly Canopus</note> in Arabic. Those in the **Taraapoz** <note>an Arabic name for Centaurus</note>—which is a figure composed of a man and a horse—those in the human figure have the power of **Venus** and **Mars**, and those in the equine figure have the power of **Venus** and **Jupiter**. The bright stars in the **Wolf** have the power of **Saturn** and a little **Mars**. Those in the **Galaxy** <note>the Milky Way</note> have the power of **Venus** and a little **Mercury**. The bright ones in the **Southern Crown** have the power of **Saturn** and **Mercury**.

<column-break/>

¶ **Haly said:** Here he completes whatever **Ptolemy** <note>the famous 2nd-century astronomer</note> spoke regarding the figures of the **fixed stars** <note>stars that do not move relative to each other, unlike "erratic" planets</note>. Before this, he will teach how you may know the power of any individual star. It is appropriate, when you find any of them having a power composed of more than one planet, that you know for certain it operates the same as those planets do—specifically by the work of the lesser power—because those planets operate in the same way. Always place the stars of the **first magnitude** <note>the brightest stars</note> in the position of greater power, and after them those of the **second magnitude**, and so you shall order their powers according to the arrangement of their sizes. Similarly, you shall grant greater power to those that are closer to the **Zodiac** <note>the path of the Sun</note> and less power to those that are far from it. Likewise, you shall grant more power to a northern star than a southern one, and more to one at the **zenith** <note>the point directly overhead</note> than to one that is not. One united with a planet in longitude and latitude (or longitude alone) has more power than one that is not. You can learn this in this way: take the locations of the fixed stars from the **Almagest** <note>Ptolemy's definitive astronomical manual</note> or another book, on a sphere or other instrument. Make a meridian circle and an altitude circle, and other things which Ptolemy teaches you in the 4th treatise of the Almagest. Find the ascendant and look on the sphere to see which fixed stars are on the horizon, which are in the middle of the sky, and which are with an **erratic planet** <note>the Sun, Moon, and 5 visible planets</note> in longitude; then mix their power with the powers of the seven planets. Thus you shall know. It is fitting for you to know that these stars are weakened or strengthened according to their place in respect to the ascendant, and by their signs in respect to the Sun, Moon, and the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>. Truly, because these stars do not return <note>they do not have retrogradations like planets</note>, they operate with **humidity** until they are separated from the Sun; they are **Eastern** until the Sun sets in their portion; they operate with **heat** from the left quarter until the Sun is opposite them; they operate with **dryness** from the opposition to the right quarter; and they operate with **cold** from the right quarter until the Sun is in longitude with them. Generally, know that whatever happens to the seven planets happens to the fixed stars. You can verify whatever Ptolemy said of their powers in the manner described by looking at their colors, if you wish to know this for yourself.

### ¶ On the Strengths of the Four Seasons. Chapter 10.

**Two** are the things by which it is necessary for us to know the general powers of the four seasons of the year. One is that when we wish to know the change of the air through the works of the stars, we shall judge what the stars demonstrate in comparison to the general composition of that season; and then we shall know whatever is in the air every day. The other is that through these seasons, we shall know the reason why the signs were divided into twelve.

---

### The qualities of the strengths of the stars in themselves, as tested from ancient times, are as follows.

**The powers** of the stars through their essence are according to the rectification of the ancient wise men.

---

### He means to say that he has now taught us the essential and accidental powers of the stars according to what the ancient sages learned through experience.

¶ The seasons of the year are said to be four: **Spring**, **Summer**, **Autumn**, and **Winter**. In the time of **Spring**, **humidity** is stronger; for after the cold of winter has passed, the heat begins, leading to a balance of humors <note>bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament</note> which were frozen by the winter cold. In the time of **Summer**, because of the Sun's approach to our **zenith**, **heat** prevails. In the **Autumnal** time, **dryness** conquers; for the heat of the past summer has dried up the moisture. In the **Winter** time, because of the Sun's removal from the place of our **zenith**, **cold** overcomes.

It also introduces the elemental qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—associated with the four seasons.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on astronomical influences, transitioning from the properties of fixed stars to a detailed explanation of the four seasons, the division of the zodiac into twelve signs, and the 360-degree system. It attempts to reconcile the views of Ptolemy and the commentator Haly regarding the elemental qualities of the seasons.</meta>

# Treatise

Similarly, there are four seasons of the year: **summer**, **autumn**, and **winter** <note>original: "estas: autunnus: et hyems"; spring is implied by the following sentence</note>. And in **spring**, moisture prevails, because after the cold of winter, heat begins to liquefy the moisture that was frozen by the winter cold; and in **summer**, heat prevails because the sun is at the zenith of our heads and in the southern climates. And dryness prevails in **autumn** because the heat of the summer that has passed dried up the moisture; and in **winter**, cold prevails because the sun is far removed from the zenith of our heads.

He means to say that in spring, moisture prevails because the temperate heat of spring thaws the moisture and draws it upward, mixing it with the air so that it becomes humid. Yet we find that **Haly** <note>original: "Hal."; likely Haly Abenragel or Haly ibn Ridwan, famous medieval commentators on Ptolemy</note> seems to go against this, where he said that the temperament <term>complexion; the balance of the four qualities of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</term> of spring is temperate. However, we wish to bring agreement between these two wise men for this reason: **Ptolemy** indeed holds that the heat of spring is such as the heat and moisture of **Jupiter**, which is temperate; and he says this previously. Nevertheless, in this place, he wished to follow more famous opinions: because a temperate temperament, which is suitable for life and growth, tends more toward heat and moisture. For this reason, there is no disagreement between these two sages. Similarly, summer heats things because the closer the sun approaches our heads, the more it heats; because it remains above the earth longer on any given day than below the earth. And because its rays fall at right angles—or near right angles—they double the ray through reflection <note>original: "reverberationem"; the medieval idea that sunlight "bounces" off the earth to create more heat</note>, and it heats us more through the joining of the rays. And because the sun lasts longer above the earth, it is fitting that heat should prevail in summer. And because summer, with its greatest heat, purges the moisture, it happens that in the coming autumn after summer, dryness prevails. And in winter, when the sun remains below the earth longer than above, the rays reach us at acute angles rather than right angles. Thus, there is reflection upon them, and only a small power from the sun’s rays is joined in the air; and for this reason, it happens that cold prevails in winter. It is visibly manifest that the cold of winter freezes moisture. Our teacher <note>original: "Doc. n."; likely referring to the author's primary authority or "Doctor"</note>, understanding that **Saturn**—because it is very cold—freezes moisture and binds it; and because heat is then produced, they are thawed and flow. For this reason, **Saturn** causes an increase in waters and streams by accident. Because the sun makes these changes by its own course through the circle of the signs <note>the zodiac</note>, it happens that the circle of signs is divided into four parts: the first part where the sun travels throughout the time of spring; the second where it travels throughout the time of summer; the third where it travels throughout the time of autumn; and the fourth where it travels throughout the time of winter. And it is fitting in every way that these parts be equal: because the sun always ascends toward the northern part until it reaches the **summer tropic** <note>the Summer Solstice</note>; and then it descends from the north until it reaches the **autumnal equinox**. Afterward, it descends toward the south until it reaches the **winter tropic** <note>the Winter Solstice</note>. Then it ascends from the south until it reaches the **vernal equinox**. These parts are indeed equal, as he showed in the **Almagest** <note>Ptolemy's definitive work on astronomy</note>. And since this is so, and we find that each of the four seasons has a beginning, an increase, a decrease, and a fading in the qualities belonging to them, it is fitting in every way that each of these four parts of the sphere be divided into three parts. Thus, the temperament of the first part of spring is near the temperament of the last part of winter; the middle part is the proper temperament of spring; and the temperament of the third part is near the temperament of summer. We shall say the same for the other seasons. And it is fitting according to the art of the **Tetrabiblos** <note>original: "quadripartitum"; Ptolemy’s four-part book on astrology</note> that these four parts be equal, not just by the art of nature; for sometimes we feel that the temperament of any season goes on increasing, then lingers in one way, and afterward diminishes. And sometimes we feel it equally, so that the time of growth, the time it lingers, and the fading are all of one manner. Furthermore, because the **Moon** traverses its course every month through the 12 signs, and meets the **Sun** twelve times in a year, each revolution produces things in the air similar to those the sun produces in a year. For this reason, it is fitting that each of the four parts of the zodiac be divided into three natural parts, so that the zodiac consists of 12 parts.

<column-break/>

These equal parts are called **signs**. The number of degrees mentioned certainly fits because it follows the daily course of the sun. For the sun travels in different ways; sometimes it goes faster and sometimes slower. The time of a whole year is 365 days and a fraction of a day. The ancient sages searched for a number from many parts in which there would be no fraction and which would be near this number; they found that it is **360**. They divided the zodiac into that many degrees because that number is easier than the others, and because this number does not stray much from the first one each day. For when we divide the 5 extra days and the quarter-day into 365, the perceptible difference does not change for any single day. Now it has been shown to you that the twelve parts are natural, and the 360 degrees are based on the establishment of the sages. For if they had been natural, it would be fitting for there to be more than 360 degrees according to the sun's daily course. The ancient sages divided each degree into 60 parts, to which they gave the name **minutes**, and the minutes into 60 **seconds**, and so on to infinity, so that the number might be easier and more certain. And since this is so, it is fitting that each sign be **30 degrees** by establishment; yet by nature, it ought to be as many degrees as the number of days the sun takes to traverse one sign. However, if the apogee <note>original: "aux"; the point where the sun is furthest from Earth</note> were movable, it would be fitting that in those same places where the sun's motion is slowed at one time, it should go faster at another time; and thus the 12-fold division is born through 360 parts, and not just by establishment.

**Therefore, since the circle of signs lacks a natural beginning—as does any circle—they placed its beginning at the sign of the vernal equinox, which is Aries.**

And since the zodiac has no natural beginning—just as no circle has a beginning—the beginning was established from the whole sign where the vernal equinox starts; and this is the sign of **Aries**.

He means to say that it does not have a specific point by nature, but they placed the point at the point of the vernal equinox; and this is the sign of **Aries**. Some people, hearing this said, believed that the zodiac is only divided into twelve parts because of the twelve figures <note>constellations</note> that are in the zodiac. But it is otherwise: because it was divided by this number, they named each part after the figure naturally encompassing that number.

**Namely, they took it from that beginning from which the moist temperament grows, just as in the first part of the ages of a life, there is a time in which their temperament is most moist.**

And they placed the beginning in the firmament at the place where the temperament of the season is most moist, just as the first age of animals is in the time when their temperament is at its most moist.

He means to say that the ancients followed nature in this and found that temperate moisture in animals is at the beginning. For this reason, they said it was fitting that the birth-beginning of the firmament should correspond to that same age: which is the beginning of spring. This is because nature makes earthly things follow the celestial bodies, and thus they are always following them.

**And in the same order, they established the other seasons. For in the temperament of all living things, moisture prevails in the first years, just as in spring. In those years, it is soft and tender. In the second years, up to the station of heat, it is perfect; just as heat prevails in summer. In the third years, in which it is near its decline and around the beginning of its lessening, dryness is stronger, just as in autumn. And in the final years, in which it reaches destruction, coldness overcomes it, just as in winter.**

And the other three seasons follow according to this: because the first temperament of an age is moist, like spring; and animals in this age are tender and mild. The second age is hot, as if the heat of the animals is complete, just as it is in the summer time. And the third age, since it begins to lessen, is dry, just as...

It establishes Aries at the vernal equinox as the starting point of the zodiacal year due to its association with life-giving moisture.</summary>

<header>Book One</header>

...in autumn: and the fourth and final age, which is near decay <note>original: "corruptionem"; referring to the end of life or the breaking down of physical form</note>, is cold like winter.
¶ He means to say that the ancients followed the justice of nature; and since nature makes earthly things similar to celestial things in every way—because the celestial are substances just as the earthly are substances, and the celestial are durable in themselves while the earthly are durable through generation <note>meaning species continue through birth even if individuals die</note>—there are traces of the celestial in the earthly. It follows from this that when we wish to demonstrate the nature of celestial bodies, we should take our evidence from the effects we see among us. And just as the first stage of a man’s life [childhood] is more moist, it is fitting that the first part of the year is spring, because it is more moist. The other seasons following spring correspond to the other ages coming after childhood, and this is a manifest reality: for we can not only understand it with our minds but feel it with our senses. And **Ptolemy** has already shown you the power that the beginning of the year holds; if I understood well what he said before, all things formed in the beginning remain firmly in that state which is generated until they decay. And by these words, it is demonstrated to you that the first quarter of the zodiac is hot and moist, like a sanguine child. The second quarter is hot and dry, like a choleric youth in summer. The third quarter is cold and dry, like a melancholic <note>original: "melicũ"; an abbreviation for melancholicum</note> man in autumn, showing the beginning of aging. And the fourth and last is cold and moist, like a phlegmatic, decrepit man in winter.

### On the strengths of the four angles and the four parts of the horizon. Chapter II.

In the same way, we must speak regarding the qualities of the four locations of the horizon and the angles from which the blasts of the winds begin toward every part.
¶ Similarly, the state of the four locations on the horizon and the angles where the movements of the winds begin through all parts.
¶ He means to say that the sun, which overcomes all things, works in these locations; and just as in the seasons of the year, the stars help him, as we will teach later.
¶ For in the part called the East <note>original: "oriens"</note>, dryness is stronger because when the sun moves through that part, it does not stop drying whatever the night has moistened; and because the winds that emit their blasts from that part—generally called Eastern winds—are deprived of all humidity and are drying.
¶ That which prevails in the East is dryness, because the sun, when in this part, begins to dry whatever the night moistened; and the winds that move in this part, which are generally called *Solani* <note>The "Solanus" is the traditional name for the East wind</note>, are without humidity and are desiccating.
¶ He means to say that dryness prevails in the air of the East for any people, relative to their Western air, because the sun begins to dry the Eastern air. Until it sets, dryness grows greatly in the Eastern parts, while what it dries in the Western parts is modest, because it does not stay there long, and when it sets, the night moistens it. The proof of this certainty is what we see in the Eastern winds: they all dry, and they almost never bring rain.
¶ The Southern part <note>original: "meridiana"</note> is the hottest, because the heat of the sun is greatest when it stays in the middle of the heaven <note>the zenith</note>; and since this part, regarding the position of our region, is to the right, the winds that proceed from that part are generally called Southern winds, which are hot and burning.
¶ And the part of the South is very hot because of the great heating of the sun which is in the middle. And this part, in respect to our habitations, tends toward the South, and the winds moving from this part, generally called *Meridionales*, are hot and burning.
¶ Ptolemy spoke very well when he said "in respect to our habitations," because if we were to place another population in the South,

<column-break/>

the North would be to them what the South is to those of us who live here. For the South is hot and burning to us in respect to our habitations because the sun is directly over that part for the whole year and creates many reflections of its rays.
¶ The Western part <note>original: "occidentalis"</note> is moist, because when the sun stays in that part, those things which the day dried begin to be moistened by the night; and the winds proceeding from there, which we generally call Western winds, soften and moisten. The Northern part <note>original: "septentrionalis"</note> is the coldest, because the causes of heat which fall upon us—due to the sun being in the middle of the heaven according to the position of our location—are very far removed from us. And since it is placed in opposition to the sun occupying the middle of the heaven, the winds proceeding from this part are very cold and constricting <note>freezing</note>.
¶ And the Western part is moist, because when the sun is in this part, things dried in the day begin to be moistened; thus the winds moving from this part, generally called Western, are moistening. ¶ The Northern part is very cold because the things creating heat through the presence of the sun in the middle of the heaven are moved very far from this part when we look at it in respect to our habitations; for it is as if in opposition to the sun when it is in the middle of heaven. The winds moving from this part, generally called Northern, are freezing.
¶ He means to say that toward the Northern parts, in respect to our habitations, the sun always approaches in the same way it does for us in winter, and for this reason, it is cold.
¶ The knowledge of these things is valuable and profitable for recognizing the temperaments <term>complexions; the balance of qualities</term> of all parts at every hour. This is because it is plain and open that the efficient power of the stars changes according to the qualities of the seasons of the years and the angles.
¶ And in these things, there is great profit and help for knowing the temperaments of all parts at any time; for it is manifest that the virtue with which the stars work is changed according to the state of the seasons, the ages, and the angles.
¶ Ptolemy said clearly here that knowing this gives great profit in knowing the virtues of the stars; and after the works of the stars receive change—as he showed us in the third chapter—it is fitting that they are changed through the temperament of the parts, the ages, the angles, and other things.
¶ For when all things are purely similar to them, their qualities will be without any mixture of anything else. Therefore, their works will be stronger. For example: stars that naturally heat are stronger in hot modes, and stars that similarly moisten are stronger in moist modes. However, their powers in the contraries of these modes are not pure, but mixed with other things and are weak, just as it happens with the strengths of heating stars in desiccating modes. We should not doubt that the same happens in all other modes according to the mixture of qualities.
¶ And when the conditions are similar to them, their quality will be pure and without any mixture, and their work will be of greater virtue; just as stars that naturally produce heat have greater power in hot conditions, and moist stars in moist conditions. And if they are in conditions contrary to them, they will not be pure, but mixed with others and weak, just as...

...the power of hot stars in cold states, and of moist stars in dry states. And all other things are according to the mixture of qualities.

<gloss>From here onward, **Ptolemy** teaches us the powers of the signs, just as he taught those of the stars.</gloss>

These things having been established, it follows that we should add the proper changes of the parts of the circle of signs <note>the zodiac</note> just as they have come down to us.

<gloss>¶ And after we have said these things in this manner, it is fitting that there follows a discussion on the natural changes proper to the parts of the zodiac signs, according to what has reached us through other wise men.</gloss>

<gloss>After he proposed to speak of the stars, times, and angles, we understand from this that the zodiac of signs is divided into twelve parts. For he said that it is fitting that we speak first of the natural changes pertaining to each sign according to the rectification <note>meaning the refined calculations or traditional assignments</note> of the ancient wise men.</gloss>

¶ These are the general temperaments <note>original: "complexionis"; the balance of qualities like hot or cold</note> of the seasons which are assimilated through them.

<gloss>¶ Because the general temperaments which any of them possess are assimilated to the seasons that occur through them.</gloss>

<gloss>The reason for this statement is what we said before: that the power of each of the signs can be understood through the general temperament that is similar to its effect; at the time when the sun is in it, it is also demonstrated by what was said before, that we understand the powers of the celestial bodies only by comparison with the sun and moon. And because the sun pertains more to the zodiac of signs—as is shown in quadrivial astrology <note>the "quadrivium" was the advanced part of the medieval curriculum, including astronomy/astrology</note>—it follows that we should know the powers of the signs through the change of its [the sun's] effects.</gloss>

¶ And also certain of their properties which are assimilated to the sun, moon, and the rest of the stars; which we will mention in the following after the aforementioned powers of the signs in themselves without any other mixture, which we assign to them only from the comparison of one to another.

<gloss>¶ Since some properties of the signs are sometimes due to the relationships they have with the two luminaries <note>the sun and moon</note> and other stars, which we will mention after we have spoken of the powers of the signs without other mixture, when they are judged by themselves in respect of one to another.</gloss>

<gloss>¶ He says that the powers of the signs are of three kinds: one is due to the relationship they have with the stars, of which he will speak hereafter; after he has spoken of the two [other] kinds, of which one is that which is proper to each sign by itself, and the other is the relationship which one has in respect to another.</gloss>

¶ Indeed, the first difference of the signs is that some of them are called **tropical** <note>also called "movable" signs</note>, some **equinoctial**, some **fixed**, and some **common** <note>also called "bicorporeal" signs</note>.

<gloss>¶ For the first differences which the signs have are that some of them are called movable, some signs equinoctial, some fixed, and some bicorporeal.</gloss>

<gloss>He wants to say that the effects of some of them change from one thing to another; some have temperate effects, some indeed fixed, and some mixed of two things.</gloss>

¶ For the tropical ones are two [sets of] 30 degrees, which follow the point of the summer solstice without interval: and they are the degrees of **Cancer**—

<column-break/>

—degrees. And also others in 30 degrees following the point of the winter solstice in order, which are the degrees of **Capricorn**. These, however, are designated by these names for this reason, since it is manifest that this happens in them. For when the sun reaches the beginnings of these two signs, it then turns back toward a motion in latitude <note>original: "latitudine"; referring to the sun's north-south movement along the ecliptic</note> contrary to the motion it had before. And when it is in **Cancer**, it makes summer. In **Capricorn**, indeed, it makes winter.

<gloss>¶ Because these two signs are movable: and these are the 30 degrees which follow the tropical point of summer, up to the end of **Cancer**. And the first 30 degrees which follow the point of the winter tropic and is the end of **Capricorn**. And they imposed such names on them because they were fitting to them: because the sun, when it is in the beginning of these two signs, changes to a motion in latitude different from the motion it had before: and when it is in **Cancer** it makes summer, and when it is in **Capricorn** it makes winter.</gloss>

<gloss>¶ He means to say that these names imposed on them are derived from the natural demonstration they have in themselves: for that which he said, that the sun changes in its motion of latitude, is shown in quadrivial astrology.</gloss>

¶ There are also two equinoctial signs: namely, the sign following the point of the vernal equinox in the first place, and these are the degrees of **Aries**. And the sign following the point of the autumnal equinox in order, which is the sign of **Libra**. Indeed, they receive this name from this, because it undoubtedly happens in them. For when the sun enters their beginnings, the days are made equal to the nights everywhere.

<gloss>¶ And these two are called signs of temperance <note>original: "temperantie"; referring to the balance of day and night</note>: and these are the first following the point of the spring equinox, and it is the sign of **Aries**. The other is the point which follows the point of the autumnal equinox, and it is the sign of **Libra**: upon which such names were imposed because they were fitting to them: because when the sun is in their beginning, the day is equal with the night in all equal parts.</gloss>

<gloss>¶ We understand from this and from other statements similar to it that the signs do not have in themselves a natural effect except insofar as the effect by which the power of the sun and other stars is changed when they are in them; and thus the signs are seen to be the matter <note>the signs act as the medium or material through which the planetary influence is expressed</note>.</gloss>

¶ Of the remaining eight signs, which are located between the tropical and equinoctial signs, four are called **fixed** and four are called **common**. The fixed ones are those which follow the two solstitial and two equinoctial signs: which are **Taurus**, **Leo**, **Scorpio**, and **Aquarius**. This is because the changes of the four seasons—which begin when the sun enters the solstitial and equinoctial signs—follow these; and they are when the air is changed to moisture, or to heat, or to cold, or to dryness. They are fixed and appear more clearly whenever the sun stays in these fixed signs. The quality of the air then naturally exists pure. For through the long durability of these qualities, it receives their powers most openly.

<gloss>¶ And of the eight signs remaining from these—namely, those which are between the movable and temperate signs—there are four which are called fixed, and four which are called bicorporeal. ...observed that the air inclines toward moisture and dryness, or heat or cold. These qualities are more firm and persistent when the sun is in these **fixed signs**, and the natural states of the air are then pure. Because they endure for a long time in these states, they receive their full power; this reception is so manifest that we feel it.

¶ This means that when the sun is in these signs, we only feel the state proper to that operation purely and without mixture, because the air remains in one state for a long time.

¶ **Common signs** <note>Also known as mutable signs</note> are those which appear immediately after the fixed signs: namely **Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius,** and **Pisces**. They are called "common" because they are placed between the movable and fixed signs, and in their beginnings and endings, they are similar to the natural change of both qualities belonging to the movable and fixed signs.

¶ **Signs of "two bodies"** <note>A literal translation of the Greek 'dikoryphos' or 'bicorporeal', referring to the dual nature of Gemini, Sagittarius, and Pisces (and traditionally Virgo)</note> are those that follow the fixed ones: and these are **Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius,** and **Pisces**. They stand between the movable and fixed signs and share in the natural change with their beginnings and ends, proper to the two states of movable and fixed signs.

¶ **Ptolemy** stated clearly in this place that two signs of the seasons <note>Aries and Libra</note> are movable, because when the sun enters any of them, the time <note>the season</note> changes. For **Aries** changes from winter to spring, and **Libra** from summer to autumn. Furthermore, he assigned the reasons why these others were called "of two bodies": because the beginning of **Gemini** has a likeness to the air of spring and its end with the air of summer. The beginning of **Virgo** has a likeness to summer air and its end with autumn air. The beginning of **Sagittarius** has a likeness to autumn, and its end with winter. And the beginning of **Pisces** has a likeness to winter air and its end with the air of spring. And since the sun's own natural movement changes through these signs, it is fitting that they have powers with which each of them performs two different operations.

### On masculine and feminine signs. Chapter 13.

They judged six signs to be of a **masculine** and **diurnal** <note>daytime</note> nature; the remaining six they referred to a **feminine** and **nocturnal** nature. They arranged them one after another for this reason: because the day adheres to the night and always exists alongside it, and because the masculine sex is near to the feminine and they are frequently joined together.

¶ Similarly, they placed six of these signs in a masculine and diurnal nature, and the other six in a feminine and nocturnal nature, and they ordered them one after another because the night always comes after the day and around the day, and because the female always goes with the male and around him.

¶ This means that the ancient wise men followed the eleventh <note>likely a reference to a specific tradition or numbered rule</note> in this division, those who had experience in this and set them down according to their position through experience, ordering them according to nature: because the female follows the male and night follows day.

¶ They took the beginning of this matter from **Aries** for the reasons mentioned before: and also because males dominate and act, it is more fitting that they should be preceding, as they are more honorable than those who are passive. For this reason, they made the beginning with a masculine sign. The signs of **Aries** and **Libra** are masculine and diurnal because the **equinoctial circle** <note>the celestial equator</note> extends over them, from which the first and strong motion—which is called the motion of the firmament—takes its origin. The order of the two signs following these is as we have said: namely, a feminine after a masculine, and

<column-break/>

after a feminine, a masculine.

¶ The beginning of this is from **Aries** for the reasons we have stated. Because the male is the leader of workers and senior in greater power than the passive one, they placed the male first. Therefore, the signs of **Aries** and **Libra** are masculine and diurnal because the equinoctial line passes through both of them, and from there begins the greatest change of the whole firmament. However, the other signs following them were ordered according to what we said: namely, one after the other.

¶ The reason which **Ptolemy** gave for starting from **Aries** is because of what the sun does in the seasons of the year, and because the power of the beginning is to be placed before that which follows. Similarly, because the motion of the whole is from east to west upon the poles of the equinox, it is fitting that **Aries** and **Libra** have senior power over those signs. And because the power of **Aries**, which is the very first, should have senior power over that of **Libra**, and because the others are ordered according to how nature ordered night after day and female after male. Since the male is the leader of workers and set over the female in power and order, it is fitting that **Aries** be masculine, **Taurus** feminine, **Libra** masculine, and **Scorpio** feminine, and so in all the others: because masculine signs are diurnal and feminine ones are nocturnal.

¶ Some, however, began the order of the sex of the signs starting from the **ascendant** <note>the 'horoscopus' or rising sign</note>.

¶ And some ordered the masculine and feminine signs beginning from the sign of the ascendants.

¶ **Ptolemy** makes us understand through this statement that the reason the ancient wise men knew the twelve **houses** is the same reason they knew the twelve signs. For the line of the horizon circle and the meridian line divide the firmament at any hour into four parts, as we said before. These places of the parts are called the **angles** of the ascendant: because these four are similar to the four points of the seasons of the year. Since according to the natural order of the year the first point is **Aries**, it is fitting that this point ascends in the ascendant so that the four points of the seasons of the year are on the meridian line and the horizon line. Similarly, this is because of the similarity of the nature of the signs that are in these points: for when one is **movable**, all four will be movable; when one is **fixed**, all four will be fixed; and when one is **of two bodies** <note>mutable</note>, so all four will be. Furthermore, when planets are rising on the horizon, the power coming from them extends to all things in a straight line to everything on the whole horizon, just like the rays of the sun, which cause the whole horizon to shine at the hour the sun rises to the ascendant. The same is true of the power of the **Midheaven angle** <note>the 10th house</note>: for when planets are there, the lines of their rays which come to a point on the horizon are equal to those which come to the other opposite point, and in all ways they will be just as far from the west as from the east. Because of this, it is fitting that the four angles have great power, just as the beginnings of the four seasons of the year have. And because the matter is as we have said, it is fitting that the firmament places itself at any hour into twelve parts for the reasons mentioned before, and each part into thirty degrees, just as the ancients divided the signs.

¶ Similarly, the wise men looked and found further that the **ascendant** is the beginning, because it will be the first thing from under the earth; and they placed it as the lord of the beginning of the soul and the body. They placed the angle opposite to it <note>the 7th house/Descendant</note> for the house of opposite pairs, and of women's affairs, and for husbands and wives. And they found the angle of the **fourth house** <note>the Imum Coeli</note> similar to the point of the summer season <note>original: "estivalis"</note>, because when **Aries** is the ascendant, the fourth will be **Cancer**. Because the power of the sun is greatest when it is in the point of **Cancer**, they placed it as the house of the father, and its opposite <note>the 10th house</note> as the house of the mother. And because the angle of the fourth house is the point beneath the earth, they placed it as the house of earthly inheritances and secret things, because **Saturn** has great power in it, who is cold and dry like the nature of the earth. Similarly, because between the sun and the tenth house there is a great similarity—for when it is in the middle of heaven, its power extends to every part—they placed the tenth as the house of kingdoms and ministries by which one lives.

Afterward, they looked to the third house and found it was cadent <note>Falling away</note> from the 4th; and because of its great similarity—for it is the house of Mercury, whose power is mixed above others and always has its course near the sun—they established it as the house of brothers, relatives, and short changes <note>Short-distance journeys</note>. Similarly, because it is in sextile to the ascendant, it has a similarity with the moon in making quick changes; they established it for the joy of the moon. And because the power of the moon is opposite the power of the sun in moistening, they established it for the joy of the sun; and because also the sun has great power in the triplicity of Aries, since Aries is its exaltation; and its triplicity is similar in name to the house.

And because the 7th is the house of equals and they are somewhat distant from the parts, just as the 6th and 7th are distant, they established it (the 6th) as the house of servants. ¶ After the ancient wise men extracted the demonstrations of the 12 houses by this reasoning, they tested them and found many times by experience that it was as they had proposed; hence they stabilized them. and because Ptolemy <note>original: "Pto."</note> did not name anything in his book except the "roots" or foundations of stability, he did not labor in explaining all of this; but he spoke of those things which are above the earth, because they have a greater influence than those below the earth. ¶ Just as some began the movable signs from the sign of the moon: since a fast motion happens to the moon more than to the other planets.

The tropics <note>The turning points of the seasons</note> are similar to those which the sun makes through all the signs each year; and for this reason, the ancients took the beginning of the movable signs from the sign of the moon; and they established a movable principle, another fixed, and another of "two bodies" <note>Mutable</note>, just as they did in the signs with respect to the course of the sun.

For a man can categorize things according to the figures from which he can help himself in this science. I feared, indeed, that it would be superfluous to declare all these things in this place.

¶ This means that the ancient wise men gave many names to the signs according to the figures of the fixed stars belonging to them and according to the figures of their operations, by demonstrating the operations of the signs by themselves and through the powers of the fixed stars that are in them. For from this comes the power by which one operates on the things that are among us, in a manner similar to that figure which is in heaven. He says that by this a man can know what we said before about the stars and signs. And because these operations change because of the movement of these figures from one sign to another over long periods of time, he held that it would be superfluous to declare it in this place. He means that whatever is necessary from that will be said later. But I want to teach you those things which happen in this our time.

And the **feathered signs** are those in which there is the figure of birds, such as the Vulture and the Hen. ### On the affinities of the four signs and their figures. Chapter 14.

Indeed, the first affinity among similar parts of the circle of signs is that which is held in the figures. Just as there are parts between which there is the length of one diameter <note>The diameter represents the "Opposition" aspect of 180 degrees</note>, and which stretch across two right angles <note>A right angle is 90 degrees; two make 180 degrees</note>: these are six signs and one hundred and eighty degrees. There are also parts between which is the trine length <note>original: *trina*; the 120-degree aspect</note>, and which contain one right angle and a third of another: these are four signs and one hundred and twenty degrees. There are also parts between which is the square <note>original: *tetragona*</note> length, which contain one right angle: and these are three signs and ninety degrees. Likewise, there are parts between which is the hexagonal length <note>The 60-degree "Sextile" aspect</note>, which contain two-thirds of one right angle: and these are two signs and sixty degrees.

¶ The parts of the sphere of signs that have a similarity with one another are, first, those that share in the figures of aspect. These are those which have between them one diameter comprising two right angles: six signs, which are 180 degrees. And those that have a distance of three [signs] <note>The text likely means the Trine, which spans 4 signs, or perhaps refers to the third part of the circle</note> and comprise one right angle and a third of another: these are four signs, which are 120 degrees. And those that have the distance of a fourth <note>The "Square" aspect</note> comprising one right angle: three signs, which are 90 degrees. And those which have the distance of a sextile comprising two parts <note>two-thirds</note> of a right angle: two signs, which are 60 degrees.

### In this, he who understands anything of geometry needs no explanation; from this is understood the error of those who spoke about the projection of rays or equal degrees.

¶ Moreover, the reasons why we ought to observe these lengths alone and no others we shall learn from what follows. For the reasons for observing the length of one diameter manifest themselves because, in its opposition, the points are distant according to a straight line. When we consider the two major parts in which there will be a harmony between the quantity of the part and the quantity of the whole, these remaining figures shall be established.

¶ You will understand the reason why these distances are only for those who judge by what we shall now say. I say that the reasoning which judges by the distance of the diameter is demonstrated of itself, because it is the opposite point along a straight line. When they consider the two major parts in which there will be a harmony of the quantity of the part and the whole, these remaining figures are constructed. Therefore, the harmony of the parts will be such that we do not accept those [aspects] in which there is no agreement, but rather those that possess more. And from these, the other aspects are made.

### Figure of the aspects.

¶ He wishes to say that the ancient sages do not judge by any other distance except by these aforesaid ones, because the diameter divides the circle through the middle and by a straight line. One point of the straight line becomes opposite the other: because when one point is in the ascendant <note>the eastern horizon</note>, the other will be in the descendant <note>the western horizon</note>; and when one is in the middle of heaven <note>the Midheaven or 10th house</note>, the other will be in the angle of the earth <note>the Imum Coeli or 4th house</note>. He says that from the arc which the diameter makes, when the major musical proportions are seen—those in which harmony falls—other distances are formed, which are the trines.

¶ Through the harmony of the part, it will be so: when we assign to the length of two right angles the proportion of the diameter's length, we take its half and its third. The half of its length is the square aspect <note>tetragona</note>, and its third is the hexagonal length <note>sextile</note>. From this [the third] doubled, the trine length is established.

¶ Regarding the agreement of any respect to the distance which makes two right angles: this is the distance of the diameter. We take the half and the third of the half: from the half comes the distance of the fourth <note>the square</note>, from the third comes the sextile distance, and from the double of that comes the trine distance.

¶ He wishes to say that regarding the distance of the diameter—because it is a manifest thing—the ancient sages took it as a rule for aspects when it has the power of participation with another. For when we take half of the arc of the diameter, it becomes the 4th <note>the square, 90 degrees</note>. When we take a third, it becomes the sextile <note>60 degrees</note>. When we take two parts [two-thirds], it becomes the trine <note>120 degrees</note>. If we double the 4th, it becomes the opposition. If we double the sextile, it becomes a trine. Thus, from the same source can come an opposition, a trine, or a sextile. It will be in a "crossroad" <note>original: *quadriuio*</note>; the manifest half and the third are the major parts if a proportion is to fall.

¶ Through the harmony of the whole, it will be so: when we have made a proportion from the square distance to the two other distances. The proportion of one will be "one and a half" <note>original: *sexquialtera*, a 3:2 ratio</note>, and the other "one and a third" <note>original: *sexquitertia*, a 4:3 ratio</note>. When we assign the proportion from it to that which is less than it, the hexagonal length <note>sextile</note> becomes the same as the "one and a half" ratio. When we assign the proportion to that which is greater, we establish the trine length as the "one and a third" ratio.

¶ To harmonize one part of the double: and thus when it is in respect to the distance of the fourth which makes a right angle.

its proportion to the two lengths is only the proportion of the whole and a half <note>original: *medij*; referring to the sesquialteral ratio of 3:2</note>; and the sesquitertial proportion <note>A ratio of 4:3</note> is another proportion of the whole and a third; and it is called "sextertia." With respect to the greater proportion of the whole and a half, the **sextile** <note>An aspect of 60 degrees, or 1/6th of the circle</note> elongation is formed; and when it is with respect to the greater proportion of the whole and a third, it is the **trine** <note>An aspect of 120 degrees, or 1/3rd of the circle</note> elongation.

He means to say that we shall take the agreement of the whole and a part in the matter: because that which is the half of the half-circle <note>90 degrees</note> will produce the sextile elongation and the trine length from it. According to this, if we take the amount as a sextile, and the half of a sextile, 4 signs are produced from it; and this proportion of 4 signs to the sextile is the proportion of the whole and a half <note>4 signs (120°) to 2 signs (60°) is a 2:1 ratio, but the text here navigates complex medieval harmonics</note>. And when we take the amount as a fourth <note>a square aspect</note> and its third more, it becomes a trine; and this is the proportion of the whole and a third. And if you understand anything of <term>geometry, arithmetic, and music</term> <note>These, along with astronomy, formed the "Quadrivium," the four mathematical arts of medieval education</note>, you will be able to understand this very easily. Indeed, Ptolemy demonstrates this in his *Four-Part Book* <note>original: *Quadripartito*; the Latin title for Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*</note>, and he does not neglect the **Quadrivium**, since he demonstrates according to nature.

<margin>Chapter 15.</margin>
<margin>Haly says.</margin>
And so, they called these trine and hexagonal <note>sextile</note> affinities "agreeing," for the reason that they are formed from signs that agree in their nature: for they are all either masculine or feminine. But those which are formed from the diameter <note>opposition</note> or from the tetragonal figure <note>the square aspect</note>, they named "disagreeing," because they are always found to be in opposition to the signs of their own kind <note>original: *genere*; gender or category</note>.

And we call the participations that are of the trine and sextile "accorded" <note>harmonious</note>, because they are composed of signs accorded in nature: since either both will be masculine, or both will be feminine. Those, however, which are in the diameter or upon the fourth <note>the square</note> are not accorded, because they are not found among signs accorded in nature.

Behold the perfection of Ptolemy's great intelligence, for he treated these elongations through gradual proportions and modes, and he wished to put them into practice until the reason for them could be known from it. You will say that these gradual lengths are agreement and discordance in another way: for the signs that are in the figure of the trine or sextile are agreeing, such that both are masculine or both are feminine. But the fourth <note>square</note> is discordant: because if one sign is masculine, the other will be feminine, and vice versa. And the signs that are upon the diameter are discordant: because the Sun makes the time in one of them according to that which it makes in the other, its opposite. Similarly, when one ascends, the other descends. In the fourth, they change the time in every single way; for this reason, it is agreed that the trine aspect is fortune, friendship, and agreement. Likewise the sextile; and the ancient wise men said that because the sextile is half of the third <note>half of a trine</note>, it is a medium fortune and friendship; and because the fourth is half of the opposition, they said it is a medium enmity.

### On the high and low signs, which are called commanding and obedient.

<margin>Haly says.</margin>
## This is another manner of agreement that the signs have among themselves according to nature.

<margin>Chapter 15.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'P' within a square frame decorated with floral motifs.</image-desc>
Indeed, those parts whose distance from any one and the same point of the **equinoctial points** is the same are called "high" and "low": and they are those whose ascensions and descensions are completed in equal times: because they are carried in equal circles on the straight circle parallel to the equinoctial circle.

Just as they call the parts that are elongated equally from one known point of the two equinox points the "high" and "low" parts: and these are those that have ascensions and descensions with equal times, because they are in equal circles among the circles equidistant from the equinox.

He means to say that the ascensions of one of them are like the ascensions of the other, and similarly the descensions: since the ascensions of the whole of **Aries** are equal to the ascensions of **Pisces** in every city; and those of **Taurus** to those of

<column-break/>

**Aquarius**; and those of **Gemini** to those of **Capricorn**; and those of **Cancer** to those of **Sagittarius**; and those of **Leo** to those of **Scorpio**; and those of **Virgo** to those of **Libra**: and according to how it is fitting that the first degree of Aries should be accorded with the last degree of Pisces, it is the same for all others.

Moreover, those parts that are formed in the middle of the **summer circle** <note>the signs near the Summer Solstice</note> are called "high" <note>original: *sublimes*</note>; and those that are in the middle of the **winter circle** are named "low" <note>original: *infime*</note>: for this reason, that when the Sun proceeds through the middle of the summer circle, it makes the days longer than the nights. But when it illuminates the middle of the winter circle, it shows the days to be shorter than the nights.

And the parts that are in the half of the summer circle are called high, and those in the half of the winter circle are called low: since when the Sun is in the middle of the summer circle it makes the day greater than the night, and when it is in the half of the winter circle it makes the [night] <note>implied correction: the night greater than the day</note> greater than the day.

Since the day is nobler and stronger than the night—because the movements of animals are stronger, and reason appears more than in the night, and by another manner through the power of the Sun, which appears by day when the virtues of all things come together—for this reason the ancient wise men said that the parts of the summer time are called "high" and noble: because the Sun, when it is in them, is at its greatest height, compared to when it is in the middle of the winter circle. Similarly, they called them "commanding" things <note>original: *comadatas*</note> and called the others "low" and "obedient": by comparing the better reason of the power which the high parts have over the low. For in all these things we gain the knowledge of two great and good things: one is the agreement that exists between these parts; the other is that when we find two births <note>horoscopes</note> that are accorded in one degree, we shall know that he whose significator is in a degree of a low sign will be **obedient** to him whose significator is in a degree of a high sign. For astrologers have said these degrees are concordant in power.

### On the signs looking at each other and being equal in their strengths.

<margin>Chapter 16.</margin>
<margin>Haly says.</margin>
## This is another manner of agreement of signs and degrees and the aspect of one to another: and Ptolemy noted this to make clear to us that the signs have many participations according to nature.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'S' within a square frame decorated with foliage.</image-desc>
Thus, just as there are certain parts that are equal to other parts in their strengths: such as those whose distance from any one point of the two **tropic points** <note>The solstices (Cancer and Capricorn)</note> is one and the same: because when the Sun passes through any of these two points, the day of one of their nights will be equal [to the other], and the times of the hours will be the same.

Just as they hold that some parts are equal to others in power: and this is when they are elongated equally from one point of the two tropics, summer or winter: since when the Sun is in either of these two parts, the day of one part is equal to the day of the other, and the night equal to the night; and the times of both hours will be equal.

This is because the Sun will be in a line equidistant from the equinox: since it will be in these two parts that are equally distant from the tropic. They also say that these parts look at one another by the aforesaid occasions: and that each of them rises from the same parts of the horizon in the East, and is occupied in the same parts in the West.

And they said that these parts look at each other for the aforesaid reason: and because each of them rises from the very same point of the horizon, and similarly sets.

He means to say that two degrees which are equally distant from the point of either of these two tropics are said to look at each other: because the days and nights of both are equal, and they both rise from one point of the horizon, and similarly they set; and because of this they are accorded, and their powers are equal.

# First Book

<margin>Commentary</margin> <image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'A' featuring a standing figure in a landscape with a building.</image-desc> Indeed, those parts <note>original: *Artes*, likely a transcription error for *Partes*</note> that are called "foreign" to one another are those between which there is no affinity based on the aforementioned relationships. They are not joined by being "perceiving" signs, nor "obedient" signs, nor by "looking" at one another as equals in strength. Nor are they among those positioned through any of the four figures that have a joined affinity: namely, through the diameter of the figures (opposition), the triangle (trine), the square (quadrate), or the hexagon (sextile).
<margin>Ptolemy</margin> And the degrees which are called "divided" and "wandering" <note>original: *peregrini*; planets with no dignity in their current location</note> are so when one has neither a similarity with another, nor any sharing of the types we have mentioned. They are not among those that command or obey, nor among those that look at one another as equals in power, nor among those that have a similarity in any of the four aspects—opposition, trine, square, or sextile.
<margin>Commentary</margin> **Ptolemy** teaches you through this order which signs and degrees look at one another, either by being on two lines equidistant from the equinox <note>original: *egnocetio*, a corruption of *equinoctio*</note>, or by both being on the same line equidistant from the equinox, or those distanced from another by a diameter, a trine, a square, or a sextile. These are the three aspects that are effectively six, because three of them are double-sided: the trine is of two types, as are the square and the sextile. He has already given you the natural reasoning for these aspects in his previous words.
<margin>Gloss</margin> However, the parts that we find are in no way associated through these modes are those between which one or five signs are contained. This is because the parts that have one sign between them do not "look" at each other; they are positioned obliquely to one another. Those parts between which five signs are located do not divide the circle into equal parts.
<margin>Ptolemy</margin> And the three types <note>of relationships</note> we find that have no sharing of any kind are those that are one sign or five signs apart. Those that are one sign apart do not look at each other because each is inclined away from the other. Regarding the five signs between them: they do not divide the circle into equal parts as the four <note>geometric</note> figures do.
<margin>Commentary</margin> Each sign near these is inclined 60 degrees from the other in ascending and descending. Those that are 5 signs apart do not divide the circle into equal parts; they have neither a "crossroads" (square) nor a "uniting" distance that could allow for agreement or disagreement. Just as the beginning of the sixth sign is inclined from the beginning of the seventh, so is the beginning of the ninth inclined from the Ascendant in the rising and setting places. Now you have been able to understand the aspect of signs with one another—the four aspects and no more. Other aspects that are not such, as Ptolemy said, are "intermediate" between joining and separating; they concern the application <note>the approach of one planet to another</note> as far as the distance of the degrees between them allows.
<margin>Commentary</margin> After we have spoken of the powers of the stars and signs, we wish to explain what Ptolemy said regarding the "participation" <note>sharing of influence</note> that parts have with the signs. If this is known, it will be useful when a planet enters any sign or degree to know what kind of power it has. Where we find that a planet rules most by its own power, we understand that sign and degree to be more suitable to that planet, and vice versa. For this will be the rule for knowing the sharing that planets have with the signs.

### On the houses of the five wandering stars, the sun, and the moon.
### Chapter 18.

<margin>Commentary</margin> <image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'A' with a profile portrait of a man's face.</image-desc> The parts <note>original: *Artes*</note> of the circle of signs which are called houses, triplicities, exaltations, and terms have a similarity; those signs in which the seven planets <note>the "wandering stars"</note> have some similarity or dignity are likened to them.
<margin>Commentary</margin> There are certain locations and parts of the zodiac signs that fall to the seven planets and are called houses, tripli-

<column-break/>

-cities, exaltations, and terms, and other such things with which they share a partial similarity.
<margin>Ptolemy</margin> **Ptolemy** holds, through the ordering of these powers, that it is fitting for a "house" to come before the "lord of the triplicity," the triplicity before "exaltation," and exaltation before "term." <note>This refers to the hierarchy of planetary strength in a specific degree of the zodiac</note>. When he mentioned "other such things," he said it because of his opinion on the sharing they have with the sun—such as the "face" <note>a 10-degree subdivision</note> and the "light," which he will discuss later. Ptolemy was not the only one to place the lord of exaltation before the lord of triplicity; for we find that Dorotheus proposed the lord of triplicity as the cause of the form.
<margin>Commentary</margin> It is the nature of the houses that I shall subjoin: Since there are twelve signs, two are northern—those namely which are closest to the zenith of our heads. These generate heat by their nature. Because these are Cancer and Leo, they were attributed to the two greatest and most noble luminaries as their houses. They assigned the sign of Leo, which is masculine, as the house of the Sun. The sign of Cancer, which is feminine, they established as the house of the Moon.
<margin>Commentary</margin> Regarding the houses, I also say this: the two northern signs of the twelve which are highest toward our zenith, and for this reason produce heat, are Cancer and Leo. Both were placed as the houses of the two great and noble lights: Leo, being masculine, as the house of the Sun; Cancer, being feminine, as the house of the Moon.
<margin>Commentary</margin> The two signs that are truly at the head of the north are Gemini and Cancer. But because Gemini heats and moistens—being the end of the spring signs—nature placed the two lights in two other stars <note>signs</note>. Gemini does not agree with them: it does not agree with the Sun because the Sun dries while Gemini moistens; nor with the Moon, which is feminine and nocturnal, while Gemini is masculine and diurnal. It was not suitable for Gemini to be the house of either of the two lights. Instead, it was fitting for Cancer and Leo to be so. Leo is the Sun's house because it agrees with his nature, being hot and dry. Since the Moon follows the Sun, it was fitting for her house to be near the Sun's house. The signs near the Sun's house are Cancer and Virgo. Because Virgo is dry, it was not suitable for the Moon, who is moist. Therefore, they established Cancer, which is moist, as the house of the Moon. When he said they are "more toward our zenith" and "therefore produce heat," he means to say that through the aforementioned region, the north comes to be such that the figures in this part are more suitable for signifying the fertility of the people than any others, because of the heat they produce in nature, by which all things grow.
<margin>Commentary</margin> They called the half of the circle from Leo to Capricorn the "Solar" half. The other half, from Aquarius to Cancer, they called the "Lunar" half. Thus, in each of the two halves of the circle—the solar and the lunar—each of the planets would have a house suitable to it, according to the order of their spheres and their natures.
<margin>Commentary</margin> For this reason, they set the half of the zodiac from Leo to Capricorn as the solar half, and the other half from Aquarius to the end of Cancer as the lunar half. This was so that each of the five wandering planets might have a house in each half of the two luminaries, according to what fits the arrangement of their spheres and their natures.
<margin>Commentary</margin> He means that the ancient wise men found that the powers of the two lights (Sun and Moon) rule over everything, and each of the five wandering planets follows them and possesses lesser power. Since they did not have power on their own without the lunar powers, this was the case before our time. For this reason, it is fitting that each of the five wandering planets has a sign in the solar half that suits its composition and is its own through solar power, and the same in the lunar half.
<margin>Commentary</margin> Because Saturn is naturally cold and contrary to heat, and his sphere is the highest and most remote from the luminaries, they assigned to him the two signs Capricorn and Aquarius, which are in opposition to Cancer and Leo. This was because these two, namely Capricorn and Aqua-
