This total agrees with the total degrees of the Egyptian terms <note>The "Terms" or "Bounds" are specific segments of a zodiac sign where a particular planet has special influence. The "total" refers to the sum of degrees assigned to each planet across the whole zodiac.</note>, and it is fitting that these terms which Ptolemy sets down are more certain than those in the Egyptian terms. For we find that they work more effectively than the Egyptian ones, although Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of astrology</note>, Dorotheus, Mellius, and other astrologers collected the Egyptian terms more than others and judged by them more frequently. Since these have been used for a great length of time, it is appropriate for us to accept them; Ptolemy himself spoke of them before others for this reason. And I say to you that it is fitting for you to act in whatever situation arises: look to the degrees you wish to examine, and see who is the lord of that degree according to the aforementioned opinions. If two opinions agree on one planet, you shall accept that one and no other. If there is only one opinion, see if there is any agreement or participation between its nature and the nature of the "luminary" <note>The Sun or the Moon</note> that is the lord of the half-sign in which that degree resides. You should accept this especially if the luminary aspects that place and is in a strong position. However, it is always appropriate to look first to the Egyptian terms, then to Ptolemy's terms for the reason he stated, and subsequently to the Chaldean terms. When the lord of the terms according to any of these opinions has some "dignity" <term>Dignity: A planet’s strength or influence in a particular sign based on its position.</term> in that sign, you should accept him before any other. This matter is consistent with what we have said regarding Ptolemy's opinion; for he had no reason to name three opinions unless he held that this was the truth. Thus, it is fitting that we do as he said.

### On the Twelfth-parts. Chapter 22.

Indeed, there are some who have divided the signs into parts even shorter than those mentioned before, calling them "places" and "degrees." Specifically, they called a "place" the twelfth part of a sign <note>original: "duodecimam unius signi partem"</note>, which consists of two and a half degrees. They also assigned lords to them: the lords of the houses according to the succession of the signs.

Others divided the dignities into even smaller minutes than those we have mentioned, and gave them the names "places" and "degrees." Regarding the "place," they said it was one of twelve parts of a sign, which are two and a half degrees each, and they assigned the lords of the houses to them according to the order of the signs.

**The calculation** for this is as follows: look at the number of degrees you wish to know the "twelfth-part" <note>Also known as Dodekatemoria</note> for; multiply them by 12, and then subtract thirty degrees for each sign, starting from the sign in which those degrees are located. Where the count ends, the lord of the house of that sign is the lord of the twelfth-part you seek. You shall mix his judgment with that of the lord of the bound <note>The "lord of the bound" refers to the planet ruling the broader segment of the sign mentioned in the table above.</note>.

Some others, however, divided the signs into other parts—namely into segments of ten—following the order which the Chaldeans followed in the order of the terms.

And others divided them differently into parts <note>The text likely refers to the "Faces" or "Decans" here.</note>, following what the

<column-break/>

Chaldeans followed in ordering the terms.

This means they divided each sign into 10, 10, and 10 degrees, so that the sign is divided into three equal parts, and in each part one planet rules. For we find that the ancient wise men used two methods: one is called the "Faces" <term>Faces (Decans): 10-degree segments of a sign, each ruled by a different planet.</term> and the other "Vorunge" <note>This likely refers to a Persian or Arabic technical term for a specific subdivision, possibly related to the "Steps" or "Degrees" of a sign.</note>. For the Faces, they gave the first face of Aries to Mars, who is the lord of the house; the second to the Sun, who follows him in the order of the spheres; and the third they gave to Venus, because she follows the Sun. And they gave the first face of Taurus to Mercury, who follows Venus, and the second to the Moon, who follows Mercury, and the third face of Taurus they gave to Saturn, and the first of Gemini they gave to Jupiter. And so on in this manner. The way to find this number is as follows: look at the number of signs from Aries to that sign, including that sign in the count; multiply this by 3 and divide by 7 until seven or less than seven remains. Start from Saturn according to the order of the planets; where the number ends, that planet is the lord of the first face of that sign, and the following planet is the lord of the next face. Another manner, which is called "Voxonege" <note>Likely a variation of the term "Vorunge" mentioned above, referring to specific subdivisions.</note>, is what Ptolemy alone mentioned: those who divided the ascending sign into three equal parts and gave the first part to the lord of the Ascendant, the second to the lord of the 5th house, and the third to the lord of the 9th, so that they would always be of one triplicity <note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note>.

And it is manifest that these people followed the lords of the triplicities in the ordering of the parts, just as the Chaldeans did in the ordering of the terms. And others divided the signs into three equal parts in another manner which you will find in books of astrology. And others divided the sign into 9 parts, and gave it the name "Neubabar" <term>Neubabar (Navamsha): A 9-fold division of a sign common in Indian astrology, later adopted by Arabic and Latin authors.</term>. But Ptolemy holds that these opinions are not reliable, nor does any experience confirm them; for this reason, in all his judgments, he casts them aside.

But since the method of these people is inconsistent, we believe it should be set aside; however, the other method which we ought to imitate, because it is consistent, we shall follow.

And after these things have been said—that they lack stability and do not follow the opinion of nature—we wish to deviate from them. And we shall begin to speak of another method which is fitting by reason.

Observe how Ptolemy teaches you to abandon words that have no stability and do not follow natural things, and how you should adhere to firm words following only the path of nature. In this you will gain much and avoid the labor and pain of a thing that is not profitable.

Therefore, regarding the Twelfth-parts and the terms, we shall begin from the two equinoctial points and the two solstitial points, as the authors of books have explained. Because the forces of nature and their similarities are properly grasped there, they began only from the two equinoctial points and the two solstitial points as we said before; nor did they have any occasion to begin from anywhere else. For if it were necessary to find another beginning besides these, it would follow that nothing could be gained in the perfection of this science, or that it should be observed and proceed in a way that is useful. For if anyone conceded...

¶ It is fitting, therefore, for us to begin the twelfth-parts <note>original: "duodenarijs"; these are 2.5-degree subdivisions of a zodiac sign, also known as dodekatemoria.</note> and the terms from the four tropical points <note>The "tropical points" are the two equinoxes and two solstices which mark the beginning of the seasons.</note>. For those who compiled the books of this art have taught us so. For if we were to establish another starting point, it would lead us to say either that the fulfillment of this art did not enter through these points, or that it is completed through them—and we would be in error if we began from another place.

¶ Ptolemy teaches us that the virtues coming to us from the stars, which change the four elements—minerals, plants, and animals—work all of this by means of the air. He teaches us that to know the virtue of any of these, one must compare it to the Sun, who rules and triumphs over all things. Since this is so, it follows that we must know the virtues of their degrees in comparison to the four tropical points.

They are also the degrees of the terms of the fortunes, and the degrees in which there are fixed stars of the nature of the fortunes—and conversely, the degrees in which there are stars of the nature of the misfortunes <note>The "Misfortunes" or "Infortunes" typically refer to Saturn and Mars.</note>.

¶ Other astrologers have spoken much about the degrees and divided them into those that are bright, slippery <note>original: "lubricos"; often interpreted as "void" or "pitted" degrees that weaken a planet.</note>, and smoky; and those from which a group is led, and those from which one is thought of; and they have spoken of many other things, as

when these points are specifically more notable and manifest among us than the others; because the Sun, which is the thing through which we know all things that are in the heaven, changes the season from one state to another when it reaches one of these points.

And because of this, Ptolemy said that for one taking this from any other place except these four points, it follows that he would say their nature is not a thing that ought to enter this art; and he who begins from another place will err. In this place, he teaches us how we may know the virtue of any degree of the signs by taking them in comparison to these four points, just as we know the virtue of the stars in comparison to the Sun. And when we know this, we will be able to arrange them well by this number. For that which has the greater harmony, we shall give the power of the House; and afterward, to the following one, we shall give the power of the Triplicity; and afterward the Exaltation; and so in the terms, twelfth-parts, and other dignities. For through this, Ptolemy gave us a way to know for certain the virtue of any degree of the signs, and what kind of harmony it has with any planet. This is the opinion of Ptolemy, which agrees with the philosophers, because it is always valid for a man to demonstrate the hidden by the manifest. We, however, find others who divided the signs into masculine and feminine degrees. And here we place an end to this our reasoning.

# Book One

...in their own **face** <note>original: "facie"; a "face" or decan is a 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign</note> because of the sharing of the geometric relationship they have with the Sun or Moon. This occurs in such a way that between any planet and the Sun or Moon, there is a distance equal to the distance between that planet’s own house and the house of the Sun or Moon. For example: if Venus were in **sextile** <note>A 60-degree aspect, considered harmonious</note> to one of the luminaries. However, it is necessary that she be "western" from the Sun and "eastern" from the Moon; and in this way, the state of being "face to face" will exist for any of the planets with the two luminaries.

**This** strength, namely, the planets gain through the relationship we observe between them and the houses of the two luminaries. For every wandering planet <note>original: "planeta erraticus"; the five planets excluding the Sun and Moon</note> has two houses because of the shared nature each has with the luminaries. Those planets that have their houses aligned with the two houses of the luminaries gain greater power when the distance between the planet and a luminary is the same as the distance between their respective houses—measured to the middle of the house itself. For example: let Mercury be in the 2nd sign from the Sun and in the 12th from the Moon; Venus in the 3rd from the Sun and the 11th from the Moon; Mars in the 4th from the Sun and the 10th from the Moon; Jupiter in the 5th from the Sun and the 9th from the Moon; and Saturn in the 6th from the Sun and the 8th from the Moon. For with such a configuration, the planet gains as much great power as if it were in its own house, because of the sharing between their houses and the houses of the luminaries.

**This** also follows the *alchinara* <note>A term derived from Arabic astrology referring to a specific type of planetary dignity or "shining"</note> which occurs when a planet is in its own **haiz** and in similar places suitable to it.

**A luminary** is also described in this way when it is in its own **haiz** or in a place that has harmony and concord with it.

**Haiz** <note>A condition of planetary strength based on the planet's gender, the time of day, and the sign's gender</note> is when a masculine planet is above the earth by day in a masculine sign, or below the earth by night; and a feminine planet is in a feminine sign above the earth by night, or below the earth by day. And that which is "similar to haiz" is when a masculine planet is in a masculine sign, and a feminine planet in a feminine sign; and when a diurnal planet is above the earth by day, or a nocturnal one above the earth by night. This is the definition upon which the community of astrologers has agreed. But **Ptolemy** says that **haiz** is when a planet is in a place suitable to it and with which it has concord. He assigned this to those planets in the **angles** <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses of a chart, representing the most powerful positions</note> or those following them (the "succedent" houses) as being "advancing," and those in the "cadent" houses as being "retroceding." Here they have taken the leadership of the planets: and this is when a planet is in its **haiz** in some "angle" of the Sun by day or the Moon by night. They say a planet is "exalted" above another planet when it is to the "right" of it, so that it is above the earth in respect to the other.

**Whenever** a planet holds two or more "authorities" <note>original: "auctoritates"; referring to essential dignities like house, exaltation, etc.</note> in a location, it is said to be in the place of its **joy** and **honor**. Their powers are then increased because they are assimilated to the signs in which they reside, which aids their strength. They are also said to "rejoice" with the signs in which they are placed in the aforementioned way, even if they are not perfectly assimilated; rather, the planets which are outside their **haiz** are assimilated to those very places—which, though the similarity may be very remote, is nonetheless present.

**And** when it happens that any planet has two or more dignities in a certain place, they say it is in the place of its joy and honor. Then its power in operation increases because of the similarity the sign in which it resides has with it, and because of the concord it has with its own nature and the help given to it. They say the planet "rejoices" even if it does not harmonize with the sign in which it exists, because of the concord we have mentioned. For places harmonize with planets that are of their own **haiz**; and though this participation is from afar, it is still participation, and therefore they gain strength.

**Ptolemy** names in this place the "states" of the planets in respect to one another; and he says that planets "rejoice" and are fortified when they have a shared participation—namely, one with another—through a secondary concord, whether natural or

<column-break/>

accidental. This is true even if the planet itself is not in a sign suitable to it. For a planet’s status is diminished and weakened when it has a relationship with another planet that is discordant to it, whether by accident or by nature. Now, these "states," according to what many of the wise have said, consist of **eleven complete modes**, for all other states are referred back to these eleven and return to a single root. This is because a light planet <note>A planet with a faster orbital speed, like the Moon or Mercury</note> always exhibits its power to a heavy one <note>A planet with a slower speed, like Saturn or Jupiter</note>, unless the light planet has so many dignities in the sign where it resides that it overcomes the heavy one in virtue.

¶ **The first mode** is **giving strength**. This is when a planet is in any of its own dignities and "applies" <note>original: "applicans"; an 'application' is when a faster planet moves toward an aspect with a slower one</note> to another that has greater power than itself; then they say it has "given its strength."

¶ **The second** they call **giving nature**. This is when a planet applies to another that is the lord of the house, triplicity, or dignity in which the first planet resides.

¶ **The third** they also call **giving nature**. This is when two planets themselves apply to each other, and each of them is in some dignity belonging to the other.

¶ **The fourth** is called **light**. This occurs in two ways: one is when a planet "separates" <note>moves away from an aspect</note> from an aspect with one planet and applies to an aspect with another; for then it "transfers" the nature of the first to the second. The other way is when one planet applies to another, and then that second one transfers the nature of the first to a third, even though the first does not apply to the third.

¶ **The fifth** they call **returning light**, and this is in two ways. One is when two planets apply to a single planet and do not "see" each other; they call this receiving planet the "collector" because it brings the light of one back to the light of the other. The other is when one planet applies to two or more, and these planets do not "aspect" each other; the one applying to them brings the light of one back to the other. And if a planet that "collects" the light looks toward any part of the firmament, they say the planet itself brings the light of the others to that very place. Afterwards, when it happens that planets which have between them a natural or accidental concord—either through any of the aforementioned dignities such as house, exaltation, triplicity, term, **haiz**, or **joy**—have these relationships between them, they possess greater strength and power in their operation.

¶ **The sixth** they call **prohibiting light**. This occurs in two ways. One is in **conjunction**, such that three planets are in one sign at different degrees, and a heavy planet is at a higher degree. For the one in the middle "prohibits" the first from applying to the heavy one until it has passed it. If the one at fewer degrees than the heavy one is in concord, it is bad; if it is discordant but the one in the middle is in concord, it is better. The other way is when two planets are in one sign and the lighter applies to the heavier, but another planet applies to the same heavy one by an aspect. The one with the heavy planet in the same sign "prohibits" the one aspecting it from applying, if the degrees are equal; however, if the one in aspect is in degrees closer to the heavy one, its application will take precedence.

¶ **The seventh** is **returning virtue**. This is when a planet applies to a planet that is **retrograde** <note>Appearing to move backward</note> or **combust** <note>Too close to the Sun, thus weakened by its heat</note>. For that retrograde or combust planet returns its power to the one applying to it. If both are in "angles" or succedent houses, or the light one is in an angle, the return will be profitable; but if the light planet is "cadent" <note>in a weak house</note> and the heavy one is in an angle, or both are cadent, the return will be with loss.

¶ **The eighth** is called **transit**. This is when a planet moves to apply to another, but before it reaches it, it leaves that sign and passes into another; then another planet of few degrees in that same sign "aspects" and applies to the heavy one with an application similar to the first.

¶ **The ninth** is **stumbling** <note>original: "cespitatio"; often called 'frustration'</note>. This is when a planet wants to apply to another, but before it applies, it becomes retrograde, and the application itself is destroyed.

¶ **The tenth** is called **disturbance**. This is when a light planet is at many degrees and a heavier planet is at few degrees; another lighter planet wants to apply to the heavy one, but before it applies, the first light planet (at many degrees) becomes retrograde and applies to the heavy one, passing through it while retrograding, and applies to the one that was lighter than it.

¶ **The eleventh** is **cutting off light** <note>original: "abscissio luminis"</note>. This is when a planet moves to apply to another, but there is a second planet in the sign next to the heavy planet; before the first can apply, the planet in the second sign becomes retrograde and joins with the heavy one, cutting off the light of the first light planet. Similarly, when a planet moves to apply to another, and that second one moves to apply to a third heavier than itself, and before the light one applies to the middle one, the middle one applies to the heavier one; and thus the light is cut off.

<summary>This page defines specific planetary strengths such as "Face" and "Haiz" and details the eleven technical modes of how planets transfer, collect, or prohibit "light" and power between one another.</summary>

# Treatise

...it cuts off the light of the middle to the light ones. For by this rule, you shall know the status of each planet, namely, when it is high.

¶ When they are found in foreign places—that is, in their **haiz** <note>original: "haiz"; an astrological condition where a planet is in a sign and quarter of the sky that matches its own nature (day/night, masculine/feminine)</note>—their own powers greatly decrease. In such cases, their temperaments are contrary to the temperaments of the signs in which they are located. Therefore, a work of two combined natures will result from this.

¶ And if they are found in foreign places within their own **haiz**, their power is much weakened, and their temperament becomes similar to the temperament of the signs in which they dwell, producing a composite work of two different natures.

¶ The virtues of the planets are weakened when they are in foreign places with which they have no relationship, neither by essence nor by accident. When they are in such a state, their work imitates nature and becomes a composite according to the mixture of their powers; and this same thing happens between planets, namely, between one and another. For planets have places in which they are strengthened and in which they are weakened, and in which they are fortunate. The places in which they are strengthened are when they are in the North, or ascending toward their high points, or emerging from under the Sun's rays <note>This refers to "heliacal rising," when a planet becomes visible again after being hidden by the Sun's glare</note>; or when a planet separates from an **infortune** <note>original: "infortuna"; a "malefic" planet like Saturn or Mars</note> and applies to a **fortune** <note>original: "fortune"; a "benefic" planet like Jupiter or Venus</note>; or when they are in the "angles" <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses of a chart, considered the most powerful</note> or in the "succedent" houses; or when the three superior planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note> are eastern of the Sun, and Venus and Mercury are western; or when masculine planets are in masculine quarters and feminine ones in feminine quarters; or when they are fast in motion and increased in light or number; or when they are in any of their **dignities** <note>Specific zodiacal positions where a planet has "home field advantage"</note> or in their "joy"; or in **Aries** or **Taurus**; or with the **Head of the Dragon**; or in the two degrees which are called those of "fortune"; or when they look upon each other with fortunate aspects; or when they are in "bright degrees"; or when they separate from a fortune and apply to another fortune; or when they are in a good aspect with the Sun or Moon—that being the fortunate part. The places where they are weakened are the opposites of those where they are strengthened. For example: when they are entering under the Sun's rays, or joined with infortunes, or in a bad state with them; or when they separate from a fortune and apply to an infortune; or when they are in the opposite of their dignities; or when they are in the **Burning Path** <note>original: "via combusta"; a specific section of the zodiac from 19 degrees Libra to 3 degrees Scorpio, traditionally considered unlucky or "burnt"</note>; and this is from the 19th degree of Libra to the 3rd degree of Scorpio; or when they are with the **Tail of the Dragon** or similar things.

¶ Now we wish to speak of the **Head and Tail of the Dragon** <note>The lunar nodes: the points where the Moon's orbit intersects the ecliptic (the Sun's path)</note>; until now, we have not had occasion to speak of this. I say that planets are strengthened when they are in the North and weakened when they are in the South. The ancient wise men established nine points where the circles of the planets intersect with the circle of the Sun: the Head and the Tail. The "Heads" are the points from which the planets depart from the Sun's circle and go toward the North; and the "Tails" are the points from which they depart and go toward the South. And because the Moon's work is more manifest—for the circle of its inclination at the point where it intersects the Sun's circle changes every day—it happens that its Head and Tail have a manifest effect, as do those of the other planets. Therefore, they said that the **Head** has the power or nature of increasing, because it increases the planet's power to a greater degree; and the **Tail** has the nature of decreasing, because planets become of lesser virtue when they descend toward the South. And some have said that the Head has the nature of a "fortune" and the Tail an "infortune"; and in everything else we have said, the reason for this is well-known.

¶ In **alictisal** <gloss>that is, joining or continuation</gloss> and **alnisigref** <gloss>that is, separation</gloss> and in other strengths.

### Chapter 24

**T**he general rule of this chapter is that planets which precede and those which seek conjunctions with others are in their **alictisal** <note>original: "alictisal"; from the Arabic "al-ittiṣāl," meaning "application" or the act of one planet approaching an aspect with another</note> unless the distance between them is greater than the sum of the two halves of the "bodies" <note>original: "corporum"; refers to the "orb" of influence surrounding a planet</note> of the two planets, whether the *alictisal* is by conjunction or by any of the stated figures <note>aspects</note>.

¶ What is appropriate for us to say in this chapter is: that when planets move to approach others, it is called their **application**, unless they are far distant from them, exceeding the half of the bodies of the two planets, whether it be a

<column-break/>

bodily application or one through the other aforementioned figures <note>aspects like the square or trine</note>.

¶ A **light planet** is one that "applies" and gives its power, and a **heavy planet** is one that receives the power. An application occurs when the distance between them is less than half of their bodies, with the light planet going toward the heavy one. When it is equal to it in degrees and minutes, the application is complete; and when it is in more degrees, it has "separated" from it. Now, the bodies <note>orbs</note> of the planets are: the **Sun**, 15 degrees in front and 15 behind; the **Moon**, 12 in front and 12 behind; **Saturn and Jupiter**, 9 in front and 9 behind; **Mars**, 8 in front and 8 behind; **Venus and Mercury**, both 7 in front and 7 behind. Nor is this the opinion of the whole community of astrologers; for **Ptolemy** holds that it is another way, according to what appears in his words. For he holds that the total body of the Sun in front and behind is 17 degrees; the Moon, 12 and a half; Saturn, 10; Jupiter, 12; Mars, 7 and a half; Venus, 8; and Mercury, 7. And he says that when there is a distance between one planet and another—whether through bodily conjunction or through a "fourth aspect" <note>a square aspect</note>—half of its body applies to the other. For the "figures" he mentioned are the four aspects, which are equally distant from the four tropical points.

¶ For this reason, it is useful to consider their **latitude** <note>vertical distance above or below the ecliptic</note> in the *alictisal* of their conjunction. Similarly, it is also helpful to consider their latitude in the **alnisigref** <note>original: "alnisigref"; from the Arabic "al-inṣirāf," meaning "separation," when planets move away from an aspect</note> of their conjunction.

¶ And because of this, it is of great profit to look at the latitude of the planets in a conjunctival application, and similarly in the separation of a conjunction.

¶ It is fitting that in a conjunction, one should look at the planets joining together: and if there is a distance of half of their bodies in latitude, it will be an application; and if more, it will not.

¶ But in the *alictisal* of the other figures <note>aspects</note>, it is superfluous to observe this, because all their rays always extend to the half of the Earth, and there they are joined from every side.

¶ In other applications which are through the figures we mentioned, to inspect the latitude is an excess, since all their rays always apply in the manner of the Earth, and are joined from all sides.

¶ Inspect the latitudes of the planets: for when one applies to another through the aforementioned figures, it is a thing that does not profit, and this is manifest: because the virtues apply through straight lines from any part of the Earth and are joined there; and a single mixture is made, distinct by itself for each of them. And **Ptolemy** places any point of the Earth as representing the whole Earth, since the whole Earth is like a point with respect to the spheres of the planets. For this is the opinion of Ptolemy.

¶ It is also manifest from the premises that the powers of all planets must be investigated from their own proper natures and from their figures <note>aspects</note>, as well as from the figures they have in relation to the Sun; the "angles" also should be considered according to the aforementioned mode of all these. Regarding the quantity of these powers, we should know that when they are **oriental** <note>rising before the Sun</note> and their proper motion is increasing, they will be very strong and capable. And when their motion decreases and they are **occidental** <note>setting after the Sun</note>, they will be as weak as they can be.

¶ We can know concerning the "light" through those things we have said in this book: that it is fitting for us to look at the virtue of the planet's own nature, the signs in which they dwell, and the figures they have with respect to the Sun, and the angles according to which we have spoken in all these matters. And it is fitting that we know the quantity of their virtue: when they are oriental and increased in their own motion, for then they will be of the greatest virtue they can be; and when they are diminished in motion and occidental, they will be of weaker virtue.

...western [occidental] and increased in motion are stronger than when they are eastern [oriental] and increased in motion. Ptolemy, however, maintains that all planets possess greater virtue when they are eastern than when they are western; for if they are above the earth, they appear before the Sun. Generally, I say that the states of the planets with respect to the Sun are these: Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, when they emerge from under the rays, are eastern and increasing in virtue until they are 30 degrees from the Sun; afterward, they are eastern and complete in virtue until they reach 60 degrees. Subsequently, they are eastern, going along while weakening themselves until they are in their first station, wishing to become retrograde; and they remain weak and eastern until they are in opposition to the Sun. Afterward, they will return to being eastern and retrograde, increased in virtue until they are direct, and they will be western and complete in virtue until they are in sextile <note>an astrological aspect of 60 degrees</note> to the Sun. Thereafter, they will remain western, going along weakening themselves until they are about 30 degrees from the Sun; afterward, they will be western and completely weakened until they are combust <note>original: "combusti"; meaning so close to the Sun that their influence is 'burned up' or hidden by its light</note>. 

Venus and Mercury, after they separate from the Sun and are retrograde, are called weak and eastern until they are 7.5 degrees from the Sun; afterward, they will be eastern and increased in virtue until they are direct. Subsequently, they will be complete in virtue as eastern planets until they enter under the rays. When they enter under the rays, they will be weak and eastern until they are at the same point as the Sun. When they are in the same minute or point as the Sun—or when there is less than 16 minutes between them—this is called **cazimi** <note>original: "canum" (likely a corruption of 'cazimi'); meaning 'in the heart' of the Sun, a position of great accidental strength</note>. And according to this rule, you must observe yourself in all other matters, for this is entirely according to the common opinion of astrologers. And you should well combine this with what Ptolemy says and judge according to your own sense. Afterward, they will be weak and western until they are 7.5 degrees from the Sun. Then they will be strong and western until they become retrograde, and then they will be weak and western. And when a planet exits from under the rays, and another does not apply to it while it is in its light, and as long as a planet is far from an application while another does not apply, it exists in that sign until it passes two terms <note>astrological subdivisions of a sign</note>. And as long as a planet is **wild** [sylvester] <note>meaning 'peregrine' or without essential dignity</note> while in that whole sign no other planet applies to it. However, they decline in strength by degrees according to their distance from the midheaven. ¶ We shall also say how they are very strong: it is best when they are in the 10th or 11th houses. And it follows well in virtue when they are in the horizon itself, and especially in the eastern part.

And if they are not in any of the aforesaid ways, they are weak and have no power. You, however, should look at the portion that the gloss has in virtue, and mix and judge according to that. ### ¶ The first treatise of Haly’s gloss on the first treatise of the second book of Ptolemy’s Quadripartitum. Haly said:

In our first treatises, we showed through the words of Ptolemy that it is reasonably appropriate for a man to trust in this art, and the proof accords with reason. We showed how much profit a man can have from this art, and that there is no art in which there is greater profit for preparing bodies and souls and such things. And whatever Ptolemy said concerning the roots and rules, we gloss word for word. And now we wish to begin glossing the rules by which a man can know all the accidents happening in this world, starting first by naming the rules by which a man can know great accidents, such as the status of kingdoms, sects, and similar great things: famine, and all matters encompassing one or more peoples. For these are the rules about which Ptolemy spoke in this second part. And because the greater virtue overcomes the lesser, and the general encompasses the particular, he spoke of great accidents before nativities [birth charts]. And regarding this, **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of astrology</note> says in the *Book of Accidents* that he who is born in a fortunate year has a great share in fortune. This affirms what he says: that if the Moon and Mercury are afflicted in the revolution of the year <note>the chart cast for the Sun's entry into Aries</note>, those worldly people who are born in that year will be, for the most part, ignorant, unless the virtue in their own nativities is so great that it can overcome the significance of this revolution. And since Ptolemy was a good and perfect man, and reasons are in agreement on this, it is fitting for anyone wishing to speak of nativities to speak of general matters first.

### ¶ Subsequently begins the second treatise of the *Quadripartitum* in which there are 13 chapters.

### ¶ On the general division of this science. Chapter 1.

Since those things which must be set forth first—those upon which individual prognostications are sustained and must be used—the things we have already set forth generally are sufficient.

¶ What we have spoken of above regarding the things one must look into in the manner of a general proposal for the particular parts of this art is quite sufficient for us.

¶ This means that the things he said in the first part are general to all parts of this art. And he says this regarding those things which are particular matters in this art, from which the whole is also composed.

¶ But since some might think that the discourse on particulars is contained within this mode of prognostication, he adds after the aforesaid things that in which we, following the direct path, shall seek out what is appropriate to natural things.

¶ And we wish now to add to this, following what we said about speaking of particulars that can be reached by this manner of prognostication, always imitating the way that pertains to the nature of the matter.

¶ This means that he will apply the particulars of this art with the universals he narrated in the first part. And what he says about "this manner of prognostication" is so he may distinguish the prognostications of this art from the prognostications of physical auguries and the like. Regarding his statement about "imitating the way that pertains to nature," he said this because everything he speaks of in this book is according to nature. For example: after the composition of Mars works heat, and heat works such and such a thing, and Mars works in such a way, and thus one thing follows another in a continuous chain, so that the later thing returns to the work of Mars because of the heat, and thus other things follow the work of Mars through the middle.

¶ We shall say that the prognostication of the stars is divided into two parts, which are its greater and more powerful parts. The first and more universal part is that which is known regarding what shall happen in regions and lands, which is called **universal**. The second part, however, which is less universal than the aforementioned, is that which is understood regarding what shall happen to each individual; it is called the **science of nativities**. I thought it worthy to set forth the universal part first, because this universal part [affects] the circumstances of the other... which is particular.

<meta>This page serves as the introduction to Book II of the treatise, shifting from the basic definitions of planetary strength established in Book I to the practical application of mundane astrology. It focuses on the hierarchy of astrological influence, emphasizing that universal events (affecting nations) take precedence over particular events (affecting individuals).</meta>

...particulars are said to be stronger and greater.

¶ And we say thus: that since astrological predictions are divided into two major and more noble parts: the first part is more general, which is that by which we can know what happens to kings, cities, and nations; and this part is called **universal**. The second part, which is called **particular**, is that by which we can know what happens to any individual person by themselves; this is what is called the art of **nativities** <note>the study of birth charts to predict a person's life and character</note>. We are bound to follow this order: to speak of the universal part first, because universal events always happen from greater causes and of greater power than those through which particular events occur.

¶ When we receive these things from the art of astronomical judgments according to nature, we find that what we receive is divided into two manners. One is universal prognostication, generally encompassing a great nation. The other is prognostication which pertains to any individual person by themselves. However, "interrogations" <note>answering specific questions based on the time they are asked</note> and "elections" <note>choosing an auspicious time to begin an endeavor</note> are quite unstable things; they neither follow a natural path nor do they look very far into the future.

¶ Therefore, because weaker natures are contained under stronger ones, and particular things under universal ones in all their qualities, it is necessary that those who seek to observe particulars should hasten to observe those things that are more universal and of greater importance first.

¶ Because noble natures are not as strong as powerful ones, nor are particular things as noble as universal ones in all matters, it is necessary for those wishing to look into particulars to first look into those things that are general and represent the greater causes.

¶ This is the rule we stated before, which is composed of two things. One is that noble natures are overcome by stronger ones. The other is that particular things are subordinate to universal ones. And thus, when we find a noble power, we will know that the strong overcomes the noble and turns it toward itself; and when we find a universal thing, we will know that the particular things under it are connected to it. Therefore, it follows that we should look first at divine matters, then laws, then kingdoms, and every universal thing of great power, before looking at those things that follow them. For example, if we wish to look into the affairs of any king: first we ought to look at the law under whose power he exists, then at his status <note>original: "regradatio"; likely referring to his rank or coronation status</note>, and then finally at his own personal nativity. And by joining the indication of all this together, we will know for certain what will become of him; and it is right that we do thus in all things regarding this art.

¶ And since from these universal observations, some judge the general state of regions, others the general state of lands, others the general impediments of the seas: such as wars, mortalities, famines, earthquakes, floods, and things similar to these. Others show impediments smaller than these aforesaid, which happen at certain hours: such as the changes of the years and seasons, the increases of heat and cold and winds, and their decreases, as well as their intensities and remissions; the abundance of rains and droughts, and similar things. And because the teaching proceeds from these two parts: it is the science of those things that will happen generally in regions, and of great impediments because of the aforesaid occasions.

¶ For by one part of these universals, we know what happens in great regions, and by another, what happens in certain cities. And by some part, we know great general pestilences, such as great mortalities, great famines, great wars, earthquakes, floods, and the like; and those things that signify pestilences smaller than these at certain times, and harsh changes that happen in the seasons of the year, whether by the increase of heat or cold or greater winds: whether concerning their growth, or their strength or weakness, or concerning the lack of food, or its abundance. And that which is of greater power first is to know those things that happen in

<column-break/>

great regions, and the great pestilences coming from great causes, as we have said.

¶ He himself makes it known in this passage by which means the prediction of great accidents is known; and in turn, it falls to us to put forward the more general and that which pertains to the greater, and to always join the particular to its own encompassing universal, and the weak indication to the strong one encompassing it; and in this way, we will know the certain indication. For this reason, he arranged his words in this part, which he related in this saying.

¶ In this knowledge, oh King, we use two things: one of which is the similarity of the signs and stars in each climate; the other is the signs occurring at various hours and in similar parts according to the eclipses, conjunctions, and meetings of the Moon and Sun, and according to the appearances of the "wandering stars" <note>planets</note> outside their rays and according to their stations.

¶ And because there are two things by which we can know all this: one is the agreement of the signs and stars with each climate. ¶ This is the major rule which you must keep much in memory: because concerning the events that he narrated, he spoke of those that encompass great regions; and among these are very great pestilences, and among them are particular pestilences; and we can know each of them before they happen by two things. One is the concordance of the signs and stars with the regions; and this is a universal thing having very great power. The other is the signs. For he taught us the signs generally in this passage when he said that these signs operate in regions that are suitable to the degrees in which they are; and their effects appear according to the agreement of those stars, and according to the places of the stars at that hour. For these signs of which he spoke, he means the eclipses, conjunctions, and such like. Wherefore, he spoke specifically of the eclipses of the Sun: because the power of the Sun is stronger and more noble than the Moon and all other powers of the stars, as we said in the first treatise. And those things that happen from it are natural; and these apply to various parts according to how the other powers of the remaining stars are mixed with the power of the Sun and Moon. For when the Moon flees from the Sun without any latitude, and the Sun is eclipsed, its power is mixed with its own, and from that, one <term>complexion</term> <note>the resulting blend of astrological influences that determines the nature of an event</note> is composed. And similarly when the Moon is eclipsed, because at that hour both are upon one straight line. And when the power of the Sun is joined with the power of the Moon, and the powers of the other stars are mixed with them, one complexion is composed from all this, by which it is bound together. There comes among us a certain spiritual power having such an effect, much greater and more general and stronger than other powers that are composed of other mixtures; and that which this power works is more a thing proceeding naturally because it draws power in turn in this complexion. And for this reason, there are powers that are bound by the Sun and Moon: because when they are joined with the conjunctions of the superior planets, such as the conjunction of Saturn or Jupiter or Mars, or these three, and the conjunction is in places having great power, from these powers occur effects that are greater and much more supreme, which we will make you understand hereafter. And this is the opinion of Ptolemy. However, those who said that the conjunctions of the planets alone have powers working very great effects spoke a vain thing; for the power of Saturn and Mars when they are joined in Cancer, or the power of Saturn and Jupiter when they are joined in any sign, cannot apply so as to have the power of working anything unless the power of the Sun and Moon is bound with them. And if they work anything, it will be weak and of little durability. However, when a conjunction or eclipse-opposition happens with them, one mixture is made from them and from the power of the Sun and Moon, having great force and virtue. Regarding this, we give such a comparison: saying that the power of the Sun is like the power of a **King**, and the power of the Moon is like that of his **Companion** [Count]; and the power of the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter is like that of his **High Judge**; and the power of the conjunction of Saturn and Mars in Cancer is like the power of a **General** of an army. And because of this, when the King and his companion and the high judge have agreed upon doing one business, it is difficult to destroy it and it lasts a long time. And similarly, if the King, the companion, and his general have not agreed in doing one business, then it is not very difficult to destroy it; and none of them can perform a great deed without the King. There are indeed certain properties of nations that occur generally along the parallel lines and the angles <note>corners or regions</note> of the earth.

¶ Because of the accordance which they have with the zodiac of signs and with the sun.
¶ A matter encompassing the people of an entire climate reaches through the accordance which the climate itself has with the sun, as being near it or far removed from it; and a matter encompassing every thing of any "angle" out of the four angles of habitation happens from the accordance which that angle has with one of the four triplicities <note>the four groups of three zodiac signs categorized by the elements: Fire, Earth, Air, Water</note>.
¶ For because that part of the earth in which we are supported is in one of the two northern quarters, those who dwell in it under the parallel lines closest to the south—and these are the lines that extend between the summer solstitial point and the equinoctial point—the sun runs directly over the zenith of their heads and burns them; therefore their bodies are black, and their hair is black and curled with roughness; their faces are dry, and their bodies are lean; their natures are hot and the qualities of their souls are for the most part cruel <note>original: crudeles; in this context, it refers to a harsh or fierce temperament shaped by extreme heat</note> because of the long and constant stay of the sun in their regions; and these are those who are generally called Ethiopians by them. And not only in these people does this quality of heat appear: but also in the surrounding air an intense heat is perceived in all animals and in the plants that are among them.
¶ And this is because the earth in which we dwell is in one of the two northern quarters: and those who dwell below the equidistant lines are further south; and these are the lines that are between the equinox and the summer solstice; and the sun passes over the zenith of their heads and burns them: and their bodies are black, and their hair is black, thick, and curly: their faces are shriveled, their bodies lean, their natures hot: their manners are for the most part wild, because the heat lasts in the places of their habitations and is continuous for them. And these nations are those who are called by the common name Ethiopians.

<column-break/>

They are so named: and not only are their bodies in this state of heat, but a great heat appears in the air encompassing them: and also in all animals and plants that are further toward them.
¶ Ptolemy makes known the natural cause reaching these people. And Haly has already demonstrated this in his book *On Airs, Waters, and Places*: that heat is in this place for two reasons. One is the greater convergence of the sun's rays, as in burning mirrors <note>speculis comburentibus: mirrors used to focus sunlight to ignite a fire</note>. The other is the length of the day and the shortness of the night; and the cold coming from the night does not overcome the heat of the day. And since the matter stands thus, the sun passes twice in a year over the zenith of their heads in those places: which are between the equinoctial line and the solstice... and it has already been proven in the *Book of Mirrors* that the rays return upon right angles, and the sun is never far removed from them at any time by a great distance. Furthermore, many rays of the sun and the length of the day are joined to these habits; and from this, a great heat is created in their environment which burns and blackens their bodies, and dries the humors <note>bodily fluids</note> of their bodies, and roasts their faces, and makes their limbs lean. And a hot complexion <note>the balance of qualities/humors</note> prevails in their bodies. And the shape and color of their hair is according to their nature and the pores from which they emerge; and because the complexion of their nature is supremely hot, it results that they are black; and because their pores are not conductive because of the dryness through which they pass, it happens that they are curly. And it is a very great principle that the manners of the soul follow the complexion of the body; and because the complexion is of supreme heat, it happens that their manners are wild without moderation; and according to this mode are the things created among them, from animals and plants. But the matter is more certain in this: the great and supreme heat of the air encompassing them. And although this follows all those dwelling in this part, it follows those on the exact equator specifically, and this makes it so that the day is not at any time of supreme heat; and because of this, those dwelling on the equator itself are saffron-colored <note>crocei coloris; a yellowish-tan</note>, and in total the air encompassing them is of less heat than that which encompasses the black peoples. Also, because the seed in the beginning of its generation is of the complexion of that generation: it happens that a black person is born in a cold region, yet a less black person than their parents; and that this person may beget another black person less so than himself, and the blackness will not cease to be thinned until it is totally removed to the limit. And this is what we wish to prove. But this name "Ethiopian" is a designation for all black people: such as those from the clouds <note>possibly a reference to a specific tribe or region</note> and the *azaganale* <note>a transliteration of an Arabic geographic term</note> and similar.
¶ However, in those who dwell under the parallel lines closer to the North, who live in places positioned beneath the Bear <note>the constellation Ursa Major, signifying the far North</note>: because their distance from the circle of signs is great and the cold overcomes the sun's heat, for that reason their humidity is great and their vegetation is abundant; nor is there heat among them to dry it. Their colors are white, and their hair is straight; their bodies are large and fleshy, and their natures are cold; likewise their habits. Similarly, they are fierce <note>original: feroces</note> because of the long and constant stay of the cold in their habitations; and also according to the qualities of those regions: a wintry quality is in their air and there is greatness in the herbs; and animals mate late. These indeed are those who for the most part are called Slavs <note>sclaui; historically used to refer to northern "barbarian" peoples</note>.
¶ And those who dwell under the equidistant lines which are in this northern part: these are those who dwell in the places under the Seven Stars <note>The Big Dipper/Ursa Major</note> which run always in a circle; because they are very far removed from the zodiac of signs and the heat of the sun, cold prevails in them; and because there is much humidity in them and much nourishment, nor is there heat there to dry it out, for which reason their colors are white, and their hair soft and long; their bodies large and thick; their complexions cold; and their manners are also wild, because the cold lasts long in the places where they dwell, and it is continuous and does not leave them. And this state of theirs is the state of their wintry air; always even the plants themselves are large, and there is greatness in the herbs; and their animals mate late. These indeed are those who for the most part are called Slavs; and their animals that live with men are few; and these are named Europeans.
¶ After he has narrated those things which happen to those dwelling in the land much...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Chapter 2 from Book II of Ptolemy’s treatise, moving from a general introduction to specific geographical and climatic influences on human nature. It addresses how the "Seven Climates" of the known world shape the bodies and minds of their inhabitants.</meta>

...due to the great heat of the sun. He now points out those things that happen to those living in a very cold land, and the things that occur due to great cold. These are the people who dwell in the **Seventh Climate** <note>In ancient geography, the world was divided into seven horizontal bands or 'climates' based on the length of the longest day.</note>, which is located between 50 and 63 degrees of latitude. This is the southern line <note>The limit of the habitable world as known to the author</note>, where the rays of the sun do not return directly to the earth, but fall upon it at **acute angles**. Because of this, they do not gather a great quantity of solar rays. Furthermore, for this reason, they experience a summer day of moderate heat and a winter day of great cold, because of the extreme sharpness of the angles and the reflection of the rays. Consequently, cold entirely dominates the air surrounding them, trapping vapors within their bodies. Because the cold dominates the surface of their skin, their colors become **white**. Due to the vapors trapped within their bodies, their hair becomes **yellow, soft, and thin at the ends**. Because of the natural heat enclosed within them, which creates humid humors from the internal vapors, their bodies grow quite large. Their characters, as well as the plants and animals found there, follow this same pattern.

And if someone should ask: "How can this be, when we see that the elephant and many other large beasts are born in hot lands?" We answer him that extremely large beasts cannot be born in very cold lands by nature, because they require a very great heat to open their pores so they can process the humors generated in their bodies. This cannot happen in a very cold land, because the great cold hinders the natural heat and does not permit their limbs to extend in every direction. What **Ptolemy** said is a general rule and true, although it happens rarely; there is another reason, and it is not the most important factor there. 

Some also say that at both ends of the habitable world—in the north as well as the south—there are **cannibals** who eat other men, and these people have faces that are distorted and hideous. I myself have seen men traveling through the world who claimed to have seen them. **Hermes** <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many astrological and philosophical works were attributed.</note> said in his *Book of Latitudes* that at the edges of the north and south dwell evil spirits and demons, as well as beasts that harm men. This may be because the extreme heat and cold, being beyond measure, pull and remove the *sigma* <note>original: "sgma"—likely a scribal error or abbreviation for 'schema' (form/appearance) or 'stigma'</note> and nature from its proper temperament. He says this hinders the generation of life because the nature of the place does not suit it; therefore, their faces are distorted and hideous, their characters are very wicked, and the animals there are wild and dangerous. He specifically named the "Plains of the Ethiopians" and those who enter among them, and others like them, such as the rural Khwarizmians <note>original: "curasmini"—referring to the people of Khwarazm in Central Asia</note> and others who dwell under the **Seven Stars** which are called the **Wagon** <note>The Big Dipper or Ursa Major.</note>.

¶ However, those who dwell between the point of the summer solstice and the *Benetnaz* <note>original: "benetnaz"—from the Arabic 'Banat Na'sh', the stars of the Big Dipper</note>: because the sun does not reach the zenith of their heads, nor is it very far from them at the hour of noon, the temperament of their air is **temperate**. Though it varies at times, it does not experience a grand variation from extreme heat to extreme cold. They have moderate complexions and their body size is moderate; they are also of good natural temperament, and their settlements are continuous. Their souls are domestic and gentle in quality.

¶ And those who dwell between the summer solstice and under the **Seven Stars**: because the sun does not reach the zenith of their heads, nor is it similarly very far from them at noon, their air is of a temperate quality. When it changes, it does not swing wildly from great heat to great cold. From this, they are of moderate color, the size of their bodies is temperate, and their natures and complexions are good; their dwellings are continuous and their manners are civilized.

¶ These are the ones who dwell between the summer solstice and the end of the **Sixth Climate**. Among these, one might surpass another in heat or cold depending on whether they are closer to the south or further away, yet they all share this: because the sun is in the middle of heaven, its rays do not fall upon them at right angles, nor at such acute angles as in those lands of greater latitude. Since this is so, **Ptolemy’s** meaning is clear and needs no further explanation. When he said that their settlements are "continuous," he demonstrates two things: first, that the settlements of the Ethiopians are not continuous because of the extreme heat and cold, which causes a great depopulation across the world, and because of the sandy deserts. Similarly, in very cold lands, settlements are interrupted by seas, snow, and winds. The second point is that for those living in moderate lands between cold and heat, there is not much "depopulation"—that is, they are densely inhabited.

¶ Of these, those who are closer to the south are for the most part of bet-

<column-break/>

-ter genius and sharper intellect, and are stronger in the **science of the stars**. This is because of the proximity of the Circle of Signs <note>The Zodiac</note> and the wandering stars <note>The Planets</note> to the zenith of their heads. Even the movements of their souls are like the movements of the stars in their sudden haste to reach a conclusion, and in the fact that they are investigators and observers of the sciences called *Attabalem* <note>Likely a Latinization of an Arabic term like 'at-ta'wil' (interpretation) or referring to astronomical tables (zij).</note>.

¶ Among these, those in the southern parts are generally more intelligent and of greater genius; they have a greater power for knowing the science of the stars because the signs of the Zodiac and the planets are more directly over their heads. The movements of their intellects match the movement of the stars, and they resemble them in finding things out quickly. They are of great study in the **quadrivial sciences** <note>The four mathematical arts: Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy.</note>, progressing smoothly compared to those who dwell in the temperate zones between cold and heat on the southern side.

¶ These are the people of the **Third, Fourth, and Fifth Climates**. I speak generally of all who dwell between 34 degrees and 42 degrees of latitude. The power of the **seven planets** reaches them through right angles or nearly right angles; in the same way, the power of the signs of the Zodiac reaches them first. Because of this, these influences work more in them than in others. Since they are of a temperate complexion, they are more intelligent overall. As **Ptolemy** said, they receive the works of the stars and signs more because they are of a balanced temperament; for great dryness (which prevents the intellect from forming ideas quickly) is not in them. Similarly, the great cold that makes men negligent and lazy is not in them. Since this is so, those in the **Sixth Climate** have less of these qualities Ptolemy mentioned, even though he did not name them specifically. As an example, **Aristotle** and **Galen** <note>original: "Sal." — derived from the Arabic name for Galen, 'Jalinus'.</note> were from this climate; **Ptolemy** and **Pliny** were from the third. Indeed, the wisest men ever found were from these climates and the regions between them.

¶ But those who are generally closer to the **East** are of greater masculinity and stronger souls; they are the revealers of all their affairs. This is because the eastern part must be said to be of the nature of the **Sun**—diurnal, masculine, and "right-handed." Just as in animals the right-side parts are more capable and are found to be stronger and more valid in vigor.

¶ And those of this eastern part are more masculine and stronger of heart, mastering all their affairs, because the eastern part suits a man, being of the nature of the Sun. This part is similarly diurnal and masculine. On the contrary, we see that animals assist themselves more with their right limbs because they are stronger.

¶ After he explained the state of those dwelling in the South and North and those between them, he now wishes to relate the state of those dwelling in the **East** and **West**, so that his entire reasoning may be completed in four parts; afterward, he will speak of the dwellings in the four angles. Because all the stars of the visible pole rise from the eastern part, the East falls on the "right" side, while the West, where the stars set, falls on the "left" side. The ancient wise men said that the East is the right side of the firmament and the West is the left. Because the power of the stars increases the more they rise from the East and weakens the more they descend into the West, they said that those from the East are stronger of heart and more masculine, nor do they hide anything of their knowledge. Such things suit the solar nature. Because of this, those in the eastern part have less power for keeping secrets, they perform miraculous things, and know more of **astronomy** than those in the western part. You will find this demonstrated in the third part.

¶ However, those who dwell in the **western part** are more feminine and their souls are softer. They also cover and hide the greater part of their affairs, because this part is **Lunar**. For the first rising of the Moon and its first appearance after conjunction is always in that part from which the west wind emits its blasts. Therefore, this part is called feminine, nocturnal, and "left-handed" in comparison to the eastern part.

¶ And those who are further toward the west are more feminine of heart...

## Book Two

In these parts, they hide and conceal all their more valuable possessions <note>The text suggests a tendency toward secrecy or protection of wealth</note> for the most part; this is because of the lunar influence, for the moon after its conjunction <note>The New Moon</note> appears from the western side. For this reason, this part is considered nocturnal, feminine, and "left-handed" compared to the eastern part.

¶ Those dwelling in this part are of this manner because the virtues of the stars begin to weaken when they are in this part. If you have understood well what we said about the eastern part, all of Ptolemy is clear and requires no further commentary. It is useful to consider the relationship between the easterners and westerners; look at those who dwell under the same line of latitude <note>original: "lineis egdistātibus eqnoctio"</note>. If you look closely at the westerners and the customs of the easterners, you will find it to be generally as Ptolemy reported: for westerners often kill their enemies when they overcome them, unless they are held back by great fear that the enemies might rise up against them another time. Indeed, their contentions are similar to the contentions of women. This is the nature of eastern customs, and it is their own; however, some westerners can be more masculine and stronger than easterners, but his **nativity** <note>The individual's birth chart</note> must have shown this, for Ptolemy expresses only that which happens **for the most part** <note>original: "vtplm," an abbreviation for "ut plurimum," meaning "generally" or "in most cases"</note>. For it is not Ptolemy’s opinion to say that a thing happens to everyone; he spoke clearly when he discussed the westerners and said "for the most part."

¶ In each of these general parts, there ought to be particular qualities regarding the characteristics of the soul and the customs of the inhabitants.

¶ And it happens that each of these general parts has within itself particular conditions of the inhabitants and their laws and customs.

¶ This means that those things which are specific to each part form, in the wills of the people of that country, their customs and laws which agree with their nature.

¶ For just as the qualities of the surrounding air in the aforementioned places differ among themselves—being for the most part hot, cold, or temperate—so too does the property of those places and lands lean toward increase or decrease, whether because of the order of the place in its layout, or because of its elevation or depression, or because of what is near it.

¶ And this, which is to have a state of surrounding air in diverse places as we have said, is because they are generally hot, or generally cold, or generally temperate. And there are locations and lands that are more or less so because of the site's position: whether it is higher or lower, or because it exists more around one place than another.

¶ Those things that happen to each part are diverse in three manners. The **first** is because of the site of the town in that part—whether it is in the middle of it or at the borders; for if it is in its middle, it happens that everything pertaining to that part appears there, and the more it is in the middle, the more it exhibits what pertains to that part; if it is at the border, it will show less of it. The **second** is whether the town is on high ground or low ground; for winds pass through high places, and from this, they carry away the vapors that are there, and those dwelling there are healthier because their customs follow their **complexion** <note>The physical and mental temperament of a person</note>; low places are different from these. The **third** is the proximity of the town to mountains, water, and flat land; for a town existing near mountains is drier, and because it is near savory <note>fertile or pleasant</note> land, it is more temperate, whereas near swampy land it is worse. And that which has many trees and stagnant waters around it suffers from corruption of the air. <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The famous Greek physician</note> explained all these things expressly in his book *On Airs, Waters, and Places*. And if you wish to understand well what <term>Ptolemy</term> said in this aphorism, look into that book of Hippocrates and you will understand it all; for it is manifest that the customs of men, their complexions, and all other virtues change according to each of these things.

¶ And as some, again, are farmers because of the suitability of their fields; some indeed are sailors because of their affinity for the sea; and some are rich because of the fertility of their region. Similarly, in each of the regions, we find the proper natures of man due to the natural similarity that exists between particular **climates** <note>Latitudinal zones</note> and the stars and signs.

¶ And so, some men are specifically laborers of the earth because their land is suitable for this; and others are mariners because 

<column-break/>

the sea is near them; and others are wealthier because they produce much fruit. And in the land of each, they find the proper natures of each of the lands from the natural connections that exist between the particular climates and between the stars and signs.

¶ Through all this, he shows what he said before. For he said later that a town changes the customs of men according to the complexion of the land itself or its proximity; the more the region changes, the more it will change the complexion of the men and their customs. For we find many laborers because the land is suitable for this, and others mariners because they dwell on the seashore, and others rich because their land is abundant. And I do not believe that any laborer has a son in the land of laboring and raised in that land who would be of another profession than a laborer—unless one could show through **astrology** in his nativity that he should be of another profession in only one way: if he moved himself from one town to another, to a custom of others suitable to his nativity. And so it is in all other things. This whole long explanation is a commentary on what he said before for himself: yet there is a rule by which it happens we must judge. When the stars of someone's nativity demonstrate that he will be a laborer, and he dwells in a land of labor, he will be wiser in laboring than others whose nativity did not show it. Similarly, if his constellation showed that he is a **physician** <note>original: "physicus"</note>, he will be wiser and a better physician than others whose nativity did not show it; we shall judge other things in this same way.

¶ These aforesaid variations, however, we have brought forward only according to the greater part; for it may be otherwise: yet not such that it could happen in every single instance as we have predicted.

¶ And these diversities which we have spoken of are in the majority of cases, not that it is so in every single part in all ways as we have said.

¶ This encompasses everything he said from the beginning of the chapter to this place; for whatever he said happens specifically to any part and any place happens "for the most part" and is not necessary for every individual. All natural things are this way: for rains come in winter "for the most part," and sometimes it happens in winter that it does not rain or rains very little, even though it is not customary to be so. This rule is general in all natural things, and in the same way, these things are found in this part, since its final works in which they operate are natural things.

¶ Now, however, it is necessary that we indicate specifically and generally, in the appropriate quantity, by name.

¶ And therefore it is fitting that we name the principal parts of these particular things from which we can profit in this art.

¶ After he narrated the state of each part of the inhabited world, he begins now to narrate the state of each **angle** out of the four angles <note>The four quarters of the world</note> that are in these parts, so that he may descend from the more general to the more particular, until he arrives at the most particular possible. For example: a general event that happens is a mortality <note>a plague or mass death</note> that happens in such a region; and within this region, it will be in such a city; for he will say specifically that it will be among all in this city and in those who have a "cutting off of life" <note>an astrological indicator of death</note> in their nativities in that year, whether it be in summer or in winter; that event will happen in this way to some specifically and not to others.

¶ On the similarity of regions with the **triplicities** <note>The four groups of three zodiac signs, each associated with an element</note> and stars.

### Chapter 3

->Haly said:<-

Ptolemy names in this chapter the provinces that are under the government of each **trigon** <note>A triplicity of signs</note>, and each sign, and each planet. And he did not speak of cities, because a city changes within a province from one place to another, and it is built under a different **ascendant** than another city whose name it took. For example: the royal city of the Caliphate <note>original: "Alyrat"</note> was first in Al-Madina and now is in **Baghdad** <note>original: "Baldach"</note>; and that of Egypt was first in Memphis <note>original: "menes"</note>, afterwards it turned to **Alexandria**, and it has not returned to **Al-Fustat** <note>original: "Alfoꝛzat," the old capital of Egypt before Cairo</note>. And if Ptolemy had wished to speak of every city as others have done, and afterwards it happened that the city was depopulated and another built under its name, his words would have been corrupted.
