### On the Qualities of Future Events. Chapter 8.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' with floral and foliate motifs inside a square frame.</image-desc>
**T**he fourth species of prognosticating the future inquires into the qualities. That is, it proposes to investigate whether things will be good or the contrary of good, or which species will prevail out of these two; this will be understood from the natures of the stars called <term>almudbebir</term> <note>From the Arabic 'al-mudabbir,' meaning the 'governor' or 'ruler' of a chart</note>, the queens who are the causes of future events, and from the mixtures of one of them with another and with the places in which they are found.

> ¶ The fourth manner of prognostication is whether the thing that happens will be good or similar [to good], and what manner of these two it will be. And this can be known from the nature of the ruling planets that govern, which create the event, and from the mixture of one with another, and from the places where they are.

¶ **Ptolemy** gives us in this chapter rules by which we may know if an event will be good—such as an abundance of food or a tempering of the air, so that bodies will be healthier—or if it will be bad, such as wars, battles, famine, and a lessening of provisions. Both of these can be known from three parts: one from the nature of the governors, another from the mixture of the powers of the rulers with the power of another planet, and from the position of the places in the zodiac in which they are located.

¶ That is, the Sun and Moon perceive and rule over the other stars. Therefore, they are the causes of the entire work and the disposition of the stars, as well as the strength of the <term>almudbebir</term> stars and their weakness.

¶ Because the Sun and Moon are the lords of the other planets, in that they both are the cause of all works and governance, and the cause of the strength or weakness of the ruling planets.

¶ In this section, he wants to express the reason why two eclipses cause grand events, and the nature of the event comes from the five planets <note>Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> without the Sun and Moon. And those planets are stronger or weaker because of the comparison they have to the two luminaries. And he says that the Sun and Moon are those that make every natural thing; and when their powers are mixed, and one power and one spirit is made from both so that both work as one, they will mix some other powers of the other planets with themselves, which inclines to the power of those planets; and they lead the work of the two luminaries into the harmony of the power of those planets. And this is the power that inclines the power of the two luminaries; and because of this, events can be known from the five wandering planets <note>original: "erraticis," referring to the planets that move against the fixed stars</note>, because the works of the fixed stars follow the works of the wandering planets.

¶ The meeting or mixture of the <term>almudbebir</term> stars with one another signifies the qualities of future events.

¶ However, one must look at the mixture of the governing planets one with another, because this signifies the events that have to happen.

¶ When we look into the mixture of the governing planets with one another at the hour of the eclipse, we will know what events will occur; and it is proper that we look to the first power and to that which overcomes, which we propose as the cause; and we then arrange the other subsequent power in dominion and strength afterward, since the accidents of eclipses are diverse throughout regions and 

<column-break/>

places. And since they are diverse, the ruling planets in any given region are likewise diverse, as we said before; and because of this, it follows that the one who prevails in one region may be different from the one who prevails in another. And for this reason, it is expedient that the works of any planet be shown to us individually when that place is the governor, or if its power prevails in the mixture.

¶ We, however, will begin to narrate the properties of the work of each of the wandering stars; but so that our narration may be more perfect, we think a certain general principle should be put forward first. It is this: that when we show the complexions of any of the five wandering stars generally, we ought to know that its work will be likened to the same nature, whether that star is named for a quality in itself or not named. This is because if some of the non-wandering <note>fixed</note> stars and some of the places of the circle of signs <note>the zodiac</note> have complexions that are likened to the complexions of that star, [the result is the same]. And if it were possible that they lacked the names of the stars, we would [still] show their natures and qualities.

¶ We, however, will begin to declare the property of the work of each of the five wandering planets, and one general statement; we will propose it thus in brief words. For we say that when we name the complexion of any of the five planets, it is proper for you to know that its work is in accord with its nature, whether that planet is named in its own state in itself, or by reason of any of the fixed stars that are likened to it, or what is likened to any place of the signs of the zodiac; thus we will be able to name their nature and state even if the stars do not have any name.

¶ He wants to say that the works of the wandering planets are those which accord with the nature of each of them, according to what was said in the 4th chapter of [this] part. And the works of any of the fixed stars are the works of the wandering planets which are of their complexion. And the works of any degree of the signs of the zodiac are the works of the lord of that place, and the works of the fixed stars which are in that boundary <note>original: "termio," an astrological subdivision of a sign</note>. And it is manifest that when we speak of the works of any of the wandering planets by itself, it will be as if we were speaking of all the works of the fixed stars and of all the degrees of the signs of the zodiac. And with as much as this is, he has given us whatever is expedient in knowing the works of the celestial bodies; and we will be able to know the work of any of them when we know in which place it is, whether we know or do not know its name; because after we have known the works pertaining to each of them, it is not necessary to know the names.

¶ And because we will also observe their mixtures, we ought to observe not only the mixtures of the wandering stars with one another, but also the mixtures of their natures with the non-wandering stars and with the places of the circle of signs, according to those similarities with the non-wandering stars which we have explained.

¶ When, however, we look into the mixtures, it is not proper only to look into the complexions of the wandering stars one with another, but it is also proper that we look into the mixture which is mixed with the fixed stars and in the places of the zodiacal signs, just as we have shown through the junctions <note>conjunctions</note> which they have with the planets.

¶ When we look into the mixture of the powers of the dominant planets, it is proper for us to mix with them the powers of the planets with which they aspect <note>form an angle with</note> each other, and the powers of the fixed stars which are with them, and the powers of the degrees of the signs in which they are, and the powers of the houses in which they are; and we will always look at what is joined from the mixture of these things until we know what signification it will have. For it happens through the mixture of all these powers that we have mentioned that one single mixture [is formed] by itself; and when we know that mixture, we will be able to know what accident will happen. And it is fitting for you to know that the whole art lies in knowing the forms of the mixture from which the works come; and to know this is difficult and much, for it requires great sharpness of intellect, great power of ingenuity, great practice, and knowing the simple natures of each by itself, in the way that a person might be able to know the truth by their own ingenuity. And what this way for knowing these things might be, we shall know.

First, the nature of the planets will prevail: and we will subtract the same amount from the nature of the fixed star that it signifies; or if it agrees with it, we will add to it. And so you must do in a matter that is composed of natural qualities. For we will add through one and subtract through another: and we will look afterward at what remains: and we will judge by that. In this way, we shall know those things which happen through the powers of the celestial bodies.

¶ When Saturn alone is the master of the disposition, it will generally be the cause of destruction occurring from cold.

¶ For if Saturn alone is the master of the governance, it will generally be the cause of the damage that occurs because of cold.

¶ For Saturn possesses a very great cold, which has exceeded its proper balance: and because of this, its works—and the condemnation of every thing agreeing with its nature—come about because of great cold.

¶ Its particular work is that when it affects humans in future events, it will generate long-lasting illnesses: and <term>phthisis</term> <note>original: "ptisiz"; a wasting disease of the lungs, often tuberculosis</note> and the afflictions that come from the humors and from the collection of humors: <term>quartan fevers</term> <note>original: "febrũs q̃rtanas"; a fever that recurs every four days, historically associated with malaria or black bile</note>, exile, stupor, anxiety, sadness, fears, and death. This is especially true for those who have already entered into their later years.

¶ And its own particular work, if it occurs in men, will be the arrival of long illnesses and wasting diseases, the failing of nature, and obstructions through the courses of the humors: quartan fevers, paralysis, anxieties, pains, fear, and mortality, especially in those who have entered into old age.

¶ He told us first the general work of Saturn, and said that the damage would be because of great cold. Afterward, he divided this summary for us, saying: if it is in men, it will be thus and so; and if in beasts, it will be thus; and if in the air, it will be thus and entirely so. It will signify nearly by itself one thing in any subject according to the event that comes to it and that it can receive. He did this for each of the planets: first giving us its general work, then dividing it according to what agrees with a specific matter. For the gloss is general and particular to all planets and fixed stars, and to all kinds of zodiac signs, as we have demonstrated. Nevertheless, in this place we wish to comment on the words of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>the 2nd-century astronomer and author of the Tetrabiblos</note>, saying it is demonstrated in the art of physics that long-lasting sicknesses are caused by coldness and dryness, and by the humors of <term>melancholy</term> <note>black bile</note> and phlegm. And the "phthisis" he mentioned is a wound of the lung. And the "failing" is like <term>diabetes</term>, flux, and <term>canine hunger</term> <note>original: "fames canina"; an insatiable, morbid appetite</note>. And what I called "obstructions of the course of humors" is a cold rheum. And quartan fevers occur because of melancholy that putrefies: and all these things happen because of cold things. And because the radical members are chilled—and the illness of diabetes, whatever it may be, occurs because of heating—the radical members are chilled by the lengthening of the illness and by great exhaustion. This indeed happens because of the nature of Saturn, which is short on life, concerning pain and death. For it is manifest that when melancholy prevails in the body of a man through strong forces, such illnesses as these must happen to him. Just as the power of melancholy produces such things when it overabounds in the human body, so the power of Saturn produces such things in the world when it chills. And after it produces hardships, it causes dearness <note>high prices/inflation</note> and a reduction of food supplies, sieges of towns, and armies. And since it is in its nature to cause fleeing and terror, it causes uprootings, defeats, retreats, and such things. Similarly, because old age is the final stage of a cold nature, it follows that this happens for the most part in men of the final age, since at that time they are in accord with such states as these. Consider this accordance which pertains to the nature of Saturn, and you shall consider all other things in accordance with the same.

¶ But when it occurs in animals which men use heavily, it will bring

Because of this, frost, fog, and thick, slippery, and excessively dry clouds occur. All this happens because of the trapping of vapor, which causes the air to putrefy. And it is manifest that when the air is in such a state, it will do such things to all that it encompasses according to its composition. For it is fitting that you compare the natural air at any time suitable to it; for when Saturn shows such signs and it is summertime, the summer heat will remove and destroy much of these damages. But if it is autumn, it will increase the damage because of the coldness and dryness of the season; and so you shall judge for the other seasons of the year.

¶ Look at how Ptolemy always follows natural reality and never separates the two. Since Saturn works in the air as he said, it is manifest that when the air mixes with the vapor that will be in the sea and rivers, wintry air is made from it. Because of the torment of winds, the sinking of ships and the danger of navigating the sea occur. Similarly, the water will chill greatly, wherefore the fish will die; and because of the cold that traps the humors in their bodies, their complexions are corrupted.

¶ In the sea, specifically, recessions and ebbs will occur. In the rivers, however, there will be great floods and the corruption of waters.

¶ When the moisture that is in the sea is trapped, great ebbs will occur in it. Similarly, the rivers will rise very high, and the waters will be corrupted because of the moist vapor that is joined to them.

# Treatise

...in the air. And when humidity prevails because of the coldness of the air, the same results in much rain and snow; for this reason, the rivers are bound to rise greatly. It is clear that the waters of the rivers are corrupted when the air surrounding them is corrupted; for this reason, the waters will be poor.

In the fruits of the earth, there will also occur diminutions, scarcities, and losses, especially in those things which humans necessarily require. Their loss will be caused by worms created in the vegetables, or by locusts, or by flooding, or by overabundant rains, or by cold, or by similar things; so that from this, a great scarcity will sometimes arise, by occasion of which people will die.

And there will happen to the fruits of the earth a lessening and damage, especially in those that are necessary to humans; and the damage that happens to them will be from worms and locusts, or from blight <note>original: "pulzone"; likely referring to plant lice or a similar pest</note>, or great rains, or great cold and the like. And so a great storm will happen because of these things, which will be the cause and occasion for many people to die.

The fruits of the earth that are necessary for humans are wheat, barley, grapes <note>original: "vve", likely a transcription of "uvae"</note>, and such things. For when Saturn cools the air, it greatly weakens the natural heat that is in the fruits; and nature does not have the strength with which to complete them and bring them to their proper state. Rather, the cold kills them if the season is cold. And many animals, such as worms, locusts, and mice, eat them, harming and destroying them. Likewise, because of great rains, the rivers will rise and destroy and carry away a great part of them. Therefore, because of all these things, it is expected that there will be a great lessening in the fruits of the earth, especially in those which are suitable for humans because they are more temperate. Now, however, observe how one thing follows another. For by this rule you shall judge in this art; therefore it is necessary that you be sharp and well-understanding, so that you recognize whatever you judge; nor should you judge a matter that is not in its proper time. For example: if the significance of Saturn happens at a time when there are no wheat harvests, it follows that you should not judge concerning the wheat with any of these things.

This is his general work: because his <term>complexion</term> <note>the combination of primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, or dry</note> is hot, moist, and temperate <note>balanced and life-sustaining</note>, just as was demonstrated in the first part; and the nature of heat and humidity, when it is in balance, is to make all natural things grow.

# Treatise

...of the planet, or such a star; I say this because the nature of that planet generates a thing in the air that is between us, or in the water, or in animals. However, when it is said that humidity prevails in the work of Venus, it means that the power of Venus generates toward us moisture rather than dryness.

Its specific and particular work in men is the **loftiness of ranks**, **honors**, **cheerfulness**, **improvement of status**, **excellence in marriage**, a **multitude of children**, the comforts of all marital affairs, the increase of substance, **clean and pure actions**, a good spirit in observing laws, a fit fleshiness, and a connection to kings and the bloodline of the powerful.

If her own specific and particular work is among men, there will happen to them an exaltation of dignities and the joys of good things, a good state of being, the improvement of marriages, a multitude of children, the praise of all marriages, an increase in riches, a good and clear maintenance of life, and good will in the deeds of the law; their bodies will grow stout, and they will become friends with princes and be honored among them.

It has been demonstrated that the nature of Venus makes things grow just as the nature of Jupiter does, except that femininity prevails in her. And since this is so, men and the dignities of men will be exalted, and many good marriages will occur, along with the generation of children and the increase of riches; and because of this, men will maintain themselves in a beautiful and clear manner, behaving as benign men of good command. Because of the femininity that prevails in the power of Venus, men will be more humble and obedient, and act as benign men of good command. Their bodies will grow stout due to the tempered moisture that Venus creates; and through the exaltation of dignities and the boldness of Venus, men will rejoice with princes and be honored among them.

But in the qualities of the air, there will happen **winds with temperance and moisture**, many feedings will occur, and the air will be pleasant and serene.

And if she is in the air, there will occur in it temperate and many moist winds, and the air will be clear, good, and bright.

Because a temperate complexion <term>complexion: the balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a thing's nature</term> of Venus prevails in the air, which leans more toward moisture, a humid vapor will arise in the air which will greatly nourish all things so that they must grow; and because of this, there will be temperate, moist, nourishing winds, and the air will be temperate and good.

As for the waters, those things which help life to arise and many rains will be present.

Ships also, sailing upon the sea, will be saved; in **trade**, profit will be made; rivers will increase and be filled.

And if she is in the waters that generate life, she will cause many rains, and ships will sail well and securely, and they will profit much in trade, and the streams will grow greatly.

It is manifest that when the nature of Venus is favorable, it will cause many moist vapors with temperance that assist in life and nourishment; and because of this, there will be many rains, by which the streams must grow; and the waters will cause all things to prosper; and because of the temperance of the air with the fortune of Venus, ships will go securely, abundantly, and safely through the sea, and they will profit much in trade—especially in sweet things and aromatic merchandise, such as good and fragrant spices, precious cloths, pearls, and precious stones, and such things.

Also, the animals which men use and the fruits of the earth will grow and be improved and prosper.

And if she is among the animals from which men benefit and in the fruits of the earth itself, they will have a multitude and abundance, and men will benefit from them.

It is manifest that when the nature of Venus happens upon beneficial animals, harmful animals will decrease; and in this way, you shall attribute to each planet an increase in things according to their agreement with it, and a decrease in those things which disagree with it.

Mercury, therefore, when he alone is the lord of the disposition, is generally mixed with the others, and his nature will be likened to them.

And if Mercury alone is the lord of governance, he will generally involve himself with the nature of any of the other planets and accord with the nature of that planet.

This means that when Mercury alone is the governor, there will be such works as those of the planet or fixed star to which he is applied; and if he is applied to none, his work will be likened to the part of the signs in which he is located; and such is the status of Mercury generally when he is the governor.

Moreover, his own specific and particular work among men is **the sharpest intellect**; and they will also be strong in that which they wish to do with a subtle mind. **The cutting off of roads**, **larceny**, and **plundering** will happen to them. In voyages by sea, however, when he is associated with misfortunes, there will be difficulty.

And his work is to move things much more than the other planets. And his work in those things that happen to men is great sharpness and subtlety in those things that a thief wishes to do, who wishes to lie in wait on the roads, to commit larceny, thefts, and robberies, and to set ambushes. Similarly, there is danger by sea if he has participation with a planet in misfortune.

When Mercury is the governor, he will perform the works of the star with which he is mixed, very quickly and with great and strong motion; and because of this, his works among men will be very sharp and involve thefts; and he will give them subtle characters, and among killers, and in ambushes. Similarly, if he is in any dignity of Mars or accords with him, he will do miraculous things in road ambushes, thefts, larcenies, killings, and hidden traps. For Mars does such things openly and discovered by the force of arms, but Mercury does them through subtle ways and arts; and if both are joined together, then miraculous things will happen.

He is also the cause of **dry sickness**, as well as **daily fevers**, **coughs**, **vomiting**, and **consumption** <term>consumption: historically "phthisis," a wasting disease usually identified as tuberculosis</term>.

And through him occur dry illnesses: daily fevers, violent vomiting, and consumption.

Mercury will cause dry infirmities because he is of a dry nature; and he will cause acute infirmities because he is of rapid motion. And since Ptolemy <note>original: "Pto." (Ptolemaeus)</note> said that Mercury performs the works of the stars with which he is involved, and of the parts of the signs in which he is, it follows that if he is in the dignity of any planet, his complexion is reduced to the complexion of that planet, whether it be the lord of the term, the house, the exaltation, or the triplicity. Nevertheless, he told us that all his works are unfortunate works; and this is because his two houses are in trine <term>trine: an astrological aspect of 120 degrees, usually considered harmonious</term> to the two houses of Mars. And because of this, it is fitting that the nature of Mercury tends toward the nature of Saturn and Mars, and tends little toward the nature of Venus, and is contrary to the nature of Jupiter because his houses are opposite to the houses of Jupiter. Yet, because the two houses of Mercury are in trine to the two houses of Venus, and nevertheless his fall is in the exaltation of Venus, it happens that he resembles the nature of Venus a little and is distanced from her as much as his nature is distanced from hers, and as much as exaltation is distanced from fall. Afterward, it happens that he does all these bad things—which Mercury does alone when he is the lord of the significance—without being mixed with another cause; and if he is mixed with the fortunes <term>fortunes: the "benefic" planets, Jupiter and Venus</term>, he will do the deeds they do, but not as completely as when he is mixed with misfortunes, where he will do much greater evils and damages than they do themselves. It is useful that you keep all these things concerning the deeds of Mercury, as Ptolemy expressed them, in your memory.

The office of **divination**, the **divine**, and those things which are to come in the inheritances of the houses of prayer; the **variation of customs** and **laws** sometimes according to his mixture with the other stars.

The diminutions of the service of God, and those things which occur in sanctuaries, the change of customs and laws at certain times, are according to his mixture with any of the stars.

# Second Book

$\P$ In the accidents <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to external events or changing circumstances, rather than essential natures.</note> of sanctuaries, customs, laws—which are the services of God—and in the common practices of any city, there will be a strength of evil and corruption at one time more than another when **Mercury** is the ruler. This depends on whether the planets with which he is mixed are **infortunes** <term>Infortunes: Malefic planets, traditionally Saturn and Mars, which were thought to bring challenges.</term> or **fortunes** <term>Fortunes: Benefic planets, like Jupiter and Venus, thought to bring growth and harmony.</term>. If he is with the fortunes, the damage will be less; if with the infortunes, it will be much greater.

$\P$ Because his constitution is dry and his motion is swift due to his proximity to the sun, and because his retrogradations <term>Retrogradation: The appearance of a planet moving backward in the sky from Earth's perspective.</term> are frequent in his revolution, he is a disturber and a repeater. Through his swift variation, he excites winds in the air, as well as thunder, lightning, openings in the earth, earthquakes, and confusion. Perhaps through these aforementioned things, harm will come to the animals and plants that men use most.

$\P$ And because he is of a dry constitution and swift motion (since he always moves near the sun and retrogrades frequently in his course), he specifically produces turbulent and swift winds in the air. These change easily and cause thunder, flashes of lightning, earthquakes, and bolts <note>original: "relampagos," a term for lightning flashes.</note> through which great damage sometimes happens to the animals and plants by which men sustain themselves.

$\P$ Now finally, regarding the first part: the constitution of Mercury dries and moistens in one manner, for he causes as much dryness as he does moisture. It was said in this place that he is dry, yet the reason was immediately given why he might cause moisture for the greater part of the time. Through the participation he always has with the sun because of his swift motion, and because he frequently returns to the sun, dryness prevails in him. He works in the air according to how the infortunes work when he is mixed with the nature of the sun; for from this mixture dry vapors are made, from which troublesome winds arise. As it was said, ships perish, the plants of the earth are harmed, and thunder, bolts, and flashes of lightning occur, just as they do through the dryness of **Mars**. And because Mercury generates dry vapors and draws them from the depths of the earth, it follows that earthquakes happen because of them, through which many places are submerged. These things are followed by the corruption of plants and trees, and of the animals from which men benefit, and an increase in plants and animals harmful to men, just as Mars causes.

$\P$ Decreases in waters and rivers will occur at the hours of his setting; however, at the hours of his rising, they will be increased.

$\P$ When he is hidden <note>This refers to a planet being "combust" or obscured by the sun's glare.</note> he works a great lessening in waters and streams, and when he appears, he increases them.

$\P$ Note that he is "hidden" when he enters again under the rays of the sun. At that time, he causes great dryness, for the dry vapors increase and the moist vapors are diminished; therefore, waters and streams are diminished. The time when he "ascends" is when he exits from under the rays of the sun; at this time alone he causes moisture, for the moist vapor increases and the dry vapor is diminished, wherefore the waters and streams must increase. Here, Ptolemy <note>original: "ꝑto." or "Ptolomeus"</note> will give you the places in which Mercury causes dryness: these are when he is in the dignities <term>Dignities: Specific signs or degrees in the zodiac where a planet is thought to have more power.</term> of dry planets, when he regards himself with them (by aspect), and when he enters under the rays of the sun. The places where he causes moisture are when he is in the dignities of moist planets, when he regards himself with them, and when he exits from under the rays of the sun. It is necessary that you understand this well.

$\P$ Therefore, each one of the planets, when it is in its own natural state, will work what is proper to itself.

$\P$ And any of those planets, when it is in its own state that is proper to it, works such things as these are.

$\P$ Any of the planets, when it is the significator <term>Significator: The planet that acts as the primary indicator for a specific person or event in an astrological chart.</term> and is not mixed with another thing, its power will remain in its own state with its own proper works. These are the works that Ptolemy described up to this point. However, when its power is changed by another thing—either by a thing that has participation with it in its rising or in its constitution—its works will be changed, sometimes to a greater degree and sometimes to a lesser, according to the power of the others that are mixed with it. For example: when **Saturn** and **Mars** rule in the governance of the world, or when one of them is the ruler

<column-break/>

and regards the other, this demonstrates from this the strifes and wars of foreign men, captivities, and very great and powerful things according to what the aspect was. If the aspect was a **trine** or **sextile** <term>Trine/Sextile: Harmonious astrological angles (120 or 60 degrees) thought to facilitate easy flow between planetary energies.</term>, there will be peace because of a great fear of the sword, so that one obeys the other for fear of killing and captivities and such. And if the aspect was a **square** <term>Square: A harsh 90-degree angle representing tension or conflict.</term>, it will signify a great strength of strifes, battles, and wars that will last a long time and return many times. If Saturn and **Jupiter** are the rulers, or if one is the ruler and regards the other, it signifies that the great damage of Saturn will be diminished, or the good of Jupiter will be diminished; and this will be according to the aspect that occurred. In this way, we say it is to be understood for all others; and you will be able to understand when you have studied well and understand the reasons of this book; wherefore it is necessary that you apply your mind well to it.

$\P$ When they are mixed with one another according to the fellowship of the figures <note>In this context, "figures" likely refers to astrological aspects or planetary configurations.</note> and the difference of the signs and their appearance in respect to the sun—and before this according to the mixture of their works—their proper work will be from different species according to this, and it will be mixed from the natures that associate with their own natures.

$\P$ And when the planets and stars are mixed, one with another through the participation of figures and diversity of signs, and according to the appearance they have in comparison to the sun, and before this the mixture they have in their works through such things as these are, their works will be of various kinds according to the nature of the mixtures which will have participation with their own nature.

$\P$ When the planet **Venus** is the ruler, and some other power is mixed with her power by some aspect from the four figures we have mentioned (without the power of the degrees of the signs or by the comparison she has to the sun), it is fitting in all ways from such a mixture that there be a very great diversity in her work. For she must always be according to the other nature that is mixed with her. It is necessary that you understand Ptolemy's words word for word: for what he said regarding "participations in figures," he means according to the **aspect** of the planets (one with another). What he said regarding "diversities of signs," he means according to whether some are in the dignity of others, and whether they are in the **angles** <term>Angles: The 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses of a chart, considered the most powerful locations.</term>, or following the angles, or falling from the angles. What he said regarding "their appearance in comparison to the sun," he said so that they might be oriental or occidental, appearing or hidden, direct or retrograde, or in their evening configurations. Everything else that Ptolemy said has been demonstrated.

$\P$ Wherefore, since the narration of a proper work resulting from every kind of mixture is inexplicable and cannot be done, and since the general narration of all these things in whatever figures they happen can be understood in many ways, this species is left to the listeners: so that they may inquire into and observe the particulars within it.

$\P$ And because to declare the works of every kind of mixture is an infinite thing and impossible—and generally all this, in whatever figure it happens, is a thing that can be understood in many ways—it is fitting through these things we have said to demonstrate this manner to the student wishing to learn, so that he himself may prepare and search out these particular things that are in it.

$\P$ Because the mixtures of the planets (of one with another, and with the degrees of the signs, and in comparison to the sun) are infinite, and similarly to explain the matter of every mixture from these composites—for this reason, they could not be placed in a book. Since this is so, it was not fitting for Ptolemy to declare to us the works of the mixtures of every composite; for it is manifest that when we know the simple natures and understand these rules by which we can know how one is composed with another, we will then be able to know the composite mixtures through the rules themselves. And it is manifest that the works of a composite mixture are these same works of the simple constitutions from which the composite constitution was composed.

### Treatise

If the works are composed together, one with another, then by these same rules the works of a composite temperament <note>original: "complexionis composite"; refers to the mixing of different planetary influences</note> can be made. Since Ptolemy taught us all these rules, it is fitting for one wishing to learn to seek out the composite temperament through the rules themselves, so that through them he may understand the workings of that mixture in any matter. And some wish to make known composite temperaments who have not followed the right path. It is fitting, therefore, for you to make good use of all the rules which Ptolemy explained, for they will set you on the path of knowing the nature of whatever thing you seek. We have placed many examples of this in our gloss <note>A "gloss" is a series of explanatory notes added to a main text.</note> and have written to you here of a secret art, so that no necessary thing remains for you, provided you have the understanding. It is fitting then that you return to it; if you reach what you seek, it is very good. If not, know that your understanding is neither sufficient nor complete; then you ought to rebuke yourself, for nothing remains for anyone else to do but you, who wish to stand around idly or not study these things, or who are occupied tomorrow with many other affairs, or perhaps your brain is not of a good temperament, and your understanding is far from it, which would separate you from the knowledge of this art.

We ought to observe these similarities of the stars—through which future events happen—in relation to the regions and lands where those future events are signified to occur, in this manner: When the **fortunes** <term>Fortunes: Benefic planets, like Jupiter and Venus.</term> are in the places where future events will happen, and the stars that are in their **hayz** <term>Hayz: An astrological condition where a planet is in a position (sign/hemisphere) that matches its own nature or "sect."</term> are similar to them, and stars of a contrary hayz do not rise above them, then the work of their nature will be of greater strength. Just as when they are not similar to those places, and stars that are contrary to them rise above them, their strength will be less. However, when their mixture is harmful and they rule over a future work: if they are similar to the places where the future events occur, and the stars of a contrary hayz rise over them, they will alleviate the harm. But if the disposition of those regions is not similar to them, and stars similar to those regions do not rise over them, the work of their harmful temperament will happen more severely in those places.

And it is fitting that you look at the concordance of the planets through which an event occurs with the regions and cities, signifying that which ought to happen. Thus, if there are **fortunes** that concord with the places in which the event occurs, and planets of a different kind do not rise over them, their work will be more beneficial. Similarly, if they do not concord with those places and contrary planets rise over them, their benefit will be less. And if they are of a harmful temperament—namely, the lords of the work of the event—and they concord with the places of the event and such planets rise over them, the damage will be small. But if they are not the governors of those regions, and concordant planets do not rise over them, the work of damage will be greater.

This is a very good rule, and it is fitting that you always keep it ready in your memory and your understanding, for it will happen that certain regions concord with a certain planet. And at some time another planet will govern the work, or this same planet will be the governor, yet another planet concordant with its temperament or of a similar kind will rise over it. Ptolemy speaks of this "elevation" in different ways: one is when a planet is in some dignity <term>Dignity: A sign or part of the zodiac where a planet has special strength.</term> of another, and when the lord of that dignity is applied to the one that is there, we say it is elevated over it. Another way is when one planet is more noble than another and is of greater power; it is elevated over the one that is weaker. The third way is when one planet is in the tenth sign from another; we say it is elevated over the other in the tenth sign. Similarly, a **fortune** planet never does damage in a region concordant with it, nor does an **infortune** <term>Infortune: A malefic planet, like Saturn or Mars.</term> do great damage in regions with which it concords. Indeed, it does very great damage in those which do not concord with it. But if it governs any region, know that in its own regions it will not do great damage; if it does not concord with itself, it will do great damage there.

<column-break/>

For I am declaring to you the obscurity and the enclosure of Ptolemy’s words through these sayings, so that you may return to Ptolemy’s words and look diligently and well into the rule itself, because in it you will find what you seek.

General events occur more frequently to people in whose birth charts <note>original: "nativitatibus"</note> the necessary places—that is, the places where the **luminaries** <term>Luminaries: The Sun and the Moon.</term> are—and the places of the **angles** <term>Angles: The four most powerful points in a chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</term> are the locations of the causes of general events—that is, the locations of eclipses or the locations opposite to them.

And general events happen most often to those who have the necessary places—namely, the luminaries and the locations of the angles in their birth charts—in the very same locations as the eclipses or their opposites.

This is another rule: just as the regions receiving an event are those which concord with the sign of the eclipse and the sign of the governing planet, so the event happens to those for whom some **hyleg** <term>Hyleg: The "giver of life," a specific planet or point in a birth chart used to determine longevity.</term> out of the five hylegs is the very location of the eclipse or its opposite, or the governing planet of the eclipse. The more this happens, the stronger the event will be for that person.

But this will be more grave and most difficult to guard against when those same parts of the eclipse locations are parts of the locations of one of the luminaries in the birth chart; and after this, when these parts are opposite to them.

And this is stronger than anything else, and that from which one can least protect oneself: when the degrees of the location of the eclipse are the very same degrees as one of the two luminaries in one's birth chart; and after this, when those degrees are the opposite degrees.

When it happens that the boundary of the degrees of the principal locations of someone's birth chart is the degree of the eclipse itself or the degree opposite the eclipse, and this occurs in the land where the eclipse's significance is indicated, it is impossible that he should escape in any way from the event of the eclipse, whether it be good or evil; he will not be able to guard himself when it reaches him. And you shall hold this same rule for the degree of that which is shown in the eclipse and its opposite, and for the signs and degrees that aspect the sign of the eclipse or its degree. Judge each of them according to the aspect and concordance it has with the sign of the eclipse or its degree. And it clearly appears from Ptolemy’s words that if the principal degree of someone's birth chart is the degree of the eclipse itself, this will be the strongest of all; after this, the location of the opposite follows that. Similarly, after that follows the one who is in the fourth or the third [sign/house].

### On the colors of the eclipse and on tailed stars and similar things. Chapter 9.

->Haly said:<-

**Astronomers** name these secondary things of the stars because they happen from the action of the stars and are very much their own because they are around them; for they similarly have powers that work upon things below them. And after he spoke about the action of the stars, he demonstrates here the action of these other things that follow them.

**In** future universal matters, it is fitting for us to observe the colors appearing at the hour of the eclipse—that is, the colors of the luminaries themselves and of those things seen around them, such as those called "haloes" and "rods" <note>original: "halcisi balela"; likely referring to parhelia (sun dogs) or similar atmospheric phenomena</note> and things similar to these.

Similarly, it is fitting that you look into the matter of universal events that occur, and also the colors occurring and appearing at the hour of the eclipse. I mean the colors of the two luminaries, or the colors of those things that happen around them, such as that which says "spears" and "rubble" <note>original: "asta et rudera"; likely describing specific shapes of comets or atmospheric disturbances</note> and such colors.

**Every** single thing among those that are generated and corrupted concords with some power of the stars and its own work.

...corresponds with the work of the star with which it agrees. And after this, we can know the significance of events through the colors of eclipses or by the **vapors** <note>original: "fumositatem"; in medieval science, these were exhalations from the earth that formed atmospheric phenomena like halos or clouds</note> that gather around the two luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>.
Therefore, when they are black or almost green, they signify those things which we said imitate the nature of **Saturn**.
Thus, when the color is black or leans slightly toward green, it signifies those things we said tend toward the nature of Saturn.
The color black is due to great burning—for it is clear that a thing which burns much later returns to a cold state—or the blackness is due to very great cold. And the color green occurs because of great cold, as demonstrated in physics. Since this is so, it is appropriate that the colors black and green correspond with the nature of Saturn.
And when they are white, they are said to signify those things which are of the nature of **Jupiter**.
And if it is white, it signifies things of Jupiter's nature.
A white color that leans slightly toward yellow (unless it is very white) signifies temperance <note>A balanced state of being, neither too hot nor too cold</note>, and for this reason, it corresponds with the nature of Jupiter.
If they decline toward redness, they designate those things which are of the nature of **Mars**.
And if it tends toward vermilion, it signifies things of the nature of Mars.
Those things that tend toward vermilion are bright red things, and it is demonstrated in physics that these colors signify heat and dryness; for this reason, they correspond with the nature of Mars.
And if they appear golden in color, they indicate those things that follow the nature of **Venus**.
And if it is yellow tending toward a golden color, it signifies things of the nature of Venus.
This is a splendid yellow color, and for that reason, it demonstrates temperance and corresponds with the nature of Venus. For the colors he spoke of correspond with the planets in two ways: one, that their color matches the planet's color; the other, because they have the same significance as the planet's own nature.
But if they are of diverse colors, they signify those things which are of the nature of **Mercury**.
And if the colors are diverse, they signify things of Mercury's nature.
He means to say that if any of these things that appear are of different colors, each color demonstrates its own proper thing. Since this is so, it corresponds with Mercury, because he is of diverse states and significations, and his colors are similarly diverse and not stable in one manner.
And it is fitting that you understand this same reasoning in all the superior signs <note>Atmospheric phenomena like halos, rainbows, or mock suns</note> that appear: for they all occur through humid vapor and dry vapor that ascends upward. When one planet dominates a part of the world's governance, it brings those vapors to its own nature; the color will then match the nature of the complexion of that planet which rules. For this reason, the significance of the planet's nature is taken from the color of the signs. Ptolemy, however, taught us through this saying how we might know the nature of the ruler when we see any of these signs above; this is a thing that helps us greatly in knowing which power prevails in the mixture made from one celestial body with another.
If, however, that color embraces the whole body of the luminary or those things around it, the event will happen in the majority of regions. But if it occupies only one part of the luminary or those around it, the event will occur only in that part which is in the direction of the side where the color appeared.
And if the color is in the whole body of the luminaries or in all the places around them, the accident <note>A specific occurrence or event</note> will be in the majority of their regions. And if it is in one part of the luminaries or in the part around them, the accident will be only in the part

<column-break/>

that stands in the direction of that part where the color is.
He means to say that the vapor which alters the nature of the eclipse gives such a color as is the color of the ruler within it. If its color is total in a total eclipse, or in the places around the two luminaries, we will know that the power which gave it such a color is very great; therefore, it will signify that the event will be in the majority of regions corresponding with the accident. And if the color is in one part of the eclipsed luminary, or in one place around it, it demonstrates that the working power will be in that part and will work in the regions corresponding with that part in which the color is. Since the power of the eclipse operates at that time, it is thereafter manifest that the superior signs which happen after the eclipse have dominion from the power of the **governor** <note>The planet ruling the astrological "house" or period</note> which is over the point of that time. For by this, great movements occur in the earthly world over a long time until those powers are completed and other similar powers occur. Since this is so, it follows that superior signs have their effects through them as long as the time of the eclipse's governor lasts. For this reason, it will have a significance corresponding with the significance of the eclipse. Thus, if Saturn is the governor, he will join the vapors and make them thick, so that sight cannot pass through them, and they will appear black or green. But if Mars is the governor, he will burn the vapors and purge them, and from this, a **comet** <note>original: "come"; literally "hair," referring to the tail of a comet</note> will be made, or rays resembling stars running through the sky, and lightnings and such things. It is the same in each of the superior signs, for they resemble the ruling planet.
Likewise, it is fitting that we observe the **tailed stars** <note>comets</note> that appeared at the hour of the eclipse or at another time, as well as other universal future things, such as those called *aleiri*, *abbocat*, *halbaueni*, and similar things <note>These are likely medieval Latinizations of Arabic terms for atmospheric phenomena like halos (*al-hala*) or parhelia/mock suns</note>. Their natures are likened to the **Martian** and **Mercurial** natures we spoke of before, because they already work through burnings and qualities that cause things to move, and the accidents that happen because of them.
It is also fitting that we look at the comets appearing at the hour of the eclipse or another hour, and at universal accidents that happen, such as **spears** and **beams** <note>original: "asta z mebla"; likely *hasta* (spears/pillars of light) and *nebula* or *nubila* (clouds/mists)</note> that appear above, black and thick, and at that which resembles a lake of water and such things.
And we shall judge their natures in all that they work according to what we said of the natures of Mars and Mercury, who work strife, wars, burnings, and things of great and rapid movement, and the accidents that happen through them.
He has already demonstrated that the accident of an eclipse happens at the time of the eclipse and in the times following it; sometimes they happen at times far removed from the time of the eclipse. The superior signs that happen again in the middle of the air are made of dry smoke and humid vapor; their forms and colors are matched with the planet dominating the governance of the world below in that hour when they appear. From this, it follows that the dry smoke that occurs corresponds with the nature of Mars or Mercury, and humid vapors with the nature of Jupiter or Venus if temperance prevails in it. Then, if it is distempered and exceeds moderation, it follows that it corresponds with the nature of Saturn. If this is so, it follows that each of the superior signs signifies those things that happen among us—to men, plants, beasts, fish, ships, and the increase and decrease of water—and their significance will be according to the planet that corresponds with them. After all these things we have proposed, listen and understand what Ptolemy wished to say. For he said that we should also look at the comet stars that were at the hours of the eclipse, as well as at other hours, and generally whatever he said in that aphorism. For he means to say that when we know the significations of the eclipse and for whom it will be, we shall look at all this together in the accidents happening in superior things concerning the temperament of the air. For if they appear in the times of the eclipse, or in the times when their works happen, and their significations are matched to that part which rules, we shall judge according to that. It can also be that the significations of these things will vary the significance of the planet ruling in the eclipse if another star rules in the time that they appear—whether it be the one that rules in the eclipse, or through another eclipse that will come, or through some joining of the planets, or through the conjunctions or oppositions that will be at that time. # Treatise

...of lakes of water: and of such things, because all these occur through a dry smoke <note>original: "sumum siccum"; refers to the Aristotelian "dry exhalation" thought to cause meteors and comets</note> that is a dry vapor: it happens that its significance agrees with that of **Mars** and **Mercury**: in disputes and wars; in the fires of furnaces, thefts, burnings; and those things that move the spirit to do evil; and in the accidents happening through such things: such as robbing and capturing, which occur because of wars; and sudden deaths, acute fevers, and other things which **Ptolemy** said are in the nature of Mars and Mercury. 

And after it is thus, it happens that the significance of temperate rains and every balance happening in the air agrees with that of **Jupiter** and **Venus**: such as the cheapness of goods, the exaltation of dignities, and all other works which Ptolemy said of Venus and Jupiter. Similarly, the significance of hailstones and strong rains and very great cold will coincide with those of **Saturn** and its works which Ptolemy narrated.

For Ptolemy said concerning the superior signs <note>Celestial omens or astronomical events</note> that they would be "accidents" <note>Events or occurrences</note>, because each of them results in many effects, such as rains: which, if they are many, will harm plants and animals; and if they are few and diminished, they also harm. Such harm would be a lack of food, scarcity, famine, and mortality. And if they are temperate, they benefit plants and animals: which indeed brings an abundance of food and health. Similarly, the rainbow appearing in the air: if it appears before rain, it signifies rain; and if after, it signifies clear weather. Similarly, any of these things signifies particular works; and for this reason, Ptolemy called them "universal accidents."

The places also in which future events will happen we shall know from their locations in the circle of the signs <note>The Zodiac</note> and from the places directly in line with the **tailed star** <note>original: "stella caudata"; a comet</note>. We shall also understand the species of the future significance and its sub-genus from the form of that accident which will then appear. From the quantity of time that the accident appears, we shall know the duration of the future event. From its affinity with the Sun, it will indicate at what hour the future event begins. For when they appear more in the morning, their future event will happen suddenly; when they appear more in the evening, the future event will happen late.

And the places in which there will be accidents will be shown through the places of these signals in the Zodiac and through the places of the signs toward which the **comet** <note>original: "stella comata"</note> points. The form of the appearing signal will show from what species the accident will be and of what genus. The time during which the signal itself lasts will signify how long the accident will last, and its relationship to the Sun will signify when it begins. Since, for the most part, if it appears in the morning, the morning accident will be soon; and if it appears as an evening star, it will be late.

After Ptolemy showed the significance of each of the superior signals, he gave us one general rule, saying that when a superior signal appears and you wish to know which accident will come to earthly things through it, and you wish to know in which regions and cities it will happen: look in what place of the signs it is, and the accident will be in the regions and cities which are assigned to that same sign. And if you wish to know what kind of accident it will be, look at its form and color: and with whichever planet it agrees, the accident will be of the nature of that planet: and the power of the accident will be according to the strength of the planet ruling there. And if you wish to know when it will happen and how long it will last: look at the hours between the signal and the **Ascendant** <note>The degree of the Zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>; do as you did with eclipses. 

I, however, saw such a sign in the figure of **Scorpio**, and in opposition to the Sun, the Sun being at that hour in the 15th degree of **Taurus**. And that star was *Al-Ançadera* <note>original: "alāçadera"; likely the supernova of 1006 AD, which Haly ibn Ridwan famously described</note> in the 15th degree of Scorpio. It was a figure of very large round shape; it could have been three times as large as Venus. And from its brightness, the whole horizon shone; its light was as much as a quarter of the Moon. It appeared moving in that sign with the motion of the firmament until it placed itself in its **Sextile** <note>An astrological aspect of 60 degrees</note> in the sign of **Virgo**, and then it was obscured. I saw all of this, as did many other wise men. The locations of the planets at the appearance of this signal were as follows: the Sun and Moon were joined in 

<column-break/>

the 15th degree of Taurus; Saturn in **Leo** at 12 degrees and 11 minutes; Jupiter in **Cancer** at 11 degrees and 21 minutes; Mars in Scorpio at 21 degrees and 9 minutes; Venus in **Gemini** at 12 degrees and 23 minutes; Mercury in Taurus at 5 degrees, 7 minutes, and 5 seconds; the **Head of the Dragon** <note>The North Node of the Moon</note> in **Sagittarius** at 23 degrees and 38 minutes. That star *Al-Ançadera* which appeared was in the 15th degree of Scorpio. The Ascendant when it appeared over the city of **Al-Fustat** in Egypt <note>original: "alfozat ciuitate de egypto"; Al-Fustat was the first capital of Egypt under Muslim rule</note> was Leo at 4 degrees, 7 minutes, and 2 seconds; and the 10th house was **Aries** at 27 degrees and 37 minutes, with all of Taurus.

I say that because it was in Scorpio, which is the sign of the law of the **Moors** <note>The Islamic world</note> and the sign of their conjunction, there occurred among the Moors great battles, fierce wars, and killings. And because of this, cities and great regions of their lands were depopulated. And a great heretic went out and rose up in the region of **Mecca** and **Yathrib** <note>original: "yetob"; ancient name for Medina</note>. And a great drought occurred, and a great scarcity of food, and great mortality because of the corruption of the air and because of the plague. So many people died from hunger, the sword, and infirmities—people without number—and thousands of men and nations. Indeed, this evil and destruction was continuous for many years after the star appeared. We shall speak of this when we place examples in such matters.

### Here begins the 2nd treatise of the commentary of Haly Heben Rodan on the 2nd part of Ptolemy's Quadripartitum.

#### On the beginning of the year. Chapter 10.

Because we wish to comment upon the words of Ptolemy, all that he spoke concerning great and universal accidents has now passed. Now, however, we wish to comment on what he said about accidents that add or subtract <note>referring to factors that increase or decrease the intensity of predicted events</note>.

Ptolemy gives us in this chapter rules by which we may know what happens in the seasons of the year: and when we combine them with other previously mentioned rules, we will know if they will add to or subtract from the universal accidents which we know through eclipses and the conjunctions of the planets; and with this, we will know the accident completely and of what kind it will be in any season.

-> After the previously mentioned universal mode of knowing those things which are in the future for regions and lands, it remains that we subjoin the particulars, namely those things which happen in the seasons of the year. <-

After we have taught the general opinion for knowing the accidents that happen in cities and regions, it remains to narrate similarly the particulars, and these are those which happen through the seasons of the year.

The **General Opinion** is the rule which he gave us in the eclipses and conjunctions of the planets; and the particulars that happen in the seasons of the year are those which occur through the conjunctions and oppositions of the months of the year. For when we join these with eclipses, they will add to them or subtract from them.

-> And the time which is called the beginning of the year: to show this, it is necessary that the beginning of the Sun's return in each revolution should be that, almost on account of its power and its name, it is plain and open. <-

In this indeed it is appropriate for us to name the station which is called the "Head of the Year": and it is manifest that it is expedient that this beginning be the return of the Sun in each revolution to its place; and this is an easy thing to understand because of its power and its name.

He who wishes to know through this art the accidents that happen in any year, it is expedient to know the hour which is called the "Head of the Year": for first, when something is bound <note>original: "ligat"; an astrological term for a fixed condition</note> in it, it cannot be undone until its four seasons have passed—which are the first increase, the peak, and the decrease—unless another thing comes which makes it stronger in another of these four times. And this is manifest in all natural things, especially in the art of physics: that which the stars have bound in the Head of the Year remains that firm binding through the whole year; except if there occurs in that year an eclipse or a conjunction of planets or another application of stars which signifies that which the stars bound in the beginning of the year, or undoes that which was bound in the beginning of the year. But all he said about its power means that what it works first will remain firm until the matter is completed...

# Second Book

...where it had its beginning: and that which he said regarding its name. He wishes to say that what the name of the "beginning" signifies, its power signifies: for the beginning of the year is when the Sun returns to the point from which it began. Because the Sun is the central point and dominates over all the planets and stars: and because of this, it happens that the year is taken from its course alone: because the courses of other planets are in comparison to it; as has been demonstrated in astrology. 

The ancient Sages valued the beginning of the year so much that they compiled many books on it, and named these books *The Revolutions of the Years of the World* <note>original: "revolutionum annorum mundi"; a standard term for mundane astrology predicting global events</note>: such as the book of "accidents" <note>occurrences or events</note> which **Hermes** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many astrological works were attributed</note> made: and because of this, many astrologers believed that the significance of an eclipse or a conjunction or any other constellation whatsoever that happens in the year is not accepted except from the "Lord of the Year" <note>the planet ruling the beginning of the year</note>: and you will find this in all their books. 

They indeed depart from the truth: for **Ptolemy** showed in the second book on eclipses that since a greater power overcomes a lesser, and the power of the two luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> is vastly greater than that of the other stars, it is clear that their conjunction and opposition is greater and stronger than the powers of the revolutions of the years. And since it is so, nothing remains for the power of the beginning of the year except to add or subtract from great events. And this is the opinion of Ptolemy.

¶ But in a circle, no one can think of a beginning absolutely: however, in the zodiacal circle, a beginning can only be understood from the points which are directly at the equinoxes and solstices.

¶ And no one can imagine a beginning in a circle; yet in the zodiac, one can understand a beginning from the points determining the four **tropics** <note>The "turning points" where the Sun changes its seasonal direction: the two equinoxes and two solstices</note>.

¶ Some say that the beginning of the year is whenever the Sun goes from the point of its **apogee** <note>original: "augis"; the point where the Sun is furthest from the Earth</note> until it returns to it. And they said that this is its own unique property in its sphere: not because the works coming through the stars in these things which are among us are not unique to the sphere of the Sun; but they are according to the zodiac of the signs: it is necessary that the beginning of the year be the course of the Sun from one point of the zodiac until it returns to it: and when we seek these points in the zodiac, we find in it four points, any of which deserves to be the beginning: and these four points are the four tropics.

¶ It also happens that men doubt concerning these locations, because they do not know which of these four is more appropriate to put first.

¶ For according to the simple nature of a circle: none of them precedes the other, such that one is more fit to be the initiation than another.

¶ And a man faces doubt in this place: how he might be able to know which of these four deserves to be prioritized more rightly. For according to the simple nature of the circumference: there is no place there which is "before" another of which we can say: that it has the right to be the beginning of the year over another.

¶ Since the zodiac of the signs has four points: any of which deserves to be the beginning. Doubt happens in this, because a man does not know which has the greater right to be the beginning. Similarly, how can there be a point which is the "beginning" of a circumference, since it is simple and round: for this does not enter the understanding; yet man arranges this by convention according to his will; but that the circumference should have it by nature: this thing is impossible. And since it is so, it leads us to look into the words of the ancient sages who spoke concerning these four points in the manner that we will find in their understandings: and that the truth may emerge from their sayings.

¶ Those who have attempted to treat this in their books have placed these four seasons in different ways: and they established each one of them as the place of the beginning: because the nature and effect of each led them to this: for to each of these times there is a certain unique property for which we ought to think that it is the beginning of the new year: because of this they placed the vernal <note>Spring</note> equinoctial time as the beginning: because the day in it begins to overcome the night: and because it is moist: for nature is very moist in every beginning of a thing when it is created: as we have shown in the preceding sections. But the summer solstitial time is placed as the beginning: because in it the day is perfected: and it is its furthest length: and because in it, among the Egyptians, is the rising 

<column-break/>

of the Nile: and in it rises the "shining one" <note>original: "aschere algemenia"; likely Procyon or a related star</note> and the equinox; but the autumnal time took the beginning: because in it is the collection of all fruits: and because future crops begin to be sown in it; but the winter solstitial time is established as the beginning for this reason: because after the shortening of the days, the lengthening of those days begins in it.

¶ And if those who have spoken of these things in their books judged that these four points are diverse: and placed each of them as a beginning: and they brought arguments reaching toward this: for these are the works of their natures: because each of these times has its own property which causes it to be held as the beginning of the year; the vernal equinox: because the day begins to be greater than the night: and because this time is moist: and this moist nature prevails much in every beginning of things which are born, as we said before. And the summer solstice: because the day is completed in it: and it is the greatest day of the whole year: and there happens in it the flooding of the Nile in Egypt: and the star rises in it which is called **Albaboz** <note>original: "albaboz"; a Latinization of an Arabic term for Sirius, the Dog Star</note>: and the autumnal equinox: because all fruits are collected at this time: and similarly at this time all seeds are sown for those things which are to come: and the winter solstice: because the day begins to increase in it after it had been diminished.

¶ "Four seasons." He means the four seasons of the year: and the significance of each is taken from its beginning: he said, namely, that the ancient sages took these four points in different ways: for among them were those who placed the beginning of the year at the vernal equinox: and others who placed the judgment of each time according to the constellation of its beginning. And since it is so, it appears through the words of the ancient sages that each of the points has its own property: and Ptolemy teaches us by what reason they came to this opinion. And he said: because they knew that a circumference has no beginning: and they found through natural experience many times: that each of these points performs works in the things which are among us: and things which follow the natures of these points: for all this made them come to this opinion: because they hold that each of them is a beginning for future things: and he wishes to say that the works of these points made them believe that all were beginnings. 

And the time of the vernal equinox: because the day begins to be greater than the night: and when the day begins to be greater than the night: heat begins to rise over the cold: and the time is of much natural moisture: so that there is much in the beginning of any generation: when much moisture is joined with the increase of heat, it becomes a thing concordant with the beginning of all generation: as has been demonstrated in physics and natural science: and because of this, the vernal time is for those things born by nature: and in it the trees put forth leaves: the birds sing and make offspring: and every thing which accords with the beginning has a greater right to be the beginning than that which does not accord: and this is the thing which he brought to all astrologers for affirmation: that this time is the beginning of the new year. 

And the point of the summer solstice similarly has the right to be the beginning: because the day is completed in it: and there is the greatest day of the whole year: and then begins the flooding of the Nile which is the beginning and the strength of the labor of the land of Egypt: and this first point has such works by which many believed that it comes through the rising of the star **Albaboz** <note>Sirius</note> which rises at that time: and they believed that these works remain for the whole year: as much as appears of the power of this time. 

And the point of the autumnal equinox time similarly has the right to be the beginning: because all fruits are then collected and managed for the future time: and sowings also occur and begin at this time: whereby all birds and all animals have life: and because of this they take from this time the significance of that which is to come in the granaries concerning salvation or corruption: and what will happen to these souls concerning the abundance of victuals: or whether a famine will occur, a great mortality and such things. 

And the point of the winter solstice similarly has the right to be the beginning: because in it the day begins to increase after it was diminished: and heat begins to increase: and when heat increases, generation comes with it: from these words also which Ptolemy said, we understand the quantity of the power of each of these four points. And that the greatest power of all is that of the vernal equinox point: and that each of these takes its significance from what has its origin in its own time: for it follows that we should take the comparison of that which happens in each of these times to that which occurred in the time that passed.
