# Treatise

...in the time of summer, it will have signified the rising of the Nile <note>original: "recentia Nili"; referring to the annual flooding of the river essential for Egyptian agriculture</note> because of the humidity that existed in the preceding spring time. According to that, there will be a rising: if there was much spring humidity, the rising will be great and large; if there was little, it will be smaller; and similarly for other things.

And what is more suitable and closer to natural reason in the observation of the year’s affairs is the observation of these four principles <note>the four "Ingresses" or the start of the four seasons</note>: as well as the conjunctions <note>the alignment of planets, specifically New Moons</note> and preventions <note>original: "preventionum"; here meaning oppositions or Full Moons</note> of the sun and moon that occurred close to and preceding those times. This is especially true of those in which eclipses occurred.

And what I hold to be better and closer to natural opinion regarding the facts of the year is to work through these four principles: to look at the conjunctions and the oppositions of the sun and moon which are closer to these principles before these times, and specifically at that one in which there will be an eclipse.

We have already said before that a "turn" <note>original: "vices"; the shifting influence or cycle</note> changes a weaker power and draws it toward itself: and you should do this for all powers that are smaller until the action of that power is completed, and another stronger turn of those same powers arrives: and thus the second shall be united with the first. And after it is so, it happens that the power of the conjunction or opposition which occurred before the sun enters any of these points <note>the seasonal points of the zodiac</note> is the mistress of the point which the sun enters. Furthermore, according to this, it follows that the sign of what will happen in each of these four seasons is a mixture of the powers of the planets at the hour of the conjunction or opposition before the sun enters the point of that season: for such is the opinion of **Ptolemy**. There are, however, others saying that the sign of any time is from the Ascendant <note>the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon</note> when the sun enters the point of that time. But this opinion is defective for four reasons. First, because the joining of the sun and moon is stronger and of greater power than the power of the sun combined only with the power of that zodiacal point. For no power is given to the whole sign except because of the sun, and even more so at the specific point of the sign.

The second reason is: because a circumference has no beginning <note>a circle, like the zodiac, has no natural starting point without the luminaries to define it</note>.

The third is: because when the sun enters the point of **Aries**, it cannot be certified; for with one astronomical table it will appear of one sort, and with another table of another: and it is not so with conjunctions and oppositions, since their ascendants agree with all tables. Through these things, you will understand that the power of a conjunction or opposition is of greater potential when the sun enters that point. And since it is of greater potential, it draws the power of others to itself, and it shall be the governor. And it follows that you should understand **Ptolemy** well regarding this, especially if there should be an eclipse there. He means to say that when an eclipse happens in a conjunction or opposition that occurred before the sun enters any of these four points, whatever sort it may be, it will be of greater power than if it occurred without an eclipse; and it will be of greater effect and change.

Thus, through the principle which is perceived from the sun’s existence in **Aries**, we recognize the quality of spring. And through the beginning of its existence in **Cancer**, the quality of summer is perceived.

Through the principle that is known from its entry into **Libra**, the autumnal quality is known. The beginning which is taken from its entry into **Capricorn** demonstrates the winter quality.

Thus we may know from the beginning of the hour that the sun enters **Aries** what the state of spring will be; and from the beginning when it enters **Cancer**, how the summer will be; and from the beginning when it enters **Libra**, what the autumn will be like; and from the beginning when it enters **Capricorn**, how the winter will be.

He means to say that we will know from the conjunction or opposition that occurred before the sun enters **Aries** what the state of spring was: if the air will be very hot, or humid, or dry. If it was very hot, we know that the trees will put forth leaves quickly, and the fruits will arrive before they are fully formed. And if it was very cold, it signifies that the trees will be slow to put forth leaves, and the fruits that were light will be much lighter. And if it was humid, it signifies the rotting of fruits, and they will be very light. And if it was dry, they will demonstrate that the fruits and other things will dry up. And through this, we can know which fruits of the earth will be many, and which few at another time; and we will know through this that the fruit which is plentiful will be cheaper, and that which is scarce will be expensive. We shall also know these things for the sailing of ships and the safety

<column-break/>

of journeys: for when we know that the ships and journeys will be safe and secure, we will know that those things which they carry will be cheap and at a good price. And by this same means, we will know that which will happen in cities regarding the things brought there: for if that which is brought is little, it will be expensive there where it is needed; and thus we will know all things. I, however, wish to show you more regarding the reason for scarcity and abundance of good things by which you may help yourself: you shall form the four angles <note>the four primary houses of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli</note>, and the stars and the other planets at the hour of the eclipse, or the conjunction and opposition of the sun and moon: just as with any other great conjunction. If there should be a planet there, then look to the angle of the Midheaven <note>original: "medy celi"; the highest point in the sky</note> and its lord; and to the place of the sun and its lord. If they should be of great power, they will signify a scarcity of money, and everything that is bought with them will be cheap. And if the power belongs to the Ascendant and its lord, and the moon and the lord of its place, it will signify a scarcity of things that are bought, such as wheat and barley, and the cheapness of money; and a small amount of merchandise will be bought for many coins. And if the moon was separated from a "misfortune" <note>original: "ifortuna"; a malefic planet like Saturn or Mars</note> and went toward a "fortune" <note>original: "fortuna"; a benefic planet like Jupiter or Venus</note> after the conjunction or opposition, it will signify a scarcity of wheat and barley; for the sun and the Midheaven accord with gold, while the Ascendant and the moon accord with the grain supply <note>original: "anona"; the state-managed grain or food market</note>, because they are similar to bodies: and every thing whose significator in the firmament is made fortunate will be expensive.

And if you have understood what we have shown, you ought to know that gold accords with the sun; and gold coinage with the sun, Venus, and Mercury—with Venus because of its beauty, and with Mercury because of its engraving. The grain supply accords with the moon; meats with Mars because of slaughter <note>original: "degulationem"</note> and cooking; fruits with Venus because of their scent and sweetness; bitter, sharp, and burning things belong to Mars; sour and astringent things accord with Saturn; sweet things with Jupiter; large things with Venus; and those of many flavors with Mercury; humid and watery things with the moon; rotten and bad-smelling things with Saturn; and those of good odor with Jupiter and Venus. Similarly, you will be able to understand colors: for blackness belongs to Saturn, and likewise for similar things; and thus you can know every thing through its correspondence. The angles accord with gold; the signs following the angles with the grain supply; and the falling signs <note>cadent houses</note> with those things which are not necessary to humans.

When, however, the "fortunes" are in the angles, the thing corresponding with that place will become expensive. And when you find the planet corresponding with a thing at the hour of the eclipse, or conjunction, or opposition, see how that planet stands there. If it is fortunate and powerful, it will signify the scarcity of that thing and its exaltation <note>increase in price/value</note>; if unfortunate, it will signify its utility <note>abundance or low price</note>. Indeed, add this to what we said about what the air will do to all fruits, and the safety of ships or their sinking: for when that thing you wish to look at is before that time, you will know how things will become cheap or expensive, and you will know the things that follow. For example, when we know that one of these things will struggle against another, we will know that he whose land is abundant will overcome him whose land is scarce and similar; because

You will also know the fact of scarcity and abundance because of the multitude of waters and their strengthening, and from cold and heat. For when the stars signify many and humid vapors, many rains occur from them; and if they occur in a time when they are necessary, they will demonstrate an abundance of victuals; but if in a time when they are not necessary, they will demonstrate the ruin and lessening of them. Heat and cold do the same: for if the heat is in a time when it is expected, it will signify the saving of all fruits from rotting; but if it is in a time when it is not expedient, it will dry up all the fruit of the earth before it is complete and it will perish. Similarly regarding locusts, grubs <note>original: "guasanis"</note>, and mice: for if they grow in great numbers they will destroy all the fruits of the earth, and if they are few, the fruits can be saved. You can know all these things through astronomy, and you will know that which is to come before it happens. So that the first is in the mode of the beginning of a thing; the second in the mode of increase; the third in the mode of the end; and the fourth in the mode of decline.

# Treatise

...they are fast: sometimes truly they are slow: because they remove themselves from the zodiac of signs: some toward the north, some toward the south. And he <note>Referring to Ptolemy</note> spoke of that which pertains to the fixed stars in the 9th chapter of the first part: and expressly of the meaning of the signs and the triplicities <term>triplicities: groups of three zodiac signs sharing the same elemental nature (fire, earth, air, or water)</term>. And although he expressed all these things, it remained to narrate the properties of each sign and its parts.

**A**ries and its sign in general, because of the equinox <term>equinox: the moment when day and night are of equal length, occurring as the sun enters Aries</term> occurring in it, brings thunder and flashes of lightning.

**I** say that the nature of the whole sign of Aries, because of the equinox that is in it, is the maker of thunders and lightning. For the sign of Aries makes thunder and lightning because when the sun enters it, it dissolves the cold humidity that joined together in winter: and because of this, a moist smokiness <note>original: "fumositas"; likely referring to water vapor or atmospheric haze</note> is gathered in the air: and from it clouds are made: and when one runs against another and they move strongly, thunder is made because of the sound of that motion: and because of the strike of the motion, lightning is made.

**B**ut the nature of its parts in increase and decrease is understood from the properties of the fixed stars <term>fixed stars: stars that appear not to move relative to each other, as opposed to the "wandering" planets</term> which are found in it.

**A**nd the nature of its parts in adding or subtracting can be known through the nature of the fixed stars which are in it.

**H**ere you must understand by this saying that which the philosophers said: since the signs are mansions <term>mansions: stationary divisions of the sky</term> which have no works of their own; the works are actually of the fixed stars which are within them. Because the sun runs through all these in one year, each sign is named according to what the sun performs while within it. And because each of the fixed stars remains in a single degree of a sign for 100 years according to the ancient opinion, or 70 years according to the new <note>This refers to the "precession of the equinoxes," where the positions of stars slowly shift over centuries. Ancient astronomers like Ptolemy estimated 1 degree per 100 years; later medieval astronomers corrected this to roughly 1 degree per 70-72 years</note>: it happens that the work of one part is of the star itself as long as it lasts there. When it is moved to another part, the work of that first part will change accordingly. For the work of the star is fixed: and because of this it pertains to the specific degrees of the signs and takes the same name, because the fixed star remains there a long time. 

If Ptolemy <note>original: "ptol."</note> had wished to narrate the power and work of every star, his book would have been too long; yet he taught you the way in the 9th chapter of the first part so that you might know this. He divided each sign in this place into three parts <term>decans: divisions of a zodiac sign into three segments of 10 degrees each</term> and extracted the complexion <term>complexion: the specific mixture of qualities—hot, cold, moist, or dry—governing the temperament of a celestial body</term> which is made through the mixing of the powers of the fixed stars found in each of the three signs of the triplicity. Follow this way so that you may judge by them: observe the approach of the stars and their change from place to place: and according to this you shall change your judgment, as we have told you in the glossary; for this is a very subtle method and reasoning. Therefore, look into it and understand it yourself.

**F**or the beginning of this sign makes rains and winds, and its middle is of a temperate complexion. But its extreme part is truly burning and generates mortality <note>original: "mortalitatem"; referring to death or pestilence caused by unseasonable or extreme heat</note>.

**A**nd the beginnings of these signs are generating rains and winds: and the middle parts are temperate, while the ends cause mortality.

**H**e wants to say that the fixed stars which were in his time in the beginning of Aries have a complexion which does not mix with the complexion of the sun: which pertains to the whole sign of Aries. Because of this, a certain power occurs there which draws the moist vapors that are the matter of rains and winds. Similarly, the fixed stars which were in his time in the middle of Aries have a complexion that does not mix with the sun's general complexion for Aries; there occurs a certain power which is likened to the temperate power of Jupiter and Venus. Similarly, the fixed stars which in his time were at the end of Aries have a complexion not mixing with the sun's, and there occurs a power likened to the burning power of Mars; it is a generator of mortality because it makes the humidities gathered in winter putrefy. 

When things are thus, it happens that when any of these stars moves into the sign of Taurus, a mixture is formed between them and the work of the sun in Taurus. For example: we already understood that the sun's complexion in Aries generates the moist vapors that make clouds, thunder, and lightning. We know that when the powers of the fixed stars are mixed with this complexion (as they were in the beginning of Aries in Ptolemy's time), a mixture generating rains and winds occurs. It is declared that this complexion of stars also generates moist vapors. When these stars are moved toward the middle of Aries, and their power to create humidity is mixed with the power of the sun in Aries, there will occur no

winds and fewer rains. According to this rule, you should understand the other signs, since he has already stated the works proper to each part. It may be that these works are increased or diminished by that which will be ordained in the complexion that existed before—without opposition—and by eclipses and conjunctions of other planets and other applications <term>applications: the movement of one planet toward another to form an astrological aspect</term>.

**B**ut those stars which are in the north heat and destroy; those truly which are in the south congeal and make cold.

**A**nd those which were in the northern parts will be harmfully hot: and those in the south will be very cold and will generate great frosts.

**A**fter he said each sign is divided into three parts, and each part into 10 degrees, he assigned to each part the works of the fixed stars that were in that part during his time. Many fixed stars remained in the northern and southern parts of each sign; he joined the works of the north into one grouping and the works of the south into another; thus each sign takes five such groupings. It appears by his saying that all the complexions of the fixed stars in the northern part of Aries are of the nature of Mars, and those in the southern part are of the nature of Saturn. And when an eclipse occurs in any of these two parts, or the latitude of the moon <term>latitude: the distance of the moon north or south of the ecliptic</term> at the time of a conjunction or opposition, or the ruling planet, then the work of these conjunctions is mixed with the work of the eclipse or the ruling planet. Understand the remaining stars in other signs according to this.

**T**he sign of Taurus truly signifies both complexions; but yet it is more inclined toward the signifying of heat.

**A**nd the whole sign of Taurus signifies two complexions: and tends a little toward heat.

**H**e wants to say that when the sun is in Taurus, it dries and moistens equally. The dryness is caused by great heat, and the humidity by the attraction of the moist vapors that existed previously. Because of this, it creates more heat here than when it is in Aries; consequently, the sign of Taurus receives these works from the sun. Similarly, every sign and its parts receive from the sun and fixed stars a power with which they operate; this is a general principle for the whole.

**A**nd its first parts, which are around the Pleiades <note>original: "pleiades"; a prominent star cluster in Taurus</note>... make winds and clouds. The middle of the same sign moistens and cools. Those which are northern are of a temperate complexion, and those which are southern cause instability and disordered motions.

**A**nd its first parts, those following the Pleiades, are makers of earthquakes, winds, and clouds; those in the middle cool and moisten. Lastly, those from the side of Aldebaran are of the nature of fire, ignited with lightning and flashes; those from the northern side are of a temperate complexion, and those from the south make terrible motions as a rule.

**B**y this saying, Ptolemy shows that the Pleiades were in his time in the first 10 degrees of Taurus, and that their nature was to create dry vapors from which winds and earthquakes are made. Through the joining of its work with the work of all Taurus, clouds are made by the attraction of moist vapors. Now, however, in our time, the Pleiades are in the middle of Taurus; they still produce winds, but because the vapor is scattered by great heat, they do not produce clouds or earthquakes except on rare occasions. It appears from his words that the power of the fixed stars which were in the first 10 degrees of Taurus in his time were of the nature of Mercury. Those in the middle of Taurus had the power of Venus; those at the end had the power of Mars; those in the north had the power of Jupiter; and those in the south had the power of Mercury mixed with Saturn. Each part of Taurus received the powers of the fixed stars within it.

**A**nd the whole sign of Gemini creates temperance.

### On the Investigation of Particular Qualities. Chapter 12.

Ptolemy teaches in this chapter how the things he predicted are divided in a way that we may know them with certainty, because we need to know them at every hour.

Therefore, having promised these things, we shall subsequently describe the modes of particular significations. One of these modes is the observation of a matter generally, which is understood through the observation of each of the four quarters of the year.

<column-break/>

In this, we should observe the nearest conjunction or prevention <term>prevention: a term used for the syzygy or full moon (opposition) preceding a solar event</term> of the Sun and Moon that precedes the solstitial and equinoctial points, as we have said. We should then set all the angles for the hour of the conjunction or prevention in each climate <term>climate: a geographical zone or latitude</term> for which we wish to investigate, just as we set a birth chart <term>nativity: a horoscope or birth chart</term>. Afterward, we should observe the planets that are the *almudbebir* <term>almudbebir: from the Arabic 'al-mudabbir', meaning the governor or ruling planet of a chart</term> of the places where the conjunction or prevention occurred, as well as the disposition of the angle which these places follow, just as we showed in the matter of eclipses.

¶ And after we have said this, the particular significations will be in this manner which I wish to say and show. One of them is to look at the matter generally: and this is what a person can know from the nature of any quarter of the year in the way we described. It is necessary to look at what is contained and applied in the first conjunction of the Sun and Moon, or the opposition that was before the four tropics <term>tropics: refers here to the four turning points of the year—the solstices and equinoxes</term>. We must rectify the angles at the time of conjunction or opposition in whatever climate we wish to know, just as we do in birth charts. Afterward, you will take the planets governing the places of the conjunctions or oppositions and the governors of the angles that follow these places, just as we calculated in the matter of eclipses.

¶ The first thing we must do is to know the general accident <term>accident: a non-essential or changing quality, such as a weather event</term>—namely, what it will be, when it will be, and in what land. We will take the operation from the ascendant <term>ascendant: the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific time</term> for the specific matters of that quarter. Afterward, we will rectify the ascendant of the conjunction or opposition that occurs before the Sun enters the point of that quarter, as well as the other angles, properties, and fixed stars. We will look at what all this signifies in that quarter. Once we have certified this well, we will look at the entire signification; we will see which influence prevails, and we will judge according to it. This is the proper method of Ptolemy, if you have understood his words well.

¶ Next, the general properties of the quarters.

¶ Afterward, we shall know the general matter from the properties of the quarters.

If the accident is heat and it happens in winter, we will judge that the winter will be warm, with little cold or rain, and all other things in this manner.

¶ After the things we have said, it is necessary to observe this knowledge. When, therefore, a conjunction <note>original: "coniunctio"; the alignment of the Sun and Moon</note> occurs near a solstitial or equinoctial point that preceded the part, we shall observe clearly until the intersection of that same quarter; and when a prevention <note>original: "preventio"; likely referring to the preceding Full Moon</note> occurs near any of those points, we shall attend to the points until that quarter is finished.

¶ And it is fitting that we retain what I wish to say: I say that when a conjunction happens near one of the four tropical points <note>The solstices and equinoxes</note> that has passed, we shall look to the conjunctions until we reach the next quarter that follows it. And when an opposition <note>The Full Moon</note> happens near one of those points, we shall look to the oppositions until we reach that quarter which follows it.

¶ After the time for the sign is taken from the conjunctions and oppositions, it follows that there is a month from one conjunction to another, if it was a conjunctional quarter, or from an opposition if it was an oppositional quarter. Thus, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*</note> holds that the first certain time is not simply when the sun enters any of the four points; rather, he holds that it is from the conjunction or opposition that occurs around these four points. This remains and lasts as the governor until that quarter has passed, just as we showed before. And after this is so, we shall see if the quarter was conjunctional: we will make the start of the first month of the quarter from that conjunction, and the second conjunction that comes afterward will be the start of the second month of that quarter, and the third conjunction the start of the third month. We will judge each month according to the significance of its conjunction and its comparison with the whole quarter. We will do the same with oppositions if it was an oppositional quarter.

¶ Likewise, we must observe the angles and the stars of each of the predicted places of the <term>almudhebir<gloss>The governor or manager; a planet that "manages" a specific period or chart</gloss></term>.

For we shall look at what will dominate in one and the other; and he who is more in agreement with the properties of that quarter and with the accidents of the world will be seen, according to what we see of the power or weakness of that virtue.

¶ We should investigate the appearance of the approaching stars and the <term>alictisal<gloss>Application; when a faster planet approaches an aspect with a slower one</gloss></term> and <term>alinsiref<gloss>Separation; when planets move away from an aspect</gloss></term> of the wandering stars <note>Planets</note>, and the properties and qualities of those stars, and which winds they themselves move, as well as the signs and the parts of the signs in which they are. Again, we have observed toward which sign the blowing of the winds and the latitude of the moon declines when it has declined from the zodiac circle, so that in the majority of the qualities of the months, through all these things, we may foreknow what will prevail and their blowing.

¶ And we should look specifically at the appearance of the fixed stars that are nearby, and the appearances of the planets, and the application or elongation of one from another, and at their properties and states, and which winds these stars move, and the parts of the signs in which they will be. Similarly, we will look from the direction of the wind where the latitude of the moon is, if it is removed from the zodiac of the signs, so that through all these things we can know which of its winds will most prevail in the state of the month.

¶ When we know what is united in the quarter and what is united in the month, what will happen in that quarter and in that month of the quarter from both parts—and from the appearance of the fixed stars that appear nearby, and from the applications of the planets one with another, and their elongation, and their declination, and of the latitudes, and the properties of the signs of their parts in which they are—through all these things we will mix one with the other. We will know the prevailing power and judge by this the thing happening at any time, in any quarter, and in any month. This is the place that is sufficient in this art for the one who understands it well and has looked into it well; however, he who does not understand it will be far removed from this art. This, however, is how one can understand it well: by understanding everything we have taught up to this point

<column-break/>

from the words of Ptolemy, and by having it clear in his intellect, and by having a subtle and healthy power of consideration, using it much and looking into it.

¶ The third way, however, is that we should observe the stronger signifier which signifies over the weakness and strength of the matter, and from the fellowship of the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note> in particular figures—not only in the figures of conjunction and prevention, but even in those which are detected in the <term>dichotomy<gloss>The "halving" of the moon, referring to the first and third quarter phases</gloss></term> of the moon.

¶ The third proposal is to look into the more subtle signification which shows the mildness or strength of the matter; and this is the thing that can be known from the participation of the Sun with the Moon in particular figures, not only in figures of conjunction and opposition, but in those which occur when the Moon is halved in light.

¶ He gave us rules for the four times of the year and for the months; and we understand through them what will happen in the middle of any month by the opposition, if the month was conjunctional, and by the conjunction if it was oppositional. For we assume that some month is conjunctional. We can then know that which will happen in the middle of the second month through the opposition which occurs after that conjunction. And now he gives us a rule in this place by which we may know what will happen in any quarter of the four quarters of the month, saying that this can be known from the Moon when it is halved in light; and at this hour the Moon will be in the quarter of the Sun. Thus we take the sign of the middle of the month through the conjunction of the Moon with the Sun, or through their opposition; likewise, we will take the sign of what will happen in any quarter of the month from its own quarter phase. And when we see the comparison of one to the other, we will know the strength of the accident, or its mildness, and all the other things we have said. Similarly, it is useful that you calculate the angles in the quarters and judge by them just as you judged the oppositions and conjunctions.

¶ And the beginning of the alteration will more frequently be the figure three days before the Moon is with the Sun; and perhaps this work will be the three days that happen upon equal longitude.

¶ And the beginning of the signified change will be for the most part either three days before the Moon is with the Sun, or it can happen three days after, so that it will be in the elongation of equal parts.

¶ The Moon runs through a whole sign in two full days and one part of a third. Ptolemy set this as a full day for brevity, and because the virtue of the body of the moon is 15 degrees before and after; and because of this, it was three days. This in Ptolemy is understood in two ways: the first is that the Moon passes two complete signs in six days, and by passing through two signs, it arrives at the same number as there are in the firmament. And after it is so, it happens that it applies to the point in all signs in the three preceding days and in the three following; and at the hour it reaches them, that signification is moved. The second is that the virtue of the Moon turns with the virtue of the Sun for three days before application, and so it remains mixed until three days after its application, because the body of the Sun is 15 degrees before and 15 after, and the body of the Moon is 12 before and 12 after; however, the first way agrees more with the opinion of Ptolemy. Nevertheless, both have their reason.

¶ Likewise, it is detected from the fellowships of those two with the wandering stars in these or other qualities, such as in the trine and sextile <note>Astrological aspects: trine is 120 degrees, sextile is 60 degrees</note>.

¶ Similarly, we will know this from the participation they have with the planets in the figure and in any of these states, and others such as in the sextile and trine.

¶ Look at the words of Ptolemy, how one follows another; and how he placed the root of the signification upon the application of the Moon to the Sun. For in this place, it is intended that we can know what will happen in the month and in the middle of the month from the participation of the planets at the hour of conjunction or opposition. Afterward he did this, saying that this is to look at the participation of the planets and signs with the luminaries at the hour of the fourth, or sixth, or trine aspect. And then the root is this: that in any application which the Moon has with the Sun, we ought to form the ascendant and the angles and look to the planets and fixed stars, how they dwell at that hour by always joining...

# Treatise

How shall I know a particular matter alongside a universal one? That is what we wish to know before it happens. For Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, 2nd-century astronomer and author of the Tetrabiblos</note> adds to this whole demonstration for us both the text and the glosses.
¶ And because these things imitate the natural order.
¶ Because these things which I speak of follow the natural reality.
¶ What he means is this: that from the point where the Sun and Moon are joined, it will be so: from which all the planets that shall rule through many dignities at the hour of that planet's mixing will appear in their effects in things when we measure them in this way.
¶ We shall arrive at the quality of variation when the natural similarities held by the signs and stars which are observed are imitated by the surrounding air and the winds.
¶ And we will be able to know the state of change by following the natural agreements of the planets which they receive, and of the signs with the air surrounding us and the winds.
¶ He means to say that when we inspect the angles <note>The four most powerful points in an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note> and the locations of the planets at the hour when the two luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> apply one to the other, and we know the nature of the ruling planet, the universal state will be changed only so much. By taking a comparison of its effect with the effect of the first governor <note>The primary planet ruling the period</note> and with the properties of the air and winds at that time, we shall know from this how much a thing will increase or decrease.
¶ Truly, the strength of these particular qualities that occur daily will then be most apparent when the fixed stars <note>original: "non erratice stelle"; stars that do not move like planets</note> of greater brightness and stronger effect appear in the morning or evening, in the east or the west, according to their affinity with the sun; for this reason, they change and alter particular qualities to their own natures for the most part.
¶ And the hours of these particular states that occur on any given day will be specifically influenced by the fixed stars which are of greater light and effect when they appear in the evening or morning on the eastern or western side with respect to the sun: and this is because they change and reduce particular states into their own nature for the most part.
¶ Fixed stars of greater light are those of the first magnitude: and those of the second magnitude follow them in power: and those of the third magnitude follow them. For the power of any of these increases when it appears in the morning under the rays of the sun, or in the evening around its entry under the rays: because its power is mixed with the power of the sun. And it is manifest that although the power of the sun is the victor, it tends toward the power of the stars that are mixed with it. Likewise also regarding the moon. And since this is so in the fixed stars, it will be even more so in the planets: and when we mix these things according to what happens each day, we shall know by this the particular accidents <note>Specific occurrences or events</note> of any given day.
¶ Likewise, this will be no less when the luminaries are in any of the angles. For the weaknesses and strengths of the qualities of each hour will happen when the luminaries proceed into these places. Thus the flow and ebb [of the tides] are proven to happen when the moon is in these angles: and the change of the dispositions of the winds is near; it only happens at the course of the two luminaries toward these cardinal points: and their change is toward the wind toward which the latitude of the moon declines.
¶ Similarly, this will be no less than what we have said when either luminary passes through the angles: so that the gentleness and strength which will be in the states of any time happen when the luminaries pass through these places; thus both the increase and decrease are through the passage of the moon through these places: and the change of the states of the winds will specifically occur when the luminaries pass through these angles: and their change will be to the wind which will be from the direction where the latitude of the moon declines.
¶ He means to say that when either of the luminaries passes through any of the angles that were in its first application, it will signify an addition or a subtraction of the event of the application: and there will be an addition when the signification of its passage is the same as the sign of the root <note>The original planetary alignment or "base" chart</note>; and there will be a decrease when there are two different signs. And since it is so that when both luminaries apply to the governor or in the first degree of the sign, it will do the same: and it happens that you should know that the degree of the sign is the degree of the luminary

<column-break/>

which is above the earth: thereafter the degree of the sun is the degree of the sign. Likewise, according to the strength of the agent, the strength or gentleness of the thing will be: for the angle of the ascendant and the 10th house have greater power than the 7th and 4th houses. And Ptolemy confirms his neighboring reasoning by that which appears in the rising and falling of the sea: because when the moon is in one degree of the sign, it causes an addition in the flow.
For example: when it is the ascending degree of the preceding conjunction or opposition at the entry of the sun into Cancer or another sign, then when the moon passes through that sign, it will demonstrate the increase of the Nile. Likewise always when a planet applies to the governor: and when it passes through the place of the conjunction or opposition that was there: except if another greater sign happens which might disturb it. Likewise, the winds move from one part to another at the hour in which either of the two luminaries passes through any angle of the angles of the ascending signification according to the direction toward which the latitude of the moon shall decline.
¶ In every place, however, we ought to know that the first general occasion is stronger. Those things which follow are the occasions of particular accidents: because the effect is most certainly verified and corroborated when the stars which are of the nature of general things are associated with the "Almudbebir" <note>original: "almudbebir"; an Arabic term for the 'Governor' or planetary ruler of a chart</note> in the figure of particular natures.
¶ And it follows that we should understand in every place that the first universal cause is prior: and that which follows is the cause of particular accidents. And when we find the governing stars of universal natures that agree with the natures of the particulars in the figure, the work will be certified and strengthened.
¶ He means to say that when we know a universal accident from a cause having greater power, and we know a lesser accident from a cause following the first: and so we shall go from the greater to the lesser, declining; and from the universal to that which is particular until we reach the end of all things, ordering one after another. And when we have done this, we shall inspect because we shall find the things stable and agreed in one, and we shall put them in one place and make all of this one thing. For we shall do this when there are two signifiers, or three, or more at one and the same hour. And when we have done this, we shall inspect their comparison to the nature of that time and to the stronger cause: and we shall judge that which shall be according to that which prevails: because when many stars signify one thing, whichever it may be, it happens that if other parts or stars signify that which agrees with the first constellation, that signification itself will be stronger and certain: and if they are diverse, nothing will be certain except from that which is stronger and more nearly relates to the nature of the time in which the sign occurs: for this is in all general rules which, if observed by you, will succeed in every place.

### On signs which are taken from other signs. Chapter 13.

->Haly said:<-

Now we have demonstrated that superior signs <note>omens or celestial signals</note> always happen from the powers of the stars, and the superior sign is always assimilated to it: and its signification to the power of the ruling planet and its sign. Whence Ptolemy showed us rules in the superior signs so that we might know through them particular accidents, just as he showed us rules in these signs so that we might know universal accidents, in the same way he did with the planets and fixed stars.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring an avian figure surrounded by scrolling floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

Truly, in the prognostication of particular significations, it is useful to observe the signs which are around the sun and moon and the stars.
¶ Particular significations of prognostications hold great profit when one looks into the signs appearing around the sun and moon and the stars, each in its own time.
¶ Inspecting the superior signs which are around the sun and moon and the shining stars brings great profit for knowing particular accidents: which, when they happen universally before they are completed, help in knowing the prevailing complexion and that which happens in the air through it.
¶ That also which happens from these to the sun must be investigated for the knowledge of daily qualities when it emerges [rises]. In the knowledge of nocturnal qualities, however, it is fitting to observe and scrutinize when it sets.
¶ And it follows that we should inspect that which happens from this to the sun: when it rises, for knowing those things which shall be of the day: and when it sets, for knowing those things which happen of the night.

## The Second Book

¶ Since we shall know through the significators of the fourth year and the fourth month those accidents which will occur in the air, such as winds and rain, and we wish to know the daily occurrences arising from these, we shall observe the Sun as it rises in the morning and the exhalation <note>original: "fumositatem"; in medieval science, weather was thought to be caused by "vapors" or "fumes" rising from the Earth</note> which is joined around it. For that which happens during the day will correspond with that exhalation: if the vapor is dry, we know that winds and such things will happen that day; and if it is moist, we know there will be the softness of rain and similar things. The force of the event will occur in the direction where the vapor was most closely joined.

¶ Truly, to know the qualities whose spans extend through the hours of the associations of the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>, we shall consider them in the figure. This is because each of the qualities from that hour until the hour in which the Moon is in the following figure signifies, for the most part, what is to come.

¶ And for the sake of knowing those things which endure for many hours, look to the hours in which the Sun participates with the Moon and the figure; for those figures demonstrate, for the most part, the state that will exist from that hour until the hour when the Moon is able to enter the figure coming afterward.

¶ Since the Moon has a participation with the Sun in another bound figure, a certain power is held there which is not released except through another figure of the kind that releases it, as we have shown. And since this is so, it is appropriate that when a face appears around a luminary with a particular significance, some other of the superior signs should endure in that significance until another figure arrives; and this we have already taught well.

¶ When the Sun rises or sets, if it is clear and not covered by anything, and free from clouds, it signifies serene weather. But if its circle is of diverse colors, or if it declines toward a fiery redness, or if the rays of the Sun which proceed from it or are around it are red, or if the clouds which they call "mock suns" <note>original: "soles"; these are parhelia, bright spots in the sky caused by ice crystals</note> appear on one side of the Sun, and have the color of clouds declining toward redness, and its rays are extended long and separated from each other outside the circle, they signify very strong winds. These winds will be preceded by blasts from the directions in which these signs we have mentioned appear.

¶ Because when the Sun rises or sets being clear and bright without clouds or anything else covering it, it signifies serenity. And if its circle is of diverse colors or the beams are vermilion like fire, or if the rays coming from the Sun or around it are vermilion, or if there are clouds which are called "mock suns" on one side of it, resembling the color of a cloud tending toward vermilion, and its rays are extended and long, they signify strong winds; and these winds will move from the direction in which these signs appear.

¶ The clarity of the Sun when it rises and sets shows that the air is clear of all exhalation; and because of this, when it rises, its clarity shows that the day will be serene. And if it is clear when it sets, it shows that the night will be serene. And when the circle of the Sun is of diverse colors, it shows an exhalation of the nature of Mercury. And if it tends toward the vermilion of fire, and the rays coming from the Sun or around it are vermilion, it shows that the exhalation is of the nature of Mars. And if there are clouds called "mock suns," they are those which reverberate the rays of the Sun. When they tend toward vermilion, they also signify that the exhalation is of the nature of Mars. Similarly, if the rays of the Sun are extended and long, they demonstrate a dry and long smoke; and all these things demonstrate strong winds which will move from the direction of those signs.

¶ But if it rises black or declining toward greenness, or if it sets cloudy, or if one or two circles are around it, or if it has clouds around it which are called mock suns

<column-break/>

and thus their rays are declining toward greenness or are black, they shall indicate wintery weather <note>original: "hyemalem"; refers to stormy or harsh weather, not necessarily the season of winter</note> and rains.

¶ And if it rises black, or if it tends toward green, or sets with clouds, or has clouds called mock suns on both sides, or the rays which go out from the Sun tend toward blackness or green, it will signify wintery weather and rains.

¶ When the Sun rises or sets, if it appears black or green, it entirely shows that the exhalation around it is of the nature of Saturn. And if the clouds which reverberate the rays are green or tend toward blackness, because of this, it signifies—when they appear at the rising of the Sun—that the day will be rainy; and if they appear when it sets, the night will be rainy. The whole significance of the superior signs is certain if it agrees with the primary figures of the luminaries, for they have such significations, and thus you shall understand through all things.

¶ Likewise in the Moon, we ought to observe the same place on the day which is three days before the conjunction <note>The New Moon</note>, and the same before the opposition <note>The Full Moon</note>, and the same before the dichotomy <note>The Half Moon</note>, as well as three days after these hours.

¶ And it is also appropriate that you look to the place of the Moon on the third day before the conjunction or opposition. And the third as if it were halved in light; or the third day after these hours.

¶ After he has taught us the signs of the Sun, he now gives us those of the Moon, since we shall otherwise know the accidents, both enduring and coming, through the figures with the Moon. He began by having us look at the Moon on the third day before the figures and the third after; and if we see the Moon with such a significance, the judgment will be certain. And if they are diverse, we shall hold ourselves to the stronger reason of those three days which we have already demonstrated.

¶ Therefore, when it appears, if it seems thin, clear, and bright, and there is nothing by which it is surrounded, it will signify serenity. But if it is thin and red, and everything which it does not illuminate appears clear and as if it is seen to move, it will signify that blasts of wind are coming from that direction toward which it declines. But if it is black or green and thick, it will announce wintery air and rains.

¶ And if it is clear and does not hold anything around it, it demonstrates serenity. And if it is thin and vermilion, and that which remains of its circle or light is clear, resembling something that moves, it signifies the motion of winds from the side to which it declines. And if it is black or green and thick, it signifies wintery air and rains.

¶ When the Moon is thin and clear, and does not hold any circle around itself, nor a cloud, it demonstrates that the air is clear of exhalations. And if it is thin and vermilion, it signifies that the exhalation around it is of the nature of Mars in its dryness. And if the part of its circle in which there is no light is clear, resembling something that moves, it signifies a dry exhalation which moves; and because of this, it signifies a course of winds from the direction where the exhalation itself is. So too if the Moon is black or green and thick, it signifies that the exhalation which is joined around it is of the nature of Saturn; and because of this, it signifies wintery air and rains. It is appropriate that you join all these things with the significations of the planets standing in the figures of the two luminaries, and join it all with the property of the fourth year and month, and that which we have said.

¶ Likewise, it is appropriate that we attend to the circle which is formed around it: if it is one and clear and gradually shortens, it will designate clear air. But if there are two or three, they will demonstrate wintery air. If they decline toward a red color and are as if cut off, they will announce wintery air which will happen through powerful winds.

¶ And it is also appropriate that you look at the circle which is made around...

### Treatise

Concerning it: because if it <note>Referring to a halo or circle around a celestial body mentioned on the previous page</note> is single and clear and gradually fades, it signifies clarity of the air. If there are two or three, it signifies wintery weather. If it tends toward a vermilion circle and is broken, it signifies wintery weather coming with strong winds.
¶ When the circle is single, it shows that there is little smokiness <note>original: "fumositas"; in medieval science, weather was believed to be caused by "fumes" or vapors rising from the Earth</note> in the air. When there are many, it demonstrates that there is thickness and density in the vapor; many circles are formed because the rays reflect—namely, one to another. A reddish circle demonstrates vapor of the nature of Mars <note>Mars was traditionally associated with heat, dryness, and the color red</note>. When it is broken, it demonstrates the movement of the vapor; for this reason, any of these things signifies strong winds.
¶ If, however, they are turbid and thick, they will indicate wintery air that will come through a "wind-snow" <note>original: "ventiniuium"; a storm of wind and snow</note>.
¶ And if it is turbid and thick, it signifies wintery air with fine hail.
¶ The thickness of the circle signifies thick, cold vapors of the nature of Saturn <note>Saturn was associated with cold, contraction, and density</note>; and for this reason, it produces wintery air with clouds and echoes.
¶ And if they decline toward a blackish green and are broken, they will signify wintery air which happens by the occasion of both; and when there are more circles, there will be more effects according to what we have said before.
¶ And if it tends toward green with black and is broken, it demonstrates wintery air by these two things; and the more circles there are, the more of these things we have mentioned there will be.
¶ The blackness and greenness of the circle demonstrate cold and thick vapor in the air; when it is broken, it shows the movement of this vapor; and when these two are joined, they demonstrate wintery air which will be with cold winds and snows. Many circles show much and thick vapor, because one reflects the rays to the other; for this reason, many signify the strength of the thing they demonstrate.
¶ Likewise, a circle which appears around the wandering stars <note>The planets</note> and, among the non-wandering stars, around the bright ones, will signify things resembling the colors of those circles and the natures of those stars which they surround.
¶ Similarly, a circle around the Pleiades and bright stars demonstrates things concordant with the colors of those circles and with the natures of those things they encompass.
¶ This statement does not need a gloss <note>An explanatory note</note>, as it has already been demonstrated. Similarly, it can be understood that each of the stars draws to its own part a vapor concordant with its own nature; when this vapor appears in great quantity in the region of any star, it demonstrates that the power of that star prevails; and we shall know what kind of event will occur by the color of that vapor.
¶ It is also appropriate for us to observe the non-wandering stars, such as the Pleiades, Alfeca <note>Alphecca, the brightest star in the constellation Corona Borealis</note>, and similar ones, so that we may inspect their clusters where many stars approach one another, and so we may perceive their colors without considering their size.
¶ And it is appropriate that we look at the fixed stars, and at those which are very much in unity, one around the other; and that we look at their magnitudes and colors.
¶ There are stars that stand one near another, like the stars of Gemini and Scorpio. Truly, this does not need a gloss in this place, if you have understood the other gloss on everything we have said.
¶ For when they appear and are of greater light and greater size than usual, they will signify blasts of wind from that part in which they are situated.
¶ Thus, when they appear of greater and greater light than they are accustomed to be, they signify the paths of winds from the part where the stars are, from whatever direction they may be.
¶ This is because of the qualities of the dry vapor from which winds are made; and when this

<column-break/>

vapor penetrates the rays of sight, as is proven in the 5th treatise on optics <note>original: "aspectuū"; likely referring to a work on Perspective or Optics</note>, the stars appear with greater or lesser light than usual.
¶ Similarly, in the same way, those stars which specifically resemble Aldebaran <note>original: "aladeba"</note>, such as those called "Nathra" <note>The Manger or Praesepe (M44) in Cancer</note>, which are often mentioned, and those like them: when in clear weather they appear as if not visible or thick, they indicate many rains and wintery air. But if they are clear and shining, they announce powerful winds.
¶ Similarly, "nebulous" stars—specifically those stars called the Manger <note>original: "pesebre"; the Praesepe cluster</note> and others like them—if they stand covered and appear in clear weather as if they are thick, they signify much water and wintery air. And if they are clear and resplendent, they signify strong winds.
¶ There are stars that stand near one another—namely, around each other—and are of the 6th magnitude, or are from the nebulous ones; when they are hidden so that they are scarcely visible in clear weather because they do not have light for themselves, they show that there is a certain smokiness in the air that hinders them so that you cannot see them well; and therefore they signify rains.
¶ The manner of those things which happen at certain times from other conditions is similar. For the praised stars that resemble Aldebaran always show winds and dryness of the air; and the strength of what happens from this will be according to the multitude of those things and the length of their space.
¶ Similarly, those things which sometimes appear as signs, such as hairy stars <note>term: "stellae comatae"; comets</note>, always signify dryness of the air and winds; and what happens from them will be according to the number of these things.
¶ <margin>X</margin> Comets and "albançadere" <note>term: "albançadere"; a medieval Latinization of an Arabic term for meteors or shooting stars</note> are all made of dry vapor. And if they appear nebulous, it shows that there is little density in that vapor; for this reason, these things signify many winds and dryness of the air; and the winds and dryness of the air will be according to the magnitude of the comet and the meteor, and they will last according to the time that they endure.
¶ And the "throwing of stars" <note>Shooting stars</note> and their running: if it is from one of the corners <note>Cardinal directions</note>, it will signify that blasts of wind are coming from that part; and if they appear from different corners, it will announce disordered winds. If they are seen from four corners, one shall judge it to be wintery air from many directions; so that we shall not doubt that thunders, lightnings, and similar things will come from it.
¶ And the path of the stars, if they are from one corner, signifies the path of the winds from that part; and if they run from diverse corners, they signify winds that will run without order. And if they run from four corners, they signify diverse wintery air, so that they result in thunders and lightnings <note>original: "relampagos"</note> and such things.
¶ Aristotle and Theophrastus <note>Famous Greek philosophers who wrote on meteorology</note> have already demonstrated that "albançadere" <note>meteors</note> are made of dry vapor, and that winds are similarly made from this vapor. And since it is manifest that many shooting stars demonstrate many dry vapors in that part where they appear, by this they signify the paths of winds from that part. Truly, the "corners" spoken of in this place are those which we have said to be between the North and the West and all the other four corners.
¶ In the same way, when the qualities of the clouds resemble tufts of wool <note>Cirrocumulus or altocumulus clouds, often called a "mackerel sky"</note>, they will perhaps signify wintery air.
¶ And similarly, clouds that resemble fleeces of wool sometimes signify wintery air.
¶ If such clouds are formed, they are made of very thick and cut-up vapor; and this smokiness is accustomed to make the air wintery and bad.
¶ Also the Rainbow <note>original: "Iris"</note> which is sometimes seen: when it appears in clear times, it will pre-signify wintery air; and when it is formed in times of wintery air, it will announce clear weather.
¶ Similarly, the bow which sometimes appears, if it appears in clear time, demonstrates wintery air; and when in wintery...

## Second Book

...it will form from the evils of the air and will announce clear weather.
The **rainbow** occurs in the air through the reverberation of the rays of sight; it is seen near water in the light of the sun. When it appears in clear weather, it demonstrates an accumulation of watery smokiness <note>original: "fumositas"; medieval science viewed weather as the result of "fumes" or vapors rising from the earth</note> in the moist air; and when the air itself thickens, rain and wintery weather occur. And if it appears during a time of heavy rain in wintery air, it demonstrates that the smokiness which was accumulated in the air is being diminished and scattered; for this reason, it signifies clear weather.
Generally, however, we say that for the most part, the actual colors that appear in the air will indicate qualities similar to the events signified by those aforementioned colors.
And I say generally that many of these proper colors which appear in the air signify things that harmonize with the events signified by the colors we have discussed.
In this place, **Ptolemy** added what he said before, stating that the color of the smokiness which is joined in the air demonstrates that the event happens because of it.
These things, therefore, have been said in a general way for the investigation of general and particular matters. In the following sections, we shall explain the prognostication of nativities <note>Individual birth charts</note> as the order requires.
This is what we said in the general demonstration of universal and particular things; and we shall note the prognostications that will occur in the nativities of all men, which fits this arrangement.
Ptolemy finished the second part with this speech, saying that the universal and particular prognostications which happen in any region and any city will be according to what we have said. And after that universal nature of the ancestors has been joined with the event, the event itself will be received, which he then discusses in nativities. I, however, have seen fit for the good to add to this treatise the words of **Hermes**, in which he spoke in his book on events about things by which we can help ourselves in universal prognostications.
Hermes said: "Order the significators <note>Planets that indicate the outcome of a situation</note> by the stronger first, then the weaker, because their glory must have a participation in the sign with the one that is stronger." And he said that according to the state of each planet, the hour of the significator will be the state of that thing in which that planet rules. For if the **Sun** is in the second house, it will signify the movement of kings from one land to another; and if a fortune <note>A benefic or "lucky" planet like Jupiter or Venus</note> joins it, their journeys will be for good and for peace; but if a misfortune <note>A malefic or "unlucky" planet like Saturn or Mars</note> joins it, they will be for war and evil. And he said the **Sun** is the significator of kings, and the **Moon**, when she is in a sign that belongs to the Sun, is the significator of the sons of kings. And he said that **Jupiter** is the significator of great men, judges, religious people, and the wise; and if he is unfortunate, whatever he may be, it will be according to the nature of that misfortune. And he said: "Look at all people and kings from the lord of that house which rules." And he said: "When a fortune is the governor and moves toward a misfortune, there will be a change from good to evil, and vice versa." And he said: "When any planet or any sign is unfortunate at the hour of the sign, every matter over which it rules will be unfortunate; and it will be much worse if the misfortune is retrograde <note>Appearing to move backward in the sky, usually considered a sign of weakness or corruption</note> in the sign of its significance." And he said: "When any misfortune is in the exaltation <note>A specific sign where a planet's influence is most powerful</note> of another planet, it greatly harms those who are in the participation of that planet; for if the sign of **Aries** is harmed by some misfortune, it will harm the flocks, the cattle, the harvests, and the trees." And I said: "Look at the hour of the sign; the places of all planets in the region will be joyful and well-fortuned, and especially if that same planet is in a good place in the Ascendant—by day in a good aspect to the Sun, and by night to the Moon." Similarly, if it is in a good aspect with the misfortunes, its work will be of greater power; and if in a bad aspect, its work will be debased. And he said: "When a misfortune is retrograde in the exaltation of any planet and passes through the degree of exaltation, it will harm the people who are in the region of that planet." And it signifies that the king of that region will commit acts of pride and malice; for when that planet is retrograde, he is like one who departs from obedience; and the worst retrogradation of planets is that of **Saturn** and **Mars**. And he said: "Look at the kings and the governor and the magnates and the powerful from the planet that follows them in strength, and the people from the planet that is in strength, if one has participation with the other in the sign." of any planet, or its exaltation or triplicity, or from its trine aspect at that hour, look at the Ascendant; if the fortunes behold the governor from the tenth house, the king will have great good and all kings will fear him, and it will be to those people according to the planet looking upon him: if it is masculine, it will be of the barons; if feminine, of the women; if it is of a royal sign, it will be of kings; if it is a sign of two great men, it will be of such; and if a son, it will be of such; if it is from the second house, it will be on the part of wealth and riches; and if it is from the Ascendant, it will be regarding the matters with which he involves himself."

### Treatise

**Saturn**, when it aspects <note>An "aspect" is a specific geometric angle between planets that astrologers believe creates a relationship between their influences</note> [the significator of death], they will die with the pains of winds and [torn] sails; and if **Mars** aspects, they will die by the sword and fire. And if Mars is in a **bicorporeal sign** <note>Signs with dual nature, such as Gemini (the twins) or Pisces (the fish)</note>, they will die by arrows and diverse things. And he said that if the **fortunes** <note>Benefic planets, usually Jupiter or Venus, believed to bring positive outcomes</note> aspect and the planet is under the sun's rays, they signify ruin; and what the fortune signified [will happen], and if an **infortune** <note>Malefic planets, usually Saturn or Mars</note> aspects from its own place, there will be evil through thieves. And when the fortunes aspect while being **retrograde** <note>Appearing to move backward in the sky</note> or in **station** <note>When a planet appears to stand still before changing direction</note> under the sun's rays, they signify heresies and some strife. And when the sign of fortunes and infortunes is equal, they signify that the people will experience good and evil as one. And he said that when **Mercury** is "damned" <note>Poorly positioned or afflicted by negative aspects</note>, it signifies that scribes and servants will incite the king to commit injustice; and if Mars aspects Mercury in this state, it signifies many thieves. And he said that when the **Moon** aspects Mars and Mercury, it signifies that warring peoples will seek a truce among themselves. 

And he said that when the planet of the nobles and the people is an infortune appearing retrograde or in station, and it aspects the lord of the region with a bad aspect, men will rise up who are not from their own land, even their enemies. And if the aspect is a **trine** or **sextile** <note>Harmonious aspects of 120 or 60 degrees</note>, their enemies will be men of their own house and their kindred. And when the **Hyleg** <note>original: "vannum," the planet or point that determines the length of life</note> is strong, look at the place where the opposition is; and say for certain that on that day he shall die. And if the fortunes aspect, judge that the king will conquer and escape with his people, unless that infortune is falling. And if Mars aspects him, his death will be hastened; and if Saturn is there, he will have imprisonment for a long time until he dies. And if both Mars and Saturn aspect, he will be captured and afterward killed. And if this occurs in a bicorporeal sign, many will be killed in prison with him. And if one infortune is in a bicorporeal sign and the other in a **fixed sign** <note>Signs representing stability, like Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, or Aquarius</note>, it will not happen only once but many times; and there will be damage in that land until the infortune leaves that place, or until a fortune aspects, destroying that constellation. 

And he said it is appropriate that God provides a comparison of the signs of the king to the signs of the **luminaries** <note>The Sun and the Moon</note>; for if the Sun is slow and the Moon diminished at the hour of the signing, and the significator demonstrates strife, it will be greatly prolonged. And if the Sun is swift and the Moon increased in light at the hour of the signing, the matter will be reversed; and when the signs demonstrate strife occurring by day, the strife will be hasty and not prolonged.

¶ Here indeed we have added many of the sayings of **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of astrology and alchemy</note> from which you may profit, if God wills. And it is expedient that you look well upon and understand those things which we have well spoken in these two prior parts. And if you understand them, you will know well that which will happen in the world, whether of little or much, with the help of the Most High God.

¶ Here ends the gloss of **Haly Aben Rodan** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note> on the 2nd part of the *Quadripartitum* of Ptolemy.
¶ Here begins his first treatise on the 3rd part of the *Quadripartitum* of Ptolemy, which is the 7th treatise of the gloss. Said Haly:

**[Image: A decorative square initial "J" containing foliate motifs.]**

Now we have glossed the first and second parts of the treatises, and we have demonstrated in them the reasoning of the words of **Ptolemy**, which were rather brief. Now, however, we wish to gloss in the same manner the 3rd and 4th parts; and we say that Ptolemy narrated to us in these two parts the rules by which we may know the future accidents of any person through their whole life and at any time. In one part, indeed, he demonstrates to us the rules regarding those things that happen to the essence of a man in his body; and in the other, he demonstrates the rules of the accidents that happen to a man from outside himself. And when Ptolemy completed this, he considered some things he had left for later in the matters of **interrogations** <note>Horary astrology, used to answer specific questions</note>, **elections** <note>Choosing the best time to start an action</note>, and similar things. And we say that he showed all these things in what Ptolemy spoke in this book: whenever we wish to take the **ascendant** <note>The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment</note> of a question or an election, or such things, we will first look at it. And this is the hour of the person asking the question, or the hour in which we wish to choose something; and we shall adapt the **twelve houses** and the planets upon that first point and the place of the preceding **conjunction** or **opposition**, and the rulers; and we shall look at all these things and what they signify; and we shall say what such a person is, and such an election, in the same way that we do in their nativities and their revolutions. And the difference that exists between these things lies in joining the sign of the form with the matter that receives it. For example: the form which we take from eclipses and conjunctions of the planets, as we have already demonstrated, pertains to **general accidents**; such are kings, kingdoms, battles, famine, abundance of food, mortalities, pestilences, and similar things. And the form which we take from the ascendants of men who are being born, we shall show that it pertains to the accidents that happen to each man by himself. We shall likewise show that the form

<column-break/>

which we take from the **revolution of the nativity** <note>A chart cast for a person's birthday each year, also known as a Solar Return</note> pertains to the accidents that happen to each man in each year by himself. Thus we have demonstrated that the form which is taken from the **revolution of the years of the world** pertains to the accidents that happen to the world in each year by itself; similarly, the form which is taken in a question or election pertains to the matter in which that accident happens. And since it is so, the methods of the whole art are prepared, and the diversity is in nothing else except the matters receiving the accidents. And since this is so, all questions and elections are included in the words of Ptolemy which he spoke regarding nativities and before nativities. And if someone should say, "if it is so, it would be appropriate that what he narrated in nativities should have entered into the general rules he narrated"—we respond to this that the matter is so: but it was not his place to divide and judge many particular things in nativities which he did not divide in general matters. And if someone should say that it would similarly be appropriate to divide them in elections and questions, we respond and say that if the general matters of eclipses and the strong conjunctions of the planets agree with the significations of the nativities and their revolutions, it will be a grave thing to destroy the sign of such matters. And since this is so, questions and elections do not have the power to prevail in anything against the things signified by those other strong [general] indicators; and for this reason, it is superfluous to speak of them. Nevertheless, a man can extract what has been predicted in necessary matters; and therefore Ptolemy did not labor to compose a book on such things, because he held that this whole art would be fulfilled by what he had narrated—and this is the truth. Whence, he who has used and studied well in this *Quadripartitum* can indeed extract all elections and questions. And after we have shown this, we shall return to glossing the words of Ptolemy as we began.

### The third treatise of the third book of the *Quadripartitum* of Ptolemy begins, in which there are fourteen chapters. The Prooemium [Preface] of this treatise.

**[Image: A historiated initial "P" depicting a scholar or scribe wearing a cap and robes, seated at a lectern or desk with an open book.]**

After we have demonstrated the **general accidents** in those things which were set before us from our observation—because their observation is more appropriate to be presented first—we will now strive to explain how we may perceive the future things of each man in the properties of his own nature. This part of the work, therefore, is called the **prognostication of the matters of nativities**.

¶ After we have narrated before and begun in general accidents—because it is more appropriate that they be put forward—we now wish to show how those things which happen to any man in his own proper nature can be known; and this is the part of this art called the prognostication of the nativities of men.

### General accidents are those which happen to one people or many at some time, such as earthquakes,

strong winds, great floods, the inundation of rivers, new laws, new kingdoms, abundance of food and famine, mortalities and pestilence, the flight and depopulation of goods from one region to another, battles and robberies, conflict, diverse deaths, famine and war, the submersion of ships, the multiplication of evil beasts, the mortality of domestic animals, the wars of one king against another, the appearance of new customs in men, and such things. And we have already shown through the glosses of the second part all the rules by which we can know each of these before it happens. And it is manifest: when such a matter has a greater right, it should be spoken of before nativities, because general things are of greater power and overcome particular ones; for which reason it is appropriate for a master of this art to take a comparison of the particular to the universal; and thus his speech will always be firm and his judgment right.

Because, however, the power of these two parts is one in the way of work and science, it is not inconvenient to know them. For the movement of the sun and moon and the stars is the occasion of each proper and general accident. The difference, however, is in the nature of those things which were predicted and the similar movements, and the observation of those which the celestial things move; and those things which surround them are the occasion through...
