<meta>This page continues the transition into Book III of Ptolemy's work. The previous page ended with specific planetary aspects concerning death and social strife. This page establishes the theoretical framework for "particular" astrology (individual birth charts) and explains how they relate to "universal" or "general" astrology (world events), emphasizing that major world events always take precedence over individual destinies.</meta>

# Third [Book]

...by which the prognostication of these **accidents** <note>In this context, "accidents" (Latin: *accidentia*) refers to external events or happenings that occur to people or nations, rather than random mistakes.</note> shall be.

¶ It is fitting that we know that the power of these two kinds is one in its operation and in the knowledge of them. Because that which causes any of the accidents, whether general or particular, is the course of the planets, as well as the Sun and Moon; and furthermore, the knowledge of accidents before they happen consists of the diversity of the natures of all these aforesaid things and the rectification of their similar movements, just as the celestial bodies move within the things they encompass.

¶ Of the two kinds he mentioned: one is of **universal accidents**, which he described in the second part; the other is of **particular accidents**, and he describes this in the third and fourth parts. He says thus: that the power of what happens through universal and particular accidents—how we may know when they happen—is one and the same. And he proved this by saying that the thing causing any of the accidents is the movement of the stars, and everything else he said. And **particular accidents** are **nativities** <note>Individual birth charts.</note>, while the **universal** ones are those he described in the second part. Because these accidents come through the courses of the Sun, Moon, planets, and other stars and celestial things, just as we said in the commentary on the first part; so that through them, at any given time, a measure and a **complexion** <note>The specific "makeup" or temperament of the time, determined by planetary positions.</note> is created that is different from that which occurs at another time because of the diversity of their natures and their applications to the Earth. And because of these compositions, where one is composed with another, all accidents come about; and by the rectification of these compositions, we know things before they happen, all of which we demonstrated in the commentary on the first part.

¶ Except that general accidents are greater and do not need the supplement of the other; particular ones, however, do not stand alone.

¶ Since universal accidents are stronger and more complete in themselves, particular accidents are not so.

¶ After he shows that the power of the two kinds is one and the same, he now distinguishes between them. He says that the power causing universal accidents will be stronger and more complete in itself because it does not require an introduction in what it operates; and so that we may know this, the power of the three [planets] causing particular accidents is weaker than it, nor is it complete in itself. For it is necessary that it is not completed without the affirmation of the prior power; if that first power has not affirmed it, one falls into a great error. For a nativity may happen to someone signifying a life of 50 years, and in some year of his life, a weak **abscission** <note>A "cutting off" or a point in an astrological chart where life is threatened.</note> will occur; and in that year, some strong power from the first [universal] causes will occur, signifying a general **submersion** <note>Often referring to a flood or mass drowning, but used here as a metaphor for a general disaster.</note> or something even more general in which many people die, or a great mortality because of the **corruption of the air** <note>A reference to the miasma theory of plague or pestilence.</note>. And that man will die before he completes 50 years, because the great power subverts and overcomes all others that are below it, as is shown in the **science of physics** <note>Latin: *scia phice*. This refers to natural philosophy or the study of nature, likely referencing Aristotle's *Physics*.</note>. And for this reason, we say regarding such power that this dispute shall be so. If, however, the individual power accords with the general one—and it is fitting that you understand from me a thing that the physicists demonstrate—it is that all weak powers are not subverted to the greater ones unless they are in accord with them. And because of this, an abscission does not happen to anyone unless they have some sign of it in their nativity.

¶ Nor is it necessary that we think the hours of the principles themselves—in which we place the qualities of the celestial things and by which we strive to foreknow what is signified by the assembly of figures formed in those hours—are one and the same principle. Rather, we ought to think that there are many beginnings of general accidents, because we cannot find the beginning of everything in that whole. Indeed, these principles are not always found from the subject things themselves, but the occasions of future things are found from the surrounding things. For we, for the most part, investigate all accidents through the greater **eclipses** and through the stars that move with manifest motion. In individual men, however, one and many principles are found. For one principle is the beginning of the collection that is within us; but many principles, with respect to the first, are the other reasons that happen afterward from the surrounding things. Therefore, one beginning is more 

<column-break/>

fitting to be set forth in this place because all others occur only by occasion of this one. Therefore, since these things are so, the general properties of the collection are perceived from the observation of the first beginning; from the remaining principles, however, we shall learn that which happens in each of their hours from increase or decrease, according to what we shall subjoin from the divisions of times.

¶ And it is not fitting for us to understand that the hours of all principles—in which we apply celestial things for the sake of knowing those things which ought to happen because of the figures that will be in those hours—are all one and the same principle. Rather, it is necessary for us to know that the principles of universal accidents are many, because the thing that encompasses all is not one principle alone. Nor do we always take these principles from the subject things receiving them, but rather from the things surrounding them from which the accidents come. So it is that, for the most part, we take care to know these accidents from eclipses, which are more complete, and from the planets running in a manifest course. We find, however, for each of these by itself, one principle and many principles: there is one principle when it is first formed, because we have this aforesaid principle; and there are many principles which are the many changes that happen afterward through the surrounding things in comparison to the first principle. And one principle has the greater right to be placed first in this place, because all other principles come through it. And since this is so, we can know through the first principle the properties of the universal composition; and from the [secondary] principles, we will know whatever will happen at any time regarding increase and decrease, just as we shall hear in the divisions of times.

¶ **Ptolemy** says that the knowledge of accidents before they happen is divided into two kinds: one is to know general things, and the other is nativities. He taught us that either of these two parts happens by the nature of the stars, since it is their power that operates the accidents which we must foreknow before they happen. And he showed us that we can know this when we know their powers and works, and everything else he said in this reasoning. But now he shows us in these [chapters] how we shall know the times in which these powers happen, which result in works; and the beginning of that which happens in that which is to come. And he said that the times of the principles in which these powers happen are not one and the same, but rather many. And first, he taught us what he showed us in the [previous] part regarding these things. And he says that some of them are strong, and these are the complete times in which eclipses happen and the great **conjunctions** <note>When two or more planets appear in the same spot in the sky.</note> of the planets, the beginning of years, of quarters, and of **comets** and such things. And there are minor beginnings, such as the beginning of building cities, castles, or the houses of kings, and that which pertains to any city regarding the diversity of these eclipses and conjunctions from the aspect of its latitude and longitude and such things; because these are minor powers not having the strength to destroy the strong ones, but only to add to or diminish a single quantity in them. And after he reminded us of these things which he demonstrated to us completely in the second part, he begins afterward to tell us what he wants to show in the third and fourth parts, so that our intellects may be prepared for all he wishes to say. Just as the great beginning of a nativity having a power greater than another is the constellation of the **firmament** <note>The sphere of the stars.</note> at the hour it begins to be generated; because the power of the operation in that hour works into the body all the accidents that are never separated from the man his whole life. But the other beginnings that follow these are those which signify the parentage of nativities according to sons, and the revolutions and divisions leading to ... and such. And all these are minor beginnings compared to the first, having the power of adding or diminishing in the works of the first principle. And when you apply your mind to his words, according to this commentary, you will understand them well word for word.

# Treatise

...if you have understood, you will understand Ptolemy more fully through this treatise, and you will know through him as much as a human can know of this art, and how it is practiced.

### Chapter 8: On the falling of the seed and the birth of the infant.

->Haly said:<-

After Ptolemy taught us that nativities <note>Individual birth charts.</note> have a true beginning, and that other beginnings which come after it have no power except for adding or diminishing, he now first wishes to investigate what this primary beginning is, which is a matter of some doubt. Is the beginning the hour when the seed falls into the mother's womb, or the hour when the creature emerges into the light? And he finds through arguments that the beginning is that hour when the creature is separated from its prior state, and it begins to speak from there.

Since the temporal beginning of human existence has a start, this beginning is natural when the seed falls; yet it is potential and accidental <note>In medieval philosophy, "accidental" refers to a property or event that is not part of the essential nature of a thing, rather than something happening by "accident." Here, birth is the "accidental" start because the "essential" biological formation began at conception.</note> when the infant emerges at the hour of birth. It is appropriate for those who have grasped the hour of the falling of the seed—either by chance or by careful observation—to use this for their investigations when they wish to know the specific qualities of the body and soul, operating from this and from the configuration of the stars at this specific hour, that is, the hour of the falling of the seed.

Since the generation of humans has a temporal beginning, and the beginning which is according to nature is when the seed falls, nevertheless, the potential and accidental beginning of the creature is the very hour in which it is born. Therefore, it is fitting for those who know the hour of the falling of the seed—either by rectifying the time or by setting their minds to it—that when they wish to know the states and accidents of the body and soul, they should seek them from the work that the configurations of the stars perform specifically in this hour, which is the hour of the falling of the seed.

What Ptolemy called a "temporal beginning" is a distinction between that and what is not in time—such as light, which comes from a luminous source and has no temporal beginning, and many other things that lack temporal beginnings, such as good things. And such things are generated in a temporal beginning; and he says "humans" meaning every person as an individual, but the general species of humans requires a higher philosophy than what we are speaking of now. And when he says the primary beginning is the falling of the seed, he means that the seed gives nature to the <term>menses</term> <note>original: "menstruo." In Aristotelian biology, it was believed the mother's blood provided the physical matter of the fetus, while the father's seed provided the "form" or "spirit."</note> so that from it one body may be made, such as that from which the seed came. This nature is both active and formative; and it follows that the beginning of its work is certainly the hour it falls into the womb, and after it has fallen there, the menstrual matter begins to be transformed, and its works will be continuous until its work is completed. For this reason, it is useful for us to know what happens to the body and soul—whether they will be completed or not, and if completed, what manner of person or <term>complexion</term> <note>The physical and psychological makeup of a person based on the balance of their "humors."</note> they will be. We can know all of this through the configurations of the natures of the stars at the hour the seed falls into the womb; and the nature of this beginning is the falling of the seed. This can be known by rectifying and applying the mind to the configurations of the stars at that hour. Perhaps it can even be known by understanding which day and hour it was, and the constellation that existed at that hour will be observed. And as for what he says—that birth is the beginning of humans only through potential and accident—he means that the nature of the seed has no other task except to create the creature, and when it is completed, it is moved by its own nature to emerge. Therefore, the exit is related to the nature of the seed by accident, because the seed does not have the extraction of the fetus as its primary nature.

Wherefore, when the seed has once in the beginning happened to receive a quality that comes to it from the surrounding things, although that quality in this may happen to be varied afterwards from the things and hours of the body, nevertheless it will naturally attract to itself an increase of matter similar to itself. And when that manner of things has grown, it will be likened to the primary qualities which are proper to the seed.

So, since the seed has prepared itself at one time to receive some state at the beginning from the surrounding things, although that state itself may change,

<column-break/>

afterwards, the form within it is what draws to itself, by nature, the increase of matter convenient to it and nothing else.

And when the matter has grown, it returns similarly to the likeness of the first state pertaining to the seed.

These are words that are very dense and obscure; when you look into them, you will find that this was a good man, very wise in the wisdom of philosophy and mathematics, following the philosophy of Aristotle and his sect. For these men considered well all the things that are in the world, and they found that the seed and things similar to it are prepared in the air to receive virtues from the firmament with which they perform all their works. And later Aristotle said in his *Book of Animals* that the seed is a "thing of God" in which He placed a virtue for moving the menstrual matter, so that the creature might be generated from it. And he said in his *Book of Natures* <note>Referring to the *Physics* or *Generation of Animals*.</note> that "man and the Sun generate man." He meant that the seed of a man specifically receives from the Sun a generative and formative virtue to make another such man as the first. From this, it follows that it has a greatness over all earthly things as great as the Sun has over all celestial bodies. And when you apply your mind to this, it also follows that the Moon must have great power in that which concerns the nature of the Sun. For this reason, the nativities of humans are held specifically with the two luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note> and their conjunctions and oppositions; and the nativities of other living things are held with their own stars—that is, whichever stars they accord with. You will find this distinct and divided in the words of Ptolemy; yet in this place, insofar as he understood this reasoning of philosophy regarding the seed, he demonstrated to us that when the seed is separated from the man and falls into the womb, it receives in that moment, through the mixing that happens from the nature of the stars, a virtue with which it moves the menstrual matter. With this virtue, the natural powers afterwards perform all their works. This is what Ptolemy wishes to say in this place. Look upon these words many times until you understand them well. And if anyone should say that Ptolemy ought to speak separately about the falling of the seed and its constellation, just as he spoke about the emergence of the creature, we would say to him: we see how much he has to say on that separately further on. If you understand well, you will know that no more was necessary.

However, when the hour of the falling of the seed is unknown—as is found to happen many times—it is necessary to observe the beginning which is the emergence of the infant. This is the same "greatest beginning," nor does it differ from the first except in what follows: through the first principle, that which is before birth may be known beforehand.

And when you do not know the hours of the falling of the seed, which happens frequently, it will be necessary for you to look into the beginning which is the hour of the creature's emergence. This is the greatest beginning, and it does not differ from the first except as much as I shall tell you: that through the first beginning, one can know those things that happen to the creature before it is born.

We have already demonstrated in the preceding sections that from the configuration of the firmament at the hour the seed falls, one can know what happens in the workings of the seed regarding its increase or diminution. However, because the majority of men are drunk when they lie with their women, or are in some other state such that they do not consider the hour when the seed falls, it is therefore very difficult to know this beginning. It is necessary that we look at the other beginning, which is the hour of the creature's emergence from the mother's womb. Although this beginning is second in terms of time, it nevertheless has great power, because in it the creature receives a different virtue than it had before. This beginning does not diminish from the first, except that we will be ignorant of what happened to the creature before it left the mother's womb. From the words of Ptolemy, some believe that through the first beginning (conception), everything that will happen to a man in his whole life can be known; but he did not speak of this beginning except to propose it as a matter of doubt, and to destroy that doubt further on. Through demonstration, he proved that the second beginning (birth) is the true beginning of a man, while the first is only for knowing what happens to the seed.

For the first is a beginning, but another similar one shall be the beginning; it can be sufficiently declared because the last of these is in...

While conception is the natural beginning of biological formation, the text concludes that birth is the practical "true beginning" for a human life, especially since the exact time of conception is rarely known.</summary>

...in time: and perhaps its quantity [of the beginning] lies in the perfection of its strength. First: it is appropriate that we more frequently call the first beginning the start of the human *seed*. The second, however, may be called the start of the *human being*.

**And** if anyone should say that whichever of these two belongs to the prior is the beginning of truth, and the other is merely like the beginning, we shall say that the last and second in time is also of greater strength and more complete than the first. And it happens for the most part that we say the first beginning is the generation of the human *seed*, and the second is the generation of the *man*.

**In** this word, Ptolemy clarifies a doubt and destroys it. The doubt is: if anyone says that the first is the "certain" beginning, and that the second merely follows the first. Ptolemy, however, destroys this doubt with what he said: that the second beginning is of greater strength and more complete. For the first is the beginning of the human seed, and the second is the beginning of the generation of the man; for that which nature began to generate as a man could not become a man at the first beginning—it made an animal body prepared to become a man. And this is what nature did in the first beginning: it made an animal body prepared to be a human, yet in the second beginning, nature made a human being out of that animal body. If it were otherwise, there would be infinite beginnings, for before that first one there would be another when the sperm is formed in the father's body. And Ptolemy demonstrates this with propositions which no one can contradict.

**Because** of this, the infant then acquires those things which it did not have while enclosed in the womb; and along with this, it also acquires properties which are only in the nature of man, and the quality which happens to its body.

**So** that the creature then receives a thing which it did not have before in the time when it was in the matrix <note>The womb.</note>, and similarly receives properties belonging solely to the nature of man and the state which comes to be in its body.

**The** things which the creature receives when it exits the mother's belly, which it did not have before when it was in the matrix, are such as receiving food by its own mouth, the exiting of superfluities <note>Waste products.</note> from behind and before, and breathing with the chest and lungs <note>Original: "filia," likely a variant or error for "pulmonia."</note>. For these are natural things which it did not have before. And nature prepared for it limbs which it would not use except after it exited the mother; for it breathed in the mother through the pores which are between its veins and the mother's veins, and it was governed through the veins which are connected from the umbilical cord to the veins through which the menstrual blood comes; and the superfluities of its body exit through the pores between it and the mother, and through the ears. The properties which he said belong to the nature of man alone are such as laughing, crying, and beginning to imagine, to understand, and to have discretion gradually. And the "state" which he said happens to its body is the movement of its limbs and using them, as well as sleeping and waking, and the rest—namely, the senses. And of all these things it had nothing when it was in the matrix, because when it is generated inside, it is like a plant <note>In medieval science, the fetus was thought to pass through a "vegetative" or plant-like stage before becoming a "sensitive" animal and then a "rational" human.</note> prepared to receive the hour when it shall come forth with the power to use its animal and human works through the celestial bodies. And this is the end of its natural essence. Or, just as the seed, when it is separated from the man, is prepared to receive from celestial things the power with which it forms the creature and makes it ready to receive celestial things (just like this beginning from which it becomes a man), for this reason it is appropriate in every way that the second beginning be of greater strength and lordship than the falling of the seed.

**Likewise**, that which surrounds us at the hour of birth, although in making the nature it may be thought to help nothing—as if it were merely the quality of that which exists—nevertheless helps so that its appearance and exit be according to the proper quality of the surrounding environment. Because nature, after its perfection, causes it to be moved to the exit, and it will be assimilated to the quality that formed it.

**Similarly**, the state of things that encompasses us at the hour of nativity, although some believe it does not help in any way in forming the creature in the matter which it is, nevertheless helps so that its exit and appearance be according to the proper state of the thing encompassing us. Because

<column-break/>

nature makes its exit in a movement similar to the state in which it formed it, from the first degree to the next, after it was completed.

**Ptolemy** shows us through these words how much participation <note>Resonance or interconnectedness.</note> there is between the first beginning and the second. And he spoke of it according to a credible argument. For although it might not have been proven that the first and second beginnings are of greater strength and more manifest than the first, yet it happens through this participation between them that the first and second have a power through which we might know what will happen after birth when we do not know for certain the first beginning. For only a few times can a man observe and know that moment [of conception]. And this participation exists because the nature which we say is the power the seed receives at its falling through the celestial bodies—this same nature similarly moves the creature to exit in the hour that occurs through those things which are among us, a force similar to the first beginning through the celestial bodies. For example: the Sun always accords in the hour of birth with the place where it was at the falling of the seed; for it will always be in the 7th, 9th, 10th, or 11th house. And Hermes said that the location of the Moon at the hour of the falling of the seed is itself the Ascendant <note>The rising sign.</note> at the exit of the creature; and the Ascendant at the hour of the falling of the seed is the location of the Moon at the exit of the creature. <note>This relationship is known as the "Trutine of Hermes," a rule used to check the accuracy of a birth time.</note> And I have tested this saying of Hermes, and I found it certain many times, and sometimes uncertain; yet the Moon always accorded with the Ascendant, and in this there is no error. And since it is so, it follows that there is a concordance between the two beginnings. And since there is a concordance between them, we can know from the second beginning whatever will happen to the creature. And this is the reason he gives us here; and when we take it with the first proof, we shall know for certain that the second beginning has the greater right to show us what will happen to the man.

**It is necessary** therefore that we consider the quality of the stars at the hour of the infant's exit to signify these similar things again; not that the stars themselves perform these things, but necessarily and naturally they are assimilated in strength to the "maker" <note>The natural formative process.</note>.

**And** it is appropriate for us to hold the state of the planets at the hour of the creature's exit, because they similarly show such things as are their makers without doubt; but through nature, it is assimilated to the maker through power.

**This** is the conclusion of the statement he narrated concerning the concordance that exists between the two beginnings; and we have already glossed this.

**Since** in this discourse our intention is to manifest this part of the science by a skillful path, as we promised at the beginning of this book—where we proved that this method of prognosticating could be reached—and since the most ancient way of prognosticating, which is according to the mixture of all stars or the majority, is of many modes and almost infinite when someone attempts to examine it clearly and openly. Especially in particular future things which are sought by observers of nature, which can be found in the narrations said by them; and because of the weight of its use and the difficulty of its explanation, we have decided to pass these over. However, we intend to narrate concisely the prognosis of that mastery by which each species is apprehended in the manner of searching, as well as the working powers specifically related to the stars, which can be followed with perfection through the path of natural conjecture.

**And** therefore it is our purpose in this statement to narrate this part of the art with a certified opinion, as we promised in the beginning of this book when we showed how one can reach such a manner of prognostication. And the opinion of the ancients in speaking of things before they are—through the mixture of all the stars or the greater part of them—is of many kinds, so that they can be without end, if anyone wished to certify, demonstrate, and declare much, especially in particular accidents...

...things which the wise of nature <note>The "wise of nature" refers to natural philosophers or scientists of the era.</note> seek concerning those beginnings we have heard spoken of. Since we are determining such a matter—one that is very powerful in its operation and very difficult to demonstrate—we wish to proceed to describe the very prognosis <note>original: "pnosticatiōē", referring to the predictive capacity of astrology</note> of the art. Through this, each thing can be known according to the method of inquiry, and we shall describe the creative and specific virtues of the stars completely, so far as a person can briefly follow such a matter through natural consideration.

I desire to certify the whole wisdom and science of the art, which is to well-certify the certain and true rules through which the whole art is joined to the human intellect. If one understands all the rules well, one can proceed through all the particular matters of the art. Regarding this, Ptolemy said in this statement what he had said at the beginning of the first part: that his purpose was to describe these rules completely in this book. And after he described all the general rules of the art in the first part, he described in the third part those things pertaining to great nations, and in the [other] third part those things pertaining to every individual person, and in the fourth part those things pertaining to "accidents" <note>In medieval philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential properties or events that happen to a person, such as health, wealth, or travel.</note> that happen to a person from outside themselves. The ancient opinion he mentions is that of the astrologers who came before him, for none of them described all the accidents in this art; rather, each of them described particular accidents. For example: someone says such and such a sign signifies such and such a thing when it is the ascendant of a certain creature, and such and such a planet demonstrates such and such a thing when it is the lord of the ascendant. All such things are those for which there is no following rule, and moreover, they are infinite and difficult to narrate. Therefore, it was necessary that we set aside the sayings of such people so that we might proceed to the rules of which this art is solely composed. And regarding what he said about the "manner of natural consideration," he means that the rules are accepted through the science of nature; therefore, his consideration of future things will be in harmony with natural science.

It is necessary that our intention be passed down through the qualities of hidden things, by which every accident that happens to a human is understood. But more generally, it is appropriate that we [coordinate] the creative powers of the bodies <note>the celestial bodies/planets</note> with their similar places. We follow the manner of the victory of dominion, just as we do in the shooting of an arrow; for the future things in this subject species are gathered through a collection of many things for the one who has deliberated upon them and sought them out with insight. Thus, we leave the observation to the archer when he successfully hits the mark.

And it is not our purpose to proceed solely into the states of hidden things from which any accident occurring to humans can be known; but with all this, it is appropriate that we join the creative virtues that come to the bodies with the places that agree with them in the manner of power and dominion. This is like the shooting of arrows; and as for the accident that is joined in the subject species from a composition of many natures, we will not omit the inquiry into those who have thought deeply upon it, just as a crossbowman does who aims precisely at the mark.

Ptolemy demonstrates to us in this statement the rules he gave us in this art; and the reason for his words is this: he means it is not possible for you to seek out all the virtues that compose a thing, because it would be impossible to reach them, since the combinations are infinite. "But I declare to you the roots and simple rules, and I will show you the manner of their composition, so that from my words you will be able to extract the power that arises from every combination." For example: when the Sun is in the 10th [house], it is fit to be the <term>hyleg</term> <note>original: "byleg"; the Hyleg is the planet designated as the "giver of life" or "life-meter" in a birth chart, used to calculate longevity.</note>. He means the "signifier of life," since the Sun in this place has dominion and great power; and if it happens to be in another of the places of the <term>hyleg</term> in its triplicity or exaltation, and some planet having dignity in that place looks upon it with a good

<column-break/>

aspect, and there is no other planet there having greater power than it, then it will be the <term>hyleg</term>; for the <term>hylegs</term> are the planets having the greatest power in the nativity. And since all that we have heard from Ptolemy's words is like this, it is a root and a rule which we must follow and work according to. And when we have done this, we can go through whatever part of the art we wish. And he specifically gave you the metaphor of the arrow: because arrows are drawn toward the mark from any side. Because of this, it is appropriate that you take Ptolemy's word as a certain and authenticated thing by which you may guide yourself and observe in every constellation who "wins" <note>The "winner" refers to the Almuten, or the planet with the most calculated dignity and strength in a specific chart.</note>; and you will know through their shared virtues that the outcome follows the planet that wins, and you shall judge by it.

We shall place the beginning of our discourse on universal things at the start, which is at the appearance of the infant's exit, as fits the proper order. Since through this beginning we can reach the existence of all things having this nature, as we have said. However, the properties which are born at the hour of the falling of the seed <note>conception</note> are perceived through this same observation by one who will sagaciously scrutinize and subtly investigate the properties that were in that same collection.

And we wish to place the beginning of our speech on universal things after they appear at the start, since the birth is the creation. Just as one can reach the facts of all good things that have this nature through this beginning, as we said before, the properties that happen at the hour of the falling of the seed can be known in this same manner by anyone willing to study much and refine their skills to enter into the properties that are solely in the composition itself.

After he demonstrated to us in the preceding statement that what he has narrated in this book are the roots and rules, those he begins to narrate first are the universal things for a person that can last with them through their whole life—such as their appearance, character, the build of the body, and every limb. And he tells us what he demonstrated before: that these things can be known from the first [beginning], which is the hour of birth. And since he has narrated all these things, we can extract from them the matters pertaining to the first beginning, which is the falling of the seed, when we know the hour well. For the creature receives through the celestial bodies at the hour of its exit virtues that are innate to the body and soul, binding the accidents that are never separated from it in its whole life. Similarly at the hour of the falling of the seed: for the seed receives from the celestial bodies, and similarly the works pertaining to itself while it stays in the womb, such as being formed, shaped, and drawing in the appropriate materials for its nourishment.

### On the Knowledge of the Ascending Degree. Chapter 2.

->Haly said:<-

After Ptolemy demonstrated to us in the first chapter that the beginning which is the exit of the creature <note>birth</note> is a greater beginning than the [conception] in the nativity, he now shows us how we shall know this beginning for certain, and he says:

<image-desc>A large decorative blackletter initial 'C' containing intricate vine-like scrollwork and a central sun-face or floral motif.</image-desc>
**Since** in the first matter, which is the support—that is, the ascending degree <note>The "Ascendant," the sign and degree rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note>—doubt very often arises regarding the hour of the infant's exit. For in the majority of cases, the hour of birth cannot be known without error except by one who has observed it among all the instruments of the hours by the **astrolabe** alone. Indeed, other instruments of the hours by which many of those who work in these matters look, perhaps often fail and deviate from the truth. For even those for whom the Sun indicates the hour, it happens [that they fail] because of their crude decline in the positioning of **sundials** <note>original: "scioterorum", from the Greek for shadow-measurers</note> and because of the crookedness of the **sundials**. Moreover, with instruments of the hours that are adapted through the flow of water <note>water clocks or clepsydras</note>, it happens because of the retention of the water or the dominance of the flow, which occurs due to different occasions or any other circumstance happening to it.

**Since** doubt very often falls upon the first thing in which we ought most to trust—which is the ascending degree at the hour of the creature's exit—one who knows this power for certain...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the accuracy of astronomical instruments and the specific methodology for determining the "Ascendant"—the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon—at the moment of birth.</meta>

...is greater than that which is inspected through the astrolabe alone among other time-keeping instruments. This is because these other instruments, with which people observe things, can often measure falsely and recede from the truth. If one of those instruments that observes the hours by the sun is used, error occurs because of the inclination of the sun in that location and because of the distortions of its appearance. A great error also happens in water-based time instruments <note>original: "instrumētis hozay aque"; referring to the clepsydra or water clock</note> because of the clogging that happens in the water, and because it flows in different ways due to various impediments.

**What** he said: the first thing in which we must consider is the ascending degree at the hour of the creature's exit <note>In this context, "creature" refers to the newborn infant</note>. He has already spoken plainly here, for the first of these is verified through the hour, and in that we must place our trust. Therefore, he said that one can know the hour of the creature's exit for certain if they observe through an astrolabe <term>astrolabe: a complex hand-held tool used by astronomers and navigators to solve problems relating to time and the position of the stars</term>. This is a well-known instrument, and it is said that its first inventor was Abzacham <note>likely a corruption of Abraham</note>. It is also said it was invented in the time of King Solomon, son of David, or even before him. Some say a man named Lab invented it, along with Astoz—meaning the lines—from which it is called an "astrolabe," that is, the "lines of Lab" <note>This is a popular medieval folk etymology for the Greek word 'astrolabos'.</note>. Its measurement cannot be corrected unless it has certain divisions, and the one who observes through it must be very wise so that an error in rectification does not occur. For in rectifying, error often occurs when the star being observed is near the Midheaven <note>original: "mediū celi"; the highest point in the sky</note>; the observer might not know if it is exactly in the middle, or might be slow to place the rule <note>original: "regulā"; the alidade or sighting arm of the astrolabe</note> upon the degree, so that much time passes in the firmament before they move it. Or perhaps they rise too slowly to observe after being told the creature has been born. Thus, they will necessarily have a high degree of the ascendant after the birth, or there will be an error in the astrolabe itself, or in the division of the altitude degrees, or in the rule, or in the whole quadrant of altitude. Rarely does a person escape such things without them happening. For if an error of one degree of altitude occurs, the found ascendant will not be that of the birth; and even in an error of one minute, the ascendant will be wrong. Ptolemy told us that in all other time instruments, a great error occurs. In shadow instruments <note>sundials or gnomons</note> with which the sun is observed, error occurs because the sun is not equidistant to the surface on which the instrument is placed, or because the lines of sight are distorted so the shadow is not certain. He also said there will be error in water instruments because of things happening in the water: either it is thick, or something obstructs it, or the hole becomes blocked, or it flows inconsistently—sometimes the hole widens, or there is much water and it flows quickly, or little water and it flows slowly, or it is hot or cold. Since this is so, there is no instrument a man can be secure in for certifying the hour when the creature is separated from the mother. However, one can show a time near to it. The most true instrument is the astrolabe; after that, the shadow instrument; after that, the water instrument. Because of these errors occurring in instruments, it happens that he shows you all the rules and foundations with which we can verify the matter.

**Necessarily** it follows that we should indicate the way in which the degree of the circle of signs <note>the Zodiac</note>—which by natural, sequential reason ought to be the ascendant—can be grasped. Thus we almost grasp the degree of the ascendant by the way of ascensions through the hour attributed to us.

**It is fitting** in all ways that we teach the manner through which we can know which degree of the zodiac belongs to the ascendant according to the natural way which we always follow. This is done by knowing beforehand, through the hour given to us by estimation, the degree nearest the ascendant through the chapter on ascensions.

After he demonstrated to us that instruments are not sufficient for rectifying the certain ascendant of a birth, he taught us this rule: that it is fitting in every way to first teach the rules by which we can know the natural degree of the ascendant at the hour of the creature's exit. I have seen births, and among those I had rectified, some

<column-break/>

deviated from this natural path because of some disturbance happening there. I found the matter in these births just as he said in the chapter on the imperfection or wasting of limbs, and in the chapter on those not receiving food. This disturbance can be because of the narrowness of the mother's womb, or the weakness of the force pushing the creature out, or because of some infirmity happening to the mother. For because of such things that occur, the exit of the creature is delayed. It is most manifest that the celestial bodies cause these disturbances. I have searched into this and applied my mind to it for a long time, and I found that it happens in these as in other births, for sometimes error falls in them. Since this is so, it is fitting for us to seek only natural, particular things. Ptolemy says we can know this natural thing by taking an ascendant near to the natural one, whether that ascendant is rectified or not, because through it we can know the natural ascendant.

**It is appropriate** therefore that we find the degree of conjunction or prevention <note>original: "preuentionis"; in astrology, this refers to the Full Moon or Opposition preceding the birth</note> which was closest before the birth, and that we learn it truly.

And we say that it is fitting for us to take the conjunction or opposition preceding the birth—whichever of them was closer—and we will apply our mind to knowing its certain degree.

We have already demonstrated through the preceding words the harmony that exists between the nature of man and the nature of the Sun and Moon. We mentioned what Aristotle said on this, and Ptolemy's opinion is the same, according to what he found through experience and natural arguments. Similarly, we demonstrated in the second part that the work of the conjunction must last until the opposition, and the degree of opposition has the power to last until the conjunction; and that the power of each of these two degrees increases and diminishes at every hour according to the planet winning <note>ruling</note> that hour. After these things are explained and completed, it is fitting in all ways that the ascendant of the creature's exit have a nature connected with the nature of the planet governing the degree of the conjunction or opposition preceding the birth. And when he says, "we will well apply our mind to knowing its certain degree," he means to say for certain which degree will be the conjunction, or which degree they will give to the opposition.

**If it was** a conjunction that we found, we shall take the degree of both luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon are at the same degree during a conjunction/New Moon</note>. If instead it was a prevention <note>Full Moon</note>, we shall observe the degree of the luminary existing above the earth.

And if that which we take is the conjunctional one, we will take the degree of the two luminaries. If it is the oppositional one, we take the degree of that luminary which is above the earth.

**Since** planets above the earth are of greater strength than those existing below the earth, it follows that we take the degree of the luminary existing above the earth. This statement can be understood in two ways: one is to take the degree of the luminary existing above the earth [at the time of the syzygy]; the other is to take the hour of birth as the hour of opposition, and this is more well-known. Similarly, if one luminary is in the east and the other in the west, whether at the hour of birth or the hour of opposition, it follows that we should take the degree of the one in the ascendant, because we must always take that which has the greater power.

**After this** we shall inquire which of the planets of the birth hour is fitting to have the disposition <note>rulership</note> of that degree.

**We shall observe** afterward which planet has the greater right of disposing that degree at the hour of birth.

He means to say that when we take the degree of conjunction or opposition, we will observe which planet will rule in it at the hour of birth only. This is because the one who governs it at the hour of conjunction or disposition disposes it specifically, and this pertains more to the birth. If it happens that the one who is the general disposer is simply the specific one, he will be firmer, and it will demonstrate that the birth is that of a great man.

**Specially** however, the way in which it is fitting for a planet to dispose is explained by these five things: triplicity, house <note>domicile</note>, exaltation, term <note>bounds</note>, and appearance—or affinity to the sun in the figure.

### Treatise

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, when your matters are to be arranged, there are five dignities <note>original: "dignitates"; these are the five ways a planet gains strength based on its position in the zodiac</note>: triplicity, house, exaltation, term, or appearance—so that they may have a participation with the sun in the figure.

<margin>C</margin> Of these, four are essential and one is accidental. The essential ones are the dignities of triplicity <note>original: "triplicitatis"; a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note>, and he <note>referring to Ptolemy</note> ordained this before the others. And it was shown in the first part on behalf of Ptolemy that in every triplicity, he does not agree with the stars. And if you wish to operate by the *animodar* <term>animodar: a traditional method used to rectify a birth chart when the exact minute of birth is unknown</term> according to his opinions, you will have to operate through all the triplicities. And the one that follows is the lord of the house; and the lord of the house is followed by the lord of exaltation; and the lord of exaltation is followed by the lord of the term. These are the four essentials which you can know from the first part of this book. The fifth is accidental, which happens when a planet is appearing under the rays of the sun, or that it has participation with the sun in the figure by beholding itself with the same through a trine, a sextile, a square, or an opposition <note>original: "3o vel sextili vel 4o vel opposito"; these are the 'aspects' or geometric angles between planets</note>, or in any other way of those which he narrated in the first part.

<margin>C</margin> The disposition of that place will belong to the planet which had more than one of these strengths in it, or all of them.

<margin>C</margin> And the disposition of that same place belongs to the planet that had more than one or two of the dignities in that place, or all of them.

<margin>C</margin> Ptolemy always seeks the greater factor in the composition; and we have already shown through his own words that it happens that when you know the degree of the conjunction or opposition <note>the New Moon or Full Moon</note> preceding the birth, and you look at the hour of birth, that planet has the greatest power in that degree. And you will know this through the five things said; and whichever planet you find having the greatest strength in that place and the greatest accordance, you should look to that one.

<margin>C</margin> But if we find all or many of these things for one planet, we will observe its degree in the sign in which it was at the time of birth, found truly at that hour. We will say that the degree of the sign—accepted through the ascensions <note>original: "ascensiões"; referring to the rising times of the signs</note>—which equals it in number, shall be the degree of the Ascendant <note>the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon</note>. But if we find two or more planets associated with each other, we will look at the number which each one traveled at the hour of birth. Whichever number is closer to the degree of the Ascendant that appeared to us through the ascensions, that itself shall be the Ascendant of the hour of birth. If we find that the number of degrees of two or more planets is close to the number of the ascending degree that resulted for us through the ascensions, we will follow the one that has more authorities in the angles <note>original: "angul’"; the four most powerful houses in an astrological chart: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th</note>, and we shall imitate the one whose *hayz* <note>original: "baiz"; a specific condition where a planet is in a sign and hemisphere matching its gender and the time of day</note> is in that place. But if the distance of the degree of the *almudebir* <term>almudebir: a planet that acts as a "governor" or "giver of life" in a chart</term> from the degree of the Ascendant—found without subtle observation—is greater than the distance of the syzygy <note>original: "suiphus"; likely a corruption of "syzygia," the alignment of the sun and moon</note> from the degree of the Midheaven <note>original: "medij celi"; the highest point in the sky at the time of birth</note>, by that same way of inquiry we will restore that same number of degrees to the Midheaven, through which we will equalize all the other angles.

<margin>C</margin> And if we find all the aforesaid things or most of them in one planet, we will look well to see in which degree of that sign it stays at the hour of birth, and we will certify it greatly; for in as many degrees of the sign as we previously took by the estimation of the elevations, that will be the ascending degree. And if we find that two or more planets have participation in the disposition, we will look at the number which each of them wants at the hour of birth. And for whichever we find the number closer to the degree of the Ascendant that resulted for us by the elevation, then that will be the degree elevated at the hour of birth. And if we find the number of two planets or more existing around the ascending degree that resulted for us by the elevations in an equal way, we follow the planet having more dignities in the angles, or which is in its *hayz*. And if the degree of the planets disposing it was further removed from the Ascendant than what we took

<column-break/>

by estimation than from the degree of the Midheaven, we will adapt all the other angles upon it.

<margin>C</margin> All these words have one root: the matter that the planet is the *almuten* <term>almuten: the planet that holds the most mathematical dignity or power over a specific point in a chart</term>, that is, which has the greatest power and most dignities in the constellation. Thus, when we wish to know which planet rules the hour of birth in the degree of the conjunction or opposition preceding it, and we have applied our mind to those five things by which a planet will be the dispositor: if we find one planet ruling in that degree, we will set the number of degrees of the Ascendant, or the degrees of the Midheaven, to be as many as the degrees it held in its sign in which it stays in an equal way. And if that number is closer to the degree of the Ascendant given to us by estimation, the degrees of the Ascendant will be as many as the degrees of the planet in an equal way. And if the degrees which the planet traversed are closer to the degrees of the Midheaven—that is, the conjunction or opposition—as many as the degrees of the planet in an equal way; nevertheless, if in the degree which was before, two or more planets rule and are equal in strength, we will consider the planet whose degrees are closer to the degrees of the Ascendant or the Midheaven and we will work through it. And if the degrees of one are equal to the degrees of the other or nearly so, we will take that planet of them which had more dignities in the angles of the birth; and we will prefer the one which was of the stronger *hayz* and in more accord with the sun. And let us understand from these words that we must always take and judge by the planet which is of greater strength and greater accordance with the matter we seek.

<margin>C</margin> ->On the division of the discourse on nativities. Chapter 3.<-
->Haly said.<-

**After** it was demonstrated to us in the preceding 5th chapter how we shall know the natural beginning of the human being's exit <note>referring to the moment of birth</note>, he begins in the 13th chapter to show us all that we can know through this beginning, so that our understanding may be applied to each of them. And he gives us in these things three rules which he spoke of before.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial P containing a seated scholar figure at a desk with astronomical or medical instruments.</image-desc> **After** the premises of these things are placed, we shall add that when one wishes to distinguish the general observations of nativities in an ordered and competent division, they will find that of those things reached by the natural path, some are accidents that happen before birth, such as speaking of the parents. Others are accidents that happen before birth and after birth, such as speaking of brothers.

**And** after we have proposed this, we say—not that some wish to divide or distinguish the judgment of nativities with an ordered division—and through the rules, one will find that some of these things which a man can reach according to the natural way are accidents that happen before birth, just as a man judges concerning parents; and some are accidents that happen before birth and after, just as a man judges concerning brothers.

**That** which he says "after we have proposed," he means to say that it has already been demonstrated in the preceding locations that the beginning which will be the hour of the creature's exit is the same as the beginning of the natural generation of man. And this is more worthy of entering into signification. He likewise demonstrated how we can know for certain this beginning, and what happens to one wishing to look into the natural significance of this principle: that he should first judge concerning the parents, afterward concerning the brothers; and he gave the reason why. And he said that parents are before the birth, and brothers can be before and after. And someone can ask and say: after the seed comes out from the parents, when some event happens, each of them has a birth chart signifying their own measured state; how can the birth of the sons give a significance of the parents? And the same can be said of the brothers. To which we respond, saying: always when the father is joined to the mother, the same creature is not always generated; rather, it is when it happens that they are joined at an hour in which that constellation accords with the birth of the parents. And it happens that this same accordance exists between the birth of the parents and the son. And because of this, the birth of the son signifies all of this concerning the parents. And it is manifest that the birth of each of the sons has accordance with the birth of the parents; and things which have accordance with one and the same thing are in accord—that is, one with the other—and because of that, it happens that the birth of any...

### Third Book

**Similarly**, the status of brothers <note>original: "fratrum"; in this context, it refers to siblings generally</note> marks the state of other brothers: and these five concordances mark five fortunes and five misfortunes; five good things and five evil. You will find all of this demonstrated and detailed in its proper place hereafter.

**But** those things which happen at the very same hour of birth are nothing but one and the same, plain and evident, just like what we predicted. Truly, the last of the occurrences that can be known is said to be that which happens after the birth. It is not doubted that this category consists of many modes and various parts.

**Since**, however, that which will be in a nativity is not one single thing alone, just as the things we have narrated; the later thing which we can reach among the occurrences is that which happens to them after birth: and this part is of many types and modes.

**He** <note>referring to Ptolemy</note> divided the judgment of the state of the one being born into two parts. One is that which happens at the hour of the birth itself, and the other is what happens after the time of birth. Neither of these types is simple, unlike the judgment of parents and siblings: for each of those judgments is simple. Therefore, he said that the judgment of either of these two modes is of many types, and he intends to demonstrate these hereafter.

**Of these** things, therefore, which happen in that same hour of birth, those which we wish to know are to speak of males and females; and whether she will give birth to twins or more at once; to speak also of monstrous forms; as well as of those who will never grow.

**And** that which we wish to know from what happens at the hour of birth is: to judge concerning males or females; or if two are born together; or if the one being born is of imperfect build; or if it will not receive nourishment or food <note>This refers to infant mortality or the "nurturability" of the child</note>.

**This** is one mode of the two composites of which he spoke, and he divides it into four modes. The first is to judge concerning male or female. The second, if more than one is born. The third, if it is of imperfect build. The fourth, to judge concerning those who do not receive food.

**From these** things, and what follows after birth, the things we seek to know are: to discourse upon life; the composition of those who grow is not linked to these narrations; but after these, to speak of the form of the body, and of the infirmities and impediments happening to the body. Next, to discourse upon the qualities of the soul and its accidents. Then to speak of the fortune and misfortune of the native; and of his kingdom, exaltation, and his high rank; and afterwards to recount the good things which will be achieved through his works. Next, to discourse of his marriage and the time spent with a wife; and of the good things that happen regarding his children; as well as of his mixing and familiarity with men and of his friends. Then to show his travels; and finally, to judge the manner of his death, which in strength is likened to the discourse made concerning life. However, its order must be placed after these aforementioned things.

**That** which we wish to know from what happens after birth is to judge concerning life, since this is not a matter held within the judgment of those who do not receive food. And afterwards, to judge the form of the body, and the infirmities and plagues happening to the body; and after, to judge the good things of the state of the soul and spiritual accidents; and after, the good things of the form of the native and his substance <note>wealth or essence</note>, honor, and exaltation; and after, the good things of his state, namely, which mastery <note>profession or craft</note> he will involve himself in; thereafter of his marriage, and how he will behave with a wife—or a wife with her husband; and what kind of children he will have; and what kind of society or participation with men; and what kind of friends he will have; and thereafter to judge if he will be a traveler in foreign lands; and by what death he will

<column-break/>

die. Finally, to judge what is fitting through the power of the judgment of life; and it is fitting that its order be after all these things.

**This** is the number of those which are in the second part, which is composite: and he divides it into thirteen modes. The first is to judge life; and it is said that this mode of judgment does not hold itself with the judgment of those who do not receive food: because they do not have a life well-measured in comparison to the course of the sun, which is the measure of all our plantings; and that which helps it to have a quantity, it is fitting that it be made by the course of the sun so that it completes its course at least once: and this is one year. The second mode is to judge the form of the body. The third, to judge infirmities and plagues of the body. The fourth, to judge the state of the soul. The fifth, station and exaltation or his depression. The eighth <note>The text skips 6 and 7 in the numbering</note>, which mastery he will involve himself in. The ninth, the marriage of the native: and how many he will be coupled with, and in what manner, and how long he will last with those to whom he is coupled. The tenth, concerning the children the native will have. The eleventh, what kind of life he will have, and what society with men, and what kind of friends. The twelfth, look to what kind of journeys he will make, and to what lands. The thirteenth, of what type his death will be. And since we shall aggregate these thirteen modes with the above-mentioned ones of parents and siblings, there will be fifteen; and in the fourth part there are four modes: as you will find there. And when it is said that it is fitting through the power of the judgment of life, and it is fitting that its order be after all these, he means to say that the judgment of death is a matter that agrees with the judgment of life; for the thing that gives life is the thing that gives the native one time in which are his natural deaths and his virtues from the body; and the good time lasts until another thing comes which cuts it off: and this is that which gives death. For this reason it is fitting that the judgment of death be concordant with that of life; and although there is a priority between them through power, it is fitting that it be ordered after all of this, since this is the end of the matter.

**We** shall narrate the mode of each of these generally: and when we speak of the strengths of our narration accompanying these things, we shall say them as we manifested above. But those things which have been spread about by very many people foolishly and superfluously—in which there is no probable reason, though they generally suit the occasions arising from their own nature—we shall postpone. Of these, we shall follow that which we can reach, not through lots nor through numbers <note>The author is rejecting numerology and "Lot" systems (like the Lot of Fortune) in favor of pure planetary positions</note>, which do not have the reasons for which these things must be; but we shall investigate through observations of the figures of the planets and their similitudes with their places.

**And** we shall also speak of these things generally beforehand: and we shall name the simple virtues which each of these made as we said before; and we shall omit the vanities which many men have narrated, in which there is nothing perfect, nor anything that should be heard, nor anything that is guided by reason which comes from its own nature. We shall name those things which we can reach from the aforesaid: not through lots or numbers having no reason, but by looking into the figures of the stars and in the concordance which they have with their places.

**Place** for one hour these things and your mind with me, so that you might be able to understand this so noble a saying; for if you understand it, you will emerge from great labor and long pain, and from the vanities which many have compiled, making many books about them. And it is a great marvel since they did not apply their minds to this book, which was made now a thousand years ago; and because they have not glossed it nor demonstrated the reasons which it intends to say; and they have not followed it alone. No, for they would not have involved themselves in vanities nor in the fables of old women. I, however, do not believe they left it for any other reason than laziness or malice. If through laziness: it was because this book is very obscure, so that they were unable to understand it. And if through malice: it was because some understood it and led men away from the understanding of it, compiling other vanities in which men might labor, so they would not look into this book. And if we wished that any of those who were before did not understand as much as I believe of this book to speak the truth—if you apply your mind well to my gloss, you will hold me to be truthful in this my order. I do not wish to prolong further, but to the words of Ptolemy.

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*, specifically focusing on the methodology for interpreting a birth chart. # Treatise

He shows you the reasons. Because, as he said, we will describe each of these things generally. He means to say that these things he will describe are only the <term>rules and roots</term> <note>original: "regule et radices"; fundamental principles</note>: for this entire art is composed of rules and roots, while the specific details lie in the particular cases of the art itself. And when he said, "we will describe the simple virtues that operate in these things," he means that along with these rules, he will provide examples taken from the powers of the stars. Because, as he said, "we have set aside vanities in which there is no reason," because those who spoke them said nothing that holds up with primary nature. He means that such things had no basis in the celestial virtues which operate upon the things existing among us. And he clearly says that they demonstrated this matter well through direct proofs: for they showed that God, who created the heavens and the stars, placed virtues in them for the governance of all earthly things. This is a well-affirmed matter in the science of philosophy; <term>Aristotle</term> and those of his sect, and <term>Ptolemy</term>, spoke many things about this in their books. He wished to show us through the aforementioned that it is proven in philosophy that all things which happen among us occur through the will of God: for He is the one who moves the heavens and whatever is in them, and because of their motion, all <term>accidents</term> <note>events or non-essential qualities</note> in this world come about, concerning both generation and corruption. And afterward, the master Ptolemy is right to disdain and despise the vanities that others have compiled, because there is nothing in them except for the virtues derived from the aforementioned things of God. And he says they were vanities because he and all philosophers consider that there is nothing in the world that happens except through celestial disposition; if one believes otherwise, it is vanity. And if anyone should say that a good person can do something by themselves—like a king—nevertheless, that power which he has follows a will pertaining to itself, which is his own. And when he said, "we will seek out those things which we can reach among them, not through lots nor computations which have no reason," he means that he disdains <term>lots</term> <note>points calculated mathematically, like the Part of Fortune</note> and all those parts and numbers which have no rational basis in this art. These are parts taken from one place which, by their nature, have no relation to another place in terms of their power—such as the numbers described by Velius, or the number of miles and hundreds of years, and other things which were applied to this place from elsewhere. And as for what he said regarding "setting the goals in the figure of the stars and in the concordance they have with their places," he means that the rules and roots he will demonstrate in this art are according to the participation that exists between the configurations of the stars and the things they operate upon. Thus, he will demonstrate in the judgment of "parts" the participation that exists between a "part" and the Sun. And it is clear that through parts and numbers that have such participation, it becomes possible to judge—such as the <term>Part of Fortune</term> and the number of other planets and other similar things.

**Wherefore**, lest it be necessary to repeat the words in each of the prescribed chapters, it is fitting for us to set them forth here for all of them generally.

**And** so that we do not many times weary the readers with the things we have already said, it is fitting that we speak of the one God in all things generally.

**Afterward**, he will demonstrate to us that what he has spoken of in this matter will be the rules and roots from which the doctrine is composed in each of the seventeen aforementioned modes. He says in this place that since he does not wish to return to this statement many times, he comes to give general rules in this place; and these rules are three, as you will understand shortly.

**From** the chapters, therefore, of the observation of the <term>nativity</term> <note>birth chart</note>, let us consider the place of the zodiac which is similar to that species of the fifth chapter. For example, there is a similarity between the place of the <term>midheaven</term> <note>the 10th house; the highest point of the chart</note> and a person's works, and the place of the Sun and matters concerning <term>fathers</term> <note>original: "pijs/pites"; likely a scribal contraction for "patribus"</note>. Afterward, we should observe the planets which it is fitting to assign here to govern those places from the aforementioned five species.

**It is fitting** that we first look in the zodiac for the place that corresponds to the matter we are seeking and those things we wish to judge. For example: if the place of the midheaven agrees with the professions and works with which the native will involve himself, or if the place of the Sun agrees with matters pertaining to fathers. And afterward, we will look to see which planet has the right of governing that place through the five modes we have mentioned <note>The five "essential dignities": House, Exaltation, Triplicity, Term, and Face</note>.

**This** is the first rule which we will want to observe in each of the seventeen modes to know what will become of it: we will first seek the participation or proportion that exists among those three celestial things; and this propor-

<column-break/>

tion and concordance is that which concerns the places of the "parts." Thus, the place of the Sun pertains to fathers, and the concordance which is through the place of the signs, such as the 10th house, pertains to profession. Because when we know these, we will inquire which planet has the <term>disposition</term> <note>management or lordship</note> of that place, and we will know who the "dispositor" will be through the aforementioned things: namely, <term>triplicity</term>, <term>house</term>, <term>exaltation</term>, <term>term</term>, and the <term>aspect</term> under the rays—so that it has an aspect with the Sun in the figure, as we have already said.

**And** if one planet is ruler of that place in all these modes, we will attribute the disposition of that matter to it. If, however, two or three rule it, we will give the disposition to the one who has the strength of the greater number of dignities.

**And** if the house of the <term>triplicity</term> of the place belongs to one planet, we will give all parts to it as the dispositor of that matter. And if there are two or three for the place, we will set them as the dispositors since they have more dignities by number.

**He means** to say that if the lord of that place is one planet through each of the aforementioned modes, that one alone will be the dispositor of that matter. And if there are two or more, we will take the one of greater virtue and most dignities: we will give it a "helper" planet which follows it in virtue and number of dignities; and in all other modes we shall do the same.

**Then** let us consider the quality of the future: the investigation of which will be from the natures of those stars to which the disposition comes, and from the natures of the signs in which the planets are, as well as from similar places.

**Afterward** we will look at what the <term>accident</term> <note>the specific event</note> will be, and the time, according to the planets who have the right of disposing and according to the signs in which those same planets are, and from the places concordant with them.

**He means** to say that what happens in each of the seventeen modes, and generally concerning accidents, can be known through three things. The first comes from the nature of the disposing planet. The second is the nature of the place where that disposing planet is. The third is the nature of the place concordant in habit with that matter—just as the place of the Sun agrees with the father, and the place of the midheaven with professions. You mix one with the others, and you extract from that composition what will come of that accident. For example: if that concordance is of one nature, nothing more needs to be looked at. But if it is diverse, we will say that the accident will be composed of those three. And let us suppose that the Sun is in the 11th house, in the house of <term>Saturn</term>; and Saturn is in the 10th house, surrounded by <term>Jupiter</term> and <term>Venus</term> in the house of Jupiter. When we see this, we will say that the part will be of a good life in his law after this birth, and he will do good through his soul, such as entering religion; and he will be of noble race because of the nobility of Jupiter which comes to him through Saturn, and through Venus... and Saturn, who does not aspect himself with the Sun.

**After** this, we will take up the investigation of the quantity of the future and their strengths: considering whether they exist as strong in their qualities in the <term>world</term> and in the <term>nativities</term>, or if they are weak. In the world, they are said to be stronger when they are in their own places or others [favorable ones], and when they are also <term>oriental</term> <note>rising before the Sun</note> and increased in number <note>referring to their speed/motion</note>. In nativities, truly, they will be stronger when they are in the <term>angles</term> <note>the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses</note> or in places rising toward an angle; but especially in the first two, which are the <term>Ascendant</term> and the <term>Midheaven</term>. They will be weaker in the world when they exist in foreign places or those dissimilar to them, or when they are <term>occidental</term> <note>setting after the Sun</note> or diminished in their travel. But in nativities they will be weaker when they have receded from the angles.

**Afterward** we will seek the quantity of the accident through strength: and we will see if they are in a state of power and strength in the world, and if they are in such a state in the nativity. And if so, the greater power they have in the world is when they are in a pertinent place and are concordant with them, and when they are oriental, and when increased in number. And the greatest strength they have in the nativity is when they are in the angles.
