# Treatise on the Form of the Body

In their **complexion**, heat and moisture will prevail. But if he [the planet Jupiter] should be occidental, the native will be white-complexioned, though not as clearly white as we said above. His hair will be flat and he will be bald on the front part of the head; his eyes will be of medium size, and his body of medium stature; in his complexion, moisture will overcome the other qualities.

**When** Jupiter is the lord disposing of the aforementioned places, and he is oriental: the form of the native will be of a white color, with good hair, and eyes of medium, well-proportioned size. He will be of good height and will be a man who is honored or well-ordered; heat and moisture will prevail in his complexion. And if he should be occidental, the native will be of a medium whiteness—not as much as we said before—with thin hair, and he will be bald at the two sides of his forehead. His eyes and his body will be of a medium quantity; moisture will prevail in his complexion.

**I wish** to distinguish for you the substance of Ptolemy in this second place, and I shall open it to you in such a way that you may afterward take examples in other matters. I say that when he said "when Jupiter is the lord disposing of the aforementioned places," he means that when Jupiter alone holds the signaling power, he will signify just as a temperate city signifies: a temperate kind of good men. And if his signaling is not separate <note>meaning, if he is not the sole ruler but shared with another planet</note>, it will be in the manner signified by simple things. And what he said—if he is oriental, the native will be of such and such a form—means that when Jupiter is oriental and strong, he signifies such a color and such a form as he described. And what he said regarding the occidental position means that when Jupiter is occidental, weak, and of small appearance and splendor, he signifies those things he mentioned. And because the nature of Jupiter is temperate between heat and cold, and tends more toward moisture, it is fitting that he gives heat when he is oriental, and does not give heat when he is occidental. Therefore, it follows that when he is oriental, he gives a hot and moist complexion, and the complexion he gives when he is occidental is moist alone; and according to this rule, you shall judge in other cases.

**And whenever** Mars is oriental, the native's form will be of whiteness and redness; he will be of a good size and adequately fleshy; his eyes will be varied <note>original: "vary," likely meaning sparkling or of different colors like hazel</note>; the hair thick and medium in length. In his complexion, heat and dryness will prevail. If, however, he should be occidental, the native will be of a purely red color and of moderate body size, having small eyes, and sparse, flat, yellow hair; dryness will overcome his complexion.

**And** if Mars is the lord of the disposition of the places we have mentioned and is oriental, the native's form will be between white and red, of good magnitude, with a thick body, red eyes, and thick hair that is medium between curly and straight. Heat and dryness will prevail in his complexion. And when he is occidental, the form of the native will have much redness in color, a body of temperate size, small eyes, and sparse hair that is straight and blonde; and dryness will prevail in his complexion.

**What** has been demonstrated to us through the nature of Mars is a state of burning and maximum dryness. When he is oriental, he receives a hot and temperate nature and much moisture, such that they thicken the body and the eyes become "cardines" <note>original: "cardines," likely referring to a sky-blue or clear celestial color</note> because of the moisture that prevails. The hair is thick due to the many vapors <term>vapors: "fumositates," internal gases or heat believed in medieval medicine to produce hair</term> that are in the body on account of the great heat. When you understand this, you will understand what Ptolemy says about the form signified by Mars.

**The works** of Venus are indeed similar to the works of Jupiter, except

<column-break/>

that those things which happen through her are more beautiful and more pleasing; and her beauty is more like the beauty of women. He [the native] will also be of a better figure and a more suitable quality of soul, and the body is softer. Also, from her properties, she makes the eyes "subiuffos" <note>original: "subiuffos," likely meaning sparkling, moist, or slightly reddish</note> and fitting.

**The bodies** [signified] by Venus are similar to the works of Jupiter, except that what she works is more beautiful, more pleasing, and more delightful to the sight. Her beauty is more like the beauty of women; the native will be of a more beautiful figure, of better will, and of a thicker body. It is her property to make the eyes "picratos" <term>picratos: likely from the Greek 'pikros' or a medieval term for bright, multi-colored, or sharp-sighted eyes</term>, beautiful and of mixed colors.

**That** which happens through Venus is like that which happens through Jupiter; yet because she has a greater appearance than Jupiter and is feminine, it follows that she differs from the works of Jupiter in the things described.

**When** Mercury likewise is oriental, the native will be of a honey color; he will be of moderate body size, well-proportioned, with small eyes and medium hair. Heat will prevail in his complexion. But if he should be occidental, the native will be somewhat blackish and participating in a saffron color, lean, having a thin voice and hollow sockets. The pupil of the eyes will be like the pupil of a goat's eye, declining toward redness. It is not doubted that dryness prevails in his complexion.

**Similarly**, if Mercury is oriental, the native's color will be like the color of honey; the size of his body temperate and of good composition; with small eyes and medium hair; heat will prevail in his complexion. And if he is occidental, the native's form will be between a dark and red and saffron color, with a black body and a subtle voice, with concave eyes. The pupil of his eyes will be likened to the pupil of a goat's eye tending toward redness; and dryness will prevail in his complexion.

**We** have already said that a planet gains a good appearance and heat through being oriental; and if it is occidental, it loses it. Since the proper nature of Mercury tends somewhat toward dryness, he signifies the aforementioned things for that reason. It is manifest that if he is mixed with another planet, these things will incline toward the nature of that planet. And after Mercury acts according to his own nature—and in a temperate city produces a color medium between dark, red, and saffron when he is occidental—he will produce even more blackness when he is in a "burning city" <note>A metaphor for a very hot climate or a harsh astrological placement</note>. Mercury has this nature among all other planets because he is always "combust" <term>combust: an astrological term for a planet being too close to the Sun, which was thought to burn or weaken its influence</term> and under the rays of the Sun, just as a very hot city is.

**Each** of these stars is aided by the Sun and Moon when they are associated with them in figure.

**And** the Sun and Moon help each of these planets when they participate with them in figure <term>figure: the "aspect" or geometric relationship between planets</term>.

**A doubt** arises when the Sun or Moon is the dispositor of the native: how should we take the signification from the Sun or Moon regarding forms? The answer to this is what we have taught many times before: that the Sun and Moon are the princes over all stars. When the signaling belongs to one of them, it signifies the natural thing of the whole genus without any inclination toward a distinct head. The distinction in their signaling is found in what Ptolemy says in this statement.

**For the Sun** aids in the figure and beauty as well as in the fatness of the body. The Moon, however, generally helps in the temperament and in leanness or moisture. Especially when she is separated from him [the Sun], her help will be particularly according to the properties...

¶ The Sun similarly helps and gives a beautiful appearance and a thickness of the body, and the Moon generally helps in every temperament <note original="temperie">The mixture of the four primary qualities: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>: both in the leanness and the moisture of a humid complexion. It is also clear that the Moon generally gives temperance, leanness, and a humid complexion; this happens specifically when it separates from the Sun and its light appears. This causes it to grant salty phlegm <term>flegma salsum: one of the "humors" of the body, believed to be influenced by the Moon's light</term> through the increase of its light, and it gives acidic phlegm through the diminishing of its light; particularly, however, it gives different states in its various phases. When they precede the Sun, they make the bodies temperate; but when they move in their second station <note>the point where a planet stops before resuming direct motion</note>, they make them weaker. When they set, they will bring about misery, impediments, and heaviness.

¶ Generally also, when the planets are matutinal and visible, they make large bodies; when they are in the first station, they make them strong and hot; and when they are preceding [the Sun], they make them temperate. When in the second station, they make them weaker. And when they have hidden themselves so that they are not visible, they make them base, for pestilences and miseries befall them.

¶ When planets are matutinal, they are stronger and larger; because of this, they make the bodies stronger and more complete. They always increase in this until they reach the first station, at which time their virtue or power is perfected. For that reason, they make bodies that are rigid, strong, and durable. From there, the power itself goes on diminishing until they are in opposition to the Sun; then they make the bodies weaker, and that weakness grows until they become vespertine <term>vespertini: "evening stars," planets that set after the Sun</term>, until they enter under the rays of the Sun. Then they make the bodies prone to suffering, because miseries and pestilences quickly befall them; and you must understand this regarding Venus, Mercury, and so on, according to what we demonstrated in the gloss of the first part.

¶ He [Ptolemy] wants to say that the figures of the places in which the disposing planets are, and the figures of the place of the Moon and the Ascendant, similarly help the planets in signifying the build of the body. They change the build of the body, its figure, and its complexion according to their natures, if they are of a nature contrary to the disposing planets, as he demonstrated before.

good size, of a thick body, of good eyes, and heat and moisture conquer in him.

¶ The quadrant, however, which extends from the summer solstice to the autumnal equinoctial point will grant the native a temperate and medium body size, suitable fleshiness, large eyes, and thick and curly hair; heat and dryness will conquer in him.

¶ And the quadrant from the summer solstice to the autumnal equinox makes the native temperate and medium in size, of a thick body, of large eyes, and of much and curly hair; and heat and dryness conquer in him.

¶ Because this fourth quadrant is cold and moist, and black color comes from great heat—as the physicists have proven—and sometimes it comes from great cold. Because this fourth quadrant is of great coldness, it signifies a black color like the summer quadrant, but the beauty of the Sun and Moon disturbs this. And what Ptolemy wanted to say is that any of these quadrants helps the planet that accords with it, and diminishes all the work of that which does not accord with it regarding matters pertaining to itself; and he wants to show us what each of the signs works by itself, so that this may be joined with everything he said before.

¶ Particularly, however, the places whose figure is assimilated to human figures—namely among the figures of the circle of signs [the Zodiac] and outside it—will form bodies of fit and temperate composition.

¶ The particular matter is such that those places whose forms are similar to the forms of men (from those which are in the zodiac and outside the zodiac) make bodies of good, temperate composition.

¶ It is fitting that the forms outside the zodiac indicate these things, because those that have the power of working are those that stand above the circle with the disposing planet from the circles we spoke of before; and we have already demonstrated these forms in the gloss of the first part.

# Treatise

¶ Those whose figures <note>In this context, "figures" refers to the constellations or signs of the Zodiac.</note> are not inclined toward a temperate body are proven to imitate the forms they resemble, and their limbs are made like the limbs of those things they represent through similarity. For these signs tend to cause greatness or smallness, strength or weakness, and a well-proportioned or poorly-proportioned gathering of features.

¶ However, those that are not of this specific form but of others change the bodies according to what suits their own forms; they make the limbs similar to their own by inclining them somewhat toward a greater or lesser size, or toward strength or weakness, or toward a good or bad composition.

¶ The thing that best suits the human form is temperance <note original="temperantia">The ideal balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, as Haly demonstrated in his *Book of Complexions* <note>Haly refers to Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arab astrologer whose commentaries on Ptolemy were standard textbooks in Europe.</note>. For when the forms that are separate from human forms share in the influence of the disposing planets, they change those bodies and pull them toward their own nature, making them somewhat similar to themselves. The words of Ptolemy have been declared, and he wishes to explain them better by what follows.

¶ Those signs that produce greatness are Leo, Virgo, and Sagittarius; those that lead to smallness are Pisces, Cancer, and Capricorn.

¶ Those which tend more toward greatness are like Leo, Virgo, and Sagittarius. And those which tend toward smallness are like Pisces, Cancer, and Capricorn.

¶ Since the figures of Leo, Virgo, and Sagittarius are large in the heavens, they signify greatness. Similarly, the figures of Pisces, Cancer, and Capricorn, because they are small, signify smallness.

¶ Furthermore, regarding Aries, Taurus, and Leo, if the beginning of their influence is used in the higher art <note original="altiori arte">Likely referring to the more precise calculations of astrology or the primary dignities of the planets.</note>, it will make the limbs better and more inclined toward fatness. But whatever is located toward their lower parts and their extremities, it applies more to leanness. On the contrary, whatever of Sagittarius, Gemini, and Scorpio is placed toward their beginnings causes a decline toward leanness, while that which claims their extremities for itself makes them more inclined toward fatness.

¶ Similarly, those signs like Aries, Taurus, and Leo, according to their front parts, make the limbs tend toward thickness. And their back parts pull the limbs toward leanness and weakness. And those that are of another sort, such as the front of Sagittarius, Gemini, and Scorpio, tend toward leanness, while their back parts pull the limbs toward thickness.

¶ This is another similarity, because the figures that resemble beasts pull the human figures toward the shapes of beasts. Thus, because the front parts of Aries, Taurus, and Leo are larger than their back parts, they produce such a result in human bodies; through this gloss, you will be able to understand everything Ptolemy wishes to say.

¶ Furthermore, Virgo, Libra, and Sagittarius produce a body tending toward temperance and good proportion. Scorpio, however, along with Pisces and Taurus, removes the body from temperance.

¶ Similarly, Virgo and Sagittarius incline bodies toward temperance and good composition; Scorpio, Pisces, and Taurus incline bodies toward distemperance and bad composition.

¶ Those that create temperance do so because they are of the human figure <note>Virgo (the Maiden), Libra (the Scales, often held by a human figure), and Sagittarius (the Centaur, whose upper half is human) were considered "human" signs compared to animal signs.</note>; and those that are far removed from human figures cause distemperance.

¶ Therefore, one must observe the qualities of the figures in various ways.

¶ It is also fitting that we apply our minds to the other figures.

¶ He means that applying our minds to the figures is according to this reasoning which Ptolemy stated before.

<column-break/>

¶ It is fitting for us to compare them with one another and to project the properties found therein, joined together in the form of the bodies, their complexion <term>complexione: the specific temperament or "chemical makeup" of an individual's body</term>, and the mixture of all those things.

¶ But we shall take the comparison in its entirety—namely, one with the other—and we will understand those same properties which are joined by the composition of these things in the form of the body and its complexion.

¶ This is a general rule for all: whenever we find that there is one disposer <note>The planet that rules or dominates a specific sign or point in the chart.</note> and all other things agree with it, we shall judge by that disposer. But if another thing is contrary to it, we shall subtract as much as that thing pertains to him. And if we find that more than one planet has lordship over the disposer, we shall take the one that has the greater testimony <note>A technical term for the number of astrological "points" or strengths a planet holds in a specific location.</note> and all other arriving factors, and we shall subtract or add according to this. By this, we shall know the figure of the body, its complexion, and its form.

# Third Book

If the planet is in its own place, or in the fourth house, or in opposition on the same diameter, it leads us to believe that pestilences <note>In historical astrology, "pestilence" often refers to sudden physical blemishes, accidents, or acute defects, rather than just contagious plague.</note> and infirmities will affect the body of the newborn. This is especially true if both luminaries <note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and the Moon.</note>, or even one of them, are found in the angles of the manner we described: whether both are in one angle or in two opposite angles. In such cases, they do not only grant misfortunes when a malefic planet <note original="infortuna">Usually referring to Mars or Saturn, planets traditionally associated with hardship.</note> rises after the luminaries in an angle that causes pestilences and infirmities—which are signified by the locations on the horizon, the signs, and the nature of the malefic planets and the stars that participate with them—but they will also give them the power to do the same if they ascend before the two luminaries.

¶ If you apply your mind to these words and join them with the words of the chapter on those who do not receive food <note>This likely refers to a chapter on infant mortality or "non-rearing," where the stars suggest a child will not survive to eat.</note>, you will understand this well. The rule that Ptolemy taught us in this chapter is a general rule by which we can know the pestilences and infirmities occurring in the body of the newborn. This rule teaches us to look at the Ascendant <note>The 1st House, representing the self and the physical body.</note>, the seventh house, and the sixth house—which has no aspect <note>An "aspect" is a specific geometric relationship between planetary positions that allows them to "see" or influence each other.</note> with the Ascendant—and to the planets existing in these places and the planets looking upon these places. If you find these locations afflicted by malefic planets, or even just two of the places—specifically the seventh and sixth houses—we know for certain that infirmities and pestilences will happen to the body of the newborn. And if we find one of these afflicted, we look to the two luminaries; if they are in the angles or in fortune <note>In a favorable position.</note>, we will know through this that pestilence will happen to the body. One should look at these five places: the Ascendant, the seventh, the sixth, and the locations of the Sun and Moon, to see if any of them is separating from a malefic planet or moving toward one. One is as significant as the other, though the planet moving toward a malefic causes greater harm than the one separating from it, as we said in the chapter on those who do not receive food. What we must keep in mind here is that the powers of the planets are mixed together. You should know that the pestilences and infirmities happening in the body will be according to what the ascending sign and the seventh sign signify—for these are above the horizon—and according to the signs in which the significators <note>The specific planets designated as "pointing to" a certain life area.</note> stand, the nature of the malefic planets, the afflicted locations, and the planets participating in the figure with them; all of which Ptolemy teaches from here on.

¶ Because the parts of each sign surrounding the part that receives light from the parts of the hemisphere, I say that the part receiving the impediment signifies that part of the body in which the event will occur. They also designate whether the event will be a physical defect <note original="impedimentum">A physical disability, injury, or blemish.</note>, an infirmity <note original="infirmitas">A chronic or internal disease.</note>, or both. The natures of the stars also specify the types of impediments and accidents.

¶ Thus, the degrees of each sign that encompass the degree receiving the harm—from the degrees of the horizon—signify the location on the body where that accident will hit, and whether what happens to that limb will be a pestilence, an infirmity, or both. However, the natures of the planets determine the specific types of their occurrences.

¶ This means that the degree which receives harm from the malefic planets—whether it is among the degrees of the Ascendant or the degrees of the 7th house—signals the limb in which the pestilence or infirmity will occur. This is because that degree will always be in the "term" <note>A "term" is a sub-division of a zodiac sign ruled by a specific planet.</note> of some planet, and therefore it happens that it governs the limb belonging to that planet. Furthermore, the natures of the planets that cause the types of pestilences and infirmities similarly cause the origins of these types. Since this is so, once we know the specific limbs assigned to the planets, we will know everything that belongs to this chapter.

¶ Because Saturn has, among the more noble parts of man:

¶ Because Saturn possesses, among the principal limbs of man, the right hearing and the *barum* (that is, the spleen), the bladder, and phlegm.

It has the *barum* (the spleen) because of the black bile <note original="meliam">A corruption of "melancholia."</note> which is of its nature, and the bladder because it participates in the channels of superfluities <note>Waste products of the body.</note>, and phlegm because it sometimes causes great cold and sometimes great moisture.

¶ Jupiter, however, governs touch, the lungs, the ribs, the cartilage, and the sperm.

¶ And Jupiter has touch, the lungs, the ribs, the pulse, and the sperm.

¶ It has these because it is hot and moist, and tempered toward moisture in another way, and these things suit those qualities. For touch comes from temperament; the lungs, ribs, and pulse suit heat and life (which exists because of temperament), and sperm for that same reason.

¶ Mars, however, has the left hearing, the kidneys, the veins, and the testicles.

¶ And Mars has the left hearing, the kidneys, the veins, and the virile members <note>The male reproductive organs.</note>.

¶ This is because Mars often participates with the Moon, and therefore participates in the disposition of the left hearing. Because of the "baseness" of the places through which superfluities pass to these limbs, the kidneys, veins, and virile members belong to it.

¶ The Sun governs sight, the heart, the brain, the nerves, and all the limbs of the right side.

¶ The Sun has sight, the brain, the heart, the nerves, and all the limbs of the right side.

¶ Since the Sun is more noble than all other stars, it is taught to have the most noble limbs in man and those on the right side; for the right side is nobler than the left. Similarly, it is because the Sun participates with other parts in the terms of the halves of the greater firmament.

¶ Venus governs smell, the liver, and the flesh.

¶ Venus has smell, the liver, and the flesh.

¶ You already know that Venus is [harmonious] according to sound and is distinguished as being female, and that she herself is beauty; therefore, it is fitting for her to have these parts.

¶ Mercury governs speech, deliberation, memory, the tongue, bile, and the nostrils.

¶ Mercury, however, has reason, speech, thought, the tongue, bile, and the foundation from the lower part <note original="fundamentum a parte inferiori">A polite reference to the anus or rectum.</note>.

¶ You already know that Mercury by itself tends toward dryness and is of a convertible nature with whichever planet it is mixed. You know that it always travels near the Sun, which is the great prince. Thus it is fitting that it has speech, reason, thought, and the tongue—since it is always near the Sun and tends toward the nature of every planet—and it has bile and the lower foundation because of the mixture it has with the malefic planets.

¶ The Moon governs taste, swallowing, the stomach, the belly, the private parts of women, and all limbs of the left side.

¶ And the Moon has taste, the throat, the stomach, the belly, the matrix <note>The womb.</note> of women, and all limbs of the left side.

¶ Since the Sun has the limbs that have the most dominion in the direction of life, it follows that the Moon has the limbs that follow those principal ones and serve them. Therefore, the belly, stomach, womb, and throat are under the dominion of the Moon. Similarly, the Moon participates with the planets in the disposition of the limbs that are in the lesser half of the firmament. We have demonstrated the words of Ptolemy in these matters so that you may always take an example for yourself, to give each planet what is fitting to it.

¶ Generally, physical defects will occur for the most part when the malefic stars that cause them are oriental <note>Rising in the east before the Sun.</note>. Infirmities, however, will happen when those same stars are occidental <note>Setting in the west after the Sun.</note>.

### Treatise

Because each of these two paths is distinct. For a blemish <note original="impedimentum">In this context, a physical defect or sudden injury.</note> will only occur once and will not last long. Infirmities, however, will either endure for a long time or will occur through recurring episodes. 
¶ A general occurrence of pestilence <note original="pestilentiarum">Here, "pestilence" refers to a sudden, permanent physical affliction or blemish rather than a contagious disease.</note> will happen when the fortunate planets causing them are oriental <note>Rising in the east before the Sun.</note>; however, it will be an occurrence of infirmity when these planets are occidental <note>Setting in the west after the Sun.</note>. For there is this difference between their powers: a pestilence happens at one time, and the pain of it does not endure. An infirmity, however, lasts always and sometimes has recurring attacks.
¶ When the unfortunate planets <note>Traditionally Mars and Saturn.</note> causing such things are strong, they give pestilences; when they are weak, they give infirmities. This is what Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text for this work.</note> means. Indeed, he gave one example for strong planets—so that you may take it as a model for other strong positions—and the example is this: oriental planets are stronger, and occidental ones are weaker. This is the distinction between a pestilence and an infirmity. Because of this, he said that a pestilence happens once and its pain ceases while the defect itself remains and is not removed—such as blindness, deafness, or the loss of use in one side of the body <note original="proditio unius lateris">Paralysis or a stroke.</note>. But in an infirmity that occurs, the pain lasts until the person is cured or it comes in recurring attacks, such as gout <note original="podagra">A form of inflammatory arthritis, historically associated with humors.</note>. His words are useful here in this general rule; from here on, he wishes to speak about particular cases.
¶ In matters through which particular accidents are grasped, when the figures have been properly tested and observed, and the qualities of the infirmities and signs of defects are found, what is grasped comes from the accidents that follow and happen for the most part according to the properties of the stars in their qualities.
¶ There are three ways by which we can know particular accidents when they have been well-calculated by finding the figures and states signifying pestilences and infirmity. These are to know them through the accidents that follow and occur in the majority of cases according to the state of the planets that are similar in their condition.
¶ After he showed us the things by which we can generally know the pestilences and infirmities that happen to the newborn, he wishes to show how we recognize them in a particular way, and he spoke thus: "When I wished to be well-instructed and to know, I looked at and calculated these things specifically, and I found that each of them happens through its own proper figure," and he distinguishes them further on.
¶ Indeed, there will be a loss of sight in one of the eyes when the Moon is alone in the aforementioned angles, and at that hour there is a conjunction or a full moon <note original="proventio">likely a transcription error for "preventio," often used for the syzygy or preceding full moon.</note>; or when it is in another figure with the Sun and is associated with any of the stars of <term>alaceba</term> <note original="alaceba">An Arabic-derived term for nebulous star clusters or "cloudy" stars.</note> which resemble clouds and are in the circle of the signs <note>The Zodiac.</note>. Examples include the nebulous star in <term>Cancer</term> <note>Specifically the Beehive Cluster, or Praesepe.</note>, and the <term>athoraie</term> <note original="athoraie">The Pleiades star cluster.</note> in <term>Taurus</term>, and the tip of the arrow of <term>Sagittarius</term>, as well as the tail of <term>Scorpio</term>, and that which is around the <term>aldahera</term> <note original="aldahera">The "tuft" or mane of the constellation Leo.</note> in the parts of <term>Leo</term>, and also the <term>calber</term> <note original="calber">Possibly a corruption of 'Kalb' (heart) or a specific star in Aquarius.</note> of <term>Aquarius</term>.
¶ Thus, the loss of sight happens to one eye when the Moon is only in the aforementioned angles and at that hour there is a conjunction or opposition. Similarly, when it is in another of the figures it holds with the Sun and applies to any of the nebulous stars in the zodiac, such as the nebulous star in Cancer, and the <term>Pleiades</term> in Taurus, and another in Sagittarius, and the tip of the tail of Scorpio, and those which are in the circuit of the Lion's hair, and the <term>altarssim</term> <note original="altarssim">Likely referring to stars in the face or eyes of the constellation Aquarius.</note> of Aquarius.
¶ This is the specific figure that causes blindness or infirmity in one eye only: that the Moon be in the Ascendant or the descendant and be unfortunate, and that the Sun be with it or in opposition to it. For this constellation causes infirmity in one eye or blindness in it. Similarly, if the Moon applies to the Sun while it is in any angle

of those which are the Ascendant and descendant and is unfortunate, and any nebulous star exists with it upon one of the circles that resemble the horizon—which we previously described in the chapter on life—such a constellation causes blindness in one eye or infirmity in it.

### Third Book

[The defect] may occur in a sign of fire <note>original: "signo calo" (signo calido/ignis)</note>; it will be because of fire. And if it occurs in the terms <note>Terms are specific subdivisions of zodiac signs ruled by different planets.</note> of Saturn, it will be because of iron. You should take this as an example for all other matters, because what **Ptolemy** said will be the rule from which you take your examples. It is necessary for you to know in this place the infirmities of the eyes from the physicians, and the cause of each of them, and you shall judge each one according to what pertains to it. You must also hold in your memory what we said in the chapter on those who do not receive nourishment. And if this harm <note original="nocumentum">A physical injury or defect.</note> is very great, it will be an occurrence around birth; if it is not great, it will be prolonged. Similarly, [see] if any fortune <note>A benefic planet like Jupiter or Venus.</note> testifies to it. You will know the time in which it happens through the rules you have learned regarding the times at which dangers occur; this has already been stated. Similarly, you will know this through the revolutions of the years <note>Annual horoscopes used to predict events for a specific year.</note>.

¶ Likewise, when **Venus** is in any of the aforesaid **angles** <note>The four most powerful points in a chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note>, and especially in the western one [the Descendant], and stays with **Saturn**, or is associated with him in the figure and they have exchanged their places <note>Mutual reception, where each planet sits in a sign ruled by the other.</note>, and **Mars** is elevated above her or in opposition to her: it happens from this that men do not have children, and for women there are abortions and untimely births.

¶ Similarly, if **Venus** is in any of the aforesaid angles, especially in the west, joined to **Saturn**, or aspects him by exchanging places, and **Mars** is high above both of them or in opposition to them across the diameter: it will happen because of this that men will not produce children, and it will happen to women that their children will die, or they will give birth before the proper time.

¶ There are other rules that are taken through the figures of **Venus**. The first is that **Venus** be in the **Ascendant** <note>The Eastern Horizon</note> or the **West** <note>The Descendant</note>, which is stronger than the former; and let her be joined with **Saturn**, or let him aspect her. The other rule is that **Saturn** be in the place of these two angles with **Venus** joined to him, or aspecting him. And if in these two circumstances **Mars** aspects **Venus**, or is in her opposition, it will happen to men that they will be <term>maneri</term> <note>Sterile or impotent men.</note> and will not produce children, and to women that their children will die, or they will give birth before the proper time.

¶ Also, mutilations of children <note original="puerorum detruncationes">This can refer to birth defects, injuries, or even sacrificial rituals in historical contexts.</note> will happen from this, especially in **Cancer**, **Virgo**, and **Capricorn**, and when the **Moon** from the east has any trial <note original="tial" (likely triality/aspect)> with **Mars**.

¶ It will similarly happen to them that the creatures [fetuses] will be cut apart in their wombs; and this happens especially in **Cancer**, **Virgo**, and **Capricorn**, with the **Moon** applying to **Mars** from the oriental side.

¶ This means that when **Venus** is in the state he described, and it happens in this way in **Cancer**, or **Virgo**, or **Capricorn**, with the **Moon** applying to **Mars** from the oriental side: the dismemberment of the creatures will happen to women.

# The Third [Book]

And it will happen from this that one will suffer because of burning <note>original: "combustione"</note> that will occur to him: or through perforations in hidden places by way of an evil occasion: such as **fistulas** <note>Abnormal tunnels or passages in the body tissue.</note> and **hemorrhoids**: or things that are born in the body either through very hot and burning wounds: or through sores that eat away the flesh: and with this it will happen to women that the children they carry in their wombs will move, or that they will rot or be lost within them.

And "humors that descend": he wants to say the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance was thought to determine health.</note> that descend through the urine: and that through sour and salty phlegm the body becomes thin: and wounds of the internal members occur because of the humors that descend there: it happens that he who is in such a state becomes very wasted. # Treatise

¶ He means to say that when the **malefics** <note>original: "infortune"; these are the "unfortunate" planets, Saturn and Mars, traditionally associated with hardship.</note> have caused some infirmity in the body, and no **benefic** <note>original: "fortuna"; the "fortunate" planets, Jupiter and Venus, associated with growth and healing.</note> testifies to the malefics or to the **luminaries** <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>, then neither those infirmities nor the pestilences will be cleared; instead, they will be greatly harmful. Similarly, this occurs if the benefics testify only weakly, while the malefics are in positions of greater power.

¶ However, when the benefics are in their more dignified figures <note>Astrological positions where a planet's influence is strongest.</note> and are stronger than the malefics (which are the causes of the afflictions), then there will be no shameful impediments, nor any leading to disgrace. There will also be light infirmities that are quickly quieted; this likewise happens when the benefics are **oriental** <note>Rising in the east before the Sun, considered a position of strength and action.</note>.

¶ If the benefics are in oriental figures and elevated above the malefics that are causing the condition, then the pestilences will not last long, nor will they be foul; the infirmities will be light, will quickly quiet down, and will change easily for the better. The same will happen if the malefics themselves are oriental.

¶ He means to say that when the benefics testify and are strong in themselves, while the malefics are weaker than them, foul pestilences will not occur, nor will the body be worth less because of them. The infirmities will likewise be light and will quickly cease; and if, in addition to this, the benefics are oriental and emerge before the Sun, the person will be healed quickly.

¶ For **Jupiter** indeed hides impediments and causes infirmities to cease through the help of others, attributed to reasons of wealth or uprightness.

¶ Because it is the nature of Jupiter to cover over pestilences and to remove or mitigate infirmities with the help of the good care provided to the patients by other men.

¶ He means to say that when Jupiter regards the pestilences, he covers them and gentles the illnesses with the help that men provide to one another, and some will help themselves by mitigating the sickness.

¶ And when he is with **Mercury**, he will wipe out infirmities with medicines, or through the healing tools of physicians. **Venus**, however, will adorn the impediments by a certain grace, for the sake of decoration: through divine occasions or **prophets** <note>Those perceived to have divine insight or healing powers.</note>. She also eases infirmities in whatever way possible, making them cease with medicines proceeding from a divine occasion.

¶ And if they are with Mercury, the illnesses are quieted through medicine and the care of good physicians. And Venus alleviates illnesses and pestilences with a great alleviation through a divine miracle, or through some prophet or holy man; she gentles the illnesses with medicines or care proceeding from God.

¶ He means to say that when Venus regards them, she beautifies somewhat the pestilences that the malefics cause; those who have them, she makes them as servants, so that his good works make him have the love of men, and he will not be weary of that pestilence. Men will then consider that this good man has this from God. And if it is an infirmity and not a pestilence, they will quiet down through things made of **incantations** or some **character** <note>A magical sigil, symbol, or amulet.</note> which is placed around the neck, and other such things that are accepted from the friends of God, or through dreams coming from friends.

¶ But if **Saturn** is with her, it will be well noted and manifest, or something equivalent. And if Mercury is with her, this will be done with profit and gain for the patient, which will happen to the patient because of this.

¶ And if Saturn is with her, that matter will be made plain and detected and similar things; and if Mercury is with her, it will be with help and profit which the person suffering the pestilence or illness will have through that which he possesses.

¶ He means to say that when Saturn is with Venus, the pestilences and illnesses and their beautifying and gentling will be matters clearly

<column-break/>

demonstrated and very apparent. And if Mercury is with her, he will have profit and utility from that illness or pestilence; for men will believe that God wished to take it away or beautify it for him through the love He has for him; and because of this, men will desire to do him favors and good.

<margin>Chapter 13.</margin>
->On the qualities of the soul of the native.<-
->Haly said.<- <note>Referring to Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer whose commentary on Ptolemy was widely used in medieval Europe.</note>

¶ After he has completed the rules by which we can know the conditions of accidents happening to the same [body], he now wishes to show us the rules by which we can know the state of the part of man which is the **soul**.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial M featuring stylized floral patterns and foliage.</image-desc>

The method indeed by which the accidents of the body are recognized is this which we have said before. Regarding the qualities of the souls, that which pertains properly to the intellect and reason is always recognized through the qualities of **Mercury**.

¶ For the part through which we seek to know the accidents of the body is as we said before; however, the state of the soul in the **rational part** <note>The faculty of logical thought and intellect.</note> can always be known from the state in which we see Mercury. The states of the soul are good morals, which are called **virtues**, and malice, which are called **vices**. And the disposition for receiving each of these things from the state in which we see Mercury is the **complexion** <note>The overall "makeup" or balance of qualities.</note> which he will have at the hour of birth. And this state is weighed from the sign in which Mercury stays, and from the lord of that sign, and from his application to or separation from other planets, and from the things that are shown in this. The rule by which we can know the "face" of the rational soul and its whole state is taken from the complexion of Mercury, which is composed of these things we have mentioned.

¶ That, however, which is the height of **irrationality** <note>The emotional, instinctive, or vegetative part of the soul, as opposed to the logical mind.</note> is understood from the luminary near to the dense bodies, which is called the **Moon**, as well as from the stars associating with her in the figure, and those having *alictisal* and *alinchibref* <note>Latinized Arabic astrological terms: *al-ittisal* (application) and *al-inkiraf* (separation), describing the movement of planets toward or away from an aspect.</note> with her.

¶ And that which concerns it in its natural [vital] part can be known from the luminary which is near to the dense bodies, which is the Moon, and from the parts with which it shares a figure through application to them or separation from them.

¶ What he said regarding its natural part: he means to say concerning the goodnesses and in other things that are in the **vegetative and vital part** <note>The basic biological functions and instincts.</note>. And what can be known of this from the luminary near to dense bodies: he means to say from the bodies [signs] in which the Moon stays. And he teaches his words well through a rule by which we can know the knowledge of the whole state of the irrational soul; we ought to take it from the complexion of the Moon—namely, those things that are in her from her own nature, and the sign in which she is, and the lord of all her dignities, and the place in which she is in comparison to the **angles** <note>The four most important points in a horoscope: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note>, and from her application and separation, and from all her other states which we have narrated. And since it is so, the rule by which we can know the knowledge of the whole soul generally is from the state which Mercury and the Moon have at the hour of birth: the rational soul is separated [discerned] by the state of Mercury, and the irrational by the state of the Moon. And it is well known that when these two have applied to each other, or there is some concord between them, the action of the soul will be ordered, and there will be concord between them. And if Mercury is stronger, the irrational soul obeys the rational; and if the Moon is stronger than them, similarly, he who is in a **direct sign** <note>Signs of long ascension, which rise more slowly and are thought to be more stable.</note> will be the lord of him who is in a **tortuous sign** <note>Signs of short ascension, which rise quickly and are often associated with irregularity.</note>.

¶ Wherefore, since the movements of the soul and its qualities are of many kinds, their investigation does not proceed by one and the same smooth path, however far it goes; but they must be attended to by many observations and diverse considerations. For all the signs in which the Moon and Mercury and their lord are found greatly assist the qualities of the soul’s properties. Furthermore, the associations of the figures of the stars in the aforesaid respects to the Sun and the angles having a part: the qualities also of the natures of each of the stars specifically assist the movements of the soul.

# Third Book

¶ Since the matter of the soul's movement and its various states involves many different modes, our inquiry into them should not be a simple thing, nor should it be done haphazardly. Rather, it must be performed with great diligence and various rectifications <note>In astrology, "rectification" refers to the precise calculation and adjustment of a birth chart to ensure accuracy.</note>. This is because the differences in the signs in which **the Moon** and **Mercury** are found—along with the planets that are their **dispositors** <note>A "dispositor" is a planet that rules the zodiac sign where another planet is currently located; it acts like a landlord influencing its tenant.</note>—greatly assist in determining the soul's properties and provide great strength to them. Similarly, the participation of the signs and planets, which they have in what we have said regarding their relationship to the **Sun** and the **angles** <note>The four most important points in a chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note>, as well as the specific natural states of any of the planets, aid in the movement of the soul.

¶ This teaching is a gloss and interpretation of the state in which **Mercury** shall be, and the state in which **the Moon** shall be at the hour of birth. Since each of these states can exist in many and diverse configurations, such that each signifies something different about the soul's condition than another, it is necessary that the judgment of the soul's qualities be made in many ways. It is fitting that the inquiry into the soul's qualities is not just one single thing however it happens, but is done with maximum diligence and the rectification of various figures and the different positions that Mercury and the Moon will hold. This is because the diversity of the natures of the signs in which each of these two planets is found, as well as the participation of one with the other, and the diversity of the natures of their dispositors, and the participation they have with them—both their position in the world <note>Their placement in the sky relative to the horizon.</note> and their position in the birth chart—gives each of these things its own separate property to the native's soul. And since this is the case, the accidents <note>In a philosophical sense, "accidents" are the traits or characteristics of a person that are not part of their essential being.</note> of the soul and its demonstrating states can be known by applying the mind to all these things separately in each matter. For when we know the simple elements and find how many of them are joined (2, 3, or more together), we will compose them and judge according to the prevailing composition, as we have shown many times. Indeed, I have seen some astrologers who knew nothing of this chapter; and when I applied my mind to them, I found that they understood nothing of everything that has come before in this book. I understood that the weakness of their intellect was in this chapter because they understood nothing of the preceding chapters. For example <note>original: "v. g." (verbi gratia)</note>, how can someone understand what Ptolemy taught at the end of the chapter on the division of births, or at the end of the chapter on parents, if they cannot understand the reasons contained in this book which Ptolemy organized? For this is just like what is found in Euclid and books of geometry: the reasoning of these books cannot be understood unless the preceding concepts are understood first. He who neglects to understand the first things will not be able to understand the latter. Such is this book. Thus, he who does not understand **syllogisms** <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> will not be able to understand a demonstration; and he who does not understand the premises will not understand the syllogisms; and when you do not understand the parts of the premises, you will not understand the premises themselves. Similarly, he who does not understand the particular details we take from the soul, from which the general rule is composed, does not understand the general rule. And now I will list these particular things, and they are six: 

First is the nature of the signs. Second is the state that Mercury will have in comparison to the Moon. Third is the participation both of them will have with other planets. Fourth is the nature of the planets that are their dispositors. Fifth is that which the state of their position does in comparison to the world and in comparison to the Sun. Sixth is that which the state of their position does in the birth chart and in comparison to the angles. And Ptolemy teaches each of these particular things and says:

¶ From the signs, therefore, the **movable signs** <note>Also called "Cardinal signs": Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn. They represent the start of the seasons and are associated with initiative.</note> generally make the soul love matters of union and universality, as well as cities. Furthermore, they compel the soul to affect praise, to think upon divine things, and to be of sharp wit—a seeker of truth with praiseworthy movement: liberal, of good reputation among others, and skilled in the judgments of the stars.

¶ The movable signs generally make souls lovers of many things and of cities; they similarly make them lovers of praise, burdened with divine matters, subtle, of good and praised movement, of great benefit, of great inquiry into things, doing good for others, of good thoughts, and having a good likeness to things; wise 

<column-break/>

in the judgments of astronomy and condemnations.

¶ He wishes to speak of the signs in that which he said generally, which are of a "participable" nature; because of this nature which they have, they signify a specific thing, and each of them has its own specific signification pertaining to itself. And because these movable signs signify the beginnings of the four seasons, it is fitting that they signify, according to this nature, things concerning the people, and the good fame of cities and towns, and finding things accepted from God which were conquered in the law. And it is fitting that they signify, according to their nature, subtlety and all other things that Ptolemy related, because they are always of greater strength than those which follow them.

¶ **Common signs** <note>Also called "Mutable signs": Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces. They represent the transitions between seasons and are associated with flexibility or instability.</note> make the soul multiform, easily changed, difficult to know, agile, unstable, deceitful, desiring many things, a lover of music, talkative, of perceptive intellect, and prone to regret.

¶ Indeed, the signs of "two bodies" <note>Another name for the Common/Mutable signs, often depicted as dual figures (like the Twins or the Fish).</note> make souls of diverse character: light in changing themselves, but it is heavy for men to understand those who wish to be foolish and light to move themselves. In two ways, they are lovers of many and diverse things, covetous, lovers of music, lazy, slow, and quickly repenting of that which they do.

¶ Because the signs of two bodies signify according to this particular nature which they have, it is more fitting that such a signification in the soul similarly agrees with this nature, as Ptolemy related.

¶ **Fixed signs** <note>Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius. They represent the middle of seasons and are associated with stability and persistence.</note> indeed make the soul upright, unfailing, immobile, of good genius, quiet, intelligent, patient in labor, tolerant, rigid, restraining pleasures, envious in will, effective, imitative, loving, contentious, transgressive, and unchangeable.

¶ And fixed signs make souls just, who do not deceive themselves, of a fixed and firm nature, of great maturity, intelligible, patient, lovers of labors, hard and strong against exhaustion, abstaining from vices, and restraining the appetite for anger; they are demonstrators of good counsel, yet can be treacherous, sweet in disobedience, and not easily moved for a small matter.

¶ For the common quality which the signs have is to create the durability of the four seasons and to rest in their natures that are fitting to them; and therefore, the fixed signs signify in every matter a signification according to their nature. Thus it is expedient that they signify in the states of the soul things according to their nature, and those are what Ptolemy said.

¶ From the qualities of the stars and their figures: that which shall be **oriental** <note>Rising in the East before the Sun.</note> and ascending—specifically that which shall be in its own proper face <note>A "face" or "decan" is a 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign.</note>—will make the soul free, suitable, and confident in its own counsel: rigid, of sharp wit, generous, and open.

¶ And the state of the oriental planets and their figures: I say that those which are oriental and ascending—especially those which shall be in an aspect of a form pertaining to themselves—make the soul free, simple, separate with its own counsel, strong, subtle, sharp, and not easily changed.

¶ After he related the common natures of the signs and planets which they have through their position in comparison to the world, he said that every planet which is oriental and ascending—and especially if it is in an aspect of its own face (and you know all this from the gloss of the first part)—if such a planet is the dispositor of the soul's work, it signifies that the soul will be free, simple, separate with its own counsel, strong, subtle, and sharp. It will by no means retreat, because such a state of the planets signifies the great power which planets have when they are in a good state; and therefore it is fitting for them to have such a signification.

¶ Regarding the **matutinal** <note>Appearing in the morning.</note> stations of the stars, and when they are in the **mid-heaven** <note>The highest point in the sky at the time of birth, associated with public life and career.</note>: they make souls thoughtful, firm, of good memory, quiet...

# Treatise

...intelligent, magnanimous, unshakeable, unchanging, without deceit, knowledgeable, industrious, investigative, and skilled in true sciences.

¶ And the station of planets that are morning risers <note>original: "matutinales," planets that rise before the Sun</note> or those located in the Midheaven <note>original: "medio celi," the 10th house, representing the highest point in the sky</note> create thoughts that are great, strong, unchanging, mindful, serious, intelligent, courageous, fixed, without fraud, possessing good discretion, active and inquisitive, noble, and of certain wisdom.

¶ Regarding what is said about the "station of morning planets," he means the **first station** <note>The point where a planet appears to stop before turning retrograde</note>. We have already shown in the preceding text that planets in this state are at their full strength; therefore, it is fitting that they signify things in the soul that accord with such power. And as for what he said regarding the "Midheaven," he means the **10th house**; for when a planet is in this narrow point, it is at its most complete strength compared to all other twelve houses, as we have demonstrated. Thus, it is appropriate for planets to have the same status in this location as they do when they are at their full strength. When a planet is in either of these two places or states—that is, in its first station or in the Midheaven—it will signify in the soul that which **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundation of Western astrology</note> described.

¶ Furthermore, the risings of stars at the beginning of the night and their settings make souls light, agile, weak, unable to endure labor, easily influenced, unfortunate, small-minded, efficient yet petty, hesitant, weary, slow, changeable, and solitary.

¶ Planets also rising at the start of the night and those in the East <note>oriental</note> make souls light, foolish, weak, unable to suffer labor, easily changed, base, unhappy, doubting, and shifting between worthlessness and an un-tiring weightiness of hard movement.

¶ When planets rise at midnight, they are then in opposition to the **Sun**. Similarly, those that set at the end of the night see their power diminished every day; thus, it is fitting that in such a state they signify matters pertaining to themselves within the states of the soul.

¶ The stations of certain evening stars <note>original: "vespertinali," planets rising after the Sun</note> and when they are in the Midheaven beneath the earth <note>the 4th house, or Imum Coeli</note>, as well as the evening setting of **Venus** and **Mercury** during the day, and their morning settings when it is night, will render the soul clean, pure, and sensible, yet with an inconvenient memory. It makes the soul prayerful, no lover of labor, an investigator of secret things, and a seeker of the occult—such as the hidden arts of <term>necromancy: here used to mean the study of spirits or hidden forces</term>, the highest matters, the science of instruments and machines, wondrous works, and the judgments of the stars <note>astrology</note>. It also makes the soul prophetic, skilled in the arts of augmentation, an interpreter of dreams, and similar things.

¶ And the station of evening planets and those in the angle beneath the earth—such as when **Venus** and **Mercury** are evening risers and occidental <note>setting in the west</note> and it is a day birth, or if they are morning risers and occidental and it is a night birth—these will produce in the soul great subtlety, good sense, and good intellect. However, such a person will not have a good memory, nor be a hard worker, nor love to be fatigued. Nonetheless, they will be an inquirer into complex and secret things and hidden matters, such as necromancy and the remaining arts of knowledge, like the making of instruments, the creation of strange devices, and <term>prestidigitation: "trasgettamẽta," or sleight of hand and illusions</term>, and the judgments of astrology. They will love philosophy and 

<column-break/>

auguries <note>divination by the flight of birds or omens</note> and will be an interpreter of dreams and similar things.

¶ The station of evening planets is the **second station**; it is manifest that their powers in this state are mediocre, between strength and weakness. When a planet is in the Midheaven beneath the earth, it is in the angle of the **4th house**. It is clear that their powers in this state are also mediocre. Because they are in the angle of the 4th, they have a known power, but because they do not cross the earth <note>remain invisible</note>, they have a weakness. Thus it is fitting that both of these things signify things in the soul that accord with such a state. And because **Venus** and **Mercury** do not have an opposition with the Sun, their state is added here. He described a state between weakness and strength so that through this we might understand other states. He said that when Venus and Mercury are occidental and evening stars during the day—meaning when they are occidental to the Sun in daytime births—they are mediocre. And he said when they are oriental <note>rising in the east</note> at night—meaning in nocturnal births—they are also mediocre. This agrees with the station of the superior planets. This teaching shows that when Venus and Mercury are occidental in nocturnal births, they are heavy <note>slow or influential</note>, and similarly in day births if they are oriental. Then they will signal the things described regarding the superior planets when they are in their first stations. You should take this as an example for other matters. After completing this, he gave the reason why it must be understood that planets which are mediocre between strength and weakness signify things in the soul that accord with such a nature: the soul is subtle and has good sense, yet is of a restful nature, neither a worker nor a lover of labor. And because this is so, the person will be a seeker of complex things and a requester of secrets, such as necromancy and higher matters, the making of crafts, and instruments for estates or manors, strange things and miracles. They will seek the judgments of an astrologer through philosophy; they will also love auguries, the interpretation of dreams, and the like. And of these states which **Ptolemy** described, some result from the quality of the zodiac signs, which provide strength or weakness—such as sharpness of sense, which comes with modest memory and laziness. These exist because these indicators are covered under the rays of the Sun, or move as if hidden under them; thus they seek hidden and secret things, as Ptolemy described. This is the interpretation of his words. Furthermore, we understand that he gave us four planetary states: the first is what they signify when they are oriental and ascending; second is what they signify when they are heavy in their second station (to know what they signify when weak); third is what they signify when opposite the Sun (to know what they signify when under the Sun's rays); and fourth is what they signify when they are mediocre between strength and weakness. Thus, when we find a planet that is not in one of these four configurations, we mix its state according to its operation between the two ends the planet falls between, and we give the interpretation to the side it most leans toward. Thus you shall understand and thus you shall judge.

¶ Likewise, the stars that rule the disposition of souls make the properties of the soul fit and clear when they are in their own places and in their own <term>bounds: "baiz" or "termini," specific degrees of a sign ruled by a planet</term>, as we explained in the premises. Their effects can be hindered by nothing, and each part will remain solo and prosper. This is especially true when the same stars are rulers of two places—that is, if they are associated with the configuration of **Mercury** and have frequent aspects with **the Moon**. If it is not as described, or if they are in places not their own, their own natures will make the qualities of the soul hidden and imperfect rather than open, and they will not prosper.

¶ Similarly, if with these planets the governors of the soul's actions are in their own bounds pertaining to them and...

# Third

...accord themselves with them, as we have shown above: they will make the soul <note>original: "animam"</note> strong; nor will anything disturb it from completing what it desires. It will happen that such a person rules both themselves and the matters they begin. This is especially true if the two governing planets are both in a place belonging to one of them, and if they share a connection with the location of Mercury, wherever that may be, and if it separates from the Moon as it applies to itself. For if this is not the case, as we have said, or if they are in places not pertaining to their own proper natures, they will make souls that are not strong, but fearful and hidden—souls that do not complete what they start nor set it before themselves.

¶ In this statement, he shows us two contrary things so that we may understand the two middle states between them. For it is manifest that just as we know one contrary, we can know the other through its opposite. This contrariety of which he speaks in this place is one where it is more complete for a planet to be in its own place pertaining to it—such as its **House** <note>The zodiac sign where a planet is most "at home"</note> or **Exaltation** <note>A sign where a planet's influence is heightened</note>, or within its **Term** <note>A specific degree-range within a sign ruled by a planet</note>. Or it may be in its **Hayz** <note>original: "baiz"; an astrological dignity where a planet is in a sign and sector matching its own gender and sect (day or night)</note> pertaining to it; and this occurs when a diurnal planet is in a diurnal place, or a nocturnal one in a nocturnal place. Generally, it is when it is in a place of "accordance" with it, even if it is not its House, Exaltation, Triplicity, or Term. This is one of the two contraries which gives strength to the planet, through which the states of the soul possess qualities pertaining to that strength: that the person will be strong in their actions, rule themselves by their own counsel, and complete whatever they begin. The other contrary is when the planet is in such a place or Hayz that does not pertain to it. This gives the planet weakness, causing the states of the soul to have corresponding qualities, such as showing no good, but rather diminution and worthlessness in all their ways, never completing what they begin. Everything else that **Ptolemy** <note>The 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer</note> says explains this fully to us.

¶ The natures of the stars ruling over them, or those elevated above those human souls, produce rigid works that are harmful to their subjects. These are like unjust and wicked men, to whom these things happen because of a likeness to the **Infortunes** <note>original: "infortunatarum"; the planets Mars and Saturn, traditionally associated with hardship</note>. When these rule, they make the movements of those souls quick to impede others, so that nothing will stop them and no difficulty will stand in their way. However, when these souls are ruled by stars that are in a Hayz contrary to them, they make them of weak reputation, nor will they prosper, and they shall suffer punishments from them.

¶ And the natures of planets exalted above them make the actions of souls strong and harmful toward those in power, such as the proud and the wicked in whom this occurs through the accordance of the malefic planets. If they are governors, they make the people agile and light in doing evil without any disturbance or labor in the task; and they do this without restraint. And when another planet, being in its contrary Hayz, rules over these planets, it will cause the person's soul to be despised and unfortunate, and they will suffer penalties and disgrace.

¶ He means to say that the planets governing in the administration of Mercury and the Moon, if they are in their Fortunes <note>Venus or Jupiter</note> and exalted above them, and are powerful, they will signify that the native will be proud, burdened by evil, and agile in doing harm to others. If, however, in doing so they are faithful in their fortunes, they will signify otherwise: that the native will be proud and wicked. If those which are elevated above them are in accord, yet are in a contrary Hayz to one another, it will make the native wretched and unfortunate because of the evil that makes them a receiver of harm.

¶ These are not like just and equitable men, to whom these things happen by a likeness of the Fortunes. When nothing is elevated above them, they will rejoice in doing good to others and will be commended for it. No harm shall come to them from it; rather, their own goodness

<column-break/>

will be the occasion of their profit. But when stars of a contrary nature are elevated above them, the opposite of what was said will happen: through their softness and their love for people—even in praise and piety—they will be despised by men, blamed, and have violence done to them.

¶ Just as the good and just, who exist through the accordance of the fortunate planets, if no other planet is elevated above them, they will be happy and joyful for the good they do for others. They will consider themselves fortunate and praised for it, and will have a will toward it. No evil will come to them from it, but a great abundance of good and profit. Likewise, if another contrary planet rules over these planets, the opposite will happen to them despite their gentleness and piety: through their love and the giving of gifts, many will do them great injury.

¶ The births of the good and just are those where the fortunate planets rule over Mercury and the Moon, provided no other planet is exalted over them. For such births signify that the native will be happy and content with the good they do for others, and will be praised for it without regret. By doing good, great profit and wealth will come to them. However, if the fortunate planets rule Mercury and the Moon and exalt themselves over them, yet are in a Hayz contrary to them, they will make the native gentle but despised because of the love they have for people and the good they do, and they will be dishonored. Similarly, many will rise against them to flee them, nor will they be able to defend themselves. Thus, Ptolemy taught us in this saying and the preceding one how we can know if a native will be good or evil, and what dignity they will have in any of their states—and if you look well into his words and this gloss, you will understand more than we have said.

¶ This, therefore, is the general way in which the qualities of sensitive and rational souls are prognosticated. We shall now teach by a general discourse the properties of particular things which occur from the natures of the stars according to their dominion, until we reach the "mixture" which is understood by the general path.

¶ This is the general and common rule by which we can know the part of man that concerns morals and virtues. We wish to enumerate generally the particular states arising from the natures of the planets according to their increases, until we apply them to the composition that appears according to the general rule.

¶ The general rule of which he speaks refers to the rule composed of the rules he showed us regarding the state of the soul. When he says "the part of man that is in virtues and morals," he refers to the **irrational soul** <note>The part of the soul governing emotions and instincts, as opposed to the rational intellect</note>; for spiritual passions are in this part alone, as **Aristotle** taught in the *Ethics*. And when he said "we wish to say the particular states that happen because of the natures of the planets generally according to their lordships," he means he will relate what the nature of each planet does when it is not acting alone, but in participation with another planet. We should keep this ready so we may take from it what is necessary, and through it, join the significations of the general rules and roots taught previously. By this, we may know how to add the state pertaining to any native. It is vital that you keep this ready in your memory for this and other such chapters.

¶ When **Saturn** alone, therefore, rules the disposition of the souls and is the lord of the Moon and Mercury: if he is well-placed in respect to the world and the **Angles** <note>The four most powerful points in a chart: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note>, the native will love just men. He will be rigid and of deep counsel; he will remain firm in his own counsel. He will be industrious and a debater. Sometimes he will decline slightly from the truth; he will be wealthy and a seeker of power <note>original: "regni"</note>, versatile, a hoarder of treasure, solitary <note>original: "subterraneus," literally 'underground' or 'hidden'</note>, and envious.
