# Treatise

¶ And if **Saturn** alone should be the governor of the state of the soul <note>original: "statu anime"</note>, and is the lord of the places of **Mercury** and the **Moon** in a good condition relative to the world and relative to the **angles** <note>The "angles" are the four most powerful points in an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note>, he will make the native a lover of the land, one of great and firm counsel, hardworking, a seeker of secret and divine things, a lover of kings, a consumer of others' wealth, and a speaker of treasures.

¶ The "good condition" that planets have relative to the world occurs when a planet is in its own **house**, **exaltation**, **triplicity**, **term**, or **face** <note>These are the "Five Essential Dignities," representing various levels of a planet's strength and comfort within specific signs and degrees of the zodiac.</note> belonging to it. This "state" also means the planet is powerful, such as when it rises in the morning, moves in a direct path, or moves quickly. The "good condition" it has relative to the angles occurs when the planet is located in an angle, or in its **hayz** <note>original: "baiz"; a condition where a planet is in a sign and sector of the sky that matches its own gender and nature.</note>, or in the houses following the angles. This must be arranged according to the ranking of the strengths of the twelve houses, which we have already made clear many times. It is manifest that when Mercury is in this manner, he will be in the best state he can have. For this reason, it is fitting that in matters of the soul, what pertains to this should be as **Ptolemy** said: so that if other rules he mentioned before signify other things, he will help them with these matters. You shall take these things which you find in agreement and judge according to them, and you shall judge according to that which you find to have the greater significance; and so you shall do with every planet. It is necessary for you to understand this; do not ask me to tell you this again for the other planets.

¶ But if Saturn exists in the contrary of what we have said—that is, in an inconvenient state—the native will be unclean, vile, small-minded, ignorant, stubborn in his own counsel, envious, timid, a recluse, deceitful in words, a lover of secrecy and mourning, shameless, unfortunate, a lover of labor but loving no one, a deceiver of friends, never rejoicing, and malevolent toward the good.

¶ And if Saturn’s condition is perverse and not in a good state, he will make the native foul, vile, small-hearted, without discretion, of poor understanding, ruling himself by his own whim, envious, a vile solitary person, separated from everyone, a liar, a deceiver, and false. In secret, he will love **sorcery** <note>original: "endichiertaz"; likely a corruption of a Greek or Arabic term for magical arts or incantations</note> and shameless lamentations; he will be unfortunate, a lover of labor, having no love for anyone, horrible and false to his friends, always sad and grieving, and he will abhor good people.

¶ Planets that are "turned away" from what we have said are in a "bad state." This means having a position relative to the world that is opposite their own house or exaltation, or being in the dignities of planets that disagree with them, or being an "evening star," or **retrograde** <note>appearing to move backward in the sky</note>, or slow in motion, and similar things. A bad state relative to the angles is being in the 12th or 6th house, not being in its "hayz," and things like this. Here, Ptolemy teaches us two contrary facts about Saturn so that you may gather what lies between these two extremes. If you find a planet between these two states, look at which state it is closer to, and give that state more power than the other. Subtract from its effects as much as the other part pulls away, and retain what you understand. Afterward, add this to the general rules of this reasoning, and you shall judge according to the prevailing significance and that which is most joined to a single thing. Then you will judge correctly and will not err; and according to this, you shall do for every other planet.

¶ And if Saturn is like **Jupiter** according to what we said before, and its quality is commendable, the native will be just, will honor elders, and will be of sound counsel, a helper to the kingdom, knowledgeable, magnanimous, a lover of friends, quiet, intelligent, patient, and a philosopher.

<column-break/>

¶ And if it is in accord with Jupiter in the way we describe and in a good state, it will make the native free, a respecter of good people, a protector of the elderly, of good counsel, a helper in others' affairs, always a known associate of kings, of great eloquence, a lover of his parents, mild, intelligent, long-suffering, and wise.

¶ And if it has concord with Jupiter such that both he and Jupiter are the governors, or if **Venus** is present and another planet beholds it with a good **aspect** <note>An "aspect" is a specific geometric angle between planets that determines how their energies interact.</note>, or if one of them is the governor and the other is the "governor of that governor" (meaning he is the lord of his house, exaltation, triplicity, or similar), this is the reason for concord. It is necessary that you understand this applies to the other planets as well. And when it says "if it be in another state," it is necessary to understand that there is a good kind of concord between them, such as a good aspect or a "reception" between them, and that each of them is in a good manner relative to the world and the angles.

¶ But if the quality of this star is contrary to the things aforesaid, the native will be ignorant of doing good, senseless, dealing in diabolical and perverse things, dwelling in oratories <note>perhaps implying a false or superstitious piety</note>, predicting the future, abhorring his own children, having no friends, dwelling in crypts and caves, not associating with men, nor will anyone trust him. He will be foolish, evil, weak, not loving honor, full of regret, poorly received, of bad choices, and a sufferer of labor.

¶ And if the state of these planets is the reverse of what we said, it will make the native one who does not practice good, ill-mannered, of evil sense, meddling in diabolical and evil things; he will love to always stand in oratories, a diviner, a slanderer of his own children, having no friend, separated from all, unfaithful, seeking evil for men, of an evil heart, weak, tedious, not loving honor, a worker of poor reception, content with every evil thing, a vile passer-by of things, and a scatterer.

¶ This means that there is a "bad concord" between Saturn and Jupiter when they are the governors of the soul's disposition. This happens when they are both in an unfriendly aspect, or in a bad position relative to the world or the angles, or when one of them is the governor of the soul in such a state, and the other looks upon it with the same aspect in another such state, as shown in the commentary for the present and other preceding glosses. You shall know that when you find such a constellation, the native will be as Ptolemy said. It is fitting, as we said, that we add these significations to the first rules so that we may know the proper state of the native. Ptolemy taught us the good states of concord between Saturn and Jupiter and the bad concords likewise; so that when you find a mediocre concord between them, you shall judge accordingly and compose a judgment of the things he said in those two states. With this, you will be able to understand this entire saying of Ptolemy and what he says regarding the other planets.

¶ If Saturn is also like **Mars**, and he himself is of good quality and praiseworthy, the native will be one who does not recognize <note>perhaps meaning ungrateful or unobservant</note>, very hardworking, wretched and weak, harmful, attempting things with great fear. He will be a heavy brawler, not pious, considering everything trivial, immoderate, warlike, putting his soul in fear, loving disturbances, a traitor, a disturber of others, of the worst envy. By some specific event, his soul will be changed; he will make men labor, he will overpower others, a transgressor, hating kings and princes, loving hypocrisy and victory, envious, of evil depth, difficult to tolerate, full of rusticity, intolerable, a boaster of himself, unjust, harming men, vilifying them, and hating them. He will not be moved or altered, and will meddle in many things...

### Third Book

...he will easily withdraw from them: he will be an artisan and a student in general; he will also prosper.

And if he should be in concord with **Mars** and in a good state <note>As established previously, a "good state" refers to a planet being in a strong zodiacal position, such as its own house or exaltation.</note>, he will make the native <term>native: the person born under these stars</term> of bad reputation, a hard worker, and useful in all things; sometimes bold, and sometimes remiss in bad company; without piety, a dishonorer of good people, or a harsh brawler. He will put himself in great danger, being a lover of strife, false, unfaithful, a killer, and one who holds onto anger badly. He will be talkative, unstable in deeds and words, a hater of good things, a lover of flattery and pride, and of bad will. He will be strong in enduring, yet austere and cruel to men, a doer of evil, quarrelsome, a wicked violator, a robber, and a dishonorer. He does not change himself, nor does he turn away from evil; he is warlike, sharp, a completer of all these evils, and yet fortunate in them.

Observe the nature of the two <term>malefics: Saturn and Mars, traditionally considered the "unfortunate" planets</term> <note>original: "duaz infortunaz"</note> when they participate together in the governance of the soul and there is concord between them while in a good state; or when one of them is the governor and the other is in concord with him, both being in a good state, notice how they make the souls of the native prone to these things that incline greatly toward evil.

But if this star <note>Saturn</note> should be in the opposite of the aforesaid state, he will make the native a plunderer, a highwayman, wretched, of bad quality and bad profit. He will not fear God, nor will he love anyone; he will be a blasphemer, a disturber, a thief, a deceiver, a traitor, a killer, evilly incestuous, impious, a murderer, a **necromancer** <note>original: "nigromanticus"; one who practices magic involving the spirits of the dead</note>, a plunderer of houses of prayer, a fornicator, a violator of tombs, and generally he will be wicked in all things.

And if the planet should be turned away from what we have described, the native will be a robber, a layer of snares for all in every complete manner, of a bad life, and bad profit. He will not fear God, nor will he have love for Him; he will be a dishonorer, a bringer of shame, a killer, a trickster, a necromancer, a robber of oratories and altars, given to wicked lust, a stripper of the dead, a traitor, and wicked in all his other deeds.

These facts signify the nature of the two malefics existing in a bad state; they are modes of many pure malices and bad vices. And know that the native will possess these traits when you join this with the other rules that **Ptolemy** stated regarding the state of the soul.

If **Saturn** is joined with **Venus**, and is of a good quality, the native will abhor women and love the elderly and those who are reasonable. He will be poorly received by others and will not seek honors. He will abhor beautiful things and will be envious and of bad company. He will separate himself from men and trust in his own counsel; he will fear God and be zealous in his advice, though of a "bad law" <note>This likely refers to being an adherent of a marginalized or condemned belief system</note>. He will love hidden things, be a diviner, and think upon divine matters. He will be peaceful, modest, a lover of knowledge, faithful, abstinent, deliberate, keeping himself from the impure, yet tedious and jealous regarding women. 

However, when this star is in the opposite of the aforesaid, the native will be a fornicator and impure; he will commit foul acts among his own people, be a foul adulterer, and allow himself to be deceived by women—especially by his own kinswomen. He will be very wretched, weak in every way, and will be constantly occupied with sexual acts without intermission. He will abhor beauty, be a curser, proud, and secretive of his mind. He will be vile, criminal in foul intercourse, and will subject himself to lust against nature. He will desire to do this with the aged and with vile people, and against the law; he will even desire to do so with beasts—

<column-break/>

—he will not fear God; he will scorn secrets, houses of prayer, and chastity; he will scorn all things. He will be a necromancer and will meddle in everything.

And if he is in concord with **Venus** and in a good state: the native will be an abhorrer of women, a lover of the old and of hermits, and poorly received. He will not love honor nor beautiful things; he will be envious, of bad company, and will separate himself from everyone. He will rule himself by his own counsel, read secrets, know the laws, and be a lover of secrets and a diviner. He will love God and His law, and be a lover of the things of God. He will be chaste, a lover of journeys, and prompt in lawsuits and wars, putting himself forward for the defense of the law. He will be a faithful lover of philosophy, law-abiding, of great abstinence and thoughtfulness; he will guard himself from a bad reputation, though he will be sad and jealous of women. 

And if the planet is turned away from what we have described: the native will be a fornicator of great foulness, without discretion or purity in his lust. He will be deceived because of women, especially by those of his own blood. He will be of bad reputation, dishonored in all his affairs, and a follower of luxury. He will hate every good deed, be of bad reasoning, a drunkard, and a lover of secrets and lusts against nature with those older than himself, and with vile people outside his law, and with beasts. He will not fear God, will be a despiser of oratories and of those religious in the law; he will love necromancy and similar things.

If you are mindful of all the glosses we have expressed clearly before this, you will be able to understand this saying; but if you have forgotten them, look back at what we have glossed: for you have one virtue combined with another of those things we have told you many times.

If **Saturn** is associated with **Mercury** and is of a good quality: the native will be a king and an establisher and investigator of laws. He will love the science of medicine and hidden things; he will be a deliberate thinker of secrets and will do wonders. He will be a sophist, nimble, an organizer, of good genius, of an eager soul, a sharp investigator, and a lover of intelligence and its works; and it will go well for him. 

But if this star is in the opposite: the native will be envious and of a turbulent soul, hardworking, and hateful. He will have trouble with his relatives, be a lover of labor, and sad. He will be disturbed at night, a bringer of omens, a deceiver in his business, and will not associate with men. He will be a thief, knowledgeable in evil, a necromancer, an enchanter, shifty, and will not prosper.

And if he is in concord with **Mercury** regarding the state of the soul and exists in a good state: the native will be an inquirer and seeker of chronicles, histories, and laws. He will love natural science <note>original: "physicaz"</note> and be a keeper of secrets, studying the secret miracles of the saints. He will be a sophist, agile among his people, a governor of the people, intelligent, of great inquiry, and experienced. He will love all that is good and be fortunate in all these things. 

And if the planet is the reverse of what we have said: the native will be a keeper of anger, of bad will, and always sad. He will be a laborer, will abhor his parents, and love hard work. He will be sorrowful and have great fear at night. He will be a layer of snares and a tempter for the sake of killing, a deceiver, and will have no company with men. He will be a thief, a poisoner, a necromancer, and a maker of magical characters and strange things ingeniously; and with all this, he will be unfortunate.

# Treatise

¶ This is similarly said of all things in the present disclosure: we wish to reveal one thing through which we may declare what we said before: you should know that when **Mercury** governs the activity of the soul while in a bad state, and **Saturn** is elevated above it, it signifies that the native <term>native: the person born under these specific planetary alignments</term> will be a traitor and a thief; and along with all this, he will be without fortune: in this, he will receive punishment for his deeds. You may understand the other planets in this same manner.

¶ **Jupiter**, however, when he stands alone as the lord of the soul’s disposition.

¶ And if **Jupiter** should be the sole governor of the soul.

¶ **Jupiter** alone will be the governor of the soul when he is the sole lord of the places of **Mercury** and the **Moon** without any participation from another planet.

¶ If he is of a laudable quality <note>A "laudable quality" or "good state" means the planet is positioned strongly in the zodiac, such as in its own house (Sagittarius or Pisces for Jupiter) or its exaltation.</note>, the native will be magnanimous, generous, just, modest, cheerful, a lover of people and beauty, liberal, fair, a man of great thought, gentle, excellent, and pious in his works; he will do good to men and be an amiable leader.

¶ If he is in a good state, the native will be of a great heart, free, clear, honest, delightful, a lover of good men, of good knowledge, merciful, and he will value himself highly; he will possess good abstinence, be spiritual, and be recognized by all for his good deeds toward good men; he will cause himself to be loved by everyone through his good understanding and good governance.

¶ Observe how a planet of fortune, when it is powerful, exhibits all the good virtues.

¶ Or if he should be in the opposite of all the aforesaid, the quality of the native's soul will be similar to those mentioned, except it will be weaker in these things, and more hidden, without a good intellect. For in the place of the magnanimous man, he will be a spendthrift; in the place of the just man, he will serve the devil <note>original: "seruiet diabolo." In this context, it refers to extreme vice or malevolent behavior.</note> or be of bad reputation. Instead of being modest, he will be a coward, and instead of being gentle, he will be proud. He will also, instead of loving men of good quality, and instead of loving beautiful things, love base pleasures; and instead of great thought, he will be stubborn; and instead of freedom, he will be ignorant and other such things.

¶ And if he should be perverted from that which was said, he will be similar in the soul of the native to the states we predicted; yet they will be much more vile without discretion. Thus, in the place where he should have a great heart, he will be a devastator. And in the place where he should be clear and just, he will be a servant of the devil, or of false belief or an evil sect. And in the place of modesty, he will be base; and in the place of the chaste and those of good abstinence, he will be a fool. In the place of a lover of men, he will be of "good will" <note>Here used ironically to mean someone who is overly compliant or weak-willed</note>; and in the place of loving beautiful things, he will love vices without restraint and similar things.

¶ **Ptolemy** <note>original: "Ptol." Referring to Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century author of the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text for this treatise.</note> did not care to give us rules in every single place to match these, because fortune always grants what agrees with its own nature. If it is in a good state, it will draw forth good virtues; if it is in the reverse, it will give in the place of good virtues things that resemble them but are not, as Ptolemy reported in this place. He said that in place of having a great heart, he will be a devastator, and in place of being clear and just, he will be a follower of idolatry or great heresy, like the religious of the heretics and those holding a bad law. And in place of a lover of men, he will be of "good will"—meaning he wishes to appear so suave and gentle that he never becomes angry—and all the other things he said.

¶ Or if **Jupiter** is in concord with **Mars** and exists in a laudable quality, the native will be truthful, an advocate, warlike, an organizer, very strong in action, and will humble himself to no one; he will also be a man of armies and great works, desiring to be avenged and to completely overcome; he will make himself singular. He will be an inventor of things and will not be ignorant of the truth of a matter; he will be provident and magnanimous, and he will prosper. He will also seek to be honored; he will be quick to anger but a knower of things,

<column-break/>

and he will command many things to many people. But if this same star stands in the contrary of the aforesaid, the native will be a blasphemer, a disturber of words, impudent, a concealer of nothing, a despiser of others, a hypocrite, a physician <note>The term "medicus" here may imply a charlatan or someone who manipulates nature improperly, given the negative context.</note>, proud, disobedient, a plunderer, easily changed, quickly repenting, unstable, vile, unfaithful, of no knowledge or counsel, senseless, a robber, a loser of his friends, and generally he will be of various and mutable qualities.

¶ And if he should be in concord with **Mars** regarding the soul and be in a good state, he will make the native bad <note>This "bad" seems to refer to a rugged, aggressive nature rather than pure evil, as the following traits suggest power</note>, unhidden, a striver, a wrangler, of great cunning, a governor of others, disobedient, sharp, a director of beasts and cavalry, of great prevalence; he will want to avenge himself, a doer of slights to many; he will always love to win and be great over others, an inventor of things, a man and a strengthener in all his deeds, free, a giver, always a victor, of a great heart, a lover of good things, angry, a commander and a forbidder. And if the planet should be the reverse of what we said: the native will be of the dishonest, very cruel, he will not spare anyone, a striver; he will always be flattering with his followers, disobedient, a fool, a thief, light and mobile; he will quickly repent, nor will he be stable in any matter; simple, unfaithful, without discretion and counsel; he will quickly speak evil, saying what he wishes to say like a senseless man; and generally he is of various manners.

¶ Now he has taught us in what has passed about the two contrary concordances between **Saturn** and **Jupiter**; and we have commented on it in such a way that it is not necessary to return to the other planets another time. Therefore, we do not have to comment in this place on these two contrary concordances that occur between **Jupiter** and **Mars**. For the words of **Ptolemy** in this place are manifest and declared if you are mindful of the past commentaries. It is useful in this place, if you find that **Jupiter** is the governor and has concorded with **Saturn** and **Mars**, that you join one significance with the other; and after you join them all, you should know them according to the rules he spoke of in the "Chapter of the Fathers" <note>Likely referring to a specific chapter in an Arabic or Latin astrological source text</note>, and you will join all the rules and judge by them.

¶ Or if he is like **Venus** and exists in a laudable quality, the native will be simple, loving neatness and mastery, and an investigator of things; he will be a singer, seeking jests and feasts; he will be of a good quality of soul, pious, of a healthy heart; he will love God and serve Him; he will also desire to be hardworking for the love of God. He will be sensible and loving, humble, of a splendid soul, gracious, and munificent; he will by no means abhor the reading of books. He will be a king of knowledge, and temperate regarding the legitimate acts of Venus <note>Meaning he is moderate in his romantic and sexual life.</note>; he will also love his kinsmen, and desire the beauty of honor and a name; generally, indeed, he will be just and upright. But if this star should be in the contrary of the aforesaid, the native will be unlaborious, of a delicate life, of a feminine soul, a dancer; his anger will be like the anger of women; he will be a spendthrift, senseless in the affairs of women, a suitor, lustful, delinquent, a lover of hair ornaments; he will extol himself, and he will rejoice in the ignorance of his own losses; he will be easily hindered by the shame of men; he will be self-composed, of a feminine sense; he will prevail in the love of ecclesiastical things and will precede in these matters. He will be a concealer, and faithful, ignorant of all evils, and subject to all. In his works, he will be commendable and liberal in all that he does.

# Book Three 72

And if this planet <note>Referring to Jupiter, the primary subject of the preceding section.</note> should be in concord with **Venus** and in a good state: the native will be clear-minded, cheerful, and delightful; he will love to keep himself clean and well-presented; he will delight in the ministry of singing and seek out all kinds of musical songs and instruments; he will eat well, be happy and well-disposed toward others, a doer of good, a painter, of a healthy heart, a servant and lover of God; he will love to fight in the service of God <note>This likely refers to the crusading ideal or "spiritual warfare" common in medieval thought.</note>; he will be sensible, a lover of people, of good abstinence, a giver of thanks, and a rewarder of good; he will love to study books and possess good discretion in matters of luxury, being temperate, and a lover of the good fashion of his own property; a lover of health and generally complete in all goodness. 

But if this planet should be in the opposite state <note>original: "de converso" — meaning the planet is poorly placed or in "detriment."</note>: the native will be a lover of bodily games, feminine in his will <note>A medieval stereotype associating "softness" or lack of resolve with femininity.</note>, and in his anger he will be like the anger of women; he will be a wasteful spender and a lover of women; he will be deceptive, greatly lustful, and without abstinence; he will love to be adorned and well-combed; he will be a laugher at vain things, a self-destructor, and a critic of people; they will seek after wanton kisses <note>original: "catugultis," likely a corruption of the Greek-derived "cataglottis," referring to lascivious kissing.</note>; he will have the mind of a woman, be weak of heart, yet will love places of prayer and follow them; he will love secrets and hearing pure things; nevertheless, he will be faithful, without any joyful release <note>possibly meaning he lacks a sense of humor or true relaxation</note>, well-received by others, a companion to all, of good will, and he shall be praised in whatever he does.

¶ Similarly, if there are two contrary states in the agreement of **Jupiter** with **Venus**: whether both or only one of them is the governor of the soul. And it is manifest that if **Saturn** and **Mars** both agree with them, the significance will be a composite and mixed one according to the previous rules and according to how we have commented on them all; and it is necessary that you apply your mind from the beginning of this chapter to this place: for if you apply your mind to what follows, you will judge better.

¶ If **Jupiter** is assimilated to **Mercury** and is of a suitable quality: the native will be diligent in reading books; he will love syllogisms <note>Formal logical arguments used in medieval scholasticism.</note> and will be a geometer skilled in the <term>quadrivium: the four higher subjects of the seven liberal arts (Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy)</term>; a poet and a public speaker, of sharp wit, humble, a giver of good counsel, praiseworthy in his morals, a benefactor, an organizer, of a good quality of soul, generous in assembly, a lover of good reputation; he will perfect things well and suddenly once they are begun; he will be a man of good governance, of good faith, a physician to the king, a lover of God, of a lovable soul; he will love his kinsmen; in his studies <note>original: "doliis" — likely a scribal error for "scholiis" (scholarly works).</note> he will be a good lover of knowledge, and a man of riches. Because if this planet obtains the opposite of the aforesaid: the native will be a fool, a speaker of foolishness, and will frequently fail; he will happen to be a most wandering wretch; he will cling to diviners; he will be impetuous, of a bitter soul; although he is a fool, he will think himself wise; proud, a disturber, he will place himself in the service of another; his movements will be disordered; he will be wordy, possess a good memory, a man of teaching, yet of a rigid appetite.

He will be courtly, learned, a lover of wisdom, honored and prized by everyone. ¶ All this said is manifest through the glosses <note>Explanatory commentaries or annotations.</note> which we previously spoke of in this chapter: and that which is called "contentious" is a loss of sense and the speaking of future things.

# Treatise

...hidden under the rays or beneath the earth, it makes the soul unknowing, sluggish—that is, slow and weak—and weary. And it is clear what he related regarding these states of the Moon: one state is contrary when it is at the limit of its latitude; another when it has no latitude; the remaining two are when it is ascending or appearing above the earth in the east. And its other opposite is when it is in the west or covered beneath the earth. For it is enough that he said "ascending" or "under the rays," and he did not bother to say "above the earth" or "under the earth" or "western," because it is well understood from what he did say. And thus it is fitting that you understand those two contraries are the waxing and waning of its light. And what he says regarding when it is covered by the rays can be understood as what the Moon signifies when it is full of light. And since this is so, it is fitting that when you find the Moon in any of these contrary and opposite states, you should blend the significance of the two chapters.

The **Sun** also assists in some way in these things that have been said: so that with the stars that rule the disposition of the soul, he exists in a similar state. For when he is assimilated with them, if his quality is commended, the qualities of the soul will be more direct and he will be further from deviance, as well as more powerful, generous, faithful, and of a better law <note>In this context, "law" refers to one's moral code or religious adherence</note>.

The **Sun** also gives some measure of help in the matters we have discussed when he is in accord with the planet that governs the soul's formation; so that when he is in accord with it, and that planet is in a good state, the habits of the native will be more direct, harmonious, temperate, noble, and honest, and more free from pride.

He teaches us through this saying that the Sun and Moon then assist when they are in accord with the planet governing the soul. And when the Sun is in accord with a planet existing in a good state, he helps the impulses so that they are temperate and direct, and stripped and distanced from all malice.

When, however, the Sun is contrary in the aforesaid matters and not assimilated to the stars, the qualities of the soul will be worse: the person themselves will be more wretched and lowly, and will remain more under the toil of their own counsel; they will be foolish and of a heavier will, and generally difficult to improve.

And if the matter is the reverse—and the Sun does not have concordance with the planet—the habits of the soul will be viler and weaker, and separated in their will and manner, and harder in their prior will; generally very stubborn and difficult to guide.

He means to say that if the planet is in a bad state and the Sun is in accord with it, it will signify viler habits. And whatever else he showed and taught us through this saying: that if the Sun is in accord with the governing planet, even if it is in such a bad state, the Sun will diminish something of the malice in proportion to that very concordance. And we have already shown that concordance is when there is a good aspect between them—such as a trine <note>An aspect of 120 degrees, considered harmonious</note>—or when there is a "reception" of power between them, or of nature or likeness.

And we wish yet to show you in this place the "summa" <note>A comprehensive summary or totality</note> of the whole rule by which you shall judge the state of the soul in a birth; and you shall know everything about anyone's birth. This is it: when you have arranged the 12 houses and named the planets, look to **Mercury** and to the **Moon**. And if they are in concordant signs, write clearly the habits that those same signs signify. And if they are in solitary, discordant signs, write clearly what each of them signifies, and make a note of the "rational" habits of the sign of Mercury and the "irrational" habits of the sign of the Moon. And you shall look to the planet that is the "dispositor" <note>The planet that rules the sign where another planet is located</note> of each of these two. And if the dispositor of both is one single planet, that alone shall be the one we seek. And if they have individual, different dispositors, write clearly the habits of each mode that pertain to each dispositor. And if you find that one of them is more than one dispositor, you shall take that one of them which has the greater strength and more dignities in its place. And when you know who the dispositor is, look to its position according to the world, and according to the "angles" <note>The four critical points of a chart: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note>, and according to the Sun; and you shall write

<column-break/>

the habits that each of these states signifies, and afterward write the habits which the planet itself signifies when it is in a good state. Similarly, write the habits it signifies if it is in a bad state. And if it is in a median state, look at what that same median state signifies, and what the figures of the planets signify, and what the sign in which it resides signifies. Similarly, write it clearly; and if another planet—or more than one—is in accord with it, write what you find to be in accord with each of them.

And when you have done this, apply your mind to all the notes you have written. If the habits agree as one, write the rational and irrational ones clearly in another place. And afterward, apply your mind to the comparison of one with the other; and what you find to be in accord, you shall take and judge by it. And in those things that do not accord, apply your mind to which ones more closely fit the complexion of the body, and take that, and cast away what does not accord with it. And when you have done this, join what you have accepted in all the things in which the Sun and Moon assist. And whatever results from that will be the habits of the native which you seek. And those which remain behind, the complexion of the body itself will demonstrate to you; yet they will not appear in him, nor will he act through them. And you will be able to work through this rule when you have understood whatever we have said in the other glosses.

### On the impediments of the soul. Chapter 14.

->Haly said:<-

A man of great intellect marvels at what was said. For he spoke in the second chapter of this treatise concerning the facts of the native's body and the pestilences <note>original: "pestilentijs"; here meaning afflictions or chronic ailments of character rather than the plague</note> and infirmities happening in the same. And he spoke in this chapter only of the "pestilences" arising in the soul and did not say "infirmities"; for the infirmities of the soul depart quickly and do not last with the habits, because a man has that with which he may oppose them. And because of this, they are called infirmities which do not oppose the habits, and only "pestilences" are bound with them.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' with floral patterns</image-desc>
Since the descriptions of the soul's own impediments follow the narration of its properties, it is generally fitting for us to know and observe—for the knowledge of these things—the **mercurial** and **lunar** qualities in relation to each other, and their relation to the angles and the "unfortunate" stars <note>Malefic planets, usually Mars and Saturn</note>.

And because the judgment of the soul's own pestilences follows the judgment of its properties, it is fitting that we generally look to the state of **Mercury** and the **Moon** to know this matter: how one stands with the other, and how they stand according to the angles and the planets that cause misfortune.

### The general rule in knowing the soul's pestilences is to look at the state of Mercury and the Moon:
how one stands in respect to the other, and how they exist in respect to the angles and the unfortunate planets.

For when the Moon and Mercury are not joined to each other, or when any of the stars whose qualities cause impediment are elevated above them on the eastern horizon, or surround them, or remain in opposition to them, they will signify that many modes of impediments happen to the qualities of the soul.

And if Mercury and the Moon have no aspect with each other, and there is some discordant unfortunate planet elevated above them in the eastern horizon, or surrounding them, or in opposition to them, many "pestilences" of many kinds will happen in the properties of the soul.

He means to say that when Mercury and the Moon are discordant and there is no aspect between one and the other, it will signify that the two parts of the soul <note>The rational (Mercury) and the irrational/sensitive (Moon)</note> do not accord with one another; and because of this, great "pestilences" will happen to it. Similarly, if they have an aspect with each other, but there are unfortunate planets elevated above them that have no lordship in their governance—either because they are in the angles, or because they surround them, or because they are opposite to them—it will signify that great pestilences will similarly happen to the soul. And when the pestilences happening to the soul are diverse...

### Third

...it is manifest that they will be of many modes, as Ptolemy <note>original: "Pro.", referring to Claudius Ptolemy</note> teaches us the rule through which we can know each of them in what he says.

¶ We will be able to know and explain quite aptly this matter, which is drawn from the aforementioned proper qualities of the stars that are assimilated to their locations. However, in those things which we have permitted in demonstrating the properties of the soul, we have again explained many impediments <note>In this context, "impediments" refers to mental afflictions or disabilities</note> from the weaker impediments of the soul, and we have grasped enough of the works of the unfortunate stars <note>Malefic planets, usually Saturn and Mars</note>. Because of this, he called the signs of the soul's qualities "impediments" because they cannot be restrained; whether they are intensified or diminished regarding a temperate quality, he will name them properly and well.

¶ The knowledge of this thing and its distinction will be from the proper states which we have spoken of regarding the planets <note>original: "p̄tis", likely *planetis*</note> according with their locations. Similarly, we have already spoken of how they transmit the weak plagues of the soul; and we can know their strength and increase from the great works of the many unfortunate stars. Thus, those things which are called "vices" in those who lack abstinence <note>Self-control or moderation</note>—which are "plagues"—will be called true just as they are more or less mediocre.

¶ This is the general rule by which we can know each of these things that become a plague of the soul. For he intends, in what he said regarding the proper states, that they should be understood from the planets according with their locations through the states of the many stars governing the locations of **Mercury** and the **Moon**. And he added for us these states of the unfortunate stars which will belong to their rulers in the locations of **Mercury** and the **Moon**. And he placed in your mind the final thing he said in the chapter before this one: those things which happen through the bad states of the planets. And when we find this, and we wish to know the quantity of the increase of those vices in the way they become "plagues," we can know this through the great powers of the unfortunate stars. After this, however, he divided the plagues into two parts. One consists of behaviors <note>original: "mozes", likely *mores*</note> which are without abstinence and change from one manner of vice to another; such vices are those which are less than mediocre plagues. There are other vices which are more than mediocre, yet mediocre behaviors are virtues enough. And every virtue has two vices at its extremities: one is less than it, the other passes beyond and exceeds it. For example: patience is a virtue, and in a man who suffers dishonor <note>original: "debone-stationē"</note> it is a weakness of the heart and a bad behavior. Similarly, pride is mediocre, and is one evil from the strong ones. Similarly, the virtue of the heart <note>likely courage or concord</note> is less than it, and it is a bad vice where folly passes beyond this, and is a bad behavior. Philosophers demonstrate all of this in the books of Ethics <note>original: "moR", likely *Morum*</note>.

¶ That which is less than or exceeds what is fitting is like an infirmity; and that which entirely exceeds nature sits in the intellectual part of the soul, and in the part receiving the impression, as I shall say.

¶ And concerning that which is of great strength, and exists according to an infirmity or things outside of nature—that is, "adoncado" <note>A term for a seizure, likely related to being "bowed" or "struck down"</note>—this happens in the rational part of the soul and in the part receiving the action. We can know this in the manner we wish to describe.

¶ When he spoke of that which is of great strength, he spoke because of the vices of evil if they are supreme. And what he said according to infirmity, he said because of the vice if it is bad, and in a work that is according to an infirmity of the body. And what he said regarding things outside of nature or "adoncado," he said because it is separated from the nature governing the body. And what he said—that this happens in the rational part of the soul and in that which receives the action—he means to say that with these states, the rational man is impeded by that which is not rational. And for this reason he refers to the part that receives the action, because the rational part does not receive change within itself, as the philosophers have said: for the part receiving change is the animal part, because the work of the rational part is not changed according to its bodily crafts, since it does not receive change in itself as the philosophers show. And we similarly have shown this in the treatises we composed on Nature.

**Epileptics** are most frequently those in whose nativities <note>Birth charts</note> the **Moon** and **Mercury** are neither joined as we said before, nor are they connected with the eastern horizon; and with this, if in diurnal <note>Daytime</note> nativities **Saturn**, or in nocturnal <note>Nighttime</note> nativities **Mars**, is in the "angles" <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses of the zodiac</note>, provided that he himself rules over this quality.

¶ Thus, epileptics for the most part are those who do not have the **Moon** in aspect to **Mercury** in their nativities, as we said, neither one with the other nor either of them with the eastern horizon; and with this, that **Saturn** is in one of the angles by day and **Mars** by night, and that he is the lord of this state.

¶ **Epilepsy** is a convulsion <note>original: "colambziū", likely a corruption of *convulsio* or *clonus*</note> seizing the whole body for a time and is immediately destroyed; and among them is that which seizes at a known time, and that which happens at any hour, and that which seizes for the whole of a man's life, and that which happens after many years of life have passed. And among them is one that can be cured and one that cannot. And I have seen all these manners many times, and they are demonstrated in Medicine <note>original: "phīca", *physica*</note>. But the cause close to this infirmity, according to the opinion of **Aristotle**, is a vapor entering the ventricles of the brain; and according to **Galen**, it is a vapor that raises itself from some limb, just as we have recounted concerning the vapor in a boy that raised itself from a cold stomach to his brain. And there is another manner which is because of infirmity; and all this is demonstrated as being accidents or occurrences in the brain which impede spiritual works. And with this, it is clear that the infirmity which happens through these manners which **Ptolemy** spoke of in this place is that which lasts for a man's whole life, nor can it be cured in any way. For he himself spoke of this manner of epilepsy because when we know what configurations of the planets cause such a thing, and afterward see another thing similar to it, we will know then that another manner of epilepsy will happen; yet what **Ptolemy** recounted in this place is the greatest that can be. And it is fitting that we understand that he knew what would be less than this, such as the configuration he spoke of. That is, <term>Mercury</term> and the <term>Moon</term> if they do not aspect each other—that is, one with the other—nor either of them with the Ascendant; and that **Saturn** is by day in any of the angles, or impedes the place of **Mercury** or the **Moon**, or both in one. And **Mars** similarly, that he is by night in any of the angles, and that he similarly impedes the aforementioned places. For such a configuration as this will make epilepsy always durable, nor can a man be freed from it. And if by chance we find that **Mercury** does not aspect the **Moon**, yet one of them aspects the Ascendant while an unfortunate planet is existing in some angle, such a configuration makes epilepsy, but not so strong as the other aforementioned; and according to this example you shall judge in the other aforementioned manners.

¶ **The Insane**, however, are those in whom this will be contrary to what we have said. That is, the lord of the quality is **Saturn** by night, and **Mars** by day; especially when he is in **Cancer**, **Virgo**, or **Pisces**.

¶ **Fools**, however—hasty and striking men—are those whose state in their nativities is the reverse of what we said with that same state we recounted: namely, that **Saturn** is the lord of the state by night and **Mars** by day; and especially if he is in **Cancer** or in **Virgo** or **Pisces**.

¶ What he said "with that state we mentioned," he means to say that **Mercury** and the **Moon** are discordant without any aspect, nor either of them with the Ascendant. And all the rest that he says is manifest: when you find the state of **Mercury** with the **Moon** in this manner, and it happens with this that **Mars** is in some angle in a diurnal nativity, or **Saturn** in a nocturnal one, you will know that the person born will be a fool for his whole life and will strike men, nor can he be cured. And it is manifest that this is an infirmity of the body and is of many diverse manners. And

# Treatise

Ptolemy <note>original: "Pto.", referring to Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and astrologer</note> gave us a rule for a more serious matter regarding this plague <note>In this context, "plague" refers to a severe affliction of the mind or soul</note>, so that we might add another greater rule to it. For example, let it signify the revolution of any year in which such a thing happens to the person born, or the <term>hyleg</term> <note>The "giver of life," a specific point or planet in a birth chart used to determine longevity and health</note> will signify that an infirmity will happen to him in that year. Afterward, we shall judge how that man will fall ill in that year with such an infirmity that his senses will be altered. What he said specifically regarding Cancer, Virgo, or Pisces is that he means these signs particularly tend to signify such a plague. If it happens that a constellation signifies the aforementioned "folly," then in these signs the plague will be much stronger and worse.

¶ Those who are demon-possessed <note>original: "Demoniaci"</note>, or those who are called <term>aurotafelsi</term> <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek or Arabic medical term referring to those with excess fluid in the head</note>—that is, those in whose heads moisture superabounds—are those in whose births the quality of the <term>fortunes</term> <note>The "benefic" planets, Jupiter and Venus</note> was as we have said. They will be dominated by the Moon, and the Moon itself will be ascending under the Sun's rays, and its lord in conjunction will be Saturn, and in <term>prevention</term> <note>An astrological term for the moment before an aspect or conjunction</note> it will be Mars, especially in Sagittarius and Pisces.

¶ And those who are called demon-possessed are called in Greek <term>hydrocephalos</term> <note>original: "ogro fatali"; likely a transcription error for the Greek term for "water on the brain"</note>. He wishes to speak of those whose moisture prevails in their heads: these are those who have in their births (according to what we have said) the <term>infortunes</term> <note>The "malefic" planets, Saturn and Mars</note> dominating over the Moon, while she is under the Sun's rays, and Saturn dominating over her at the hour of conjunction, and Mars at the hour of opposition, and especially if it is in Sagittarius or Pisces.

¶ The "demon-possessed" are those who are defective in their limbs from the hour they are born because of the moisture prevailing in their heads, such that their brains are so moist that they understand nothing in the world. The rule of the aforementioned figures that makes them such is that neither the Moon nor Mercury aspect the <term>ascendant</term> <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at birth</note>. Furthermore, the one that shall dominate the "infortune" of the Moon as it emerges from under the rays after conjunction should be Saturn, and when it has ascended above the earth after the hours of opposition, it should be Mars. It is sufficient that he said "ascending under the rays of the sun," and there was no need to say "ascending above the earth," because these two states of the Moon are similar to one another. What we are saying confirms his statement: if it is Mars at the hour of opposition, it is manifest that neither at the hour of opposition nor after opposition can the Moon be under the sun's rays. When we say "especially in Sagittarius or Pisces," it means these two signs in such a state have a separate property that other signs do not have, and because of this, they help the "infortunes" in such a matter so that they are stronger.

¶ If both "infortunes" alone prevail in this quality, the infirmities of the soul will be incurable; however, they will not be ferocious and will remain hidden.

¶ And if in this state the "infortunes" prevail in the manner we have described, they will cause these infirmities to happen in the rational part of the soul, such that they are never cured. Yet, if they are such, they will not be foul, nor so manifest.

¶ We have already shown that these infirmities tend toward the brain so that the spiritual virtues are disturbed and cannot perform their works. Since this is so, it is worth as much as Ptolemy says: that these infirmities happen in the rational part of the soul, just as they happen in the "tools" <note>The physical structures of the brain</note> through which the soul performs its own works. What he means in this saying is: he in whom one infortune or both shall dominate without the <term>aspect</term> <note>The geometric relationship between planets</note> of any "fortune" shall never be cured. The "fortunes" have no other significance than this: because by the power they signify this thing, they do not signify it because these infirmities are foul or extracted, for they do not show such a thing unless another constellation is present.

¶ If, however, both "fortunes"—that is, Jupiter and Venus and the like—are present, and both "infortunes" are in a hidden <term>angle</term> <note>The "angles" are the four most powerful points in a chart; "hidden" likely refers to the descendant or IC</note>, while the "fortunes" remain in the oriental angle <note>The Ascendant</note>, they will generate the most ferocious but nonetheless curable diseases. But if Jupiter

<column-break/>

was the one who is assimilated, the infirmities will be cured by medicines, whether through diets or through antidotes. And if Venus was the one assimilated to it, the diseases will be repelled by prophecies or by divine help.

¶ If the two "infortunes" agree with them, and Jupiter and Venus (the "fortunes") were in the western angle, and two "fortunes" were in the eastern angle, they will cause infirmities that can be cured. These infirmities, however, will be unconcealed. If it is Jupiter who harmonizes, the infirmities will be cured by physical care through diet or medicines; and if it is Venus, the liberation will be through prophecy or on the part of God.

¶ This means that when any of the aforementioned figures signify that the infirmities will be in the brain, and the "infortune" causing this is in the west, and one or both "fortunes" are in the ascendant, the "fortunes" will have an advantage over the "infortunes" because of the improvement of the power of the ascendant. Because of this, those infirmities can be cured. The other thing he said is manifest, so there is no need to boast of it.

¶ Because if the "infortunes" are in the eastern angle and the "fortunes" are in the western angle, the diseases will be incurable and ferocious, and less manifest. The infirmities of epilepsy <note>original: "epilepsie"</note> will always endure with a cry and fear of death. The insane, lacking their senses, can in no way be restrained; they will hinder their relatives and say foul things, and other things similar to these "demoniacs," their infirmities, and the superabundance of moisture that harms their heads. We call this <term>enthusiasm</term> <note>original: "entusimesem," from the Greek for being possessed by a spirit/god</note>: being overly exposed and making impetuous leaps at people, striking them, and similar things.

¶ And if the "infortunes" are in the eastern angle and the "fortunes" in the west, they will cause infirmities that cannot be cured and will be unconcealed and very manifest. If it is epilepsy, it will be continuous and never recede, and it will be with great cries and great danger from which death can come. And if it is the infirmity of "folly" where men are struck or lose their senses, it will make the one who has it act against his parents and say foul and evil words. And if it is the infirmity which is the "frenzy of demons" <note>original: "ferica demonum"</note>, which is due to the great moisture prevailing in the brain, it will make them anxious and they will commit unconcealed follies; they will insult people and strike them and do such things.

¶ Whenever the "infortunes" are in the ascendant in the angle of these states, or some of them, and the "fortunes" or some of them are in the west, the power of the "infortunes" will prevail. The power governing the body through the "fortunes" will have the strength with which it repels the causes of the infirmity, but because the "infortunes" prevail, it cannot be cured. Because of this, such a struggle occurs between the infirmity and nature. One must pay attention to the things Ptolemy said, which he taught us here to add to what he said before: when we find "infortunes" and "fortunes" in the figures, we shall speak according to that which prevails in it. Thus, if a "fortune" is the lord of the figure and its dominion is an "infortune," and the "fortune" is stronger, we shall judge according to it; and in this way, we shall do in all other things. And what he said regarding "anxieties" <note>original: "angustys"</note>: it is an infirmity where the sense is lost and such people predict the future. Ptolemy taught us in this place that this happens because of the great moisture of the brain.

¶ Certain locations in which that quality exists will sometimes help by their own aid. For the locations of the Sun and Mars specifically help so that one becomes insane. The locations of Jupiter and Mercury help with epilepsy...

# Third Book

...[epilepsy] better helps in treating infirmities. The place of Venus, however, helps through prophecies and so that they may speak of hidden things. The places of Saturn and the Moon help those who are demon-possessed and assist the obstructions of the humors <note>In medieval medicine, the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were believed to govern health; an "obstruction" caused disease</note>.

And if it were in such a constellation as we have described, there will be folly in the divination. If it were not so, it will signify only prophesying. And if it were in those places in which Saturn or the Moon has some dignity, it will help in doing harm: such as when many humors flow, and one will have the infirmity which is called the sacred disease <note>original: "ferica demonum," likely a corruption of "hiera," the sacred disease, a common name for epilepsy</note> of demons. # Treatise

...the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> with the aforementioned qualities are positioned in feminine signs: women will behave in ways that are natural to them. Men, however, will commit those acts which are for them <term>contrary to nature</term> <note original="praeter naturam">In a medieval context, this refers to any sexual behavior deemed non-procreative or socially deviant, including same-sex attraction</note> and will overstep their natural boundaries with softness and a feminine soul. 

¶ And if the planet’s position is the reverse of what we said—that is, if both luminaries exist in feminine signs in the state we described—they will signify that women will become supreme in the matters natural to them, and men will become supreme in matters natural for women. They will overstep the natural order, becoming lustful and feminine at heart.

¶ The state he described is when the two luminaries do not <term>aspect</term> <note>When planets are at specific angles to one another, such as 90 or 180 degrees</note> each other, nor does either of them aspect the Ascendant <note>The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note>, and when some harmful <term>malefic</term> <note>Saturn or Mars, traditionally viewed as planets of hardship</note> is in an "angle" <note>The four most powerful points in a birth chart</note> hurting both luminaries or one of them. When this happens and the two luminaries are only in feminine signs, it will signify that women will greatly love men and desire to lie with them, and they will be well-known for this; and men will be so greatly consumed by this desire that they will overstep the natural state for them toward women and will greatly love this unnatural manner of lust.

¶ Furthermore, if only Venus is feminine, women will excessively fulfill the illegitimate acts of Venus; yet they will more frequently decline toward natural acts and with anyone, to the point that they will deny no sexual union, whether it be deformed or against the law. Men, however, will be effeminate and soft, and more prone to unnatural acts of love; they will prohibit no one from illicit sexual union, though they will perpetrate it mostly in secret. Likewise, if Mars is feminine, it will cause both of these—that is, fornication and disgrace—and they will perform illicit acts openly and without a blush of shame, so much so that they will be cursed and reviled for their excessive display.

¶ Similarly, if Venus is feminine, women will be highly involved in prostitution, so much so that they will exceed the natural state in this matter. They will not defend themselves from any act of lust, even if it is very shameful or against the law, just as feminine and lustful men will want to satisfy their lust against nature and will not defend themselves from other men wanting to lie with them or do other shameful things. And this will be done in secret. And if Mars is likewise feminine, he will be in every one of these evil and shameful manners; we say this is very much "uncovered" and without shame, and they will be drawn to the work and named for it, so that they will be dishonored thereafter.

¶ All of this which has been said is manifest and declared if you look closely at the previous <term>glosses</term> <note>Explanatory comments written in the margins or between lines of a text</note>. If the configurations of the luminaries signify those "plagues" <note>Referring here to social or behavioral deviations</note> while existing in feminine signs, they signify that women will be such harlots that they will behave as men, seeking lust prohibited by law and wanting others to lie with them in an unnatural and shameful way. And when a constellation such as this happens in the births of men, they will be harlots and feminine, and will similarly desire the things mentioned. This is what women and men will do in hidden and secret ways. Whence, if Mars is feminine in the place of Venus, it signifies that the matter will be public and without shame; they will not fear being "outside" <note>Publicly known</note> so that they are dishonored by all, nor will they consider it a bad thing. And if in such a state Venus and Mars are both feminine, the acts of the men and women will be suspect, somewhere between hidden and open.

¶ The oriental <note>Rising before the sun</note> and morning qualities of Venus and Mars in masculinity help in bringing things to light.

¶ And the oriental state of Mars and Venus, and the fact that they are in the morning, helps them to be manly and famous.

<column-break/>

¶ This means that they will be manly, and the men will be more masculine and stronger; and the women will be "rubbers" <note original="fricatrices">A medieval term for lesbians</note> with one another and drawn to it; and this is clear from the oriental states of Mars and Venus when they are in the morning.

¶ However, their evening and western quality in femininity helps with concealment.

¶ And their western and evening states help toward femininity and lowliness.

¶ The femininity of women is that they become harlots; for men, it is that they are in this vice against their nature.

¶ Similarly, if Saturn is with them, he will help them incur horrors, rot, and filth, as well as great shame, because his nature naturally assists each of these things.

¶ Similarly, when Saturn is with them, he will help in great and shameful pollution; it is according to his nature to help in such things.

¶ This means that if the places in which the luminaries and the planets giving them misfortune are standing—and the places in which Venus and Mars or either of them stand—belong to Saturn or he participates with them, he will help in great, shameful pollution and lowliness.

¶ But if Jupiter is with them, he will increase the beauty and grace of things, as well as a fitting sense of shame.

¶ And if Jupiter is with them, he will help in governing these matters and in having shame regarding them, so that they perform these things "beautifully" <note>Perhaps meaning with more social grace or discretion</note>.

¶ This means that if the places of the aforementioned significators belong to Jupiter, or if he has an aspect with them, he will help toward the beauty of this matter and they will act in secret.

¶ And if Mercury is with them, he will help in the discovery of things, the hastening of future events, and the multitude and increase of their varieties.

¶ And if Mercury is with them, he will help to uncover these things and toward a great movement of youth in the manners of women, and toward great use and a great increase of them.

¶ This means that if the places of the aforementioned significators belong to Mercury, or if he participates with them, he will help in the fulfillment of the things signified by him and toward a great movement of them in many ways. And with this, he completes all that he says in the second chapter: and it is clear because the "unfortunate" planets, if they are in the west, and the "fortunate" planets in the Ascendant, signify the aforementioned state—that these infirmities can be cured. Similarly, if the fortunes are more powerful than the misfortunes. And if the misfortunes are in the Ascendant and the fortunes are in the west, these infirmities will be long-lasting. Similarly, if the misfortunes are more powerful than the fortunes.

¶ And after this, the third part of the *Quadripartitum* is completed here.

¶ Ptolemy. Likewise, the ninth treatise of the gloss of Haly Eben Rodan <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note>, the physician, on this same *Quadripartitum* is completed.

¶ Here begins the tenth treatise of the gloss of Haly Eben Rodan, and the beginning of the gloss on the fourth book of Ptolemy's *Quadripartitum*.

WE HAVE GLOSSED three parts of this book in nine treatises of the gloss, showing and declaring as briefly as we could; and we still wish to gloss and distinguish this part completely and openly without abbreviation. We shall provide such examples as will make the reader mindful of those things which passed in the other parts, so that he may have greater help in understanding this book. And he who wishes to understand it must be both a philosopher and a logician, wise in the <term>quadrivium</term> <note>The four high subjects of medieval education: Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy</note> and in the practice of natural philosophy...

# Fourth Book

...are ethical: one could certainly understand our words without our commentary <note original="glosa">A 'gloss' is a marginal or interlinear explanation of a difficult text, common in medieval manuscripts</note>, yet it would require much study and labor. Since our commentary provides help for a better understanding to the majority of people who are not experts in philosophy nor even moderately wise, we are opening the channels and unlocking the enclosures that Ptolemy included by speaking of this part of philosophy. Even if the tables <note>Astronomical tables used for calculations</note> and the equations of the planets are known, great help and progress lie in my commentaries. However, for one who has never studied any part of philosophy, the best advice is not to labor over anything we have said, so that his mind may rest without the struggle. For we do not make these commentaries except for those who are knowledgeable in this science or philosophy. Let the one who knows nothing of this realize that his ignorance belongs to himself, not to the science.

Similarly, if someone understanding this book errs in any judgment of astronomy, it should be known that the error exists because he did not look properly at what was necessary to know, or did not well understand what is in the book. It is manifest to those who understand this book that a proper judgment belongs to it. For example: what will happen if someone judges that a newborn will not pass 20 years of age, or that he will gain riches from a king, or through the goods of the dead, or through a treasure he finds? If he does not specify that these refer to things pertaining to the king, he might still gain wealth by trading with the king or through inheritances coming to him from the king’s side. 

Likewise, it is not fitting for him to say simply that when this newborn reaches 20 years he will die, or fall ill with a great sickness, or go from one land to another. Yet it is fitting for him to say: "he will die utterly," and that "he will fall ill in every way" or "all this will happen," or "he will fall ill and die," so that his words are recognized and true in every matter. For he who does not distinguish with a sharp eye in judgment does not well understand what we have said; and if he did understand, he did not look well to the practical application as was fitting.

And if anyone should say that matter is not stable in a single form, and because of this an astrologer cannot certify his words in any judgment, we answer him that matter (as we have shown before) receives both particular and universal impressions from the celestial bodies. It is manifest that the particular is always predicated on the universal. He who well knows the judgments of astronomy in both universal and particular work cannot easily err, and rarely falls into error. Yet for the one who does not know these things well, all judgments are left to chance. 

And here lies another point: an astrologer may judge certain things for a newborn and say some will happen at the peak of 50 years of life, and others at 10 years; yet it could happen in either of these two times that something changes the judgment. To this we answer what we said before: that it is fitting for the astrologer to look into general and particular things, the locations of the planets, the revolutions of the years <note>Solar returns, or the chart for the year</note>, and to look well into all of them. He should give the power to the planet that has the greatest influence at any given time and judge based on the potential work pertaining to that time. We have made all of this clear and declared it in the preceding treatises, and we shall show many more things that are fitting as we move forward.

## The Fourth Treatise of the book of Ptolemy's *Alarba* <note original="Alabiæ">Likely a transcription error for 'Alarba,' referring to the Arabic title of the Tetrabiblos: Kitab al-Arba'a</note> begins, in which there are nine chapters.

### The prologue begins. Ptolemy said:

Regarding those things which can be observed before birth and those which happen at the very hour of birth, as well as everything that follows birth: that which is proper and natural, and by which our whole being exists, is proven and most clearly demonstrated.

In the matters of man, judgment can be made concerning those things before birth, and those at the same hour of birth, and things happening after birth which are proper to the newborn, and which guide them in themselves and their conditions, which we have described up to this point.

<column-break/>

The things about which a man can judge existing before birth are judgments concerning fathers and brothers. And the things he can judge at the very hour of birth are such as whether the child is male or female, or of mixed composition <note original="mutute cōpōnis">Likely referring to hermaphroditism or ambiguous sexual characteristics</note>, or if it will not receive food <note>Indicating a stillbirth or a child that dies immediately</note>.

What happens after birth is divided into two modes and manners: one is always proper to the newborn, such as judging his life, his body, and his soul. It is manifest that in all these things, the status of the newborn can be understood by their essence; these parts have already been demonstrated in what has passed, and some are shown from here forward. The other manner concerns accidental things after birth: judging the status of things that happen by accident and are outside of nature. We have already made clear in the commentary of the third treatise that all these things can be known from the <term>second beginning</term> <note original="z° pn°">Abbreviation for 'secundo principio'</note>, which is the hour when the creature exits the mother's womb.

Regarding those things that happen from without—namely, those whose explanation follows in due order—the first is to judge prosperity in the substance <note>Wealth and material possessions</note> and health of the newborn; to explain his prosperity in substance along with collective things pertaining to the body; and likewise to explain his prosperity in health along with things pertaining to the soul.

And for the things that happen to the newborn from outside, following what was said before: the first is to judge the fortune of the newborn in riches and value <note>Social standing or honor</note>. The judgment of fortune in riches is similar to things pertaining to the body, and judging what his fortune will be in value is similar to things pertaining to the soul.

When it is said that what has been signified pertains most to men, it has already been demonstrated in what has passed. It is understood that something still remains regarding the things pertaining to man which it is necessary to demonstrate. He said these words: "the fortune of the newborn in riches and value," and he joined the judgment of riches with the judgment of the body, and the judgment of value with the judgment of the soul. This is because riches are subject to value, and value in comparison to riches is according to form, just as the body is subject to the soul, and the soul is the completion and form of the body. And it is visibly manifest that one who has value and honor has many things in his power. And who would say that he has no riches? He may have other natural good things from the outside, such as mastery of a craft, marriage, children, and the like. For it cannot be that a man has such things and yet has nothing; and this is what Ptolemy wished to say in the prologue of this book.

## On the prosperity and substance of the newborn. Chapter 1.

->Haly said:<-

Because riches are subject to value and honor, and with these two things a man can have all the states that come afterward, Ptolemy placed the judgment of riches after the judgment of the soul, because it follows it.

To understand what quality of substance <note>Wealth</note> of things may come, it is necessary that we grasp the knowledge from the **Part of Fortune** <note original="parte fortune">A mathematical point in the horoscope used to signify prosperity</note> alone. We shall always learn this by observing the distance between the Sun and the Moon, and projecting this from the **Ascendant** <note original="ascendēte">The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon</note> in both day and night births, for the reasons we showed in the discussion on life.

And how the things pertaining to the gain of substance will be, it is fitting for us to inquire from the Part of Fortune alone, from that which we always know through the distance between the Sun and the Moon; it is projected from the Ascendant in those born by day and those born by night, for the reasons we stated when we were speaking about life.

You already know that the Part of Fortune is always taken from the Sun to the Moon, and we add the degree of the Ascendant to this and project it from the Ascendant. The reason why this position has power is found in the *Quadripartitum* <note original="Quadri. Prol.">The Tetrabiblos, Ptolemy's four-part work on astrology</note> of Ptolemy.
